ai-companion — Idea graph

Write down every idea in a project and connect them into a graph that can be read by clicking through layer by layer, then let the program monitor the process: if an idea is not clearly thought out, coding is not allowed; if tests have not failed first, implementation is not allowed; if a plan has not received a manual sign-off from a human, work is not allowed to start — the same graph is shared by three coding assistants: Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex, and it works the same way regardless of which repository it is placed in. It aims to solve the same root cause: ideas have never been written down, only code has been written down.

Project background

Starting from 2026-08-29, the three implementations that originally lived side-by-side (claude-companion, cursor-companion, codex-companion) were merged into a single common base: one engine, one guard, and three thin connection layers; the specification is written in companion/FORMAT.md, and everything is stored in a single file in ideas/graph.yaml.

2026-08-25 Reconstruction: commit ca7e956 moved the old monorepo (packages/ scripts/ skills/ docs/, i.e., the entire set of function-level change tracking) into the archive/ directory in .gitignore and deleted it from the working tree, leaving it only in the git history and the tag pre-archive-2026-08-24. The I-001~I-019 of the old graph describes that batch of code, which is no longer active code in this repository; therefore, the entire graph is reconstructed based on human decisions, with new IDs starting from I-041 (FORMAT.md stipulates that IDs are never reused).

Record formatTo doDefine which eight questions an idea must answer, and write programs to read, validate, sort, and render these ideas.Open →
Parent idea
—
What it is
Define which eight questions an idea must answer, and write programs to read, validate, sort, and render these ideas.
Why this idea exists
Without a fixed format, the three assistants write their own notes, making it impossible for humans to see the full picture and for programs to read them; the eight questions are the minimum set required for an idea to be reviewed by a human before code is written.
Expected result
Any idea can be read by a program, have its flaws validated, be sorted by priority, and be drawn as a webpage; someone who has never opened the repository can understand what the project is doing just by looking at the idea graph.
How to implement
Divided into two layers: first, a graph that a program can read and validate (format, reading/validation, modification records, scanning manifests, change envelopes), and then sorting and rendering on top of it (frontier, topological order, webpage, shared drawing source code, layering).
Why it is implemented this way
Format precedes the program — the program is merely the executor of the format. Reading/writing/validation and sorting/rendering are separated because the former changes everything when modified once, while the latter only affects how it appears to humans.

EnforcementTo doLet these rules be executed by programs rather than relying on self-discipline — no code writing if not clearly thought through, no implementation writing if there are no failed tests, and approval can only come from a single sentence manually replied to by a human.Open →
Parent idea
—
What it is
Let these rules be executed by programs rather than relying on self-discipline — no code writing if not clearly thought through, no implementation writing if there are no failed tests, and approval can only come from a single sentence manually replied to by a human.
Why this idea exists
Rules written in prompts are forgotten when assistants get busy; only checks attached to hooks that cannot be bypassed can guarantee that "no code writing without clear thought, no implementation writing without red tests, and approval only from humans" holds true before every single write operation.
Expected result
Before any file writing, command running, or stopping, the guard performs a judgment first; non-compliant writes are rejected with human-readable reasons; an approval code is only recorded when a human replies to the entire message.
How to implement
Divided into two layers: three gates for starting work, writing implementation, and completion (start-work check, red/green evidence, seven rules, rule core, connection cleanup, browser interception), and approval can only come from humans (approval code mechanism, and how actions on the webpage are counted as human actions).
Why it is implemented this way
Gates and approval are separate: gates judge facts that a program can determine, while approval is the matter that a program cannot determine and must be handed over to a human; mixing them would turn "human approval" into a state that a program could forge.
Where is the code

How to use in the future

What it is
Turn the five tasks—mapping, thinking clearly, doing, error checking, and viewing graphs—into individual commands that can be used identically regardless of which repository they are installed in.
Why this idea exists
Idea graphs and guards are infrastructure; what people actually use every day are the five actions: "scan, think clearly, do, error check, and view graph"; without commands, these five steps would rely on people memorizing a long string of rules.
Expected result
By typing /ccscan, /ccthink, /ccbuild, /ccfix, or /ccgraph in any repository equipped with the base, the corresponding step is completed, and it will stop and wait for a person where human sign-off is required.
How to implement
Write the five workflows into standard skill files that can be loaded by all three setups; the behavior of each command is supported by engine sub-commands (please provide the full text during approval, and align the code after submission); the endpoint is to use this process to improve itself once.
Why it is implemented this way
Commands are merely instruction manuals that link the engine and the guard, not separate logic; one main text file is copied to the three setups, so changing it in one place synchronizes all three sides.

What it is
Allow people to directly read graphs, modify graphs, and sign off on the web, with changes automatically written back to the project files after modification.
Why this idea exists
YAML is for programs to read; when people modify graphs, there must be a place that does not touch the YAML; the web is the only interface people are willing to view frequently, so viewing graphs, modifying graphs, and signing off should all be completed on the same page.
Expected result
Opening a single web page allows for layer-by-layer viewing of ideas, modifying text, adding or deleting ideas and prerequisites, and providing human sign-off for manual verification; after modification, changes are saved directly back to project files or a modified file is downloaded; the page should clearly show who is waiting for approval and who is in progress.
How to implement
Divided into two layers: modifying graphs on the web and writing back (editing, adding/deleting, submitting, write-back instructions, local small service, double-click entry, endpoint); and viewing clearly and signing off on the web (sign-off, two indices, title and page, full text pending approval, inline expansion).
Why it is implemented this way
Modifying graphs and writing back is one chain, while viewing graphs and signing off is another—the former must ensure the graph is not corrupted by writes, while the latter must ensure what the person sees is real; separating them allows one to know which chain is blocked.

What it is
Synthesize a single core by merging the respective implementations of three coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex), leaving only a thin integration layer for each, so that a single rule change takes effect across all three sides simultaneously.
Why this idea exists
Each of the three implementations is modified independently, resulting in three different versions and three different ways of applying the same rule; if a person switches to a different assistant, they must relearn everything, and it is impossible to have the three assistants take over the same project.
Expected result
One engine, one guard, one specification; each of the three providers leaves only a thin integration layer; install into any repository with just one command; the three assistants relay using the same idea graph, and a single change to the base takes effect across all three sides simultaneously.
How to implement
Divided into four layers: merge the three implementations into one (adjudication, engine migration, rule merging, migration); install into any repository with one command (single-file artifact, wiring list, installer, registry); three assistants connect to the same idea graph (thin conversion, Cursor, Codex); the base does exactly what it says (closing loopholes, finishing switches, speaking the truth in text).
Why it is implemented this way
Adjudicate before merging, otherwise merging is equivalent to picking a side at random; package the artifact as a single file, which can be installed anywhere as long as Node is present; the integration layer only performs translation without rules, ensuring a single rule change takes effect across all three sides.
Where is the code
companion · ideas.ts · guard.ts · manifests.ts · install.ts · build.mjs

Parent idea

What it is
Allow users to open a URL on any device to see the idea graphs of all their repositories that have this tool installed; modify ideas and approve plans there; after each repository pulls the code, the idea graph files will already contain the new content, requiring no manual YAML editing. Division of labor: the engine in this repository is responsible for each repository's own graph pages, write-backs, approvals, and git commits; the URL, login, and multi-repository index are handled by the portal repository LifeCopilotBeta (specifically the I-009 branch in its idea graph). First, connect both sides on the local machine, then move to a machine that is always on.
Why this idea exists
As the number of repositories increases, there is no single place to overview all projects or manage them directly on any device. Each repository's idea graph can only be viewed and modified within that specific machine and directory. What is needed is a common management terminal.
Expected result
Click into a graph of a certain repository within the portal and change an idea to blocked while writing the reason; after performing a git pull on another checkout of the same repository, that idea in graph.yaml will already be blocked and the reason will be present. Reply with an approval code on the portal's graph page, which has the same effect as replying in the terminal. Run it through on the local machine first, then repeat it from a mobile phone.
How to implement
Three things on the engine side in this repository: I-137 connect the local small service to git, I-138 move approval codes and receipts into git, I-139 open an approval entry that only recognizes host credentials (including an additional segment for I-105). On the portal side, there is one branch for LifeCopilotBeta's idea graph I-009: starting child processes and proxying (I-010), making the project page the highest level (I-011), login (I-012), forwarding approvals (I-013), and deploying to an always-on machine (I-014). Order of implementation: I-137 → Portal I-010, I-011 → I-138 → I-139 → Portal I-013 → Local endpoint I-142 → Portal I-014, I-015. companion/FORMAT.md add a section "Portal", clearly defining the division of labor and three boundaries: host credentials shall not appear in pages or logs; the identity used for synchronization and approval shall never be a human login; receipts are written only by the engine and shall not be generated or rewritten by the portal.
Why it is implemented this way
Why place the portal in LifeCopilotBeta instead of letting the engine grow its own multi-repository index: users want to eventually merge into LifeCopilot, which already has graph_repos scanning (lifecopilot/graphs.py:82), the /projects interface (lifecopilot/api.py:274), FastAPI, and a background task running once per minute; if the engine grows another one, it would be redundant. Why not use Plane (research conducted on 2026-09-09): the free tier workspace webhook cannot add request headers, so it cannot wake up GitHub Actions; the prerequisite relationship interface paths differ between the cloud and self-hosted versions, and it did not exist at the end of 2024; squeezing eight questions into the work item description box makes the dependency graph invisible; the mapping table, push, and pull components would all require new code. The always-on machine solution moves the editing, human sign-off, and submission capabilities already completed by serve and graph.html as they are; only the three git commands, one directory move, and one entry point are newly written. Why not use rclone to sync to a cloud drive: it only moves files, has no editing interface, does not produce git commits, and would result in two different truths compared to the version in git.
Where is the code
companion/FORMAT.md · Portal
How to verify
Read the "Portal" section of FORMAT.md in read-only mode, and be able to explain in your own words what the engine and portal manage respectively, what the three boundaries are, and why Plane is not used.

How to use in the future
Any host that can start child processes, proxy HTTP, and has its own login can connect to the same engine: other web pages, Discord bots, or corporate intranet portals can do so without changing a single line of the engine.

Collaboration within the same directoryTo doAllow multiple coding assistants to develop simultaneously within the same working directory, communicating what they are currently doing, with a program coordinating file usage rights and idea graph updates.Open →
Parent idea
—
What it is
Allow multiple coding assistants to develop simultaneously within the same working directory, communicating what they are currently doing, with a program coordinating file usage rights and idea graph updates.
Why this idea exists
The user wishes to retain a workflow where changes in the shared directory are immediately visible, reducing manual relaying of information, file overwriting, and loss of idea graph modifications; sessions from multiple assistants of the same model must also be distinguishable.
Expected result
Multiple assistants modify different files in parallel within the same directory; when contending for the same file, only one session succeeds, while other sessions can see the holder and the task; messages can be read by other sessions, idea graph updates will not overwrite each other, and claims after abnormal exits can be clearly handed over.
How to implement
Combine four sub-ideas without adding a dedicated assistant for coordination: I-113 provides sessions, messages, and short-term mutual exclusion; I-114 maintains long-term file claims in the message logs; I-116 reuses short-lock submission for idea graph changes; I-115 allows real assistants to receive messages at work nodes and verify ownership before writing. Division of labor is initially by file, and changes to related interfaces are coordinated via group messages; a long-term claim on one file does not hold the short-term lock for the entire project. The first version maintains a local directory on the same machine, Node 20, and a single-file artifact, without adding server or database dependencies or a chat interface. The new coordination runtime is recorded in ideas/.runtime/coord, while the long-term project intent remains only in graph.yaml; lock and session information is not written into the intent nodes within version management. Message bodies are read only as data. A process example is join→inbox/ack→claim→edit and graph update→say→release; abnormal takeover first stops the old session and in-flight writes, then verifies the claim number. Delivery is verified in two layers: this node uses multiple real subprocesses and artifacts to verify the entire protocol chain in a temporary directory; I-059 then uses real Claude, Cursor, and Codex to verify host wiring and actual visible messages. Ordinary hooks do not protect arbitrary processes; Git indices, branch switching, and public build outputs within the same directory still require separate coordination and cannot execute shared repository state changes in parallel just because source files differ. Weekly plan based on dependencies: Week 1 I-113 and verify lock recovery; Week 2 I-114 and I-116 in order; Week 3 I-115; Week 4 end-to-end verification of this node and real machine acceptance of the three providers via I-059. These are estimates based on actual commencement; Weeks 3 and 4 are especially affected by host versions, sub-assistant identities, and hook coverage. Several sub-ideas will modify the same engine or coordination module, so implementation stages will be handed over in file order; when existing in-progress ideas like I-082 occupy ideas.ts, their work must be coordinated first, rather than assuming the file is free based on the planning dependency order.
Why it is implemented this way
Leverage existing graph engines, file conflict checks, guards, wiring, and packaging instead of building a new scheduling platform. The basis within the repository is companion/ideas.ts:131, :778, :3478, :3645, companion/guard.ts:208, :1657, and companion/build.mjs:30. SQLite transactions, proper-lockfile, and resident serve have all been compared as actual alternatives (see sub-ideas and the current round of ideas/log.md research table), but under the current constraints of a local single directory and Node 20 single-file distribution, unified short-locks and a single-record stream can satisfy the confirmed requirements. Preempt by file rather than by function to avoid diff line number drift and automatic merging issues when modifying interfaces simultaneously; messages are responsible for semantic coordination, while claims are only responsible for writing ownership. The linear overhead of each log replay, explicit crash recovery, and non-instantaneous message receiving are explicit costs of the first version, rather than using "non-interference" to mask these boundaries.
Where is the code
.devcompanion/tests/test_coord_end_to_end.test.ts · End-to-end acceptance of multiple processes collaborating in the same directory
companion/FORMAT.md · Operational workflow and boundary guarantees for same-directory collaboration
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_coord_end_to_end.test.ts → exit 0; build artifacts are copied to a temporary project without node_modules, where at least three processes register, send messages and claim files in parallel, read and confirm messages, modify different nodes, release, and hand over. Assert that there is exactly one holder for the same file, different files can be processed in parallel, successful messages and idea graph updates are preserved, and old claims become invalid after takeover; the graph passes the check and matches the HTML fingerprint. Use process barriers and fault injection rather than pretending to have concurrency through sequential calls or three different names; real host interception and sub-assistant identities are still subject to manual verification by I-059.
Test file:.devcompanion/tests/test_coord_end_to_end.test.ts
How to use in the future
Multiple assistants can coordinate themselves within a shared directory; subsequent chat pages or notification services can directly consume the same messages, preserving a unique project graph.

Format for recording idea nodes: every idea must answer the eight questions CompletedI-041

Parent idea
I-119
What it is
Format of an idea node: id / name / status / needs, plus the eight mandatory questions (what it is, why it exists, expected results, how to implement, why implement it this way, which lines the code is in, how to verify, how to use it in the future), plus an append-only log.
Why this idea exists
AI hallucinations, prompts not aligning with requirements, and being unable to understand the project framework after rework — the root cause of these three things is the same: ideas have never been written down, only code has been written down.
Expected result
For the same idea, humans and AI read the same record to reach the same understanding; a cold-start stranger agent can continue working just by reading this file, without needing extra context.
How to implement
YAML, a flat list of ideas, one type of node, and one type of edge. The specification is written in FORMAT.md: companion/FORMAT.md is the version shared by the three agents, and claude-companion/FORMAT.md is the version still running on the Claude side before the migration was completed; the node templates, the eight questions table, and the two ways of writing "how to verify" in both versions must match word for word. The previous statement "each of the three companions has a basically identical copy" is now obsolete: writing separately is the source of wording drift, and it is also inconsistent with the facts — Codex does not have this file at all, the Cursor version is an old version from before 2026-08-28 and lacks the entire "how to write this graph" section. Now, only the table in the common specification counts for the wording of the eight questions.
Why it is implemented this way
Choosing a flat structure instead of a four-layer requirement/feature/module/function structure — FORMAT.md specifies at the end: the goal is "all ideas become individual modules"; a module is not a classification method, and the four-layer structure itself is the kind of complexity that makes people unable to understand the project. YAML instead of JSON, because the eight answers are all prose paragraphs.
Where is the code
companion/FORMAT.md:49-83,103-133 · A node · The eight questions

Parent idea
I-119
What it is
Read graph.yaml, check that IDs are unique, needs point to existing ideas, the graph has no cycles, done nodes must have code and verify, the code paths of done nodes actually exist, and manual verification must have a human sign-off; fields not filled in the eight questions are reported as warnings.
Why this idea exists
Without validation, the graph will quietly rot: done nodes without code, code pointing to deleted files, or two ideas depending on each other. A rotten graph is worse than no graph, because it looks complete.
Expected result
A healthy graph passes the check and exits with code 0; every way of being rotten can be pointed out and the corresponding ID can be specified.
How to implement
DFS three-color marking to check for cycles; reverse traverse from endpoints through needs to find orphans that do not reach any endpoint; use existsSync to verify the code paths of done nodes (todo nodes are not checked — those are planned locations).
Why it is implemented this way
Turn "done must have code + verify" into a hard error instead of a warning —— the code comments state that this is the prerequisite for the entire system to hold: if "done" can exist without evidence, this graph is merely a wish list. The code path for todo is intentionally not checked, otherwise the plan itself would be treated as an error.

What it is
Change an idea's status and simultaneously append a record to its own log; preserve YAML comments when writing back; reject done without code/verify, and reject manual verification without human sign-off.
Why this idea exists
Detailed records must exist for what code, what documentation, and what idea was changed, while the reason must be placed next to the idea, not in another file —— if it is placed too far away, no one will read it.
Expected result
Re-read after set: the status has changed, a new log entry is added, and the original comments remain; setting done for an idea without code will fail and explain the reason.

Use yaml's parseDocument to preserve comments and formatting, use setIn for targeted modification, write to a temporary file, and then rename.

Use Document instead of parse → modify → stringify: the latter will wipe out all comments and layout of the entire file, and comments are exactly what humans leave for themselves. rename is atomic, so a crash mid-write will not destroy the original graph (code comment: a crash mid-write leaves the old graph intact).

What it is
Render into a self-contained webpage: at the top is a complete project graph showing only idea names, which can be panned and zoomed; click any node to jump to the detail card below, which contains all answers to the eight questions, as well as its prerequisite ideas and "which ideas it is a prerequisite for", allowing for continuous clicking in both directions.
Why this idea exists
Projects without a visible shape will inevitably be rewritten. Graphs are for humans to look at, not for machines; the three things humans need to judge (too many nodes, missing edges, or failing to reach the endpoint) can only be judged if they are drawn.

How to implement
Mermaid flowchart TD (CDN) handles the layout, node labels only contain the name, and click callbacks jump to details. Zooming relies on modifying the SVG's own width/height to trigger a vector redraw, while panning relies on the wrapper's translate.
Why it is implemented this way
Use Mermaid instead of d3 / cytoscape: static HTML, no build steps, and no need to start a server. Zooming deliberately avoids CSS scale() — code comments specify that scale() rasterizes the layer once before stretching, which is exactly why it previously looked blurry; fit only scales up and never down, because putting a small image at 235% is not what anyone means when they say "fit to window."

What it is
At the start of /ccscan, list the files worth reading in the project as a list (ideas/.scan-todo); every time a file is Read, a hook strikes it off; check continues to warn while the list is not empty. ideas/.scanignore can exclude by path prefix (third-party packages, parallel versions from other agents).
Why this idea exists
"I have finished reading" is a sentence an agent can say casually. If a graph is built from only half a project, it looks exactly the same as a complete one — this is worse than having no graph at all.
Expected result
Scanning progress is a number like "Read 37/42" rather than a mere guarantee; Grep / Glob do not count, because they do not put file content into the context.
How to implement
git ls-files -z --cached --others --exclude-standard generates the list (degrades to directory traversal when git is unavailable), filtering by extension and .scanignore; strike() strikes off a line based on a case-insensitive relative path.
Why it is implemented this way
Use git ls-files instead of manual traversal because it already understands .gitignore, submodules, and case sensitivity; -z is added because without it, git escapes non-ASCII paths into octal, making those files impossible to strike off (this is explicitly stated in the code comments). node_modules is explicitly excluded because the repository might actually have committed it.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Seven mandatory rules attached to hooks that agents cannot bypass. CompletedI-047

Parent idea
I-121
What it is
A guard.ts is attached to PreToolUse / PostToolUse / Stop / UserPromptSubmit, dispatching seven rules based on events: R1 automatically logs every edit; R2 the status of an existing idea can only be changed via set; R3 implementation writing is forbidden if the test file does not exist; R4 code cannot be touched if how / why_this_way are not filled; R5 the turn cannot end if the graph has errors; R6 implementation cannot start if the graph has no human sign-off; R7 a file is only considered scanned if it has truly been Read.
Why this idea exists
The five commands are merely prompts — an agent can skip research, fabricate why_this_way, directly Edit to change the status to done to bypass all checks, or self-answer "it looks reasonable" and continue. Discipline written in prompts becomes meaningless by the thirtieth round of dialogue.
Expected result
Skipping tests to write implementation will be rejected, and it will be told which file to write first; manually changing status will be rejected, and the required set command will be provided; if the graph is broken, the turn cannot end; every edit leaves a line in ideas/log.md, requiring no cooperation from the agent.
How to implement
Exit code 2 + stderr = "intercept and tell Claude the reason"; this is the only universal mechanism across the four hook events, so a script dispatching by hook_event_name is sufficient. install.ts is responsible for writing into the target repository's .claude/settings.json without overwriting others' hooks.
Why it is implemented this way
Only enforce things a machine can judge: whether a file exists, whether fields are filled, whether status has changed, and whether it passed check. The quality of eight questions or the honesty of web searches cannot be forced; the only line of defense is to make omissions visible in check and rendering — hard-blocking something that cannot be judged accurately is worse than not blocking at all. All exception paths fail open (code comment: a guard that crashes must never block work); if the guard itself crashes, it must not lock humans out; AIDEV_GUARD=off is the escape hatch.

How to use in the future

idea Arrange by dependency order

An approval mechanism that only takes effect when a human manually inputs "approve". CompletedI-048

Parent idea
I-122
What it is
Approval is bound to the first 12 characters of the graph's sha256; it is only written into ideas/.approved when the entire message in the UserPromptSubmit event is exactly "批准 / approve / 同意"; if a single character in the graph is changed, the approval becomes invalid. The files .approved and .scan-todo, which record approval and scanning progress respectively, are blocked by PreToolUse; the agent cannot use Write to write to them directly.
Why this idea exists
Any marker that an agent can write, an agent can forge. If a "I have confirmed" marker is written by the constrained party themselves, it cannot constrain anything.
Expected result
Modifying an unapproved graph will be rejected and will require showing it to a human first; "I do not approve" will not be counted as an approval; no tool event can produce an approval.
How to implement
APPROVALS is a set that compares the entire prompt after trim + lowercase + removing trailing punctuation; newline characters are normalized before hashing to prevent CRLF detection from being read as a different graph.
Why it is implemented this way
Bind "I did it" to an event that cannot be produced without actually doing it: UserPromptSubmit is only triggered when a human manually types the message. Judge "the entire message is an approval" rather than "the message contains an approval", otherwise "I do not approve" will be counted as an approval. Known ceiling (as truthfully stated in README): an agent can still use Bash to feed a fake UserPromptSubmit directly to guard.ts. R6 blocks accidental skipping, not an agent determined to bypass it.

What it is
/ccscan reads the entire project to build a graph, /ccthink aligns→splits→researches→designs tests→schedules weekly, /ccbuild implements with tests first, /ccfix checks if the code and idea are consistent before checking the idea itself, /ccgraph only views without modifying. The engine is just a data structure; what truly determines the quality of output is "in what order things are done". If a single prompt fails to align with requirements, the cost of rework is far higher than spending twenty minutes to align first.

Why it is implemented this way
/ccthink sets "borrow whenever possible" as the highest priority rule in the command, and places research before answering "how to implement" — otherwise, research will only become a way to find justification for existing answers. /ccfix deliberately does not let the AI judge whether the code or the idea is correct: it is precisely the party that cannot judge. /ccscan explicitly prohibits fabricating why_this_way, because fabricated reasons will be treated as facts by the next agent and maintained indefinitely, which is the greatest harm this command can cause.

What it is
If ideas/graph.yaml is empty, use it and write agent: claude in the file; if it is taken by someone else, use ideas/graph.claude.yaml. Add the corresponding .approved / .scan-todo / log.md suffixes together. Once chosen, keep it fixed, because the fact that "the file with the suffix already exists" is itself the answer.
Why this idea exists
Three companions—Claude, Codex, and Cursor—reside in the same repository and all want ideas/graph.yaml. Whoever writes later will destroy the previous one.

Three sides coexist without overwriting each other; a graph.yaml without an agent: key is treated as belonging to someone else (assuming the reverse would destroy others' work).

The first to arrive keeps the clean name. Use "file existence" as the state instead of saving a separate configuration—this reduces the number of places where reality might become inconsistent. The agent: key is not decoration; code comments state that without it, the next call will misidentify our own suffix-less graph as someone else's, thereby quietly switching to the file with the suffix and discarding the graph we just wrote.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Record which repositories are installed, and be able to check if they are expired and perform batch updates. CompletedI-052

Parent idea
I-126
What it is
Every installation records the target absolute path into claude-companion/.installs.json; --status reports current / stale / missing / foreign file by file; --update refreshes everything, but does not touch foreign files.
Why this idea exists
The engine is shared so it never expires, but the five command files are copies, and copies can expire—and in the past, there was no way to know where they were installed or if they were the latest versions.
Expected result
After modifying the command file, running --status will show stale, and after running --update, everything changes to current; if someone else occupies a file with the same name, it reports foreign and will not be overwritten.
How to implement
Perform a word-for-word comparison with "what the current source file will generate now"; unify line endings before comparison.
Why it is implemented this way
No version numbers: the commit specifies "a number you must remember to bump, which will eventually be wrong, but the content knows itself whether it is correct". Normalizing line endings is mandatory — the source files provided by git on Windows are CRLF, while the installed ones are LF; if not normalized, every installation will be forever reported as outdated, rendering this check useless.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Fix the issue where scan list records are lost when multiple processes write to it simultaneously. CompletedI-055

Parent idea
I-119
What it is
Ensure that strike() does not lose writes or write corrupted files when multiple hook processes strike out files simultaneously.
Why this idea exists
This /ccscan personally encountered it: during the same round, five files were read in parallel, which meant the hook also ran five guard processes in parallel, each performing readWorklist → filter → writeFileSync. The later write overwrote the earlier write, leaving evidence in the log ("Read .gitignore (32 remaining)" immediately followed by "Read package.json (32 remaining)", the number did not decrease), and a line of incomplete content `n` was written into the list. The result was: the files were indeed read, but the ledger said they were not read — the number reported by R7 actually became inaccurate.
Expected result
After reading N files in parallel, the list should be exactly N lines short, and no lines other than file paths should appear.
How to implement
Make strike no longer rewrite the list, but change it to append only, so that race conditions no longer exist. .scan-todo becomes a list written only once (generated by scan, which is truly a single process); add a new append-only .scan-done, where strike finishes after appending one line using appendFileSync, without reading, modifying, or rewriting anything; "what remains" becomes the set difference of "list minus already read," so duplicate appending is harmless, and a torn half-line will simply not match anything. Appending must be a single write call (passing a pre-constructed full string, without using WriteStream or multiple calls), otherwise atomicity is not established. Change the return value of strike from true/false to the remaining count in its own snapshot, so that the guard does not need to read a second time when logging — otherwise, the symptom "two consecutive writes both say 7 remaining" will still appear after the fix. The contract of the return value must be able to distinguish two things, otherwise it will silently corrupt R7: if not in the list, or if no scan is running, return -1; if truly struck out, return the remaining count of this snapshot (which can be 0). Raw numbers cannot achieve this — "not in the list" and "struck out with 0 remaining" would both be 0, and guard.ts currently branches based on truthy/falsy values (`if (!struck) return OK`), and the two existing green tests happen to cover these two directions: one asserts that no log is recorded when there is no list, and one asserts that when striking out the last one, it must log "0 remaining in scan." Change the fixed temporary filename ${file}.tmp in save to a name with a process ID and a random suffix (copying the codex implementation), and add EPERM/EBUSY/EACCES retry to rename: renaming to overwrite an existing file is unreliable on Windows. .scan-done must be added to both the guard's write-protection list and ideas/.gitignore, otherwise an agent could write its own "I have read it," which is the entire reason R7 exists. Finally, perform a one-time migration for scan: list = the current project file list, already read = list minus the old remaining, and the already read items must be reconciled with the list, discarding anything that is not a known path in the list — the incomplete line `n` currently stuck in the list will therefore automatically disappear.
Why it is implemented this way
The original implementation of "align save temporary file + rename" was only a half-fix, and this repository provides immediate counter-evidence: rename makes "writing" atomic, but it does not serialize "reading". strike reads first, then writes; another process may have already read the old list in the interim, so when it writes back, it overwrites the results of others. The evidence is in lines 301 and 302 of ideas/log.claude.md — both lines write "7 remaining scanned", yet the file that was supposedly struck out remains the first line of the list to this day. The command_reviewed on the codex side is a more advanced version of the same error: it uses correct atomic writes, but it is still "read-modify-write", which still results in lost writes. Even the most complete of the three implementations failed here. Changing to append-only resolves both symptoms simultaneously: the operating system handles positioning for each append, N concurrent processes produce N complete records, and no locks, retries, waiting, or any new dependencies are required. This also holds true on Windows: the underlying library adds FILE_APPEND_DATA to append mode, which is the Windows equivalent of the POSIX semantics. I must clarify the boundaries of this evidence to avoid overstating: guard uses append for logging, and in log.claude.md, there are only three moments that truly prove "simultaneous writing" (the remaining count 32 appears three times, 19 twice, and 7 twice); the other hundreds of lines were written sequentially and do not prove concurrency. Therefore, the real guarantee is not "we tried many times and it didn't break," but rather "the growth of file length is atomic, and the upper limit for non-interleaved content is the disk sector size (512B to 4KB), while each of our records is a path of only a few dozen bytes." The first step of implementation is to measure this — first write the concurrency test, run it against the current code to confirm it actually fails (red), and then modify the implementation. Additionally, I am noting a more thorough approach that was considered but not adopted this round: Claude Code has a PostToolBatch event, which triggers only once after an entire batch of parallel tool calls has finished. Moving the strike action there would mean only one process is writing, eliminating concurrency at the source, which is simpler than any concurrency-safe implementation. The reason for not adopting it is that it would require modifying the installer to register a new event, depend on newer versions, and it would change the semantics of R7 itself (striking out by batch rather than by each Read), which is a matter for FORMAT.md to adjudicate, not something a bug fix should handle casually. The append-only approach does not conflict with it: regardless of which event triggers it, the writing method is safe, and it remains valid for the uncapped concurrency brought by sub-agents. No locks: approximately thirty lines of code would be exchanged for three new ways to fail, and stale locks are a long-term cost rather than an edge case — hook processes can be killed by the outer layer, and locks often outlive the processes. By design, guard must "allow through on error," so every lock path would need a "give up striking on timeout" branch, which would effectively reintroduce undercounting, and undercounting is exactly what R7 aims to eliminate. Node also lacks a built-in file lock to fall back on. No third-party packages: this engine has the design prerequisite that "installing in other repositories requires nothing," and since guard starts a new process for every Read, every dependency incurs a cost on every tool call. More directly, those atomic write packages only serialize writes within a single process, whereas the five writers here are in five separate processes; they do not solve the fundamental problem. Lock packages have not been maintained for years and have documented failure loops on Windows. The common foundation D30 has already ruled on this divergence: all generated state atomic writes must use process locks or single atomic appends for append logs. Known boundaries, written here to avoid being treated as a bug later: append atomicity does not hold on network drives; it is only safe on local disks when a single line is much smaller than a sector — here we store file paths, which is more than enough.
Where is the code
ideas/.gitignore:2 · .scan-done
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_ideas_scan_concurrency.test.ts → exit 0

idea Arrange by dependency order

Clean up expired hook configurations pointing to deleted code. CompletedI-056

Parent idea
I-121
What it is
There are still two hooks in .claude/settings.json pointing to packages/hook/dist/*.js, but packages/ has already been deleted in ca7e956.
Why this idea exists
These two hooks run once during every edit and fail every time. This repository itself is the first user of this workflow; its own configuration points to non-existent files, indicating that the promise that "installation is reversible and re-entrant" has not yet covered uninstallation.
Expected result
Only the claude-companion/guard.ts set of hooks remains in settings.json; there are no longer failing hook processes when editing files.
How to implement
Manually delete those two hook group objects in .claude/settings.json that are holding packages/hook/dist; the uninstallation feature will not be implemented in this round. The arrays for the two events will not become empty because of this, so no logic for cleaning up empty objects is required. After deleting, maintain the same shape generated by the installer (two-space indentation, one newline at the end), otherwise, the next time the installer runs, it will create a change to the entire file out of thin air. At the same time, add a regression test: extract the word that looks like a script from each hook command in settings.json (ends with .js/.ts/.mjs/.cjs/.py, remove quotes, parse relative path against the project root), and assert that the file it points to actually exists. This test is currently red and will turn green after deletion. Add one more assertion: each of the four events (PreToolUse / PostToolUse / Stop / UserPromptSubmit) must still retain at least one hook containing guard.ts in its commands. Without this, deleting the entire guard section would also make the first assertion turn green — a "pass by deleting everything" test, which perfectly rewards the exact kind of failure this idea should not cause.
Why it is implemented this way
First, why "delete" instead of "disable": Claude Code does not have a switch to disable individual hooks; the only switch would disable all hooks together, including the guard itself; and the hooks in settings.local.json are additive and merged, with no syntax to "negate a specific item from a previous layer." Therefore, deletion is the only way to avoid accidentally harming the guard. Second, why not just implement an uninstallation feature: the D14 of the common base has already adjudicated the scope of responsibility for install.ts — local development, old installation migration, and viewing/refreshing installed repositories; formal distribution and uninstallation are handled by each agent's own plugin layer. Creating an uninstallation subcommand now would be equivalent to building something that the common base has explicitly decided not to own. In the history of this repository, there actually was an uninstallation script (in the parent commit of ca7e956); its approach was to filter out its own entries based on characteristic substrings in the commands, and then remove the resulting empty groups — which is also the standard solution across the entire ecosystem. However, it relies on a different registry format and several files that no longer exist; bringing the whole thing back would be the kind of scope expansion that was rejected. When actually implemented, it would be a dozen lines of inversion of the four lines of filtering logic in installHooks, not something new. Finally, why a manual deletion read by a human instead of creating a new mechanism: the commit message for ca7e956 explicitly states "also deleted references interrupted by the archiving action: pointing to the hook in packages/hook/dist," and the change to settings.json in that commit only rearranged those two items from single lines into indented JSON, without deleting a single one. The reason is that the installHooks filter only recognizes its own command names, so it cannot structurally delete others'. This file has already been fooled once by an automatic fix that "looked successful"; we shouldn't let it happen a second time. There is also one risk that must be stated: this is the agent modifying the file that "decides whether the agent is managed." Cursor's specification directly prohibits this (it lists hook configuration as a locked file, with the reason being that agents are not allowed to uninstall their own constraints), whereas the common base's D24 did not put hook configuration on the protection list. The mitigation is for a human to read the changes before committing.
Where is the code
.claude/settings.json:21-64 · hooks
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_settings_hooks.test.ts → exit 0

Parent idea
I-127
What it is
Claude, Cursor, and Codex are simultaneously available within the same repository, jointly reading and writing project-level ideas/graph.yaml, logs, and evidence; when switching agents, there is no reconstruction, no copying, and no selection of another graph. This round of expansion enables multiple assistant sessions to collaborate within the same working directory simultaneously, communicating through shared messages and coordinating the writing of files and graphs.
Why this idea exists
The same project will be taken over by different agents. If switching to a different agent requires rebuilding the idea graph, then that graph is not a record of the project, but merely the memory of a specific agent.
Expected result
Once all three sides are installed, there is only one canonical graph.yaml; if any side modifies the graph, records, or completes a node, the other two sides can see the same state by re-reading. Old suffix graphs are only retained as read-only inputs before an explicit migration. During multi-session parallelism, different files can be developed simultaneously, conflicts in claiming the same file are visible and constrained, messages can be read by each other, graph updates are not lost; after an abnormal termination, an explicit handoff can be performed.
How to implement
Retain the common base migration and the relay acceptance by the original three parties, and add parallel acceptance within the same directory for I-112. First, explicitly install the products of this round in a disposable real test repository; use the actual hosts of Claude, Cursor, and Codex to open one session each to work in parallel, respectively claiming files, publishing messages, reading messages from others, and performing local updates to the same graph. Subsequently, create contention for the same file and conflicts with old values, then stop the old sessions and all in-flight writes to perform an explicit handoff. At the same time, verify that opening two sessions of the same model type does not merge identities; check the identity payload of the actual write hook for sub-assistants, rather than just checking the startup notification. Retain platform versions, input events, visible prompts, and actual file results, distinguishing between cooperative commands and verified host interceptions. Do not mark as complete until all three parties have verifiable write identities and blocking results; report unintegrated hosts or write paths item by item.
Why it is implemented this way
Continue to reuse the original common graph and the three-party connection, expanding the endpoint acceptance instead of creating another endpoint representing the same goal. Multi-process testing of I-112 can verify the file protocol but cannot prove that the real host called the hook, so manual verification is retained here. Official documentation https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks clearly states that the Codex sub-assistant follows the parent session_id; https://cursor.com/docs/hooks distinguishes between conversation_id and generation_id; identity must be verified in the actual host, and different model names cannot be used as evidence of isolation.

How to verify

Add dual-session checks for the same model type and identity checks for sub-assistants, recording host versions and actual hook input/output. Host paths that have not proven write identity or interception cannot be marked as complete. Throughout the process, only one project intent graph is retained; do not automatically modify this repository or other user repositories.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Arrange ideas according to dependency order: prerequisites always come first. CompletedI-060

Parent idea
I-120
What it is
Given a graph, return a list of ideas sorted by topological order: each idea is placed after all its prerequisites; within the same layer, sort by id (topological order is not unique, so a fixed rule is needed to ensure the same output order every time); if the graph has cycles or edges pointing to non-existent ids, do not enter an infinite loop and do not lose any nodes.
Why this idea exists
Now 'reading from top to bottom is the dependency order' is just a coincidence — this graph is built bottom-up all at once. /ccthink will make this coincidence fail by appending each new idea to the end of the file.
Expected result
Given a graph where prerequisites are written later, each idea in the returned list is still placed after all its prerequisites; the same input always gives the same output; graphs with cycles will not cause it to hang or swallow nodes.
How to implement
Add an independent function `topoOrder` in the graph query section using Kahn's algorithm: First, calculate the in-degree of each idea based on the number of `needs`; skip edges pointing to non-existent IDs directly (following the existing convention in this file—dangling edges are silently ignored, and `check` will report errors); then proceed layer by layer: extract the entire batch of nodes with an in-degree of zero, sort them by ID, and output them together, then use the nodes they unlock as the next layer, repeating this process. This is the literal meaning of "sorting by ID within the same layer"—depth comes first, ID comes second; it is neither a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue nor a greedy approach that takes the minimum at each step (both of those would move an idea from the second layer ahead of an idea from the first layer that has not yet been output). After finishing, take the nodes whose in-degree is still greater than zero (i.e., those in a cycle), sort them by ID, and append them to the end, losing none. The three orders look very similar, and a three-node linear fixture cannot distinguish them, so the tests must use the following two small graphs (I have run all three implementations, and the numbers are actual outputs, not conjectures): I. I-002 needs I-001, I-004 needs I-003 — both layer-by-layer and FIFO give I-001, I-003, I-002, I-004, while taking the minimum at each step gives I-001, I-002, I-003, I-004. This fixture catches "taking the minimum at each step." II. I-003 needs I-002, I-004 needs I-001 — layer-by-layer gives I-001, I-002, I-003, I-004, while FIFO gives I-001, I-002, I-004, I-003. This fixture catches "copying codex." Both are required; having only one would allow the other incorrect implementation to pass. The return value is the idea objects themselves, accessed by array index without going through the ID lookup table: the lookup table only keeps the last entry for duplicate IDs, and the command-line `render` never runs `check` first, so duplicate IDs would cause a card to vanish into thin air. Do not modify the existing `findCycle`.
Why it is implemented this way
This algorithm does not need to be invented from scratch—there is already a version in the Python implementation of this repository, which even defines two contracts: skip dangling edges instead of erroring, and return nodes in a cycle as data instead of throwing an exception. Borrow its shape, but the queue must be replaced: it uses FIFO (sorting only at the initial seed and each expansion), which is neither "sorting by ID within the same layer" nor "taking the minimum at each step"—the three orders are distinct, and copying it will result in the third type. To distinguish between layer-by-layer and FIFO, use the second fixture in `how`: I-003 needs I-002, I-004 needs I-001 — layer-by-layer gives I-001, I-002, I-003, I-004, while FIFO gives I-001, I-002, I-004, I-003. (The counter-example written here previously was wrong and is now void: "Four ideas A B C D, the only edge is C needs A, FIFO gives A B D C" — layer-by-layer also gives A B D C; this fixture can only catch "taking the minimum at each step" and cannot distinguish FIFO. I have manually derived the three orders one by one and am writing them here to prevent the next person from being misled by it.) This point is explicitly required by `expected`, so it must be decided and clearly documented. I choose layer-by-layer because its sole consumer, I-061, requires exactly this: "Cards are arranged from the foundation with no prerequisites all the way to the end"—read all ideas without prerequisites first, then read those built upon them. Taking the minimum at each step cannot achieve this: it would output an idea from the second layer with a smaller ID before an idea from the first layer has been output. The divergence between these three orders must be recorded in the divergence adjudication table in `FORMAT.md`, because `codex` is already running another one. Why not merge with `findCycle`: it breaks the entire traversal when it encounters the first cycle, and merging would return a truncated order, losing nodes—whereas "not losing nodes" is exactly what `expected` forbids violating. Furthermore, the required return values differ: `check` prints the path of the cycle (which only depth-first can provide), while `topoOrder` requires the complete sequence. `findCycle` is code already completed by someone else (I-042). Why not use an existing sorting library: this engine has zero-dependency as a design prerequisite; moreover, existing libraries do not provide the two things truly needed here—deciding same-layer order by ID and returning nodes in a cycle as data; re-implementing them would require an extra wrapper. To answer an obvious counter-question: I-043 once wrote "do not perform topological sort." That adjudication has not been overturned—`frontier` answers a state question (which ones can start working now), while `topoOrder` answers a structural question (in what order should this graph be read). The two are mutually exclusive, and `topoOrder` must never become aware of state, nor should `frontier` be changed to be built upon it. Known boundary: "sorting by ID" means sorting by characters. Current IDs are three-digit numbers with zero-padding, so character order happens to equal numerical order; a project using a mix of one-digit and two-digit IDs would sort in reverse. Use standard sorting (consistent with the other two places in this file) without locale-dependent comparisons—that would cause the same input to produce different outputs on different machines.
Where is the code
companion/ideas.ts:213-269 · topoOrder
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_ideas_toposort.test.ts → exit 0

idea Arrange by dependency order

Detail cards in the web page are displayed in dependency order instead of writing order. CompletedI-061

Parent idea
I-120
What it is
`render()` uses topological order when outputting the detail cards below, rather than the writing order in the YAML. IDs remain unchanged, and the YAML source files remain unchanged—only the rendered web page changes.
Why this idea exists
Humans read the web page. If the order is incorrect, readers must manually trace every `needs` in their heads to know what to look at first.
Expected result
Open `graph.html`: the foundation with no prerequisites is at the front, and every card is placed after all its prerequisites; reshuffle the writing order of ideas in the YAML and re-render, the card order remains unchanged.
How to implement
Only one change: in the line that outputs the detail cards when generating the webpage, replace "traverse by writing order" with "sort by topoOrder before traversing". topoOrder is a function already built by I-060, and to date, it has no production callers — only its own tests in the entire repository use it. This idea is its first consumer, so no additional sorting logic needs to be written, and the order does not need to be redefined (I-060 has already selected "by layer, and by id within the layer" for this consumer). There are three things that must remain untouched, each with a specific reason. 1. The flowchart above: its node declaration order comes from the shared drawing function, and existing tests assert that "the graph drawn on the page is word-for-word equal to what that function calculates"; touching it means touching the already established visual, and since the layout engine's result depends on the node declaration order, the graph would change its appearance for no reason. 2. The JSON data model embedded in the page: I-062 defines that "JSON is the sole data model for the page, and the DOM is merely its view"; card order is a matter of the view and should not move the model in reverse; a more practical reason is that every time the page structure changes, it recalculates the flowchart source code according to the order of this JSON. Once the JSON is reordered while the initial graph is not, if a person breaks a prerequisite for the first time, the entire graph will re-layout and jump instantly because the declaration order changed. 3. Anchors and jumps: card ids, links, and click jumps all find elements by id and are independent of order; after reordering, clicking a node will still jump to it — this point must be pinned down in the tests, not just relied upon through reasoning. Additionally, add a line of explanation for humans under the "Idea Details" title: "Cards are arranged by dependency order, not by the writing order in the file," otherwise readers will think the rendering is wrong if they see an order different from the YAML.
Why it is implemented this way
Compared four approaches. Sorting by id: ids are assigned sequentially as they are written, so sorting by id is basically equivalent to sorting by writing order, which is exactly the problem this idea aims to fix; furthermore, it directly violates the sentence "how it will be used in the future" — the id of a new idea is always the largest and will only appear last. Sorting by status (completed first, todo later): that answers "which ones can start working now," but frontier is already answering that question; I-043 ruled on this once, and I-060 reaffirmed it: status issues and structural issues are two different things, and the order of reading the graph is a structural issue. Moreover, sorting by status would split a dependency chain into four segments, giving the reader even more prerequisites to track. Directly reordering the ideas in the YAML to make the file order equal to the dependency order: the "What is it" section explicitly states the source file remains untouched, and this path hits two hard constraints — approval is bound to the hash of the graph content, so reordering the file is changing the content, making a graph just approved invalid instantly; the expiration check used during webpage submission also uses the same fingerprint. Changing a file that has just been human sign-off for the sake of layout involves costs and risks that are disproportionate. Reordering using a script in the browser: this is equivalent to rewriting the topological sort in the page, whereas I-076 just spent an entire idea refactoring the "graph drawing algorithm" into a single piece of source code shared by the engine and the page, precisely because a second hand-copied version would inevitably drift; since the engine side already has topoOrder, sorting once during rendering adds zero extra bytes to the page and avoids the jump caused by reordering after loading. Choosing "sort during rendering, only sort cards" is because it is the only approach that only moves the view, without moving the model or the files: the YAML remains unchanged, the ids remain unchanged, the JSON data model remains unchanged, and the flowchart remains unchanged; only the order seen by a person opening the webpage changes. Also need to correct one sentence in the original "Expected Result": it says "cards are arranged from the foundation with no prerequisites all the way to the end," but a layered topological order cannot provide this — in actual testing in this repository, five endpoints fall at positions 29, 30, 33, 34, and 40, with only the last one being exactly at the end. Topological order guarantees that "every card is placed after all its prerequisites," but does not guarantee "the endpoint is last": a shallow endpoint will naturally be placed before a deep non-endpoint. Rewritten according to what can actually be achieved.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Directly modify the text and status of an idea on the webpage. CompletedI-062

Parent idea
I-123
What it is
The detail cards in the idea graph webpage change from read-only to editable: the text of the eight questions, idea name, and status can all be modified directly by a person in the browser; changes stay on the page and are marked, waiting for submission.
Why this idea exists
When a person finds a problem while reviewing the graph, there are currently only two paths: verbally relay it to the agent (which involves an extra step and is prone to distortion), or manually modify the YAML file (which is prone to breaking the format). The place where you view the graph should be the place where you modify the graph.
Expected result
Open the graph webpage, click any idea to modify its text and status; modified parts have visible markers; changes are kept by the page before submission and will not be lost by clicking on other ideas.
How to implement
render embeds two things in the webpage: the JSON data of the entire graph (a script tag, serving as the sole data model for the page, with the DOM being just the view) and the 12-character fingerprint of the current graph content (for expiration checks during submission). Add an "Edit" toggle to each detail card: plain text fields become multi-line input boxes, status becomes a dropdown, and name becomes a single-line input box; all assignments follow textContent / value, and idea text is never concatenated into innerHTML — not all text in the graph is human-written, preventing script injection. Every modification is recorded in an in-memory change list and will attempt to save to the browser's local storage as a draft (using the project path hash as a namespace; covers all of try/catch, and if it cannot be saved, it downgrades to pure memory and explicitly states "will be lost upon closing the page" at the top of the page). Draft recovery is never silent: when reopening the page, it lists "N unsubmitted changes," and the person must confirm them one by one to recover.
Why it is implemented this way
The data model embeds JSON instead of parsing and reconstructing the displayed text from the page — the display strings for code and verify are concatenated, so parsing them back will inevitably lose structure. No frontend frameworks are introduced; native form elements are used to maintain the current zero-build, double-click-to-use state of this webpage. Drafts are treated only as a safety net, not a transmission channel (following the precedent of mermaid-live-editor); "recovery must be confirmed by a human" is because under the file:// protocol, all local webpages share the same browser storage, so things written by other pages cannot be treated as human changes (countering injection paths discovered via censorship).

idea Arrange by dependency order

Extract the algorithm for "turning one idea graph into a flowchart" into a single source code file shared by the web page and the engine. CompletedI-076

Parent idea
I-120
What it is
Currently, the algorithm for "one idea graph → flowchart source text" only lives inside the function that generates the web page, and it references several variables outside that function. Extract it into an independent function that references no external variables, so that the engine side and the browser side run the exact same source code — text purification, long name line wrapping, coloring by status, and click binding are all moved into this function.
Why this idea exists
Once the structure can be modified (adding an idea, breaking an arrow), the browser must be able to recalculate the flowchart source text and redraw it itself. There are only two ways to do this: hand-copy this algorithm again in the web page, or have both sides share the same one. A hand-copied second version will inevitably drift — if the line-wrapping rule is changed on only one side, the same idea graph will look different in two places, and no test will detect it.
Expected result
For the same idea graph, when the engine calls this function and the web page calls this function, they obtain identical flowchart source text, character for character; the existing web page's appearance, connections, and click behavior remain unchanged by a single pixel.
How to implement
Move the entire loop that generates the flowchart source text into a new function. It only accepts one idea graph and references nothing outside the function — the six items currently used by it: index lookup table, endpoint set, index-to-node-name conversion, classification by status, long name line wrapping, and text purification, are all moved inside the function body. Then, embed the function body into the web page script as a **string constant**, rather than using Function.prototype.toString to retrieve its source code at runtime. The engine side calls this function directly, and the web page side executes the same text. The way to lock in "the same source code" is a single test: for the same idea graph, calculate once on both sides and assert that the outputs are identical character for character.
Why it is implemented this way
The original plan was to "inject the page using Function.prototype.toString during rendering." This path is broken in this repository; I have tested it: tsx hard-codes esbuild's keepNames to enabled (searchable in installed packages, and there is no environment variable to turn it off), so any named const in the function body will be compiled into a call to __name(...), and __name is a free variable injected by the compiler — in other words, the prerequisite of "zero closure" is precisely destroyed by the compiler itself. I ran a function of the same shape with real tsx, evaluated the injection result, and it reported __name is undefined. What is even more fatal is that it cannot be caught: the transformation suite used for running tests does not depend on esbuild, so tests will all be green, while the page opened by double-clicking will error out directly. A failure mode that a test can never discover should not be chosen. Remediation is not impossible — write a __name shim before injection and add a test that actually spawns a child process to watch it — but that would be to preserve a mechanism that provides no benefit here, adding two new things out of thin air. Since the page generation script is already hand-written using template strings (as is already done in this file), writing the function body as a string constant involves zero extra mechanisms. The cost must be stated clearly: the string constant version loses type checking. Therefore, that test of "identical character-for-character output on both sides" is not just a bonus; it is the safety net for this decision, and without it, this choice is invalid.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Change logbook: field changes and structural changes use the same format, and browser drafts and disk files also use the same format. CompletedI-077

Parent idea
I-119
What it is
The logbook that records "what a person changed this time" on the page changes from a table of "idea ID + field name → new value" to a sequence of ordered operation records: changing a field, changing a status, creating a new idea, deleting an idea, connecting a prerequisite arrow, or breaking a prerequisite arrow. This sequence of records is simultaneously the format for browser drafts and the format for the change file submitted to the disk later — one format, not three.
Why this idea exists
Currently, this logbook can only express "what a certain field of a certain idea became." When creating a new idea, there is no ID to use as a key; when deleting an idea, there is no field name; and prerequisite relationships are a list — the current logbook compares new and old values by treating the list as a single string, so "changing two prerequisites to one" is judged as "no change" and then discarded. Structural editing has no place to land in the current format.
Expected result
All six types of operations can be recorded, saved to drafts, and read back, without missing a single one; when changing an idea's prerequisites from two to one, the log shows "which one was broken" instead of "no change"; after the page is reopened, structural operations can be restored item by item, just like field changes.
How to implement
The ledger is changed from a single table to a sequence of ordered operations, consisting of six types: modify field (with old and new values), modify status (with original and new status), create (the page only provides a temporary ID and the content of the first three questions), delete (with ID), connect a prerequisite arrow, and disconnect a prerequisite arrow. Connecting and disconnecting edges are written as a pair of "from which to which," rather than a new value for the entire prerequisite list. An envelope wraps the entire sequence of operations: format version number, project path, and the embedded image fingerprint from the page — the fingerprint is brought back exactly as is; the page never calculates it itself. This envelope serves as both the format for browser drafts and the format for modified files on disk: one single format, not three. Incidentally, this fixes an existing adjacency defect: when a draft is written, the fingerprint is stored, but when it is read back, it is never compared, meaning a draft written against an old image would be silently restored. Once operations like "delete a certain idea" exist, this is no longer harmless.
Why it is implemented this way
The existing ledger cannot be expanded further; this is based on empirical testing, not speculation: its method of comparing old and new values involves converting both sides to strings before comparing, and a list with only one element converted to a string happens to equal the element itself — therefore, "deleting two prerequisites to leave one" will be judged as "no change" and subsequently deleted from the ledger. Raw strings also cannot express "non-existence" (an empty string means empty, not deleted), and the current implementation of splitting keys by delimiters when restoring drafts will produce garbage when encountering structural operations. Therefore, this is a reconstruction, not an expansion. This sentence must be written in the node, because it is precisely the difference between "two lines of changes" and "one new module," and it is also the reason why the original sentence "make deletion a mark for deletion" sounded trivial. We choose an ordered list instead of several parallel tables: "create a temporary ID" and "connect an edge to that temporary ID" only have a deterministic meaning when there is a sequence. Edges are written as a pair instead of the entire list: this prevents two edge changes on the same idea from overwriting each other. We do not borrow JSON Patch: it locates by array index, and once this chain can add nodes, all indices become incorrect — this is also why configuration tools generally abandon it. We do not borrow JSON Merge Patch: it can only replace arrays as a whole, and it uses null to represent deletion, which directly conflicts with the "human sign-off: not yet signed" that exists in this graph. The custom operation list, addressed by ID, aligns semantically with the Kubernetes precedent of key merging, and the implementation is only about thirty lines. For the version number, we adopt the approach of online flowchart editors: add a prefix so that the write-back end can explicitly reject an old format instead of reading it in ambiguously.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Write the ID counter and the change file format into the format specification. CompletedI-078

Parent idea
I-119
What it is
Add two things to the format specification. First, the ID counter at the top level of the graph file: a number that only increases; new IDs are issued uniformly by the engine when writing back changes, and the web page only issues temporary IDs and does not touch it. Second, the format of the change file: what is in the envelope and what each of the six operations looks like.
Why this idea exists
"IDs are never reused" is a hard rule of the format, but the web page cannot see history. If the web page calculates "max ID + 1" based on the current graph, after deleting the idea with the largest ID, the next creation will obtain the ID that was just deleted; if two people open their own web pages, they will also simultaneously calculate the same new ID, and no one will notice after merging. The change file is the sole interface between the web page and the write-back command; a cross-component format that is not written into the specification would force the next person to read the implementation to understand it.
Expected result
Perform "create, delete, create" in succession; the obtained IDs increase strictly and never repeat; two change files from parties unaware of each other are written back sequentially, each obtaining a different ID. The specification allows looking up the counter field and the complete format of the change file without reading code.
How to implement
The counter is written as a field at the top level of the graph file, incremented only by the command that issues IDs; any other place is read-only. **The initial value is written as a rule, not as a number**: when the field does not yet exist in the graph, calculate it once as "the maximum ID that has appeared in this graph + 1" and write it in. The original text "the maximum ID is I-075, so the initial value is 76" is now obsolete — when that sentence was written, the graph had not yet grown to I-080; initializing according to 76 would cause I-076 to I-080 to be reissued, which is exactly what this field is meant to prevent. A hardcoded number will inevitably expire as long as the graph continues to grow. The specification clearly states two hard rules: the web page only issues temporary IDs; real IDs are issued all at once during write-back and all temporary IDs are replaced, and if replacement is incomplete, the entire write-back is rejected. The format of the change file is written out item by item according to the envelope and the six operations, with one example for each.
Why it is implemented this way
Put the counter in the graph file instead of letting the web page calculate it: ID non-reuse is a format rule, and the web page cannot see deleted IDs at all. Incidentally, correct an erroneous reason previously written in the graph — the original text said "old graph I-001~I-040 has been retired, and the page calculating max based on the current graph will collide with them," which is wrong: the living IDs are I-041~I-075, and max+1 yields I-076, which does not collide with any retired IDs. The real vulnerability occurs after deletion: if the idea with the largest ID is deleted, max retreats, and the next creation obtains the ID that was just deleted. Two web pages calculating the same ID simultaneously is a concurrent version of the same bug — this is also why Rails abandoned sequential ID migration years ago. The two matters are combined into one node because they are two halves of the same thing: both are "new things added to this pipeline that must be searchable in the specification," and both involve modifying the same managed file. Splitting them into two nodes would cause the same specification to be approved twice.
