idea Arrange by dependency order

Add and delete ideas and prerequisites on the web page. CompletedI-063

Parent idea
I-123
What it is
Create new ideas on the webpage (the page initially provides a temporary ID, the real ID is sent by the engine), delete ideas, and add or remove "prerequisite" arrows between two ideas; a newly created idea is only considered formed if at least the first three questions (What, Why, Expected Result) are filled in.
Why this idea exists
The two most common conclusions from manual verification of graphs are "missing an edge" and "this node does too much, it should be split." If only text can be modified and not the structure, these two types of high-value modifications must still loop back to the YAML file.
Expected result
Adding a node, connecting an edge, or deleting an edge on the webpage will cause the graph to immediately redraw into a new shape; new idea IDs will not conflict with any historical IDs (IDs are never reused). Since drawing requires fetching a third-party library via the network, it must be clarified what happens when offline: the graph cannot be drawn, but adding, deleting, and submitting still work as usual, and the page must explicitly state that the graph is temporarily unavailable — it must not turn into a screen full of flowchart source code.
How to implement
Four tasks, all falling within the function that generates the webpage. **Prerequisite arrows**: The "prerequisite idea" of each card changes from a read-only link to an editable one — a dropdown menu to select an existing idea to connect to, with an 'X' next to each connected arrow to disconnect it. Each operation appends a "connect" or "disconnect" entry to the ledger, writing "from which to which," rather than the new value of the entire prerequisite list. **New**: A "Create New Idea" button that produces an empty card with a temporary ID; it cannot enter the submission stage if the first three questions (What, Why, Expected Result) are not fully filled. **Delete**: A "Delete" button on the card that performs a "mark for deletion," which can be undone, and only becomes a deletion operation upon submission. **Redraw**: As soon as the structure changes, call the shared drawing function to recalculate the graph source, then create a brand-new graph element to replace the old one — the drawing library stamps processed elements, so changing text in place will not trigger a redraw. All text must be assigned using textContent. Redrawing must preserve the user's current zoom and pan; the view cannot reset to the full graph every time a change is made. This cross-module section requires two changes: move the editing script before the drawing script (it is currently reversed, meaning editing is initialized only after a cross-network module fetch); the drawing section must attach a redraw function externally after its own dependencies are loaded, following the current "click node to jump to card" approach — that is the only bridge between these two scripts today. The editing script should only perform feature detection and must never wait. **Offline**: When the redraw function cannot be detected, adding, deleting, and submitting work as usual, the page explicitly states "Graph temporarily unavailable (offline)," and the original graph source text must be hidden — currently, if drawing fails, the reader sees a screen full of flowchart source code. Prerequisite links on cards remain clickable because they are actual anchor links.
Why it is implemented this way
Why are only temporary IDs issued: real IDs must be issued uniformly during write-back; the reason is written in the idea regarding the ID counter, and this only uses it. The benefit is that this idea can start working without waiting for the format specification to be finalized. Why are edges recorded as a pair of "connected/disconnected" instead of a new value for the entire list: the ledger idea has already ruled that two edge changes on the same idea cannot overwrite each other. Why move the editing script forward: testing shows that the current editing section is placed after the drawing section, and the first thing the drawing section does is fetch modules from the CDN and uses top-level await — meaning today's editing functionality is initialized only after a cross-network request. Moving the position has zero cost, and the benefit is that editing is immediately available during network outages. Why use a global function as a bridge instead of an event bus or shared module: a bridge already exists (clicking a node jumps to a card); adding another function capable of feature detection is shorter than introducing an event mechanism and provides one less way to fail than importing another module under file://. Why redrawing must create new elements: the drawing library stamps processed elements, so in-place modification will not take effect — this is a pitfall that makes people think "redrawing wasn't triggered" and leads them to modify other things randomly. Why preserve zoom and pan: if a person is staring at a corner of the graph to modify something, and every redraw jumps back to the full view, the feature becomes unusable. Why hide source code during network outages: this is an existing defect (drawing failure = source code all over the screen); after adding redrawing, it will be encountered more frequently, so fixing it while at it is cheaper than opening a new idea. Why nodes and edges are no longer split into two ideas: they use the same machinery — the same ledger, the same redraw path, and the same shared function; splitting them would result in two almost identical nodes and two almost identical tests. The benefit of splitting is "being able to verify them separately," but here, the two sets of assertions in the same test file can verify them separately.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Webpage "Submit": if a local server exists, save directly; if not, download as a change file. CompletedI-064

Parent idea
I-123
What it is
There is a "Submit" action on the webpage that packages all changes made this time (modifying text, modifying status, creating/deleting ideas, adding/deleting prerequisite relationships) into a change record to be sent out. The page first probes whether a local server exists: if yes, it sends it directly to be saved by the server; if no (for example, if the file was opened by double-clicking), it falls back to downloading it as a file and explicitly tells the user where to put it.
Why this idea exists
Webpages in a browser cannot write to files in the project — this is the only insurmountable wall in the entire chain. A local server is the main gate to cross this wall, and downloading is the backup gate when there is no server. The two paths must deliver the exact same thing, otherwise the write-back end would have to recognize two different formats.
Expected result
When a server is present: Click "Submit" → the page lists changes one by one → user clicks confirm → changes are applied to the graph, and the page displays the new graph, without touching the file system throughout the process. When no server is present: Click "Submit" → receive a change file, along with the instruction "Put it in <absolute path>, then run this command." In both cases, the button is unclickable if nothing has been changed.
How to implement
Probing is sending a request to the server's health check address; the timeout is set very short, and a failure is treated as non-existence — a failed probe must never cause the page to freeze or trigger an error. **With a server**: Send the ledger envelope (containing the image fingerprint and a one-time token in the page) to the server; the server first returns a line-by-line comparison of changes for human confirmation, and the changes are only truly committed to disk after the human clicks confirm; upon success, the page redraws using the new image returned by the server and clears the ledger. **Without a server**: Serialize the same envelope into text and follow a two-level fallback — first, attempt to trigger a download (wrap the text into a temporary object, create a temporary link, click it, and defer garbage collection); if that fails, display a text box that allows for select-all and copying; in both cases, simultaneously display the absolute path of ideas/ (embedded in the page during rendering) and the specific command to be run. Upon successful submission, do not clear the draft, only mark it as "submitted" — wait until the changes have actually landed in the image before allowing a human to discard them.
Why it is implemented this way
Prioritize the server rather than always using files: the person's original words were "hard to sync," and inserting a file that requires manual moving is exactly what causes the lack of synchronization. The fallback is retained because the version opened by direct double-clicking must also be able to submit — the same code, one feature probe, and one fallback branch incur very low cost, in exchange for ensuring this webpage can still be entered into git, sent to others, and opened on machines without Node installed. **Reject showSaveFilePicker as the first level**: The original text stated "tested and usable under file://," but the first step in the specification for "checking if the current environment allows popping up a file picker" rejects opaque origins; file:// documents are indeed opaque origins, and three independent investigations point to this conclusion. That manual test was likely performed in a different context. It is not treated as the first level because a path that works intermittently would cause the other two levels to never see real usage and thus never be verified. If re-testing confirms it truly works in your browser, it can be an added bonus as "use it if detected," but it cannot be written as a promise. **The final level must be a text box rather than the clipboard**: The clipboard interface is also frequently unavailable under file://, whereas a text box that allows select-all will not fail in any browser — the sole requirement for the fallback level is that it must not fail. Each change carries the old value to allow the write-back end to perform line-by-line comparison and conflict display: a change record that only carries the new value can only be discarded entirely if a conflict is encountered. Do not clear the draft upon success: if the write-back is rejected (e.g., the image was modified by another session during editing — this actually occurred once on the day of the investigation), the human's changes must not be lost entirely.

idea Arrange by dependency order

A single command writes the change file back to the idea graph, preserving comments exactly as they were. CompletedI-065

Parent idea
I-123
What it is
The engine adds a new subcommand: read the change file and write every modification into ideas/graph.claude.yaml — text changes are written to specific points, status changes follow the existing "set + automatic record keeping" logic, and the creation/deletion of ideas and edges is executed according to format rules; after writing, it automatically validates and re-renders the webpage, and changes are recorded in the record file.
Why this idea exists
If write-back relies on an agent manually editing YAML, comments will be erased, status might bypass the set logic, and the format might be corrupted — these are exactly the things this tool was intended to prevent. Write-back must be a deterministic command, not an act of free improvisation.
Expected result
After applying a change file to an image with comments: every change takes effect, comments and untouched parts are preserved verbatim, validation passes, corresponding entries are added to the record file, and the webpage has been re-rendered; applying the same change file a second time will not produce any further changes.
How to implement
The engine adds a new `apply` subcommand, which is core-wise a pure function that can be tested independently: Read change file → Apply all changes in memory and run a full check; if any step fails, the entire operation is abandoned and the disk remains untouched → only then perform an atomic write to disk, re-render, and record logs. Key points: If `baseDigest` does not equal the current idea graph fingerprint, the entire operation is rejected (optimistic lock); operations are sorted by "modify fields first, then delete nodes"; after each structural operation, the in-memory snapshot is rebuilt—otherwise, writing according to old indices will cause the state to fall onto the wrong idea (this silent pollution was verified through adversarial testing); state operations are redirected to the existing `setStatus` evidence verification, and the explanatory text is also pulled from there into the log to avoid duplicate recording; new operations force the status to `todo` and strip the `log` and `human sign-off` fields from the payload—otherwise, a change file could spontaneously create "completed and signed-off" ideas; delete operations require that no other ideas depend on it, and the section comments attached to the deleted node are moved to the next node; new nodes use `doc.createNode` and set the loose text fields to a block-folding style (otherwise, shoving raw objects into a YAML document makes them unchangeable later, as verified); any completed idea whose behavior fields (`what` / `expected` / `how` / `why_this_way` / `verify`) have been modified will automatically be downgraded to `doing` and a log will be left—ensuring the three rules of "test first, think clearly, and human approval" re-apply to it. Upon success, rename the change file to `changes.applied-<date>.json`, and the end of the output will include a fixed reminder to "refresh the browser page before starting the next round"; the `set` subcommand also performs a re-render after writing to disk to ensure the web pages on disk are always fresh. **ID issuance is unified here**: Temporary IDs from the page are all replaced with real IDs in one go before application (taken from the ID counter, incrementing by one for each), and places referencing temporary IDs in prerequisite relationships are synchronized; if any temporary IDs remain after replacement, the entire write to disk is rejected. **Three ways to preserve the diff, all measured on a real graph; missing any one will turn a change into a full-file reordering**: 1. When converting the document back to text, no parameters can be passed — passing the "no line wrap" option will reorder all folded paragraphs; verified on this graph, it would move 1274/1301 lines and shorten the file by 291 lines; passing no parameters results in byte-for-byte identity. 2. When writing prerequisite relationships, a node must first be created and then marked with a single-line style; directly inserting a regular array will turn the single-line `needs: [ I-042 ]` into a three-line list, verified to move 444 lines; marking the style only moves 1 line. 3. If the deleted item is the **first** idea, that section title is not attached to it, but to the entire idea sequence — merely moving the "deleted node's comments" will orphan the title onto the new first node. This point requires its own test.
Why it is implemented this way
Writing back must be a deterministic instruction rather than agent free-play — comments, formatting, and verification will all be lost in free-play. All verification is built into the engine rather than relying on hooks: `apply` runs via Bash, and hooks cannot see it at all. This trust boundary must be honestly stated: `apply` guards "state has evidence, the graph is not corrupted, and changes are recorded," but it does not guard "changes must come from a human" (that is the responsibility of I-066). Here, I must also retract a previous overstatement: the original text said "state operations are redirected to the existing `setStatus` evidence verification," but `setStatus` on the Claude side actually only blocks two things: "missing code/verify in `done`" and "missing `human verification` sign-off" — it does not check if the eight questions are complete, does not check if prerequisites are finished, and does not check approval. The Cursor version is the one that truly gates by readiness; this discrepancy has already been noted in the specification. Therefore, the honest statement is: reusing `setStatus` for state operations is to ensure there is only one entry point for logs and to inherit its two checks; it is not "inheriting a full set of readiness verifications." To be stricter, `setStatus` itself must be strengthened, which is another idea. Writing back does not borrow existing patch libraries: research showed a package specifically for "modifying YAML via patches while preserving comments," but it itself is built on top of the same YAML library plus a patch library — and this engine already has that YAML library and the load/save read/write functions. I have verified on a real 50,352-byte graph: parsing and converting back to text results in byte-for-byte identity. In other words, this hardest constraint is obtained for free; installing that package would just be asking for something we already have, while adding a failure mode of "patch fails if the difference is too large" — and here, fuzzy matching is not needed at all; IDs are precise addresses. `check` is moved before writing to disk because the bottom line of this toolset is that bad graphs are not written to disk; "automatic downgrade of completed ideas" is the minimal fix for the largest process loophole discovered during adversarial testing — the `guard` would otherwise allow the code file of a completed idea to pass through directly, and if not downgraded, the code could be changed without approval after the graph is modified. The change format does not borrow JSON Patch (RFC 6902, which uses indices and does not recognize IDs) nor JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396, where arrays can only be replaced entirely): preserving comments requires the application side to iterate through the YAML Document interface item by item; any existing patch library application engine would be extremely heavy; we use a custom operation list by ID, aligning semantically with the precedent of Kubernetes strategic merge patch's `merge-by-key`.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Local small service: renders the idea graph to the browser on the spot and catches the changes sent back by the browser. CompletedI-079

Parent idea
I-123
What it is
The engine adds a subcommand that starts a small service listening only to the local machine: it renders the current graph as a webpage to the browser on the spot, catches the change records sent back by the browser, returns an item-by-item comparison for human confirmation first, calls the write-back logic to save to disk after human confirmation, and then sends the new graph back to the page. It ends when the human closes it.
Why this idea exists
Webpages in the browser cannot write to the disk, so after modifying, a person must manually move a file and then type a command — this is the most awkward part of the entire chain and the true source of "difficulty in syncing modified graphs." A local small service can turn this part into "save with one click." It also fixes another persistent problem: the webpage on the disk is generated and will expire; in service mode, that file does not exist at all, and what is seen is always the current graph.
Expected result
Once running, the browser can open the graph; modify one place on the page and submit, the graph file truly changes, and the page displays the new graph after the modification; if the graph was modified by another session during this period, it is rejected entirely with a clear reason; the service only accepts requests from the local machine, and write operations must include the token generated during this startup.
How to implement
Uses Node's built-in http module without importing any frameworks. It only binds to the local loopback address, not to all network cards. A one-time token is generated at startup and only written into the webpage being rendered on the spot; any write operation without the correct token is rejected. Three paths: one returns the currently rendered page, one is a health check (for the page to detect if the service is running), and one receives changes. The receiving path has two steps: first, calculate without writing and return the item-by-item comparison to the page; once the human clicks confirm, call the write-back logic with the same record. The reply uses the same apply core and never writes a separate one — so fingerprint validation, preventing bad graphs from being written to disk, and logging all proceed as before. A default port is provided, and if occupied, it increments; the final address is printed and an attempt is made to open the browser. It ends when the human presses Ctrl-C or closes the window.
Why it is implemented this way
This is the industry standard shape for this type of tool (this is how the local backend of local content management tools works). In my initial research, I rejected it because I thought it "would break double-click-to-use" — but what people want is exactly that "double-click-to-use service," so that reason no longer holds; I am recording this here truthfully. Use Node's built-in http instead of any framework: there are only three routes, and a framework is pure overhead; furthermore, the design premise of this engine is that it requires no additional installation when added to other repositories. Writing back must reuse apply instead of writing a new implementation: two write entry points mean two sets of validations, which will inevitably diverge, and the day they diverge is when "the images saved via the web and the images saved via the command line are different." The security boundary must be clearly defined: this service has write permissions for image files, and images are exactly the ledger that the guard is protecting. The judgment is acceptable because it does not provide any capability that the agent cannot currently access — the guard is only attached to Edit / Write, and Bash never goes through it; the agent can already directly run the engine's set sub-command. This is the ceiling already truthfully recorded in the repository; blocking it is a matter for another idea. Therefore, this service is not opening a new door, but adding a much more convenient handle next to the door that is already open. Implement three cheap protections: bind only to localhost, use one-time tokens, and ensure all writes always go through the full validation of apply. The documentation of the tool being referenced also warns that its service is unauthenticated and should only be used for local development; this has one extra layer because writes must pass validation — and the most critical point has not been touched: approval can still only be generated by a human typing it manually; the service cannot touch that path.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Place an entry point in the root directory that can open the idea graph with a double-click. In progressI-080

Parent idea
I-123
What it is
Place a file in the repository root directory; double-clicking it starts the local micro-service and opens the idea graph in the browser. Simultaneously, provide an equivalent npm command for occasions where double-clicking is inconvenient.
Why this idea exists
"Being able to use it immediately upon opening, like a webpage," is the prerequisite for whether this feature will actually be used. If people have to open a terminal, switch to the repository directory, and then memorize a command, then in practice, only the person who wrote this feature will use it.
Expected result
Double-click the file in the root directory in the file manager, the idea graph appears in the browser, and it can be edited and submitted directly; those who do not want to double-click run an npm command and get the exact same result.
How to implement
Place a Windows batch file in the root directory (runnable directly via double-click), the content of which calls the engine's service sub-command, and **first switches the working directory to the directory where the script itself resides** — otherwise, relative paths will all be wrong when double-clicked from elsewhere. Simultaneously, add an equivalent command to the scripts in package.json. For non-Windows cases, place a shell script with the same name.
Why it is implemented this way
The batch file was chosen because it is the only form that "runs on double-click" on Windows, and people use Windows. Do not make it a packaged desktop application: that would require introducing a whole set of build and distribution processes, and the only benefit would be an icon, whereas the design premise of this engine is that it requires no additional installation when added to other repositories. The line switching the working directory is not optional: the working directory upon double-clicking is uncertain; without it, it won't run on some machines, and such failures will only appear on other people's machines and can never be tested on the local machine. One thing explicitly moved out of scope: handing this entry point over to the installer and distributing it to other repositories. That file is claimed by another idea and is not yet finished; modifying it now would be building a prerequisite for someone else. This repository will use it first, and distribution will wait until that idea is completed.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Provide manual verification sign-off on the webpage; the sign-off is the sentence typed by the human themselves. CompletedI-081

Parent idea
I-124
What it is
Add a seventh type of operation to the change records: sign-off. On the webpage, for any idea where "how to verify" is written as manual check and has not yet been signed, an additional sign-off entry appears on the card — clicking it first displays the original text of that manual check, and below it, the user fills in their name and their own sentence. When writing back, it is saved in the exact same format as current manual entry.
Why this idea exists
Currently, the last step for 12 ideas on the graph is manual verification, and manual verification is only valid if signed by a human. Without this entry point, every time a sign-off is needed, a person must leave the webpage, tell the agent verbally, and then have the agent record it on their behalf — this wall will be hit constantly. And the promise of the "changing the graph means changing the project" chain is that YAML is never touched throughout the process; sign-off is the only link in this chain that has not yet been connected.
Expected result
Open the webpage, find an idea where manual verification has not yet been signed, click sign-off, see the original text of that manual check, fill in your name and your sentence, and after submitting and confirming, the sign-off field for that idea in the graph will be the sentence you wrote; subsequently, it is marked as completed and will no longer be rejected. Three cases where sign-off fails: the verification is not manual, the sentence is empty, or it has already been signed.
How to implement
Add the seventh type of operation `{op:"sign", id, who, words}` to the envelope; it uses the same envelope and the same write-back core, enters the ledger just like other changes, and follows the same two steps of "submit → view line by line → confirm." When writing back, it results in `<名字> <日期> —— 人的原话：「<原话>」；在网页上签的`, consistent with the current manual entry format. The engine rejects three cases: the verification for that idea is not a manual check, `words` is empty after removing whitespace, or the sign-off field already has a value (modifying a sign-off is another matter that needs to be clarified; we will not guess this round, just reject first). On the page, this entry only appears for cards where "verification is manual and the sign-off field is empty"; after clicking, **the original text of that manual check is displayed first**, followed by two input boxes; the name is stored in the browser's local storage, so it only needs to be filled in once.
Why it is implemented this way
Why it is "typing a sentence" instead of "clicking a button": A checkbox only leaves a record of "someone clicked it," whereas a sentence leaves a record of this person's judgment on this specific matter. The reason manual verification requires a human sign-off is precisely because a machine cannot judge; leaving only a click trace is equivalent to hollowing out this rule into a mere ritual. Why the original text of the manual check must be displayed before signing: One signs a specific matter, not a blank piece of paper. Requiring a person to flip elsewhere to find that sentence before signing is no different from casually clicking "I agree." Why it is implemented in the same format as manual entry: There are already several sign-offs in the graph that were recorded by an agent; having both old and new formats coexist will lead future readers of the records to believe they are two different things. **Why this does not weaken existing guarantees** —— This point must be clearly stated to avoid people blaming web-based signing as the culprit in the future: The rule where the guard blocks "hand-edited graphs" only compares states; `signed_off` is not within its protection scope at all, and an agent could write a sign-off today by directly editing the yaml. Therefore, this entry does not dismantle any gate; that gate was never closed to begin with. What truly needs to block it is I-066, which has not been implemented yet; until it is finished, the weight of a sign-off relies on convention rather than machines, and this is recorded here truthfully. **There is another harder truth that must be written down: The D27 of the common foundation has already ruled on this matter, and this approach contradicts it.** D27 states "manual verification can only pass through a manual-check challenge, writing the sign-off summary back to the graph and saving the receipt; direct editing of existing sign-offs is rejected," with the reasoning that "a signature that an agent can edit cannot prove a human has seen the result." Web-based signing produces exactly that kind of signature —— an agent can create its own modified file with a sign and run a write-back. It is not worse than the status quo (today, one can write a sign-off by directly editing the yaml), but it takes a step in the opposite direction of what D27 established; the trade-off is that humans do not need to exit the web page to find an agent for recording every time they sign, yet there are 12 ideas currently blocked at this step. The method of reconciliation is already written in D27: downgrade the web step to "proposing a sign-off request," and the actual act of landing in the graph is still triggered by a non-reusable user response —— that is the business of I-066. Until it is finished, this path is a debt incurred knowingly, and it has been simultaneously recorded in the D27 adjudication table to prevent it from being mistaken as already resolved in the future. Why not overwrite existing sign-offs: Who can overturn another person's sign-off and under what circumstances is something that must be thought through first; we will not guess in this round.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Layer the ideas: each idea must specify which idea it belongs under; the web page shows only one layer to a person at a time CompletedI-082

Parent idea
I-120
What it is
An idea can specify that it belongs under another idea —— add a field called "parent idea," fill in the ID of the first-level idea; if left blank, it is the top-most layer. The entire graph is thus a tree: a person reads from the top few ideas, and upon clicking one, sees only the layer directly below it, with a maximum of seven items per layer. This rule must be implemented in four places; if missing one, it cannot be carried to other repositories. One, define it strictly in the format specification: what the field looks like, a maximum of seven per layer, what the validation manages, how the page is split, and how the name and sentence of the top-most layer should be written. Two, the validation program recognizes this field: if attached to a non-existent ID or forming a loop, it reports an error immediately; if a layer exceeds seven, it reports a warning. Three, the web page splits according to this tree: the home page only shows the top-most layer; upon clicking an idea, the top of the page shows its own complete card, and the line below shows its direct descendants one by one; an idea's complete card appears only once in the entire text, right on its own page. Four, the instructions for the assistant regarding graph building and adding new ideas are both changed to "build the tree first, then connect prerequisites." This matter has gone through two versions, and the second version tore down the first. The first version was a flat "step-by-step overview": a list of sequential steps at the top of the graph file, with each idea tagged with a step label —— it was only one layer, and it wasn't drawn on the page. On 2026-09-05, per human request, it was changed to a tree that can be opened layer by layer; those two old fields were deleted together, the original five steps each became an idea in the top-most layer, and the sixty-six ideas replaced step labels with parent idea IDs. One matter that does not belong to this idea is written here to avoid being mistaken as completed together: the title at the top of the web page and the paragraph below it change according to the current page; that is the work of another idea (I-086), which is already finished and is not included here.
Why this idea exists
Once a graph grows to seventy-one ideas, listing them flat makes them unreadable —— the first thing seen upon opening the web page is a wall, making it impossible to see what the project is doing or where to start reading. This is not a flaw unique to this repository, but a flaw that every repository equipped with this set of tools will eventually encounter: ideas will only increase, they will not decrease on their own. Writing a few lines of introductory text for this repository only solves the problem once; defining "ideas must be layered, and how to layer them" as a rule in the specification allows any repository to follow it and obtain its own version of layering. The flat overview produced first did indeed answer half the question —— sentences like "how many things this project is doing in total, and what capabilities the project gains after each thing is finished" were the first times these were forced to be clarified when writing that overview. But it failed on two points proven by testing: it only had one layer, so seventy-one ideas spread across five steps meant that clicking any step still resulted in a long string of ten or twenty ideas, meaning the "wall" was merely cut into five pieces; furthermore, it only existed in the graph file and was not drawn on the web page at all, so a person opening the web page saw nothing extra. To make people truly able to read it, "belonging" cannot just be a list printed in a file; it must become the structure of the graph itself, with the page serving it layer by layer according to that structure.
Expected result
Open the webpage; you will only see the top layer of ideas, one per line, each with its name, status, and the first line of its "what is"; click one to enter, and the top of the page shows its own eight questions, while the bottom shows its direct descendants; click again to enter another layer. The complete card of each idea appears only once in the entire file, right on its own page. Ideas in the same layer are sorted by dependency order: a prerequisite is placed before its successor. If an idea is attached to a non-existent ID, the validation reports an error and simultaneously reports both IDs; if it forms a loop (including attaching to itself), it reports one error and prints the loop in order, reporting the same loop only once; if any layer exceeds seven, a warning is reported instead of an error, specifying which layer it is. If an idea does not have its affiliation written, the validation says nothing about it — the top layer originally has no affiliation. The boundary of this statement must be clear: if the entire graph has no affiliation written and there are more than seven ideas, the "top layer exceeds seven" warning will still appear, because that is counting the top layer, not picking out ideas without affiliation. When creating a new idea on the webpage or changing an idea's affiliation, that field is saved as a single line of plain text when writing back to the graph file, not as a collapsed paragraph; validation is performed after writing back, resulting in zero errors. If an idea's affiliation is written as a non-existent ID, the page treats it as part of the top layer and displays it accordingly — an idea cannot be lost on the page due to a typo; errors that should be reported are left to the validation to report. One more thing: running a graph construction once in a strange repository produces a tree directly, not a flattened list. The verification command below this sentence will not be triggered — those two tests check validation rules, writing back, and the page; none of them will run graph construction in another repository; and the only time that sentence received a human sign-off (2026-09-04) was for the flattened overview of the first version, not this tree, and its referenced receipt file no longer exists on the disk today. This sentence remains here waiting for a real graph construction on a strange repository, without pretending it has already been covered.
How to implement
**Field.** Add a field to an idea where the value is the ID of the parent idea; if left blank, it is part of the top layer. Only add this one direction from child to parent; do not add a reverse "child idea list." **Validation is split into two levels, intentionally.** Attaching to an ID not in the graph or forming a loop will cause the page to lose ideas or fail to render — these report errors; exceeding seven in a layer is just hard to read — this reports a warning. The method for finding loops is to climb up from each idea following the affiliation; if you climb back to yourself, it is a loop; the members of the loop are recorded, and the same loop is reported only once, using the same convergence method as finding dependency cycles in a graph. **Webpage.** All pages are written into the same file and are all hidden initially; the script in the page displays one specific page based on the ID in the address bar; changing the ID changes the page, and the browser's forward and back functions work as usual. The home page is the top layer; an idea's page consists of "its own complete card + direct descendants, one per line." The dependency graph is shared across all pages, and when switching pages, it is redrawn using the descendants of the current page; if the current page has no descendants, the entire graph is hidden without leaving an empty frame. At the top of the page, there is a path counted down from the home page, constructed by following the affiliation all the way up. The order within the same layer follows the already established dependency sorting (that was a task completed by someone else; this is just another user of it). The "how many ideas in a group, how many completed" functionality uses the shared small function left over from the first version, so the count and legend on every page always share the same source and cannot conflict — that piece of code survived, and the comments still bear the version number of the first version. **Writing back.** Both creating a new idea and changing a field recognize this field; it is an ID, not prose, so it is saved as a single line of plain text. An idea created by a person on a specific page defaults to being attached to the idea on that page — wherever the person builds it, that is where it grows. **Specifications and two commands.** A new section is added to the specifications, clearly defining the field, the maximum of seven per layer, the four validation rules, and the appearance of page switching; it also separately defines the name of the top layer and how that specific sentence should be written — four rules plus one real counter-example (the graph in this repository itself once had three "buckets" used for categorizing authors like "known defects," "endpoint," and "reading order," which, if copied as top-level ideas, would cause readers to immediately ask "is reading order something this project needs to do"); a "provenance" section is left at the end, stating that the predecessor was that flattened overview and why/when it was changed. The exported specification and the source file are identical byte-for-byte. The graph construction command is changed to "after extracting ideas, before connecting prerequisites, first build the tree"; the new idea command is changed to "fill in the first three questions before writing the affiliation; to start a new top layer, you must explain why this project has a large new block." **Cost, stated clearly.** The two fields from the first version were deleted, and the step labels already attached to sixty-six ideas are also invalidated. This is tearing down and restarting a task that was already completed and tested; this cost is being paid because it was known to be necessary. **One unfinished task, written here to avoid being mistaken for completed.** The tree in this repository itself only has two layers: among the five top-level ideas, four each have eleven to twenty-three descendants, and the validation is currently reporting these four warnings. The rules are established, but the middle layer has not yet been built.
Why it is implemented this way
**Why is it "one parent per idea" instead of adding another type of arrow?** In this record, "prerequisite" is the only relationship. Adding a second type of arrow would mean every time a reader sees a line, they have to ask what kind it is. Ownership only answers one question: under whom does this idea belong. It does not participate in "who must finish first," so an idea can still be a prerequisite for an idea on another branch; the page renders that prerequisite as a cross-page link. If this point is ambiguous, layering will be mistaken for a new sequence of precedence, and someone will attempt to schedule project timelines based on it. **Why replace the entire flat step-by-step overview with a tree instead of adding a layer to it?** There are three concrete reasons. First, a flat layout is inherently single-layered: its shape is "a sequential table at the top of the file + one tag per idea." To add a second layer, you would need another table and another tag, and both tables would each require maintaining their own order; a tree uses only one field to support arbitrary layers. Second, "steps" are a second type of thing that appears out of thin air: they are not ideas, they cannot be depended upon by other ideas, they have no status, and they do not have their own page. After changing to a tree, a "step" becomes just an ordinary idea—answering the eight questions, following the status flow, and having its own page—meaning the specification, engine, and write-back each require one fewer field. Third, the word "step" itself implies precedence, whereas there is no precedence between several ideas belonging under the same idea—precedence only exists via prerequisites. Credit must be given to the first version: the five sentences it wrote have today become the five ideas in the top layer, word for word, without a single change; this is empirical proof that it got half the answer right. **Why not use the existing section comments in the graph file for grouping?** This was the approach chosen by humans at the start of the first version, but it was rejected after research, and the reasons remain valid today. Comments can be used today—tests show they can be split into ten sections, and the numbers and legends match perfectly. However, they will **silently tell lies**: new ideas created on the web are appended to the end of the file, so every idea created via the web will automatically fall into the last section. This cannot be seen in the change logs or on the page; only the sentence "this section has X ideas" quietly becomes a lie. Two other reasons: comments are a verbal convention, they have never been written in the specification, they do not exist in newly created empty graphs, and if moved to another repository, they become a blank void; furthermore, the library that reads and writes this file format states in its own documentation that its comment handling is not entirely stable. **Rules must be portable; they cannot be built upon something that cannot be carried away.** **Why set the limit at seven?** A layer exceeding seven lines is not an overview, it is a table of contents—a human cannot scan it in one glance, so they won't scan it. This number can be checked by a machine, so it is a rule, not a suggestion. Fewer than seven is not a complete set, because the few that do make a set tend to become "buckets": this repository itself has produced three ("Known Defects", "Endpoint", "Reading Order"), and they fail to explain "what capability this project gained after completion." Therefore, even that counter-example is written into the specification—if you only write rules and not counter-examples, the next person will make the same mistake. **Why is a wrong attachment an error, while exceeding seven per layer is only a warning?** Attaching to a non-existent ID, or attaching in a loop, will cause the page to actually lose an idea or fail to render, while the page looks perfectly normal—that is bad, not just unattractive. "This layer has eight" simply means a human cannot scan it in one glance, but the graph itself is still correct; reporting it as an error immediately would cause every repository that has installed this tool to turn red instantly, which would be making others' repositories pay for our new rules. The cost must be stated: warnings are often overlooked, so "maximum seven per layer" currently relies on self-discipline rather than enforcement; once this field has stabilized across various repositories, we will consider tightening it. **Why does an idea say nothing if it doesn't write its own ownership?** In the first version, this had to be split into two tiers: if steps were declared but an idea had no ownership, a warning would be issued. The cost was that the numbers on the page would be undercounted, and warnings are often overlooked—that was a conscious trade-off. A tree does not have this cost: an idea without written ownership is simply an idea in the top layer, which is a valid state; the page will still display it and include it in the count. Thus, that tier of warning, along with its cost, has disappeared—it wasn't overlooked. **Why does each idea only write "who I belong to," and not "who belongs to me"?** Storing both directions would result in two sets of potentially contradictory facts, and when contradictions occur, no one knows which one counts. To clarify the weight of this statement: this repository has never actually stored a reverse subordinate list, so this rule is avoiding a problem based on experience elsewhere, rather than fixing a problem that occurred here. The half that can be verified is: by only storing the child-to-parent direction, the parent's subordinate list is recalculated every time. The cost is that retrieving an idea's subordinates requires scanning the entire graph, but with only dozens or hundreds of ideas, this overhead is negligible. **Why does a complete card for an idea only appear on its own page, with only one line placed on the parent page?** This is not a layout preference, but a mechanism: editing, draft recovery, and human sign-off on the web all find elements in the document by ID. If the same ID appears twice, these processes will silently misidentify one. A single line containing the name, status, and the first line of "what it is" is sufficient to decide whether to click into it. **"The entire graph is one file" was not a choice this time, but an inheritance.** It is written here because it explains why the page looks the way it does, not because other methods were compared this time: from day one, this web page has been a file that can be double-clicked to open and sent in its entirety to others; write-back, human sign-off, and drafts all find elements by ID within the same document. Therefore, page splitting can only be "all pages are in this one document, hidden first, and then one page is displayed according to its address." The cost must still be noted: rendering seventy-one ideas results in 1.44 million bytes, and it still opens very quickly; if it becomes ten times longer, the math should be recalculated. **Why is ownership stored as a line of plain text, rather than as a collapsed paragraph like other answers?** It is used for precise comparison with the IDs of other ideas. When a collapsed paragraph is read back, it has an extra newline at the end, making the comparison result always "no one," and this is completely invisible on the page—this is the most expensive kind of error. **Why are the descriptions of two commands being modified, rather than injecting logic into the program?** A machine cannot determine how to divide a project into major blocks or how to describe each block in plain language; this can only be done by the party that has read the project. What the program can do is validation; what it can write are only descriptions. The reason the description only references that section of the specification and does not copy the rules into it is because this tool has already paid the price for "writing the same thing in three different places" once before—the copied version will inevitably differ from the original, and no one will know which one counts. **Why is this one idea, rather than three?** The rules, the validation, and the two commands were originally three separate ideas. What actually happened was: the rules were written without validation to support them, the validation was done without the commands following, and all three were describing the same thing. The only effect of splitting them was to make people think that two-thirds of the layering work had already been completed. After merging, according to the rules of the specification, the smallest ID is kept; the other two retain their IDs, are set to blocked, and the record specifies which one they were merged into—IDs are never recycled, and the human sign-off on one of them remains exactly where it was.

How to use in the future
From now on, whenever adding any new structure to an idea graph, follow this procedure: the specification defines the rules, the validation catches violations, the page displays accordingly, and the two creation commands are written accordingly — if any of these four elements is missing, this rule will fail to propagate to other repositories. The first version was missing the latter two. This round also leaves behind one piece of experience specifically for "replacing an already implemented structure": retain the old idea's ID, set it to blocked, and clearly record in the notes which idea it was merged into; at the end of the specification section, leave a "provenance" paragraph stating what the predecessor was and why/when it was changed — this way, if someone asks six months later "did this field used to look different", they can find it through the specification without having to dig through commit records. The most important next step is to build the middle layer: currently, the four ideas that carry eleven to twenty-three sub-items each should be split into one more layer, so that those four warnings drop to zero. The rules are already there; this will be the first time they are executed through the entire process. Moving further down, the most natural step is to draw cross-layer prerequisites more clearly on the page — currently, the same page only draws dependencies between siblings, while cross-page prerequisites only appear as links within cards. Once installed into a foreign repository, its first time building a graph will directly yield a tree belonging to itself, without needing anyone to teach it.

idea Arrange by dependency order

The engine recognizes step-by-step overviews and validates them — misassigned steps are reported on the spot BlockedI-085

Parent idea
I-120
What it is
The engine recognizes the top-level step list and the affiliation field for each idea; the validation command checks these things: assigning to a non-existent step is an error; if steps are declared but some ideas have no affiliation, or the step count is outside the three-to-seven range, or if a step has no ideas, it is a warning; a graph with no steps written at all reports nothing. Newly created ideas on the webpage are allowed to include an affiliation field. Simultaneously, all existing ideas in this repository are assigned to steps in one go.
Why this idea exists
A rule without validation is just a suggestion. Misassigned steps, missing affiliations, and uncontrolled step counts — if these are not reported on the spot via validation, they will become lies on the page that no one notices — and since the numbers on the page will always look correct, that is exactly where the danger lies.
Expected result
Assigning an idea to a non-existent step triggers a validation error; missing affiliation, out-of-range step counts, or empty steps trigger validation warnings; a graph with no steps written at all (such as a newly created empty graph) reports nothing. After all ideas in this repository are assigned to steps, validation shows zero errors.
How to implement
Two additions to the engine's graph structure: the top-level step list and the affiliation field for each idea. **Validation is split into two levels, intentionally**: assigning to a non-existent step — reports an **error** (that is a definite typo, and it would cause the numbers on the page to decrease for no reason); if steps are declared but some ideas have no affiliation, the step count is outside three to seven, or a step has no ideas — reports a **warning**; if the entire graph has no steps written — **reports nothing**. The fields allowed for new ideas include affiliation; otherwise, ideas created from the webpage could never be assigned to steps. Then, extract a small two-line function to count "how many in a group of ideas, how many completed," so that the page legend and the step-by-step overview share the same calculation method. Finally, assign all existing ideas in this repository to steps at once — this is the first example following the newly defined rules, and it also tests whether the rule is written clearly enough: if it cannot be written, the rule is not clear. The write command also recognizes this field (both the "new idea" and "modify field" paths recognize it; values are stored as a single line, not as a collapsible paragraph). For this repository, the step assignment was intended to be written via a single change file using apply, but the guard does not allow the agent to create change files on any unclaimed paths (D16), and adding paths to this idea's code would invalidate the recently obtained plan approval (D7), so the 61 steps were written into the graph one by one using the edit tool, with comments preserved as is.
Why it is implemented this way
**Why misassigned steps are an error, while missing affiliation is only a warning**: Assigning to a non-existent step is a definite typo with no second interpretation; whereas "not yet assigned" is a normal state in a world where this field has just been added — reporting an error immediately would cause every repository that has installed this tool to turn red instantly, which would be making other people's repositories pay for our new field. We must be honest about the cost: **reporting missing affiliation only as a warning means the number on the page will be undercounted, and warnings are easily overlooked by people**. This is a conscious trade-off, not an oversight; once this field has stabilized across all repositories, we will tighten it into an error. **Why nothing is reported when no steps are written at all**: A newly created empty graph, or a project that hasn't decided how many steps it has, should not be nagged by the tool. Rules are for those who want to use them, not to punish those who do not. **Why "count how many, completed how many" was extracted into a small function**: The page legend currently flattens the entire graph count into a single string, which cannot be parsed. The step-by-step overview counts by step; if they use different methods, the legend and the overview will eventually disagree — and having two conflicting numbers is more damaging to the page's credibility than having no numbers at all. **Why step assignment is included in this idea rather than being a separate one**: It is the first user of the rule. If done separately, the rule would be written but never used, and no one would know if it was written clearly enough.

idea Arrange by dependency order

The title at the top of the webpage and the paragraph below it change along with the idea you click into. CompletedI-086

Parent idea
I-124
What it is
The title at the top of the webpage, the paragraph below it, and the paragraph above the graph shall always describe the idea of the current page being viewed. On the homepage, the title is the project name, and the paragraph below is a single sentence explaining what can be done after this project is completed; upon clicking into any idea, the title immediately changes to the name of that idea, and the paragraph below changes to the first sentence of that idea's "what it is"; the text displayed on the browser tab shall change accordingly. Any remaining historical descriptions in the project paragraph (which commit moved the old code, why the numbering restarts from a certain point) shall not be deleted by a single word, but moved into a default-collapsed folding area that only appears on the homepage; if there is no extra text to collect, the entire folding area shall not be output.
Why this idea exists
On 2026-09-05, this graph changed from a "single-layer step-by-step overview" to a tree that can be expanded layer by layer, but the page header failed to keep up. Today, when clicking into any idea, the title at the top is still the project name, and the paragraph below is still a historical description mentioning a certain commit ID, a certain tag name, and which directories were moved — completely unrelated to the graph in front of you; one has to scroll down to the cards to know what this page is about. This remains a genuine accessibility defect: this webpage has 72 pages sharing the same title; a user using a screen reader who pulls up the title list will see 72 lines of identical text, unable to distinguish which page they are on.
Expected result
Open the webpage: the top of the homepage is the project name, followed by one sentence explaining what can be done after this project is completed, with the historical description still present but requiring a click to expand; upon clicking into any idea, the title immediately becomes the name of that idea, the paragraph below becomes its "what it is", and the browser tab changes accordingly; pressing the browser's back button changes both back to the previous page. On a graph that contains only one paragraph and no historical description, that folding area shall not appear at all (not as an empty box). There shall always be only one H1 title in the entire document, and only one source for the flowchart.
How to implement
Change one place: hand over the two currently hardcoded lines (`<h1>` and `<p class="overview">` of `companion/ideas.ts:2657-2658`) to the existing page-switching function `showPage` (`companion/ideas.ts:2919`) to rewrite the text; it is already there to rebuild breadcrumbs and redraw flowcharts. For values, use the two existing functions on the page: the title takes `nameOf(owner)`, and the paragraph below takes `effectiveField(owner, "what")` (`companion/ideas.ts:2867`) — these include drafts that have not yet been committed, so the page header and the breadcrumb line directly above it will always say the same thing. For the first sentence, use the existing method on the page, copying it exactly without writing a new one: `String(x ?? "").split("\n")[0].trim()` (`companion/ideas.ts:2475`, which is how the summary in the sub-idea row is generated). Leave the remaining sentences for the folding area. There is one detail that must be written correctly: in `ideas/graph.yaml`, `overview: >` uses a folding syntax where the empty line in the middle is collapsed into only **one** newline, so split it according to `\n`; splitting by "empty line" would split a section within this repository's own graph, causing the folding area to always be empty, and test cases would fail to detect this if they simply switched to another writing style. The folding area uses the browser's built-in element, which is already in use on the page (the "modification record" of each card and the two indices below the graph; the two comments `companion/ideas.ts:2412` and `2436` have already written down the rules): default collapsing relies on **not writing the open attribute**; writing it as `open="false"` actually expands it; if there is no content, the entire block is not output. The text in the browser tab is changed together within the same function, taking from the same source as the title, rather than being stored separately. Three names that must be avoided have been verified item by item against the code and tests, rather than just copying old descriptions: do not use the class name `mermaid` (tests and page scripts both take the first `pre.mermaid`, `test_render_order.test.ts:86`, and `companion/ideas.ts:2946`); do not use the class names `graph` and `graph-hint` (`companion/ideas.ts:2937` will hide all of them on pages without sub-ideas, and most pages have no sub-ideas); do not create a new `<section>` with a `idea` class name (`test_render_order.test.ts:66` and `:76` assume the first `section.idea` on every page is the card for that page). In the old version of this entry, it stated "attribute names cannot end with id", but that statement is false: the only place in the entire test directory that locates by the `id="…"` string is `id="graph-data"`; the two tests that truly locate by card number are in `archive/tests/` and were deleted from the working tree in the last commit. Finally, rewrite the first paragraph of `overview` in `ideas/graph.yaml` into a single sentence: it currently says "three sets of workflows living side by side", whereas the three sets were merged into a single common base on 2026-08-29 — if not rewritten, the first thing seen on the homepage will still be an outdated sentence. The subsequent historical paragraph remains as is, handled by the folding area.
Why it is implemented this way
**Why change that one title instead of printing one on each page**: The entire document should only have one H1 title; this is consistent with HTML specifications and various accessibility guidelines (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/sections.html). Furthermore, the position of the header in the document is **above** the flowchart; printing one on each page would mean they could only be printed below the diagram —— which is not the position you want. **Why the title must change accordingly, instead of letting people look at the cards themselves**: A static title is itself a defect. With 72 pages sharing the same title, a screen reader's title list cannot distinguish between pages; replacing it is fixing an existing bug, not introducing a new risk. **Why the text in the browser tab line is also changed together**: This is the only point explicitly stated by standards —— WCAG 2.4.2, when discussing pages where "content changes dynamically at the same URL," requires the title to change along with the current view (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/page-titled.html). The cost is one line. **Why not "move the focus to the new title after page changes"**: That action is only supported by user research and has no standard requirement (https://www.gatsbyjs.com/blog/2019-07-11-user-testing-accessible-client-routing/); it would require adding tabindex to the title, designing a specific set of focus styles, and distinguishing between the initial opening and subsequent page changes. We are not doing it this time; it remains in "how to use in the future." **Why use the browser's built-in disclosure element instead of writing custom show/hide logic**: Writing it yourself requires handling clicks, states, keyboard interaction, screen reader annotations, and finding ways to ensure in-page search can find collapsed text; the built-in one has all of this, with a cost of zero lines of script, and "collapsed text can still be searched for and automatically expanded" is implemented by all three browser engines (an Interop 2024 completed item, https://github.com/web-platform-tests/interop/issues/491). To be clear about the cost: this behavior cannot be tested in automated testing; it can only be checked manually once. **Why the historical explanation is tucked into the disclosure instead of being deleted**: That passage contains real history (which commit moved the old code, why the numbering restarts from a certain point); if deleted, there would be no other place to record it. It just shouldn't occupy the first screen. **Why the entire block is not output when there is no extra text**: An empty disclosure box would make people think it is broken. This is also the only boundary case in this test that is absolutely indispensable —— without it, an implementation that "always outputs an empty box" could pass all existing rendering tests, because none of the sample images in those tests wrote `overview`.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Commands for graph building and adding new ideas, written and maintained according to the specification to produce that step-by-step overview. BlockedI-087

Parent idea
I-109
What it is
The command for building a graph in a strange repository for the first time, writing the step-by-step overview according to that section of the specification and assigning each idea to a step; the command for adding a new idea, assigning an affiliation to the new idea, and if necessary, adding a new step and explaining why an extra step is needed.
Why this idea exists
The rules are written in the specification, but these commands are what actually do the work of writing the graph. If the commands are not followed, the specification is just a document no one reads, and the graph in a strange repository will still lack an overview—and "being able to get the same result when installed in another repository" is the entire purpose of this task.
Expected result
Run a graph build once in a strange repository, producing a graph with a qualified step-by-step overview where every idea has an affiliation; run the add new idea command once more, where the new idea has an affiliation, and if it starts a new stage, the command will explain why this extra step was added.
How to implement
Modify the description text of two commands. **For the graph building command**: add a step between "reading the project and extracting ideas" and "drawing edges"—first write this step-by-step overview, then let each idea claim a step; directly reference that section of the specification in the description instead of re-copying the rules (copying it once is equivalent to creating another drifting duplicate), only adding one sentence unique to this command: the steps are derived from the project just read, not copied from another repository. **For the add new idea command**: add a step after "filling in the first three questions"—assign this idea to a step; if it does not belong to any existing step, add a new step and **must explain why this project has an extra stage**, because there is a limit on the number of steps, and adding a step consumes a slot. Both commands remind: if the overview exceeds seven steps, it should be merged rather than continuing to add more below.
Why it is implemented this way
**Why modify the command description text instead of injecting logic into the engine**: This overview is something that requires thinking — deciding how many steps a project has and how to describe each step in plain language is something a machine cannot do; it can only be done by the party that has read the project. What the engine can do is validation (that was the matter of the previous idea), and all it can write is descriptions. **Why reference specifications instead of copying rules into the command**: This toolset has already paid the price for "writing the same thing in three different places" once — the copied version will inevitably diverge from the specification, and no one will know which one counts. **Why adding a step requires explaining the reason**: Three to seven steps is a hard upper limit; adding steps without a reason would cause the overview to expand uncontrollably into a table of contents — and a table of contents is exactly what this rule aims to prevent. Requiring an explanation for adding a step is the cheapest form of braking. **Why this can only be manually verified**: What is being modified is the prompt for the agent, not the code. A machine can assert that those few lines of text exist in the file, but it cannot assert that they were "followed" — that kind of test looks green, but actually guarantees nothing. There is only one true verification: running a real graph construction in a strange repository and seeing if the resulting graph includes a qualified overview.

idea Arrange by dependency order

A collapsible index below the graph: lists all ideas waiting for manual verification and human sign-off. CompletedI-083

Parent idea
I-124
What it is
Add a default-collapsed area below the graph; clicking it expands it to list all ideas where "how to verify" is manual check, but the sign-off column is still empty. Each row displays the idea name and the original text of that manual check; clicking a row jumps to the corresponding idea card.
Why this idea exists
Currently, there are twelve ideas waiting for human sign-off, scattered across more than forty cards. The newly implemented sign-off function on the webpage is stuck at the step of "not being able to find which ones to sign" — people have to flip through them one by one to find which idea card has an empty sign-off column.
Expected result
Open the webpage; below the graph, there is a collapsed area stating how many items are currently waiting for sign-off; click to expand and list the name of each item and the matter it requires a person to look at; click any row to jump the page to that idea's card. When there are no ideas waiting for sign-off in the graph, this area does not appear at all — an empty list is more likely to make people think it is broken than not appearing at all.
How to implement
Below the graph and above the detail cards, output a default-collapsed folding area with the count in the title. **Use the same judgment condition currently used by the sign-off button on the page**, without changing a single word: "There are no automated verification commands available, and the sign-off column is empty". This must be written very clearly because it is not the same as the original description of this idea — the original text said "verification is manual check and the sign-off column is empty", but the actual judgment used by the button does **not** include the clause "must be manual check". Both happen to match twelve items on today's graph, but they are different sets: an idea that has both a command and a manual description should be listed according to the original text, but its card has no button. Both places must use the same judgment, otherwise the index will point to a card with no button to click. Each row is a link to a card (idea name), followed by the original text of that manual check. **The link must include the actual anchor address**; it cannot rely solely on script jumping: that smooth-scrolling function resides in a module that needs to fetch the drawing library from the network, so if you open it via double-click without internet, the entire module does not execute — the anchor is the only way that works in all four scenarios, while the script is just a finishing touch. **The row must absolutely not contain the sign-off button marker**: the existing sign-off test uses that marker to locate elements; adding one more will silently hijack five assertions. The index is only responsible for taking the person there; the sign-off still happens on the card. If the count is zero, the entire block is not output.
Why it is implemented this way
**Why reuse the sign-off button's judgment instead of writing it according to the original text**: If the two judgments are inconsistent, it will result in "the index says this needs to be signed, but clicking it leads to a card with no button" — and people will think the page is broken rather than realizing the two judgments are different. Research and testing showed that both currently hit twelve items; it is precisely because they coincidentally match that discrepancies are easier to miss. **Why each row must include an anchor address**: This was found through research — the jump function and the drawing library are in the same module, and the first line of that module is to fetch the drawing library from the web. When a page opened via double-click has no internet, the entire module does not execute, causing all script-based jumps to fail. With an anchor, the browser can jump by itself, though without smooth scrolling or highlighting. This is also why we don't write our own jump set: the existing set is better when it works, and provides a fallback when it doesn't. **Why not place the sign-off button directly on the index row** (the first instinct would be to do this to save a jump): The existing sign-off test uses that marker to find elements in five places; since the index is above the cards, the extra marker would be found first, causing all five assertions to test something else — and they would still remain green. This type of change, where "the test is still green but is no longer testing the original thing," is much more dangerous than a test turning red. **Why the entire block does not appear when the count is zero**: An empty box saying "(0)" would make people click in only to find nothing; whereas the absence of this block itself indicates there are no pending tasks.

idea Arrange by dependency order

A collapsible index below the graph: lists ongoing ideas and who each one is waiting for. CompletedI-084

Parent idea
I-124
What it is
Follow the same approach as the index above, listing ideas with the status of "ongoing". Each row displays the name and which prerequisite ideas it is still waiting for (only listing those that are not yet finished). Clicking a row jumps to the card.
Why this idea exists
Ongoing ideas are those that "have been started but are not yet finished," and they are the easiest to forget. Currently, finding them also requires flipping through cards, and even if you find one, you cannot tell exactly what it is stuck waiting for.
Expected result
Open the webpage; below the graph, there is a second collapsed area stating how many ongoing ideas currently exist; click to expand and list the name of each and the prerequisites it is waiting for; if no prerequisites are not completed, explicitly write "no prerequisites are blocking it"—note that this sentence only states that no other ideas are blocking the way, not that someone is working on it. If there are no ongoing ideas, this area does not appear.
How to implement
Use the same approach, the same collapsible element, and the same "do not appear if zero items" rule as the previous index, but change the predicate and the row content: list ideas with the status "ongoing," displaying the name in the row and its prerequisites that are **not yet finished**. "Not yet finished" must be written as "does not equal completed," and **cannot be written as "equals todo"**—if a prerequisite is blocked or ongoing, it also blocks the way, but filtering by "equals todo" will miss it, causing the page to say "no prerequisites are blocking it" when there actually are. When no prerequisites are blocking it, write a clear sentence; do not use that existing dash to represent "none"—the dash reads like "no information" here, whereas we need to state a certain fact.
Why it is implemented this way
**Why share the same approach with the previous index instead of writing them separately**: Aside from the predicate and row content, the two indices are exactly the same. Writing them separately would result in two sets of almost verbatim identical code and two sets of almost identical tests, and sooner or later, one would be modified while the other is forgotten. This is also the reason for that prerequisite edge between these two ideas. **Why "not yet finished" must be written as "does not equal completed"**: A pitfall identified during research—if filtering by "equals todo," a blocked prerequisite would be treated as not blocking the way, causing the page to state something contrary to the facts. This type of error will not manifest on today's graph (none of the three ongoing ideas have prerequisites that are not completed), so it can only be caught by tests, not by the naked eye. **Why the phrase "no prerequisites are blocking it" requires careful wording**: The original expected result for this idea was written as "that means it is truly being worked on, not stuck"—actual testing shows this cannot be inferred: among the three ongoing ideas, two have no prerequisites that are not completed, and these two happen to be stuck waiting for human sign-off. Therefore, this sentence can only say "no other ideas are blocking the way," and cannot imply "someone is currently working on it," otherwise the page would be lying about two-thirds of the rows.
