idea Arrange by dependency order

A human approves the modifications made on the webpage, while the approval mechanism is not weakened. To doI-066

Parent idea
I-122
What it is
Design and implement: after changes are written back, how this new graph obtains the status of "human approved"—while maintaining the existing bottom line: approval can only come from a human's manual action, and an agent cannot fabricate it.
Why this idea exists
If the graph changes, old approvals become invalid; this is an intentional feature; however, the person changing the graph this time is precisely the approver themselves. If the webpage requires a full graph review and approval process to be repeated exactly as before after changes are made, this feature saves no steps.
Expected result
After a human finishes modifying on the webpage and the changes are written back, a single manual action (not an agent action) allows the new graph to enter the approved state; the agent still has no way to forge this step.
How to implement
Three things. First, block existing bypasses: the guard adds a new rule for Bash—any command text touching .approved, .scan-todo, .applied, graph files or change files, or direct calls to guard.ts must be intercepted, allowing only calls in the form of ideas.ts subcommands; simultaneously, narrow the Bash allowlist in settings from "any npx tsx" to "npx tsx <engine path>". Second, after apply writes to disk, write (pre-write fingerprint, post-write fingerprint, hash of changed files, field-by-field change list) into a ideas/.applied receipt that receives equal protection, and print the field-by-field diff for the human to see. Third, expand approval words: the full sentence "approve <12-digit fingerprint>" only takes effect when Parameter == Current Graph Fingerprint == Post-write Fingerprint in the receipt—after apply, any single change the agent makes to the graph will cause the three to mismatch, automatically invalidating the fast track and reverting to full graph review; if fingerprints do not match, error out immediately and explicitly, rejecting the message, and do not allow silent failure—silent failure will train humans to only paste fingerprints without looking at the content.
Why it is implemented this way
Counter-review overturned two assumptions of the original design. First, the current state of "agent cannot fabricate approval" is false: the guard is only attached to Edit / Write, Bash never goes through it, and the allowlist permits any npx tsx—an agent can just write a script to run it and directly write to .approved. We must block this door first before discussing anything else; blocking this door also closes the known ceiling mentioned in the README about "using Bash to feed fake events to guard.ts." Second, "fingerprint equality = human has seen this graph" does not hold: a fingerprint proves freshness, not source; an agent can sneak in unauthorized changes after apply and then print the real fingerprint—therefore, the fast track must be bound to the protected apply receipt, not just the fingerprint. The boundary of honesty: this mechanism raises the cost of forgery to "must pass through human permission prompts," rather than being mathematically unforgeable. The explicit rejection solution: a headless pipeline feeding "approvals" (claude -p) can be run by any script, which is equivalent to tearing down the door.

.claude/settings.json
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_ideas_guard.test.ts → exit 0
How to use in the future
Any "human-initiated modification" can henceforth use the same channel to obtain rapid approval.

idea Arrange by dependency order

After submission, a human types one command, and the agent aligns the code to the new graph. To doI-067

Parent idea
I-109
What it is
A person executes a single command, the agent reads the current idea graph, identifies inconsistencies between "what the idea says" and "what the code does," and adjusts the code to comply with the graph following the test-first discipline: write tests first, confirm failure, then implement, and only mark as complete after verification passes.
Why this idea exists
The complete requirement is "changing the graph means changing the project": writing changes back to YAML is merely an intermediary step; the final deliverable is code that complies with the new idea. If this step is not connected, humans will still have to initiate implementation themselves, causing the link to break in the last meter.
Expected result
After an idea in the graph is modified, executing this command triggers the agent to start working automatically; upon completion, the verification command for the modified idea passes, the code is consistent with the answers to the eight questions, and parts of the graph that were not modified are left untouched.
How to implement
A new slash command /ccapply (the command file body contains the string "ideas.ts"—the installer relies on this string to identify its own files; if missing, it will be judged as an external file and never updated; use install.ts --update to distribute to installed repositories). Process: find the change file in ideas/ where the baseDigest equals the current graph fingerprint (report and ignore stale ones one by one; if none are found, remind to "check if it was saved to the download directory") → run apply → report to the human item by item: field-by-field diff, check results, new fingerprint, and "which ideas' eight questions are incomplete and will not be implemented in this round (newly created three-question ideas on the web fall into this category; running /ccthink to complete them before approval can save one redundant approval process)" → human types "approve" or "approve <fingerprint>" → the agent implements only the ideas touched by this change that have complete eight questions according to /ccbuild discipline (test-first, status via set, mark complete only after verify passes) → the end report includes a fixed reminder to refresh the browser page. For change files with fingerprint mismatches, there is a clear replay path: the agent confirms each change (including the old value) against the new graph with the human one by one; after confirmation, it regenerates the change file with the current fingerprint and then applies it.
Why it is implemented this way
An interactive slash command rather than a headless pipeline: typing /ccapply itself is a real UserPromptSubmit event, all hooks function as usual, and the approval step remains in human hands. The scope of implementation is limited to the ideas touched by this change; aligning the entire graph is the responsibility of /ccfix—a single submission should not trigger a full repository roam. The division of labor for lightweight modifications is also written into the command: it is faster to simply say a typo correction in the dialogue (since modifying loose text fields allows the agent to use Edit), while the value of the web link lies in batch modifications of loose text and structural changes like adding/deleting nodes and edges.
Where is the code
Not yet implemented
How to verify
A real walkthrough: modify a field on the web + create a new three-question idea, submit, /ccapply—the report shows a complete diff, the new idea is listed as "incomplete, not implemented," and after approval, the modified idea is implemented and verify passes.
Human sign-off: Not signed
How to use in the future
"Change a sentence on the web, and the code changes accordingly" becomes a matter of a single command from now on.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Arbitrate the divergences between the three sets of implementations item by item and write them into a common specification. CompletedI-069

Parent idea
I-125
What it is
A single unique specification file (companion/FORMAT.md), using D1–D34 to item by item arbitrate the format, approval, verification, path, hook, distribution, and shared state of the three sets of implementations. The common foundation must allow all three sides to share one project graph and retain the strongest existing verifiable guarantees of all three sides, rather than regressing to the lowest common denominator.
Why this idea exists
The first draft only arbitrated up to D15, but a completeness audit discovered 19 real divergences; among them, old arbitrations would delete Codex's RED→GREEN evidence and relax Cursor's fail-closed, which contradicts "no regression of existing functions." If divergences are not arbitrated before merging code, it will only hide the contradictions of the three sets within a single file.
Expected result
Every item from D1 to D34 includes a three-sided current status, a ruling, and a reason; the specification clearly defines one idea graph, two regular approvals, current RED/GREEN evidence, strict path ranges, and common Skill and hook normalization. An unfamiliar agent will know exactly what is writable, when it can act, and how to verify just by reading this document.
How to implement
Retain YAML, four states, needs, endpoints, and the short version of the eight questions; revise D7/D8/D9/D10 to incorporate Codex content binding approvals, RED/GREEN, and path evidence, and incorporate Cursor's default rejection, doing readiness, and overlap checks. Add D16–D34, covering shell bypass, unknown paths, runtime protection, atomic writes, common CLI/Skill, single-file release, and explicit legacy migration.
Why it is implemented this way
First rule to ensure, then shape the code; sharing a core does not mean selecting the weakest intersection. The base remains in the top-level companion/, while platform differences are confined to input/output mapping and the three manifests, avoiding the recreation of an entire abstraction framework.

I-125
What it is
Using claude-companion/ideas.ts as the substrate, establish a common engine in the companion/ directory: graph reading, validation, calculating "what can be done now", viewing individual ideas, changing states, rendering web pages, and scanning manifests are all ported over; the default file changes from the agent-suffixed graph.claude.yaml to a single ideas/graph.yaml, removing the logic of "selecting files by agent name"; add a new paths command to print all standardized paths for graphs, web pages, records, and evidence, so no one has to guess where files are. claude-companion/ is kept exactly as is, without changing a single word.
Why this idea exists
The first step of the common base is to let the engine reside in a neutral directory and read/write graphs belonging to the project rather than a specific agent. The suffixed files are precisely the source of the "three versions of truth in requirements" (ruling table D10); if the engine does not move, the subsequent guards, skills, and installers will have no common foundation.
Expected result
In a temporary directory, use the companion engine to complete the full workflow of graph building, validation, rendering, and state changes on a ideas/graph.yaml; paths prints all standardized paths; all existing engine tests pass after being moved over; git shows zero changes to the claude-companion/ directory.
How to implement
After copying claude-companion/ideas.ts to companion/ideas.ts, perform subtraction: delete the entire logic of selecting files by agent name (AGENT/agentName/nameIsTaken/graphPath), and set the default file to ideas/graph.yaml; consolidate all standardized paths into a single paths() function with a paths subcommand; unify backslashes into forward slashes at the input boundary (in Windows events, file_path contains backslashes, but official documentation explicitly requires normalization before comparison). Existing engine tests are copied into the test_base_engine series, pointing to the new engine and removing suffix assertions.
Why it is implemented this way
Alternatives are to write a "clean" engine from scratch, or to let the three engines coexist and merge slowly. "Copy the Claude version and perform subtraction" was chosen because it is the most feature-complete and has the most tests among the three (2221 lines, 19 test files), and the D1/D2/D13 rulings were originally based on its format; writing from scratch would mean re-implementing all the edge cases refined over the years, such as preserving comments, Windows renaming retries, and concurrent appending. The suffix logic is a deletion rather than leaving a switch: D10 rules that the new base has only one project graph, and a switch would only bring old ambiguities into the new home.

Parent idea
I-121
What it is
Add capabilities to the common engine that were first implemented in the Cursor version: new (creates a new idea, takes a number from the next_id counter at the top of the graph, and increments it after use), allow (asks "Can I write now?" before writing a specific file, and the answer must be exactly consistent with the guard), status (provides an overview of where each idea is blocked); before changing the status to doing, the program checks if the plan fields are complete, if all prerequisites are finished, and if the file to be written overlaps with another ongoing idea; status can only follow a small state transition table; skipping steps will be rejected.
Why this idea exists
These checks are a unique advantage of the Cursor version; the D17/D18/D19/D28 adjudication table has ruled that they are required. Rules written only in prompts are forgotten as soon as the agent gets busy; by turning them into program checks, the precedence in the graph truly holds authority.
Expected result
If one plan field is missing, one prerequisite is lacking, or one file overlaps, the transition from todo→doing is rejected, and the rejection must specify what is missing; numbers issued by new must only come from next_id, so creating a new idea after deleting the idea with the maximum number will not cause number collisions; allow's permission/rejection for any file must be consistent with the actual result of running the guard once.
How to implement
Port three pure functions (isBuildReady / needsUnmet / fileClash) and three subcommands (new / allow / status) from cursor-companion/ideas.ts; modify new to take numbers from the top-level next_id of the graph (when the field does not yet exist in the graph, initialize and write it all at once as "maximum existing number plus one", thereafter it only increments); add a four-state small transition table in set, which runs the three checks in sequence during todo→doing, and prints exactly what is missing for the user to see.
Why it is implemented this way
Option 1: Rely only on the guard to block during code writing (I-093) — by then the human has already started working, and errors are exposed too late; rejecting on the spot during set doing has the lowest cost of correction. Option 2: Follow the current Cursor status of issuing numbers via "maximum number plus one" — explicitly rejected by format specifications (re-issuing the same number after deleting the maximum number), must use next_id. The three functions are moved directly without rewriting because they already have behavioral test endorsement from test_companion_gate.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Adopt Codex version's approval mechanism: an approval code is bound to content all at once, it only counts if a human manually replies, and the receipt is kept by the program. CompletedI-090

Parent idea
I-122
What it is
Set up an approval gate for both splitting and planning: when the agent requests approval, the program creates a summary of "the content the human needs to see" and generates a one-time approval code; approval only takes effect when the human manually replies with this approval code in the conversation, and the receipt (who, when, which summary approved) is stored in ideas/.runtime/ and kept by the program. If even one character of the content changes, or if the approval code is used once, the approval becomes invalid. Human sign-off follows the same path.
Why this idea exists
Claude's current approval is the word "approve" for the entire message, bound to the full graph hash — this prevents agent impersonation, but approving the full graph in batches does not prove the human has seen a specific split; Cursor has no approval at all. Codex's one-time approval code plus content summary is the strongest among the three, and the D7/D26/D27 adjudication table has ruled to transform it into two regular gates.
Expected result
Replying with the same approval code twice results in failure on the second attempt; if the approved content is modified and used again after approval, it fails; if the receipt file is written directly by the agent, it will be rejected by the guard; the splitting gate and the planning gate can request and approve independently.
How to implement
Reconstruct in TypeScript based on the verified behavior of codex-companion: request-approval generates a one-time approval code (cryptographically random, CC-XXXXXXXX), and writes it into ideas/.runtime/pending/ along with the gate name, involved nodes, and content summary; the summary follows the "sha256 after newline normalization" method; the splitting gate creates a summary of the full graph's numbering/name/edge/eight questions projection, while the planning gate creates a summary of the single node's eight questions plus path plus verification projection; in the UserPromptSubmit event, the entire message must strictly match "approve [approval code]" or "APPROVE [approval code]" to be consumed, and the receipt (who, when, which summary approved, original text hash) is written into .runtime/approvals/; if the approved content changes, the pending files are deleted and the reason is explained. Human sign-off and unexpected green exemptions follow the same challenge/receipt path.
Why it is implemented this way
Option 1: Follow Claude's current "the entire message is the approval, bound to the full graph hash" — the same "approve" can be replayed if the graph is unchanged, and it cannot prove the human has seen any specific split; D7 has ruled this obsolete. Option 2: Codex's five gates — too heavy; D7 has reduced them to two regular gates and two on-demand gates. The behavior of single-use approval codes and content binding is copied from codex-companion (its Python tests directly assert these properties); online Baseline projects use the same "human generates markers, agent cannot forge" approach, supporting this direction.
Where is the code
companion/ideas.ts:564-709 · requestApproval / applyApproval / validApproval / approvalSnapshot
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_base_approval.test.ts → exit 0
Test file:.devcompanion/tests/test_base_approval.test.ts
How to use in the future
The guard's check for "whether there is a valid approval" only requires reading the receipt once; web-based sign-off (D27 unresolved conflict) will also follow this challenge chain in the future.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Absorb Codex version's test-first evidence: leave one record of a real failed test first; upon completion, there must be the latest passing record CompletedI-091

Parent idea
I-121
What it is
The run-check command runs verification commands on behalf of the agent, recording the exit code, the end of the output, and the content fingerprint of the test files into ideas/.runtime/: Before implementation, there must be one record of "test actually failed" (called RED); every time an implementation file is written, the old passing record (called GREEN) expires; marking done must have a currently valid GREEN or a manual verification signed by a human. If a test passes unexpectedly before being implemented, a human must approve an exemption to continue.
Why this idea exists
Only checking "test file exists" cannot distinguish between a truly failed test and an empty file (current Claude version status); the Cursor version has no defense against test-first at all. Codex has proven that "test before implementation" can be implemented with evidence; the adjudication table D8/D20 rules that the common base is not allowed to be weaker than it.
Expected result
When there is no RED record, writing implementation files is rejected; if implementation is changed after GREEN and marked done without re-running, it is rejected; if the test file is changed, old evidence is immediately invalidated; if it unexpectedly turns Green first without a human-approved exemption, progress cannot proceed.
How to implement
The run-check subcommand carries --phase red|green: run verify.command at the project root (reusing Cursor version's 120-second timeout and retries when Windows cannot find the command), saving the exit code, the last two thousand characters of the output, and the sha256 of each file in verify.test_files into each idea record in ideas/.runtime/; the guard's write-after record increments a monotonic counter for product file writes, and the GREEN record stores the counter value at the time of its execution; when setting done, re-verify that GREEN exists, the counter has not fallen behind, and the test hash has not changed. If the exit code in the red phase is 0, it is recorded as "unexpected early pass"; thereafter, implementation writing can only be released after a I-090 exemption receipt.
Why it is implemented this way
An alternative is to retain the Claude version's "test file exists is enough" — which cannot distinguish between a truly failed test and an empty file; the D8 adjudication explicitly refuses to regress the Codex evidence chain. Use a monotonic counter instead of a timestamp to judge "expiration," because timestamp resolution is low and they may roll back, whereas the counter is driven only by hooks; test file hashes are bound to prevent "post-hoc test modification." The mechanism is ported from the verified behavior of codex-companion; its corresponding Python tests are rewritten as vitest to serve as the porting checklist.
Where is the code
companion/ideas.ts:710-836 · runCheck / redGateReady / greenCurrent / recordChange and set of GREEN gate

idea Arrange by dependency order

An explicit migration command to move three old formats of idea graphs into the same project graph; if unsure, stop and ask a human CompletedI-092

Parent idea
I-125
What it is
The migrate command reads three old formats — suffix-bearing graph.claude.yaml, graph.cursor.yaml, and Codex's one-node-one-file JSON — and converts them into one ideas/graph.yaml; transferable approval and verification evidence are also moved into .runtime/; if multiple old graphs exist in the same repository, stop and let a human choose or merge, never automatically pick a winner; fields that cannot be converted are listed in a report for a human to see. Old files are kept as-is, read-only.
Why this idea exists
Adjudication table D10 rules that graphs belong to the project, not the agent; only implementation is unified, state is not migrated; changing an agent still won't allow it to take over. Migration is a one-time, lossy, and risky operation, so it must be explicit, must be auditable, and must let humans make choices.
Expected result
Each of the three old formats has one migration sample, and verification passes after migration; when two old graphs coexist, the command stops and presents the differences to a human; the migration report lists every field that could not be converted losslessly; old files remain unchanged after migration.
How to implement
The migrate subcommand scans graph.claude.yaml, graph.cursor.yaml under ideas/, and JSONs under .codex-companion*/nodes/: when there is only one source, convert directly (Codex fields are mapped according to D2 — expected_result becomes expected, implementation.how becomes how, code_refs becomes code, eight states are compressed back to four states, and extra fields are listed one by one in the report); when there are multiple sources, print a difference table and exit, waiting for a human to explicitly choose using --pick or --merge; transferable approval receipts and test evidence are moved into .runtime/; run a check before writing, and do not commit to disk if it fails; old files are all left untouched.
Why it is implemented this way
Alternative one: The installer automatically picks the "most recently modified graph" as the winner — explicitly forbidden by D10. Alternative two: Do not migrate and let humans hand-copy — hand-copying a graph with over fifty nodes will surely result in errors, and evidence files are even harder to hand-copy. Explicit commands, human choices, and issuing a report before committing to disk is the direction already adjudicated in the I-070 original text; this is simply making it into an independent, verifiable step.

idea Arrange by dependency order

A single rule core shared by all three: when an event comes in, judge it as allow or deny, with reasons that humans can understand CompletedI-093

Parent idea
I-121
What it is
Write only one version of the guard's judgment logic: the input is a normalized event (which event, which tool, which files to modify, what the human said), and the output is allow or deny plus a reason. Rules include: files without an idea claim are denied write access by default; writing is not allowed if the idea is not ready; writing is not allowed without approval; implementation is not allowed without failure test records; no one is allowed to directly write to evidence files managed by the program; file writing tricks in shell commands (redirection, in-place replacement, one-liner file writing via interpreter) are also blocked; write operations where the target cannot be identified are directly denied; the idea graph must pass verification before the session ends. If a crash occurs during the pre-write or approval stage, block it; if a crash occurs during post-write recording, only warn and do not block (Decision Table D9); AIDEV_GUARD=off is the only escape hatch; using it will trigger a loud warning and be recorded.
Why this idea exists
The three sets of guards each have unique strengths and fatal weaknesses: the Claude version is comprehensive but "allows through on crash"; the Cursor version lacks approval and testing prerequisites; the Codex version cannot see writes from MCP tools. Rules must be written only once, so that fixing one place affects all three simultaneously, to truly qualify as a common foundation.
Expected result
Every rule has a corresponding test: out-of-bounds writes, unapproved, no failure records, shell bypass, unknown targets—all are denied with human-readable reasons; failure in post-write recording does not block a completed write; the guarantees expressed by the existing tests of the three providers are all restored under the common rules.
How to implement
A pure function decide(normalized_event, idea_graph, evidence) in companion/guard.ts executes the rule table in order: evidence files managed by the program and generated files can only be modified via CLI; idea graphs and logs are editable, but if a direct modification to the status or signed_off fields is detected compared to the old idea graph, it is denied (plugging the hole where the Cursor version "agent modifies the ledger itself to unlock"); the product path must hit a code or test_files of a ready doing idea, otherwise deny by default; then check the approval receipt (I-090) and failure test evidence (I-091); shell commands must pass three layers of regex (ported from codex-companion: redirection, in-place replacement, interpreter one-liners, package managers); write operations where the target cannot be identified are directly denied; run check at Stop. In the catch blocks for pre-write, approval, and Stop, return deny; in the catch block for post-write recording, only warn and do not block (D9); AIDEV_GUARD=off allows everything but issues a prominent warning every time and attempts to record it.
Why it is implemented this way
Rather than patching three separate guards, it is better to write the rules as a pure function and feed normalized events directly into the fixture—the closest online precedent, Probity (a TypeScript program serving the three Claude/Codex/Copilot providers), uses this architecture, proving it is feasible. The rejection order checks protected files before claims, because the most common agent transgression is touching evidence first; the crash direction is categorized by event (block before write, allow after write), where Codex's hybrid model wins among the current status of the three: Claude's full allowance would miss irreversible out-of-bounds writes, while Cursor's full blocking would halt the entire repository due to logger bugs.
Where is the code
companion/guard.ts:1-316 · decide / record and rule table
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_base_guard_rules.test.ts → exit 0
Test file:.devcompanion/tests/test_base_guard_rules.test.ts
How to use in the future
Modify only this single function for the new rules; the thin layer between the three I-094 providers and this function is the only interface.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Equip each of the three agents with a thin conversion layer: translate each provider's hook events into the same event type, and translate the judgment back into answers each provider can understand CompletedI-094

Parent idea
I-127
What it is
Place three input conversion functions and three output encoding functions in the same file: Claude's events include file_path; Cursor's native hooks.json has different event field names and requires permission JSON for judgments; Codex's apply_patch carries multiple files in one patch and requires parsing for exec and MCP tools, requiring another JSON type for judgments. Each provider is assigned a set of real event samples, which are converted before entering the same rule core. The gap where the current Codex version cannot see MCP writes is filled here.
Why this idea exists
Official compatibility only guarantees that events can be triggered, not that the JSON formats of the three providers are identical (Decision Table D15/D22). Without normalization, rules would have to be copied three times, and copying three times leads to drift—which is exactly what has already happened in this repository.
Expected result
Real event samples from the three providers result in the same allow/deny for the same behavior; every file in a single apply_patch is checked; MCP writes no longer bypass the guard; output formats can be correctly parsed by all providers (Claude exit code 2, Cursor permission JSON, Codex decision JSON).
How to implement
In guard.ts, there are three input conversions and three output encodings. The entry point selects via --platform=claude|cursor|codex: Claude reads hook_event_name/tool_name/tool_input.file_path events (backslash normalization) and rejects using exit code 2 plus a permissionDecision JSON; Cursor uses native preToolUse/beforeShellExecution/beforeMCPExecution/afterFileEdit/ beforeSubmitPrompt/stop events and returns a flat permission / continue / followup_message; Codex official hooks share the same event names as Claude, and apply_patch parses all paths one by one from the Add/Update/Delete File lines within tool_input.command (if one line cannot be parsed entirely, the whole order is rejected). MCP tools match via mcp__service_name__tool_name, and response packets only use allow/deny — official documentation explicitly states that 'ask' is not supported in Codex before writing, so returning 'ask' is equivalent to granting permission. A set of real event samples for each provider is stored in the test directory.
Why it is implemented this way
Research confirmed that Codex hooks have been officially released and deliberately use event names compatible with Claude, and Cursor also includes a Claude compatibility layer — however, the response formats and field names of the three providers remain different (Cursor uses flat permission, Codex does not support ask); pretending they are the same will cause the most critical "rejection" to fail silently. Using three small functions instead of an adapter class hierarchy is the ruling from the I-071 original text; the apply_patch parser is ported from codex-companion's regex (with test endorsement).
Where is the code
companion/guard.ts:317-612 · normalizeClaude / normalizeCursor / normalizeCodex with three encoders, entry
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_base_adapters.test.ts → exit 0
Test file:.devcompanion/tests/test_base_adapters.test.ts
How to use in the future
Integrating a fourth agent is equivalent to adding a pair of conversion functions and a set of event samples.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Five workflows written as standard skill files that all three can load, with only one version of the main body CompletedI-095

Parent idea
I-109
What it is
Five standard skill files under companion/skills/: Mapping Introduction, Thinking Clearly, Doing, Error Checking, and Viewing Graphs. The main body is merged from the existing five Claude commands and five Cursor skills, removing platform-specific names and absolute paths; all commands are written as neutral common engine calls. The manifests for all three providers point to this same directory instead of generating their own.
Why this idea exists
All three providers natively support the same skill file format (ruling table D33); continuing to generate a set of command files for each provider would just be hiding copying inside the installer — the wording has already drifted once (three versions emerged from the eight questions, D11).
Expected result
None of the five skill files contain any provider-specific paths; Claude actually loads and runs one of them in this repository; Cursor and Codex loading is verified in their respective integration ideas (I-073/I-074).
How to implement
Five directories under companion/skills/ ccscan/ccthink/ccbuild/ccfix/ccgraph, each with one SKILL.md: The main body uses claude-companion/commands as the base, integrating stronger paragraphs from the Cursor version of skills (borrowing highest priority, discovery must include line numbers, three attempts result in being blocked); all engine calls are rewritten as neutral calls to the single-file program after installation; frontmatter only uses open standard fields (name is the same as the directory, description does not exceed 1024 characters), and does not use disable-model-invocation (Claude Code currently has several related unpatched defects). Skill names changed from D33's onboard/discuss/build/debug/graph to the cc prefix; this ruling update is written into the companion/FORMAT.md divergence ruling table.
Why it is implemented this way
Research determined that one .agents/skills/ directory can simultaneously feed Cursor and Codex, while Claude Code requires .claude/skills/ bridging (official support allows symlinking by skill, but Windows git does not check out symlinks by default), so the authoritative version is placed in companion/skills/ within the repository, and the deployment method—whether to copy or link—is left to the I-098 installer. The directory name uses the cc prefix instead of the D33 short name: all three providers use the directory name as the command name; /build is too generic and would cause collisions, and user muscle memory has already shifted to /ccbuild — human sign-off has been granted for this deviation (2026-08-31).

idea Arrange by dependency order

Bundle the engine, guard, and dependencies into a single-file program; as long as node is available, it can run anywhere it is installed CompletedI-096

Parent idea
I-126
What it is
A build script bundles the companion's engine, guard, and yaml parsing dependencies into a single dist/companion.mjs file; running it only requires node in the system, no npx required, no tsx required, and the target repository does not require npm install. The source code remains a single TypeScript version.
Why this idea exists
Today there are three different running methods across three providers: Claude uses absolute paths with npx tsx to run source code (which breaks when switching machines), Cursor copies source code into the target repository and then runs npm install (which will expire), and Codex is a complete replica in another language (the source of drift). Adjudication Table D34 adjudicates single-file artifacts.
Expected result
Copy dist/companion.mjs separately into an empty directory without node_modules; verification, rendering, and guard judgments can all run; artifacts can be repeatedly regenerated by build scripts.
How to implement
companion/build.mjs is about a dozen lines: call esbuild --bundle --format=esm --platform=node --target=node20 to output companion/dist/companion.mjs, with the banner injecting two things — the first-line shebang and a createRequire shim. The shim is indispensable: the CJS build of the yaml package contains require('process'), and without the shim, the build will show all green but will crash immediately upon the first parse — this investigation has reproduced this failure on a local machine and verified the fix. The entry point companion/cli.ts simultaneously mounts the engine command and the guard subcommand.
Why it is implemented this way
Use esbuild directly; do not use tsup (it is no longer maintained, and its repository points to a successor), do not use rollup (it requires three or four plugins to be equivalent, and the artifact is only a few dozen KB), do not use bun (it has a known defect of writing the build machine's absolute path into the artifact, which hits the core requirement of a "portable single file"), and do not use node single executables (hundred-megabyte binaries that still require running esbuild first). This is the only path that has been tested and passed with this set of dependencies on a local machine.
Where is the code
companion/build.mjs:1-25
companion/cli.ts:1-14
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_base_bundle.test.ts → exit 0
Test file:.devcompanion/tests/test_base_bundle.test.ts
How to use in the future
The hook wiring and the installer for all three providers issue this same file; the risk of npx tsx cold starts swallowing approvals under a thirty-second UserPromptSubmit timeout is eliminated.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Write a small list for Claude, Cursor, and Codex that contains only the hook wiring; all three lists call the same single-file program. CompletedI-097

Parent idea
I-126
What it is
Three platform lists: four hook events in Claude's settings, Cursor's .cursor/hooks.json, and the hooks.json of the Codex plugin — each list only writes "which event, which command"; the commands are all node dist/companion.mjs plus a parameter describing itself; all skills point to the same companion/skills/. The Cursor version's "injecting a briefing of the current work status into the conversation at the start of a session" is also included in the wiring, shared by all three.
Why this idea exists
Hook event names and invocation methods truly differ across providers, which is the natural location for platform differences (Adjudication Table D14/D15); besides this, nothing else should exist in three separate versions.
Expected result
Format validation for the three lists passed; the Claude version truly triggers the guard in this repository; the two Cursor/Codex versions align with the event samples (acceptance in the real product belongs to I-073/I-074).
How to implement
companion/manifests.ts exports three wiring generation functions: Claude — in addition to the four existing events in settings, it includes ConfigChange (to intercept when the agent modifies its own wiring) and SessionStart (to inject the current graph's status briefing into the session, absorbing the unique advantage of the Cursor version); commands use the officially recommended exec form with the ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} placeholder instead of hardcoding machine absolute paths, and the UserPromptSubmit entry explicitly increases the timeout; Cursor — .cursor/hooks.json, events preToolUse/afterFileEdit/beforeSubmitPrompt/stop/sessionStart/ beforeShellExecution/beforeMCPExecution, with the critical interception item failClosed set to true; Codex — .codex/hooks.json uses an event table of the same form as Claude, the matcher covers the Bash/apply_patch/Edit/Write/mcp__ prefix (same as Probity), and the command remains a stable single-line string — Codex's trust binding uses the hook definition hash, so artifact updates should not trigger re-trusting.
Why it is implemented this way
Retaining three versions of the wiring is the D14 adjudication: event names and invocation forms are truly different, which is the natural location for platform differences; only the event tables are in the three versions, with no rules included. The exec form and placeholders are explicit suggestions from official Claude documentation for Windows (regarding shell quoting issues); absolute path wiring for the current status fails when switching machines, which is a gap recorded in this audit.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Install the common base into other repositories' installers: install with a single command, capable of checking for expiration and performing batch updates. CompletedI-098

Parent idea
I-126
What it is
companion/install.ts: install the target repository path, install the three platform manifests, skill pointers, and single-file programs into the target repository, and register them in the local installation list; --status performs a byte-by-byte comparison to check if each installation is consistent with the source (normalizing newlines first so Windows CRLF does not cause false positives); --update refreshes expired installations. All tests inject a temporary installation list and never read the real list —— the bug where existing tests write temporary directories into the real list is also fixed.
Why this idea exists
The user explicitly requested that "the experience of installing into other repositories should be the same as today's claude-companion"; today's installer only installs Claude. To achieve "one installation, three beneficiaries," the hooks for all three must be connected in a single installation.
Expected result
After executing install on a temporary repository, the three manifests and runnable single-file programs are in place, and the guard takes effect on Claude events; --status reports the latest first, reports expired after source code changes, and restores the latest after --update; after running all tests, the real installation list remains unchanged by a single character.
How to implement
companion/install.ts follows the skeleton of claude-companion/install.ts (CRLF normalization, byte-by-byte comparison, unknown target files are judged as "external" and skipped, idempotent hook merging): install copies dist/companion.mjs to the target repository (one set of artifacts shared by three parties), merges the three connection sets of I-097 into .claude/settings.json, .cursor/hooks.json, and .codex/hooks.json respectively (without overwriting others' entries), copies skills to .agents/skills/ and bridges .claude/skills/ (uses symbolic links if possible, otherwise defaults to copying on Windows), seeds ideas/graph.yaml and .gitignore; perform smoke testing immediately after installation: send one synthesized out-of-bounds write event to the Claude connection command, expecting exit code 2 —— official documentation explicitly states that incorrect hook paths will fail silently, so it must be verified on the spot. Registry functions must all accept registry path parameters, with tests injecting temporary paths.
Why it is implemented this way
Aligning the experience with today's claude-companion is a user-specified requirement; however, it has changed from "absolute path sharing engine" to "copying single-file artifacts," because the artifacts have been decoupled from the source repository dependency (D34), and absolute paths are precisely the biggest portability issue in the current state (the connections in this repository itself would fail if moved to another machine). Smoke testing is written into the installer rather than the documentation, because "silent hook failure" is a trap explicitly mentioned in the platform documentation that humans cannot rely on memory to avoid.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Close the three gaps where decisions were made but not implemented: old graphs are read-only, files that were read but have since changed automatically revert to unread, and allow provides the complete decision from the guard CompletedI-099

Parent idea
I-128
What it is
Three small tasks, each corresponding to a signed decision: (1) The guard treats migration inputs (old graphs in ideas/ with the agent suffix) as read-only and directly rejects writes (D10); (2) The scan manifest recognizes content fingerprints —— when striking out, record the file's fingerprint at that time, so that if the content changes later, it automatically reverts to unread (D12); (3) The allow command is upgraded to the guard's complete decision: it must answer all three layers—claim, approve, and failed test record—ensuring the real decision for the same file by the guard comes from the same function (fulfilling the I-089 expectation of "consistency with the guard").
Why this idea exists
An audit after the implementation of I-093/I-094 found these three instances of "decision written, code not done": old graphs could still be written, so it cannot be said that "only graph.yaml is the real truth"; it only recognized read events rather than content, so files modified after being read were still considered read; allow missed two layers, causing agent self-checks to receive answers opposite to the guard.
Expected result
Edits to old-suffix graphs are rejected by the guard with the reason pointing to migrate; changing a single character in a read file causes scan to show it has returned to unread (legacy un-fingerprinted records continue to be treated as read to avoid punishing existing stock); allow answers "deny" for files that are "claimed but not approved" or "approved but not red," matching the source and answer of the guard's decision.
How to implement
(1) guard's decideOnePath rejects the pattern graph.<agent>.yaml in the ideas/ branch; (2) when striking out, append the sha256 to the read record (append only, without breaking I-055's concurrent fixes), and readWorklist compares the current fingerprint, so if it changes, it is no longer considered read; (3) extract the guard's decision on product files into decideProductWrite and export it from guard, and change the allow command to call it —— add approval and red records to the fixtures for the two CLI tests in I-089, while the assertion semantics (answer allow if writable) remain unchanged.
Why it is implemented this way
All three tasks involve connecting existing functions rather than creating new mechanisms: the read-only rule goes into decideOnePath because it already holds relative paths; fingerprints go into the read record because .scan-done is already append-only, and adding a hash column does not affect concurrency behavior; decideProductWrite is extracted instead of having the engine call guard in reverse, because guard depends on ideas.ts, and reverse calling would create a circular dependency. The alternative "allow writing its own judgment" is exactly the kind of duplication this foundation aims to eliminate. Codex's "render fingerprint handshake" is explicitly not moved: set/apply's automatic re-rendering and checking before Stop already serves the same purpose, which is recorded as a design choice rather than an omission.
Where is the code
companion/ideas.ts:322-903 · decideProductWrite / effectivelyStruck / readStruck and allow Command
companion/guard.ts:140-151 · decideOnePath Changed to delegate to the same judgment function
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_base_gap_closures.test.ts → exit 0
Test file:.devcompanion/tests/test_base_gap_closures.test.ts
How to use in the future
The I-070 milestone "only graph.yaml is writable" has turned from a slogan into a fact; the self-check command for the fourth agent is naturally consistent with the guard.

What it is
companion/ideas.ts becomes the sole graph engine, reading and writing only project-level ideas/graph.yaml; merge Claude's scan/render, Cursor's readiness/new/paths/allow/log, and Codex's approval summary, RED/GREEN runtime, path and line number verification. migrate explicitly imports old suffix YAML or Codex JSON, without automatically selecting a winner.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Merge the three sets of mandatory rules into a single policy core, and create a thin mapping between the three types of hook inputs. CompletedI-071

Parent idea
I-125
What it is
companion/guard.ts normalizes events from the three providers and executes the same set of policies: unassigned files are rejected by default, doing readiness/prerequisite/path range, two approvals, RED→GREEN, state and runtime protection, shell mutation and Stop completion checks. Reject during pre-write/approval/Stop crash; allow with a warning when recording a crash after writing; each platform only encodes input/output protocols.
Why this idea exists
Directly moving Claude guard will miss Codex apply_patch, MCP, and Bash, and will also change Cursor's default rejection to default allowance. A common guard must share the "decision"; it cannot pretend the original JSONs are exactly the same.
Expected result
Three sets of real event fixtures produce the same allow/deny for the same behavior; unknown write paths, unapproved, no RED, out-of-bounds files, and shell bypasses are all rejected; PostToolUse recording a failure will not block an already completed write; AIDEV_GUARD=off will show and record warnings.
How to implement
Keep three small normalize functions and three output encoders within the same file, without building an adapter class hierarchy; policy functions only receive normalized events. Port Cursor gate and Codex hook tests, covering apply_patch multi-file parsing, MCP, local editing, and Stop continuation.
Why it is implemented this way
The three providers' hooks are close enough to share a policy, but not close enough to safely delete normalization. A few pure functions are the smallest thin layer, which is shorter than copying three sets of rules or introducing a general adapter framework.

All three providers natively support SKILL.md; continuing to generate three sets of commands merely hides the copying inside the installer. Current npm tests still read the real .installs.json and attempt to modify other repositories; isolation is mandatory before distribution.
Expected result
Three manifests pass validation and load the same batch of Skills; the single-file artifact can run even when separated from the source repository; installation tests only write to temporary directories and temporary registries; migration preview for seven existing local installations is available, but no writes occur without an explicit update.
How to implement
Merge the existing Claude/Cursor workflow text into a standard Skill; change the platform name and absolute paths to neutral CLI calls; bundle yaml dependencies during packaging; retain three manifests that differ only in metadata/hook paths. updateAll accepts a registry path parameter, and tests never use default values.
Why it is implemented this way
Directly sharing standard files results in less overhead than template generation; manifests are the natural location for platform differences. A single-file JS is one source code and one runtime, avoiding a re-enactment of the TypeScript/Python dual implementation.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Switching wrap-up: fix invalid assertions caused by archiving, and the issue where 2 > 1 was misidentified as a file write. CompletedI-100

Parent idea
I-128
What it is
After moving the three old implementations into archive/ and switching this repository to the common base on 2026-09-02, two items remain for wrap-up. One is three test assertions: they require claude-companion/FORMAT.md to reside in the repository root, reasoning that "the five command files installed in the seven repositories point to it by name" — but those command files were also archived, and the six external repositories now install skills, so this prerequisite itself is no longer valid, and the assertions must be moved under archive/. The other is that the guard's shell gate misidentified 2>&1 as a file write: it only sees the greater-than sign and fails to recognize this as a file descriptor operation merging standard error into standard output, which does not result in a file.
Why this idea exists
The second issue is something encountered every day: a very ordinary `npx vitest run ... 2>&1 | grep` will be rejected, and the rejection message even advises people to "remove the redirection"—that is an impossible suggestion to follow, because what needs to be seen is precisely the standard error. Once the guard blocks legitimate work too many times, people will start disabling AIDEV_GUARD entirely, which is the real loss: a bypassed gate is worse than no gate at all, because it still gives the illusion of protection. Failing to fix the first issue leaves three red tests, and this repository has just established a rule that "documentation and code must not contradict each other"; those red assertions are the most glaring counterexamples.
Expected result
npx vitest run --dir .devcompanion/tests is all green; `node .companion/companion.mjs allow` answers with permission for a read-only command containing `2>&1`; meanwhile, redirections that actually result in files, such as `printf ... > src/x.ts`, are still rejected.
How to implement
On the guard side: the REDIRECT in companion/guard.ts is now `/(?:^|[^<])(<>|>{1,2})/`. We need to extract "file descriptor copying" from "writing files"—syntax like `数字>&数字` and `>&数字` results in a descriptor rather than a file; first exclude them from the match, then judge the remaining redirections. The same applies to `2>/dev/null` and `2>NUL`: the target is a null device, not a product file; judge by the target rather than by the symbol. On the testing side: in the "the frozen twin spec" section of `test_base_skills.test.ts`, `twin()` points to archive/claude-companion/FORMAT.md, and invert the assertion "must exist in the root directory"—there must not be a second copy in the root directory; there must be one in `archive/`.
Why it is implemented this way
The reason for not directly adding the entire `2>&1` string to the whitelist is that the whitelist only recognizes this specific spelling, whereas `2>&1`, `1>&2`, `>&2`, and `3>&1` are four ways of writing the same thing; adding them one by one will inevitably lead to omissions. Judging by "whether the redirection target is a file" is what this rule originally intended to ask—this follows the same logic as this round's change of protected evidence to "defend by target rather than defend by verb," where we previously had to patch it after missing `dd`, `install`, and `tar` in the enumeration.
Where is the code
companion/guard.ts:731-742,832-838 · NON_FILE_REDIRECT, mutatingShell
.devcompanion/tests/test_base_skills.test.ts:109-143 · the frozen twin spec (H25)
How to verify
npx vitest run --dir .devcompanion/tests test_base_guard_shell_targets test_base_skills → exit 0
Test file:.devcompanion/tests/test_base_guard_shell_targets.test.ts、.devcompanion/tests/test_base_skills.test.ts
How to use in the future
This is the wrap-up for the day of the switch; once done, there are no follow-ups. The experience gained is written into D21 of FORMAT.md: every time a shell gate misblocks, it is caused by "judging by symbol" instead of "judging by the resulting outcome."

idea Arrange by dependency order

When `migrate` sees an empty seed graph, it says "no migratable location"—change it to tell the truth: migrate the empty seed directly. CompletedI-101

Parent idea
I-125
What it is
Currently, `migrate` rejects as long as ideas/graph.yaml exists, replying "project graph is in place, no migratable location." Even before rejecting, it has clearly already calculated the source of the old graph (findLegacySources), yet it doesn't mention it in a single word. The three repositories ErrorRecoveryBenchmark, LifeCopilot, and LiveCaption are exactly stuck here: the `graph.yaml` planted by the installer is only 68 to 111 bytes with zero ideas, while lying next to it is a `graph.claude.yaml` of 57 to 148 KB with 31 to 68 ideas—yet the message says "no migratable location." The fix is split in two: if there are no ideas in ideas/graph.yaml (empty seed), treat it as non-existent and migrate directly, recording "overwrote empty seed" in the migration report; only reject if `graph.yaml` already contains ideas—but tell the truth: how many ideas the current graph has, the path and idea count of each adjacent old graph, and the word "move" (to indicate which one to move). Also, modify step 0 of the `ccscan` skill: a rejection from `migrate` does not equal "confirmed no old graph"; it only counts if it explicitly says "no old format graph found."
Why this idea exists
This lie is creating opportunities for data loss, and it is happening through a process we wrote ourselves: step 0 of `ccscan` tells the agent to run `migrate --dry-run`, and if rejected, it is treated as "confirmed no old graph," after which a new graph is built next to the real data. In these three repositories, 136 ideas are being blocked by a single sentence, invisible to both humans and agents. The installer side (seedWouldLockOut) already wrote this logic correctly; it is just that `migrate` itself did not.
Expected result
An empty seed is next to an old graph: `migrate` succeeds directly, `graph.yaml` is replaced with the old graph content, and `migrate-report.md` records that the empty seed was overwritten; multiple old graphs are next to an empty seed: require `--pick` as before, do not select automatically. An old graph is next to a `graph.yaml` that has ideas: reject, with the reason including the current graph's idea count, the path and idea count of each old graph, and the word "move"; `graph.yaml` remains untouched. No old graphs exist: reply "no old format graph found" as before, regardless of whether `graph.yaml` exists. `npx vitest run --dir .devcompanion/tests test_base_migrate` is all green.
How to implement
companion/ideas.ts's migrate: First, check if sources.length === 0 (if there are no old idea graphs, there is nothing to say, so do not check if graph.yaml exists first); then, if plain exists, read its number of ideas — if zero, let it pass through the original migration path and add a line to converted.report: "Overwrote a ideas/graph.yaml that contains only a seed and no ideas"; if non-zero, reject it, using sources to list the kind, path, and number of ideas for each item in the reason (reuse the counting logic from the multiple old idea graphs section), and append at the end: The engine does not merge (D10); to migrate old graphs, move ideas/graph.yaml out of the way first; to keep the current graph, move the old graph away. If graph.yaml cannot be read (YAML is corrupted), treat it as "having something," reject it, and state that it cannot be read. In step 0 of companion/skills/ccscan/SKILL.md, add a sentence: Only "no old format graphs discovered" counts as having no old graphs; all other rejections must stop for human review. test_base_migrate.test.ts: Change the line "an existing plain graph.yaml means there is nothing to migrate onto" to allow direct migration with an empty seed, add a new case for rejecting non-empty graphs with a truthful reason, and a case for rejecting bad YAML.
Why it is implemented this way
The reason for not just speaking correctly but still rejecting empty seeds is that the agent cannot perform the step of "moving graph.yaml away" (mv is a write-disk verb, blocked by D21), so it can only wait for a human — and since an empty seed contains no information to begin with, rejecting it protects nothing; it just locks three repositories for an extra day. The decision to reject non-empty graphs instead of merging them is the ruling of D10: a human decides which of the two graphs is the truth, and the engine does not automatically pick a winner; this is the same rule as requiring --pick when multiple old graphs are present. Do not change the installer's sentence "once planted, it can never be migrated into again" (seedWouldLockOut): it was the truth at the time, and after the change, its situation (not planting when an old graph is next to an empty seat) remains correct; only the reason changes from "permanently locked" to "let a human decide first." Leave this sentence to be changed together the next time it is touched; do not expand the scope this time.
Where is the code
companion/ideas.ts:1475-1500 · migrate
companion/skills/ccscan/SKILL.md:14-24 · No. 0 Step
How to verify
npx vitest run --dir .devcompanion/tests test_base_migrate → exit 0
Test file:.devcompanion/tests/test_base_migrate.test.ts
How to use in the future
Each of the three stuck repositories can get its graph back by running migrate once, without needing humans to manually move files. The same lesson should apply to the installer: existsSync(graph) blocks the reminder "there is an old graph next to an empty seed"; next time install.ts is touched, change it to also check the number of ideas. Another pitfall encountered during development: receipts generated by request-approval --gate decomposition --node X can never pass set doing (it validates against the whole graph, not the node), yet the command neither blocks nor provides a prompt, causing humans to perform an extra unnecessary approval. The engine should either reject --node at the decomposition gate, or recognize both during validation.

idea Arrange by dependency order

When requesting approval, print the full text of the eight questions being approved to the terminal. CompletedI-102

Parent idea
I-109
What it is
Before request-approval prints the approval code, print the full content of what is to be approved. For the three gates—plan, test exemption, and manual verification—print the eight questions, code location, and verification method for the specifically named idea; for the decomposition gate, print the name, prerequisite, and first three questions for every idea in the full graph. Do not accumulate the content separately, but rather take it from the approvalSnapshot projection — currently, it discards the content after calculating the hash; change it to submit the projection before hashing, so that the "printed" version and the "hashed" version are the same in the code. Also, fill in the three columns missing from the terminal today: verify.pass, verify.test_files, and verify.signed_off. (step does not enter the approved content — it is not in the projection today, and adding it would invalidate all existing receipts; find another time for that.)
Why this idea exists
Today, this command only prints three lines, and not a single word of the content to be approved is shown (companion/ideas.ts:3655-3657). Humans can only go to a web page to view it, or trust the agent's recitation in the dialogue — but there is nothing to control what the agent recites, how much it recites, or whether it embellishes. Consequently, this human gate is a blind approval: the approval code only proves "someone replied," not "this person has seen the content to be approved." Ironically, the engine itself explicitly states in two rejection messages what humans should look at (companion/ideas.ts:1657 "please have a human review the names, edges, and first three questions of the whole graph", :1660 "please have a human review the eight questions of this idea"), yet it has never actually delivered those things before a human's eyes.
Expected result
Running request-approval --gate plan --node I-104 will first show the full text of the eight questions for I-104, the code location, and the verification method, followed by the approval code. Running --gate decomposition will first show the name, prerequisite, and first three questions for every idea in the full graph, followed by the approval code. Humans can judge whether to approve without opening a web page or asking the agent. If you change a single character and run it again, the printed content changes accordingly, and the approval code changes with it.
How to implement
Four steps. One, split approvalSnapshot (companion/ideas.ts:878-896) into two: approvalProjection(graph, gate, nodeIds) which returns the projection array, and approvalSnapshot becomes sha256(JSON.stringify(approvalProjection(...))).slice(0,12). Object literals must be moved verbatim, with key order unchanged — key order is the digest; rearranging them would invalidate all existing receipts. Three call sites (:917 requestApproval, :953 applyApproval, :992 validApproval) remain unchanged. Two, extract the eight questions loop in show (:3555-3561) into questionLines(idea), which only outputs the body of the eight questions, without status, without prerequisites, and without modification records — those three elements are not in the projection; mixing them in would be equivalent to printing "unhashed content" as "approved content". show will use this. Three, write a new verifyText(v) that covers five fields (command, pass, test_files, manual, signed_off): none of these five fields have ever been complete in one place today; show only prints one of the first two, and the web card lacks test_files. The 7th question of questionLines will use it. Four, the request-approval branch (:3646-3658) will first call approvalProjection, print items one by one, then print the three lines of the approval code, and append a boundary statement at the end: "This sentence can only be replied to by you in the dialogue; clicking anything else elsewhere will not count." **The printer only consumes the projection, not the graph** — use types to weld "what is printed" and "what is hashed" together, rather than relying on discipline.
Why it is implemented this way
Why split approvalSnapshot instead of writing another function to retrieve content: writing another one would create two parallel paths, where what people see and what is hashed evolve separately — and this idea is precisely intended to fix this decoupling. Why not use the easy method from sessionBriefing (companion/guard.ts:1773-1781) of hijacking console.log to run main(["show"]): it would print the status, the status-bearing prerequisites, and the modification records together; since none of those three are in the projection, it would be equivalent to committing the same bug in a different direction; furthermore, when show cannot find an ID, it calls console.error (:3550), which hijacking log cannot catch. Why not use the string source plus new Function approach like MERMAID_SOURCE_FN: that technique is prepared for "running the same code in two runtimes, Node and browser"; here, both places are two branches of the same main within the same process, so using it would waste type checking. Why not merge the formatting of the 6th question between the CLI and the web: codeOf (:2293-2294) uses "· symbol" plus newline labels plus "not yet implemented", while the CLI uses "(symbol)" plus commas plus "—"; the separators, connectors, and empty states are all different — merging them is a visible product change and should not be done casually within this idea. Why not add a new subcommand: adding a command requires changing three places in FORMAT.md (D28) and two test files, and changing "seventeen items" to "eighteen items"; what people want is "visibility when requesting approval," not "one more command to view." Why not include step in the projection: it would change the output of JSON.stringify, invalidating all currently valid receipts, and any todo→doing in this repo would be immediately blocked by :1657/:1660, and the six other installed repositories would also require re-approval after updating. This is a separate debt to be paid and should not be bundled in.

idea Arrange by dependency order

The web page prints "Waiting for your approval": the approval code, the level, and the full text of the approved content. CompletedI-103

Parent idea
I-124
What it is
A new "Waiting for your approval" panel on the web page: it lists every pending approval code — the code itself, which level it belongs to, which ideas it covers, and the full text of the approved content, exactly as it appears in the terminal. The panel explicitly states that this sentence can only be replied to by a human in the dialogue, and clicking anything on the page will not count — the boundary is placed where humans can see it. Simultaneously, fix two invisible issues on the card: ideas with verification commands cannot see the sign-off column on the page (verifyOf returns early), and verify.test_files is not displayed in either of the two display surfaces.
Why this idea exists
When a human finishes modifying a graph on the web and clicks submit, the server has actually sent the approval code back with the response (companion/ideas.ts:3299), but the page discards it entirely — the success branch only reads changed.length. As a result, the person signing on the web cannot see the approval code they just requested; it only appears in the terminal running serve. render does not read the pending approval code directory from start to finish, and there is no command that can list them. Humans must either stare at the terminal or ask the agent; the web chain breaks at the final step.
Expected result
Open the web page; when there are pending approval codes, a panel appears showing the approval code, the level, the covered ideas, and the full content; the panel does not appear when there are no pending approval codes. After reading the content on the page, a human can complete the approval by copying the approval code into the dialogue; no need to switch back to the terminal throughout the process. For ideas with verification commands that have been signed, the sign-off is visible on the card; for ideas that declare test files, they are listed in both the terminal and the web display surfaces.
How to implement
Four steps, the first step is the shortest. 1. The callback for successful page submission (companion/ideas.ts:3002-3011) currently only reads the number of changed items today and discards the entire set of signs (:3299) already sent by the server with the response — change this to display them, and make the approval code a selectable block. No new routes, new requests, or new token validations are needed, just three lines of DOM. 2. During render, read the pending approval code directory once: construct the path using the already exported paths(dir).runtime (do not touch the private pendingDir), and write it following the three-layer defense pattern used in validApproval (:988-1001) — early return with existsSync, then file-by-file try/catch. Newly installed repositories do not have this directory at all; a naked read will crash the entire render, and there are ten test call sites in render that pass no projectDir or a fake projectDir. 3. For each pending approval code, take its node_ids to re-project onto the **current** idea graph (using the approvalProjection sliced by I-102); if the projection does not match the summary in the file, mark it as "voided" on the spot — to prevent people from copying an approval code that will inevitably be rejected by :955-958. 4. The panel should be written following the "do not output if none exist" logic of the worklist (:2340-2344), using native disclosure elements; the blockquote should copy the styles of #sign-panel .what (:2507) and add white-space: pre-wrap — the two existing line styles (.wl-note, #restore-list span) both truncate the full text into a single line with an ellipsis. Fix two things while you're at it: first, change the early return of verifyOf (:2299), then attach the condition for the sign button to awaitingSignature (:2314). **The order is fixed** — if you don't change :2299 first, you will never reach the lines that render the sign bar.
Why it is implemented this way
Why fix "the approval code arrived at the page but was discarded" first: It is only three lines, and it is the actual wall people hit today — after signing on the web page, the approval code only appears in the terminal running the service, and the signer cannot see it themselves. Why use server-side rendering for the panel instead of copying the visibility mechanism of those four top panels (:2518-2524): Those four are state-driven within the browser, whereas pending approval codes are state on the disk, which is known during render. Following the worklist's "do not output if none exist" is more efficient and provides free keyboard accessibility, screen reader semantics, and expandable full-text search. Why re-project the content onto the graph instead of storing the content in the pending file when casting the approval code: The pending file only contains 12-character summaries (:921-924), and what truly needs to be displayed is "the content of this current graph" — if it differs from the version that was originally hashed, the person should see "this approval code is voided," not the original one. Why not print the approval code on the graph.html on disk as well: redraw (:3415-3418) produces static files; writing a one-time approval code into it would cause it to expire immediately, whereas that file is intended to be sent to others. Why both display surfaces need to include test_files: The summary is bound to it; if a person changes test_files, the approval code becomes void, yet they would find no change on the page — this is not a potential future drift, it is already drifting.

idea Arrange by dependency order

The guard can see if an agent is driving the browser; any call directed at the local service must be blocked. CompletedI-104

Parent idea
I-121
What it is
The guard can recognize if an agent is driving the browser. Today, any MCP call that does not include a file path or a content field is categorized as "other" and allowed through (companion/guard.ts:1510, original comment: "a read-shaped MCP call is not ours to block"). Change it to: first check if this call points to the local service — any address falling within the loopback address plus the serve port must be blocked with a clear explanation of why; calls to execute scripts on the page should also be blocked. The reason for blocking must be a human-readable sentence, and it must honestly state that this is a guardrail, not a sandbox.
Why this idea exists
Any button on the page with authority is effectively zero if an agent can click it. Today, this path is open: the browser tool's navigate opens pages, computer clicks buttons, and javascript_tool runs scripts directly on the page; none of these three include a file path or a content field, so they all hit that "allow" branch. Meanwhile, the entire downloader family on the shell side has long been blocked as a "write file" verb (companion/guard.ts:705), and the interpreter wall also blocks node --eval — in other words, the front door is locked tight, but a back door is left open that no one sees. This hole exists today, regardless of whether web approval is implemented later.
Expected result
If an agent attempts to open the browser to the local service address, it is rejected on the spot, with a clear explanation of which rule was triggered and why. A human opening the same address in a browser is unaffected. If the guard crashes or fails to recognize a call, allow it through as before, so as not to lock humans out.
How to implement
Three steps. First, add the rule to the dispatch table in decideInner (companion/guard.ts:164 area), **do not write it into mcpEvent**. normalize() runs outside of decide's try/catch (:1821), and there is no .catch after readStdin().then() — throwing an exception in mcpEvent is equivalent to an unhandled promise rejection, exit code 1, and the host allowing it through; furthermore, in that specific hook, both the shell wall and the pre-write wall failed to run. To effectively block it, it must be placed where try/catch can manage it. Second, the criterion must be **identified by target, not by tool name**: extract the URL from the calling parameters, and block anything falling on a loopback address — the entire loopback family, regardless of port. serve has --port (:3681), so if the port is hardcoded, the rule will be missed as soon as a parameter is added. Third, block calls that execute scripts on a page as a separate reason. The rejection message should follow the structure of the existing three: which rule, why, and where the way out is, and explicitly state that this is a guard, not a sandbox. The new event type must also modify encodeClaude (:1588-1603), otherwise the rejection will fall through to a bare exit code 2 — the host recognizes this code, but cannot obtain the structured reason, so a human only sees a single failure without explanation.
Why it is implemented this way
Why identify by URL instead of tool name: enumerating browsers by name (e.g., matching tool names containing 'browser') would both miss various differently-named integrations and immediately trigger a red failure in test_base_guard_shell_targets.test.ts:231 for "navigating to example.com must be allowed" — that test is correct; letting an agent access the internet is normal work, and only the specific instance of targeting a local service should be blocked. Why block the entire loopback family instead of just the serve port: the guard and the service are two separate processes, and the guard has no reliable way to know which port the service is currently running on. Why not assume browser tools will all be allowed today: MCP_WRITEISH (:1410) includes create and write; calls like opening a new tab or writing to the clipboard have already been rejected by the sentence in :193 "this call might write a file, but it is unclear where it writes" — new rules must avoid this, otherwise a single call will stack two sets of contradictory reasons. **The honest boundary must be written into the rejection message**: Local testing on 2026-09-05 — clicking a button with a browser tool resulted in isTrusted being true, navigator.userActivation.isActive being true, and navigator.webdriver being false, exactly the same as a manual click. Therefore, the value of this rule is to turn "something that can be done easily" into "something that requires an explicit bypass," not to make it impossible. Claiming the latter will cause the next person reading the code to overestimate this wall.
