idea Arrange by dependency order

Determine on what basis an action on a webpage counts as being done by a human, and revise the existing two adjudications accordingly. CompletedI-105

Parent idea
I-122
What it is
Adjudicate "on what basis an action on a webpage counts"; the answer is: it does not count — actions on a page can only be initiated, they cannot be finalized; the only valid landing point for approval remains the sentence manually typed by a human in the dialogue. This can be written as a new adjudication in the specification, and the existing two (D26 Approval Mechanism Security Boundary, D27 How Humans Sign Off via manual verification) should be revised accordingly. The adjudication reasons must clearly state item by item: why none of the existing three things (serve tokens, two-step confirmation, envelope fingerprints) count, why the path of biometrics and security keys is also a dead end, and the various scenarios where this set of tools becomes effectively useless. The local test performed on 2026-09-05 must be recorded verbatim as evidence.
Why this idea exists
The answer to this today is "it does not count," and the reason is written in the code comments (companion/ideas.ts:1892-1894: a modified file is not a person; an agent can write it and can also run a write-back from elsewhere). D27 was just downgraded on 2026-09-02 to "only proposing requests" based on this very reason. To allow a click on a page to count as approval would be to directly overturn this newly implemented adjudication — that would require providing a reason harder than "it is more convenient," otherwise it is simply tearing down a door that was just closed. The purpose of the adjudication table is to ensure such reversals are documented with evidence.
Expected result
Add one more adjudication line to the specification, with all three sections complete: current status, adjudication, and reason. D26 and D27 should each include an additional paragraph on the implementation status, clearly stating why the original decision was maintained this time and what new evidence was added. A person who did not participate in this discussion should be able to read these three items, reproduce that local test themselves, and judge for themselves what this system prevents and what it cannot prevent. In the future, if someone proposes "letting a click on a page count as approval," reading this single item will suffice, without needing to redo this round of research. This item can only be accepted by a human.
How to implement
Do not write code; write three sections of specifications, all contained within the companion/FORMAT.md adjudication table. One: Add a new row with all three sections complete. **Status Quo**: Actions on the page today do not produce any machine-verifiable "human-originated" evidence — the served token is process-level, non-expiring, and written in plaintext into the page without a GET / check (obtaining the token is equivalent to being able to access this port); the two-step confirmation runs the same route twice, making the effect of a script firing twice identical; the envelope fingerprint is an optimistic lock, proving freshness but not origin. **Adjudication**: Actions on the page can only be initiated, not finalized; the only valid landing point for approval is the specific sentence a human manually types into the dialogue. **Reason**: See below. Two: In the reason, record the local test results from 2026-09-05 exactly as they occurred — using browser automation to click a button, the page reads isTrusted as true, navigator.userActivation.isActive as true, and navigator.webdriver as false, exactly the same as a manual click, so the request header that is only sent upon user activation will also be sent. Record one more external fact: the browser debugging protocol's virtual security key defaults to simulating "human presence" as true (automaticPresenceSimulation defaults to true), so the path of fingerprints, facial recognition, and hardware keys is equally dead. Three: For D26 and D27, add a paragraph regarding the landing situation: whether the original judgment is maintained, what new evidence was added, and the four scenarios that are effectively useless — the escape switch being opened, exits invisible to the guard (which is exactly what I-104 and I-106 supplement), the guard itself crashing during the normalization step, and humans pasting approval codes without reading the content (the guard cannot control this at all; this is precisely the entire reason for the existence of I-102). Four (added on 2026-09-09, prerequisite for I-139), add an "out-of-band exception" paragraph to the same line of adjudication: while it was stated above that "the only structurally valid out-of-band method is a second device," this section writes it as a condition rather than a negation. If one host (the LifeCopilotBeta portal) has its own login, and after the human passes the login, the host transfers the human's original sentence along with a credential to the local small service's approval entry (I-139), this counts as a human action, provided three indispensable conditions are met: the credential is passed to the small service only via environment variables and does not appear in the page, standard output, or logs; the host's login is not something an agent can obtain (keys do not enter the repository or files readable by the agent); and the receipt is written only by the engine, not generated or rewritten by the host. If any of these three conditions fail, revert to the original judgment for this line: can only be initiated, cannot be finalized.
Why it is implemented this way
Why maintain the original judgment instead of finding a way to make it work: All three pieces of evidence point to "the local service cannot distinguish between a human and automation," and the only structurally valid out-of-band method is a second device — for a local single-person idea graph guard, that is a heavy-weight solution. More importantly, the cost-benefit analysis: the 90% of approval time saved by direct web approval has already been provided by I-102 and I-103 (content is delivered before the human's eyes, so the human no longer approves blindly); the only thing truly left to save is the single action of "copying the approval code." Using one act of copying to exchange for an entire chain of trust that requires new adjudication, new threat models, and new code paths is not cost-effective. Why it must be written down instead of just maintained verbally: D27 just adjudicated the same matter on 2026-09-02, and it was raised again three days later — this indicates that the reasons for "maintaining the status quo" were not recorded in a place that would be read next time. The purpose of the adjudication table is to ensure such repetitions only happen once. Why the reason must include actual tests rather than just citations: In this round of research, a conclusion regarding the same matter cited a fabricated specification section number, which was discovered only by resisting the check and opening the actual specification. An experiment one can run themselves is more reliable than a string of citations — and the next person can re-run it following the steps. Why explicitly reject biometric and hardware keys: They look like the most plausible answers; if we do not clearly write down why they do not work, someone will inevitably propose them again in the next round. Why manual verification: The output of this item is prose; a machine cannot judge whether it has been written clearly.

If they fail at either task, it was not written clearly.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Supplement the three wiring lists with web-fetching tools, and ensure that the omission of configuration is guarded by a test. To doI-106

Parent idea
I-121
What it is
The hook wiring lists for the three parties (.claude/settings.json, .cursor/hooks.json, .codex/hooks.json) currently only send edit-type, shell-type, and calls starting with mcp__ into the guard. Web-fetching tools (called WebFetch on the Claude side) belong to neither category, so the guard cannot even see these calls. Supplement each of the three lists with it, and also supplement the one planted by the installer into the new repository. Add one more test: if a tool that should be seen by the guard is missing from the list, it must turn red.
Why this idea exists
The rule established by I-104 in the guard adjudicates "this call is targeting the local service." But no matter how correct the rule is, if the event cannot reach the guard, it is as if it does not exist — web-fetching tools are exactly such a path: they can directly request the local service on 127.0.0.1, but neither of the two PreToolUse matchers (edit and shell types for .claude/settings.json:54, and the mcp__ prefix for :68) matches it. Currently, there is nothing guarding this type of misconfiguration: test_base_manifests.test.ts has a GUARDED whitelist, but it only asserts those things already written in the list and will not turn red if one is missing — meaning the same error will be repeated in the future, and no one will notice it.
Expected result
Send the web-fetching tools into the guard for all three lists, and do the same for the new repository planted by the installer. When an agent is blocked while using a web-fetching tool to request a local service, the reason should be consistent with the I-104 rule. If a tool that should be seen by the guard is deleted from any list, the test must turn red immediately. A human accessing the same address in a browser should remain unaffected.
How to implement
Three steps. First, for the PreToolUse of the three manifests (.claude/settings.json, .cursor/hooks.json, .codex/hooks.json), supplement the tool names used for fetching web pages on this platform. Claude's current two matchers are .claude/settings.json:54 (editor and shell types) and :68 (mcp__ prefix), neither of which covers the web-fetching tools. Second, supplement the manifest used for installing new repositories into the installer (companion/install.ts) — if not supplemented, every time a new repository is installed, the same hole will be created. Third, change the GUARDED whitelist in test_base_manifests.test.ts from "asserting these are written in the manifest" to "the manifest must cover this table; if one is missing, it turns red." Since the tool names differ across the three providers, the whitelist is divided by platform.
Why it is implemented this way
Why split I-104 into two ideas: I-104 modifies the guard's judgment, while this item modifies whether the event can actually reach the guard. Their failure modes are completely different — a wrong rule will block the wrong things, which is immediately visible to humans; a misconfigured connection results in nothing happening, with no signs at all. If merged into one idea, verification could only cover one half. Why change the whitelist to a reverse assertion: currently, this table only asserts what has already been written, so missing an entry won't turn red — meaning the same error will recur in the future without anyone noticing. This time, the hole was not caught by tests, but by a human reading the connections; the fact itself is evidence. Why not just list all tools capable of sending requests: it's impossible to list them all, and the list would expire. The true safety net is the rule in I-104 based on the target URL; what is being supplemented here is "allowing the event to reach the guard" — both are required to work together; neither is sufficient alone. This must be clearly stated to prevent anyone from thinking that supplementing the list solves everything.
Where is the code

.cursor/hooks.json
.codex/hooks.json

How to use in the future
From now on, the three connection manifests are managed by a single table. Adding a tool that should be seen by the guard simply means adding a row to the table. All three providers follow suit, and if one misses it, the test will report it immediately.

What it is
Let these rules be executed by programs rather than relying on self-discipline — no code writing if not clearly thought through, no implementation writing if there are no failed tests, and approval can only come from a single sentence manually replied to by a human.
Why this idea exists
Rules written in prompts are forgotten when assistants get busy; only checks attached to hooks that cannot be bypassed can guarantee that "no code writing without clear thought, no implementation writing without red tests, and approval only from humans" holds true before every single write operation.
Expected result
Before any file writing, command running, or stopping, the guard performs a judgment first; non-compliant writes are rejected with human-readable reasons; an approval code is only recorded when a human replies to the entire message.
How to implement
Divided into two layers: three gates for starting work, writing implementation, and completion (start-work check, red/green evidence, seven rules, rule core, connection cleanup, browser interception), and approval can only come from humans (approval code mechanism, and how actions on the webpage are counted as human actions).
Why it is implemented this way
Gates and approval are separate: gates judge facts that a program can determine, while approval is the matter that a program cannot determine and must be handed over to a human; mixing them would turn "human approval" into a state that a program could forge.

If sub-ideas are not all completed, the parent idea is not allowed to be marked as completed, nor is it allowed to undergo human sign-off.CompletedAdd a predicate to the "Completion" gate: as long as a sub-idea of an idea is not completed, the idea itself cannot be set to completed, cannot request human sign-off, and even if a human returns an approval code, it cannot be signed; the sign-off button on the webpage will be grayed out; every instance must clearly state which sub-ideas are still missing.Open →
Parent idea
Enforcement
What it is
Add a predicate to the "Completion" gate: as long as a sub-idea of an idea is not completed, the idea itself cannot be set to completed, cannot request human sign-off, and even if a human returns an approval code, it cannot be signed; the sign-off button on the webpage will be grayed out; every instance must clearly state which sub-ideas are still missing.
Why this idea exists
Today, a parent idea can be marked as completed or signed off even when none of its sub-ideas are finished; that signature is equivalent to being meaningless. This rule is currently only written in the manual verification sentences of a few parent ideas themselves — I-121 says "all seven sub-ideas completed", I-124 says "six sub-ideas completed" — those are handwritten prose, no program manages them, and adding a sub-idea turns those sentences into lies.
Expected result
When sub-ideas are unfinished, the command line will reject a completion request and state which ones are missing; sign-off requests will be rejected; the manual sign-off button on the webpage turns gray, with the specific sub-ideas blocking it written next to it; all three locations unlock simultaneously once all sub-ideas are completed; the handwritten "N sub-ideas completed" no longer requires manual counting. The "Complete" on the webpage is not within the scope of this idea — no idea can be changed to completed via the webpage; to achieve completion, one must have valid current GREEN evidence, which can only be done via the command line (D20).
How to implement
In the setStatus of companion/ideas.ts, after the existing four interceptions in the "Completed" branch, add a fifth: if this idea still has any direct sub-idea that is not completed, reject it and name which ones are missing. The predicate shape mimics needsUnmet verbatim (returning either empty or a sentence naming the items) and relies only on the graph itself (both parent and status are in the graph), because pure unit calls without the project directory also use this function; move the private kidsOf and parentKey from the rendering closure to the module scope for shared use, so "who is whose sub-idea" does not need to be written twice. Block two points on the sign-off side: the manual check prerequisite block in requestApproval blocks sending the approval code, and applyApproval performs one more check before writing the signature — if a sub-idea reverts to unfinished after the approval code is sent, only blocking the first point would allow the signature to be applied via that code. On the webpage, gray out the manual sign-off button instead of hiding it, and write in text who is blocking it; first change this button to call the existing awaitingSignature, otherwise the same thing must be modified in two places; grayed-out buttons do not carry data-sign, so the sign-off panel cannot be opened. Do not touch the "Complete" on the webpage — that gate belongs to D20; no idea can be changed to completed via the webpage. Blocked sub-ideas are counted as "not completed" per the ruling, blocking it in the same way. In FORMAT.md, add one sentence to each of the three places stating "parent is inclusion, not sequence": the completion of a parent idea implies the completion of all its sub-ideas, which is a direct consequence of the inclusion relationship, not a second type of sequential relationship; synchronize the copy stored next to the engine.
Why it is implemented this way
Every tool seen in research converges to the same skeleton: the status carries a terminal state marker, and the invariant is written on that marker, not on a state name called "Completed". What cannot be copied is their failure — Jira and Redmine have completely different architectures but identical user complaints, because both companies implement interception as "control disappearance," making it impossible for users to distinguish between a rule and a defect; therefore, here we gray out instead of hiding, and name the items when rejecting. What is explicitly not copied is "automatically marking sub-ideas as completed when the parent idea is completed": Linear makes this an option that is off by default, and GitHub rejected it directly, reasoning that a parent idea's completion does not imply all sub-ideas are completed, as some sub-ideas might be optional. We only look at direct sub-ideas rather than the entire subtree because once each layer holds its own, the entire tree is automatically established, and rejection can name an idea visible on the current page; the prerequisite for these two being equivalent is that setStatus is the only place in the entire repository where status can be changed, which holds true today. Blocked sub-ideas are not counted as completed because in this format, the destination for "Deprecated" is to retain the number, set it to blocked, and write the reason — that is a record of "this thing was not done," not "this thing was finished"; the cost is explicitly stated: a deprecated sub-idea will continue to block its parent idea; if truly stuck, one must either delete it from the graph or add an "Annulled" status (the more sophisticated approach online is that a sub-idea being annulled satisfies the parent idea, but a parent idea whose sub-ideas are all annulled should be considered annulled rather than completed), but we will not do that now.

Parent idea
Daily commands
What it is
The command for building a graph in a strange repository for the first time, writing the step-by-step overview according to that section of the specification and assigning each idea to a step; the command for adding a new idea, assigning an affiliation to the new idea, and if necessary, adding a new step and explaining why an extra step is needed.
Why this idea exists
The rules are written in the specification, but these commands are what actually do the work of writing the graph. If the commands are not followed, the specification is just a document no one reads, and the graph in a strange repository will still lack an overview—and "being able to get the same result when installed in another repository" is the entire purpose of this task.
Expected result
Run a graph build once in a strange repository, producing a graph with a qualified step-by-step overview where every idea has an affiliation; run the add new idea command once more, where the new idea has an affiliation, and if it starts a new stage, the command will explain why this extra step was added.
How to implement
Modify the description text of two commands. **For the graph building command**: add a step between "reading the project and extracting ideas" and "drawing edges"—first write this step-by-step overview, then let each idea claim a step; directly reference that section of the specification in the description instead of re-copying the rules (copying it once is equivalent to creating another drifting duplicate), only adding one sentence unique to this command: the steps are derived from the project just read, not copied from another repository. **For the add new idea command**: add a step after "filling in the first three questions"—assign this idea to a step; if it does not belong to any existing step, add a new step and **must explain why this project has an extra stage**, because there is a limit on the number of steps, and adding a step consumes a slot. Both commands remind: if the overview exceeds seven steps, it should be merged rather than continuing to add more below.
Why it is implemented this way
**Why modify the command description text instead of injecting logic into the engine**: This overview is something that requires thinking — deciding how many steps a project has and how to describe each step in plain language is something a machine cannot do; it can only be done by the party that has read the project. What the engine can do is validation (that was the matter of the previous idea), and all it can write is descriptions. **Why reference specifications instead of copying rules into the command**: This toolset has already paid the price for "writing the same thing in three different places" once — the copied version will inevitably diverge from the specification, and no one will know which one counts. **Why adding a step requires explaining the reason**: Three to seven steps is a hard upper limit; adding steps without a reason would cause the overview to expand uncontrollably into a table of contents — and a table of contents is exactly what this rule aims to prevent. Requiring an explanation for adding a step is the cheapest form of braking. **Why this can only be manually verified**: What is being modified is the prompt for the agent, not the code. A machine can assert that those few lines of text exist in the file, but it cannot assert that they were "followed" — that kind of test looks green, but actually guarantees nothing. There is only one true verification: running a real graph construction in a strange repository and seeing if the resulting graph includes a qualified overview.

What it is

Why this idea exists
The engine is just a data structure; what truly determines the quality of output is "in what order things are done". If a single prompt fails to align with requirements, the cost of rework is far higher than spending twenty minutes to align first.
Expected result

How to implement
Pure markdown, steps are fixed and cannot be skipped; stop at key points to wait for a human (ccthink step 2 reviews the split, ccfix step 1 reviews inconsistencies, and at the end of all commands, wait for "approval").
Why it is implemented this way
/ccthink sets "borrow whenever possible" as the highest priority rule in the command, and places research before answering "how to implement" — otherwise, research will only become a way to find justification for existing answers. /ccfix deliberately does not let the AI judge whether the code or the idea is correct: it is precisely the party that cannot judge. /ccscan explicitly prohibits fabricating why_this_way, because fabricated reasons will be treated as facts by the next agent and maintained indefinitely, which is the greatest harm this command can cause.

What it is
Five standard skill files under companion/skills/: Mapping Introduction, Thinking Clearly, Doing, Error Checking, and Viewing Graphs. The main body is merged from the existing five Claude commands and five Cursor skills, removing platform-specific names and absolute paths; all commands are written as neutral common engine calls. The manifests for all three providers point to this same directory instead of generating their own.
Why this idea exists
All three providers natively support the same skill file format (ruling table D33); continuing to generate a set of command files for each provider would just be hiding copying inside the installer — the wording has already drifted once (three versions emerged from the eight questions, D11).
Expected result
None of the five skill files contain any provider-specific paths; Claude actually loads and runs one of them in this repository; Cursor and Codex loading is verified in their respective integration ideas (I-073/I-074).
How to implement
Five directories under companion/skills/ ccscan/ccthink/ccbuild/ccfix/ccgraph, each with one SKILL.md: The main body uses claude-companion/commands as the base, integrating stronger paragraphs from the Cursor version of skills (borrowing highest priority, discovery must include line numbers, three attempts result in being blocked); all engine calls are rewritten as neutral calls to the single-file program after installation; frontmatter only uses open standard fields (name is the same as the directory, description does not exceed 1024 characters), and does not use disable-model-invocation (Claude Code currently has several related unpatched defects). Skill names changed from D33's onboard/discuss/build/debug/graph to the cc prefix; this ruling update is written into the companion/FORMAT.md divergence ruling table.
Why it is implemented this way
Research determined that one .agents/skills/ directory can simultaneously feed Cursor and Codex, while Claude Code requires .claude/skills/ bridging (official support allows symlinking by skill, but Windows git does not check out symlinks by default), so the authoritative version is placed in companion/skills/ within the repository, and the deployment method—whether to copy or link—is left to the I-098 installer. The directory name uses the cc prefix instead of the D33 short name: all three providers use the directory name as the command name; /build is too generic and would cause collisions, and user muscle memory has already shifted to /ccbuild — human sign-off has been granted for this deviation (2026-08-31).

Parent idea
Daily commands
What it is
Before request-approval prints the approval code, print the full content of what is to be approved. For the three gates—plan, test exemption, and manual verification—print the eight questions, code location, and verification method for the specifically named idea; for the decomposition gate, print the name, prerequisite, and first three questions for every idea in the full graph. Do not accumulate the content separately, but rather take it from the approvalSnapshot projection — currently, it discards the content after calculating the hash; change it to submit the projection before hashing, so that the "printed" version and the "hashed" version are the same in the code. Also, fill in the three columns missing from the terminal today: verify.pass, verify.test_files, and verify.signed_off. (step does not enter the approved content — it is not in the projection today, and adding it would invalidate all existing receipts; find another time for that.)
Why this idea exists
Today, this command only prints three lines, and not a single word of the content to be approved is shown (companion/ideas.ts:3655-3657). Humans can only go to a web page to view it, or trust the agent's recitation in the dialogue — but there is nothing to control what the agent recites, how much it recites, or whether it embellishes. Consequently, this human gate is a blind approval: the approval code only proves "someone replied," not "this person has seen the content to be approved." Ironically, the engine itself explicitly states in two rejection messages what humans should look at (companion/ideas.ts:1657 "please have a human review the names, edges, and first three questions of the whole graph", :1660 "please have a human review the eight questions of this idea"), yet it has never actually delivered those things before a human's eyes.
Expected result
Running request-approval --gate plan --node I-104 will first show the full text of the eight questions for I-104, the code location, and the verification method, followed by the approval code. Running --gate decomposition will first show the name, prerequisite, and first three questions for every idea in the full graph, followed by the approval code. Humans can judge whether to approve without opening a web page or asking the agent. If you change a single character and run it again, the printed content changes accordingly, and the approval code changes with it.
How to implement
Four steps. One, split approvalSnapshot (companion/ideas.ts:878-896) into two: approvalProjection(graph, gate, nodeIds) which returns the projection array, and approvalSnapshot becomes sha256(JSON.stringify(approvalProjection(...))).slice(0,12). Object literals must be moved verbatim, with key order unchanged — key order is the digest; rearranging them would invalidate all existing receipts. Three call sites (:917 requestApproval, :953 applyApproval, :992 validApproval) remain unchanged. Two, extract the eight questions loop in show (:3555-3561) into questionLines(idea), which only outputs the body of the eight questions, without status, without prerequisites, and without modification records — those three elements are not in the projection; mixing them in would be equivalent to printing "unhashed content" as "approved content". show will use this. Three, write a new verifyText(v) that covers five fields (command, pass, test_files, manual, signed_off): none of these five fields have ever been complete in one place today; show only prints one of the first two, and the web card lacks test_files. The 7th question of questionLines will use it. Four, the request-approval branch (:3646-3658) will first call approvalProjection, print items one by one, then print the three lines of the approval code, and append a boundary statement at the end: "This sentence can only be replied to by you in the dialogue; clicking anything else elsewhere will not count." **The printer only consumes the projection, not the graph** — use types to weld "what is printed" and "what is hashed" together, rather than relying on discipline.
Why it is implemented this way
Why split approvalSnapshot instead of writing another function to retrieve content: writing another one would create two parallel paths, where what people see and what is hashed evolve separately — and this idea is precisely intended to fix this decoupling. Why not use the easy method from sessionBriefing (companion/guard.ts:1773-1781) of hijacking console.log to run main(["show"]): it would print the status, the status-bearing prerequisites, and the modification records together; since none of those three are in the projection, it would be equivalent to committing the same bug in a different direction; furthermore, when show cannot find an ID, it calls console.error (:3550), which hijacking log cannot catch. Why not use the string source plus new Function approach like MERMAID_SOURCE_FN: that technique is prepared for "running the same code in two runtimes, Node and browser"; here, both places are two branches of the same main within the same process, so using it would waste type checking. Why not merge the formatting of the 6th question between the CLI and the web: codeOf (:2293-2294) uses "· symbol" plus newline labels plus "not yet implemented", while the CLI uses "(symbol)" plus commas plus "—"; the separators, connectors, and empty states are all different — merging them is a visible product change and should not be done casually within this idea. Why not add a new subcommand: adding a command requires changing three places in FORMAT.md (D28) and two test files, and changing "seventeen items" to "eighteen items"; what people want is "visibility when requesting approval," not "one more command to view." Why not include step in the projection: it would change the output of JSON.stringify, invalidating all currently valid receipts, and any todo→doing in this repo would be immediately blocked by :1657/:1660, and the six other installed repositories would also require re-approval after updating. This is a separate debt to be paid and should not be bundled in.

After submission, a human types one command, and the agent aligns the code to the new graph.To doA person executes a single command, the agent reads the current idea graph, identifies inconsistencies between "what the idea says" and "what the code does," and adjusts the code to comply with the graph following the test-first discipline: write tests first, confirm failure, then implement, and only mark as complete after verification passes.Open →
Parent idea
Daily commands
What it is
A person executes a single command, the agent reads the current idea graph, identifies inconsistencies between "what the idea says" and "what the code does," and adjusts the code to comply with the graph following the test-first discipline: write tests first, confirm failure, then implement, and only mark as complete after verification passes.
Why this idea exists
The complete requirement is "changing the graph means changing the project": writing changes back to YAML is merely an intermediary step; the final deliverable is code that complies with the new idea. If this step is not connected, humans will still have to initiate implementation themselves, causing the link to break in the last meter.
Expected result
After an idea in the graph is modified, executing this command triggers the agent to start working automatically; upon completion, the verification command for the modified idea passes, the code is consistent with the answers to the eight questions, and parts of the graph that were not modified are left untouched.
How to implement
A new slash command /ccapply (the command file body contains the string "ideas.ts"—the installer relies on this string to identify its own files; if missing, it will be judged as an external file and never updated; use install.ts --update to distribute to installed repositories). Process: find the change file in ideas/ where the baseDigest equals the current graph fingerprint (report and ignore stale ones one by one; if none are found, remind to "check if it was saved to the download directory") → run apply → report to the human item by item: field-by-field diff, check results, new fingerprint, and "which ideas' eight questions are incomplete and will not be implemented in this round (newly created three-question ideas on the web fall into this category; running /ccthink to complete them before approval can save one redundant approval process)" → human types "approve" or "approve <fingerprint>" → the agent implements only the ideas touched by this change that have complete eight questions according to /ccbuild discipline (test-first, status via set, mark complete only after verify passes) → the end report includes a fixed reminder to refresh the browser page. For change files with fingerprint mismatches, there is a clear replay path: the agent confirms each change (including the old value) against the new graph with the human one by one; after confirmation, it regenerates the change file with the current fingerprint and then applies it.
Why it is implemented this way
An interactive slash command rather than a headless pipeline: typing /ccapply itself is a real UserPromptSubmit event, all hooks function as usual, and the approval step remains in human hands. The scope of implementation is limited to the ideas touched by this change; aligning the entire graph is the responsibility of /ccfix—a single submission should not trigger a full repository roam. The division of labor for lightweight modifications is also written into the command: it is faster to simply say a typo correction in the dialogue (since modifying loose text fields allows the agent to use Edit), while the value of the web link lies in batch modifications of loose text and structural changes like adding/deleting nodes and edges.
Where is the code
Not yet implemented
How to verify
A real walkthrough: modify a field on the web + create a new three-question idea, submit, /ccapply—the report shows a complete diff, the new idea is listed as "incomplete, not implemented," and after approval, the modified idea is implemented and verify passes.
Human sign-off: Not signed
How to use in the future
"Change a sentence on the web, and the code changes accordingly" becomes a matter of a single command from now on.

What it is
Allow people to directly read graphs, modify graphs, and sign off on the web, with changes automatically written back to the project files after modification.
Why this idea exists
YAML is for programs to read; when people modify graphs, there must be a place that does not touch the YAML; the web is the only interface people are willing to view frequently, so viewing graphs, modifying graphs, and signing off should all be completed on the same page.
Expected result
Opening a single web page allows for layer-by-layer viewing of ideas, modifying text, adding or deleting ideas and prerequisites, and providing human sign-off for manual verification; after modification, changes are saved directly back to project files or a modified file is downloaded; the page should clearly show who is waiting for approval and who is in progress.
How to implement
Divided into two layers: modifying graphs on the web and writing back (editing, adding/deleting, submitting, write-back instructions, local small service, double-click entry, endpoint); and viewing clearly and signing off on the web (sign-off, two indices, title and page, full text pending approval, inline expansion).
Why it is implemented this way
Modifying graphs and writing back is one chain, while viewing graphs and signing off is another—the former must ensure the graph is not corrupted by writes, while the latter must ensure what the person sees is real; separating them allows one to know which chain is blocked.

What it is
Let every idea on the webpage speak for itself: three bullet points under the title explain what it is doing; expanding one line reveals which ideas are hanging under it; blocked ideas print why they are blocked; at the bottom of every page is a timeline of changes for this idea and its descendants.
Why this idea exists
To understand an idea today, you must click into it and read all eight questions; blocked ideas only show the two words "Blocked", so no one knows what is stopping them; change records are hidden inside each card, making it impossible to see which part of the project has been moving in the last few days. If you send this graph to someone who hasn't opened this repository, they won't be able to read it.
Expected result
Open any layer, and there are three bullet points under the title explaining what this page is about; expanding one line allows you to see what its own sub-ideas are and their respective statuses; blocked ideas come with a sentence stating "why they are blocked"; at the bottom of the page, a list of every change for this idea and its descendants is shown in reverse chronological order.
How to implement
Three bullet point introductions (I-131), the list of its own sub-ideas in the expanded line (I-132), the reason for being blocked (I-133), and the change timeline at the bottom of every page (I-134). All four items only modify the render section in companion/ideas.ts and its adjacent engine functions; no new files or dependencies are added.
Why it is implemented this way
These four things could have been attached separately, but they are placed under the same idea because they share the same set of read-only derivatives—sub-idea list (kidsOf), status count (tally plus countsOf), first sentence extraction (the expression that is identical word-for-word between the line summary and the page header today), and collapsible blocks (worklist)—and every single item in the repository already exists in only one copy. By grouping them together, all four changes will pull from that single copy; if dispersed into I-123 and I-124, a second copy will inevitably grow. Another path was to stuff everything into I-124, but that was rejected by the "maximum seven per layer" rule, and furthermore, I-124 is about "who is waiting for you to process," which is not the same thing as "has this page explained itself clearly."

What it is
Synthesize a single core by merging the respective implementations of three coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex), leaving only a thin integration layer for each, so that a single rule change takes effect across all three sides simultaneously.
Why this idea exists
Each of the three implementations is modified independently, resulting in three different versions and three different ways of applying the same rule; if a person switches to a different assistant, they must relearn everything, and it is impossible to have the three assistants take over the same project.
Expected result
One engine, one guard, one specification; each of the three providers leaves only a thin integration layer; install into any repository with just one command; the three assistants relay using the same idea graph, and a single change to the base takes effect across all three sides simultaneously.
How to implement
Divided into four layers: merge the three implementations into one (adjudication, engine migration, rule merging, migration); install into any repository with one command (single-file artifact, wiring list, installer, registry); three assistants connect to the same idea graph (thin conversion, Cursor, Codex); the base does exactly what it says (closing loopholes, finishing switches, speaking the truth in text).
Why it is implemented this way
Adjudicate before merging, otherwise merging is equivalent to picking a side at random; package the artifact as a single file, which can be installed anywhere as long as Node is present; the integration layer only performs translation without rules, ensuring a single rule change takes effect across all three sides.

Collaboration within the same directory To doI-112

Parent idea
—
What it is
Allow multiple coding assistants to develop simultaneously within the same working directory, communicating what they are currently doing, with a program coordinating file usage rights and idea graph updates.
Why this idea exists
The user wishes to retain a workflow where changes in the shared directory are immediately visible, reducing manual relaying of information, file overwriting, and loss of idea graph modifications; sessions from multiple assistants of the same model must also be distinguishable.
Expected result
Multiple assistants modify different files in parallel within the same directory; when contending for the same file, only one session succeeds, while other sessions can see the holder and the task; messages can be read by other sessions, idea graph updates will not overwrite each other, and claims after abnormal exits can be clearly handed over.
How to implement
Combine four sub-ideas without adding a dedicated assistant for coordination: I-113 provides sessions, messages, and short-term mutual exclusion; I-114 maintains long-term file claims in the message logs; I-116 reuses short-lock submission for idea graph changes; I-115 allows real assistants to receive messages at work nodes and verify ownership before writing. Division of labor is initially by file, and changes to related interfaces are coordinated via group messages; a long-term claim on one file does not hold the short-term lock for the entire project. The first version maintains a local directory on the same machine, Node 20, and a single-file artifact, without adding server or database dependencies or a chat interface. The new coordination runtime is recorded in ideas/.runtime/coord, while the long-term project intent remains only in graph.yaml; lock and session information is not written into the intent nodes within version management. Message bodies are read only as data. A process example is join→inbox/ack→claim→edit and graph update→say→release; abnormal takeover first stops the old session and in-flight writes, then verifies the claim number. Delivery is verified in two layers: this node uses multiple real subprocesses and artifacts to verify the entire protocol chain in a temporary directory; I-059 then uses real Claude, Cursor, and Codex to verify host wiring and actual visible messages. Ordinary hooks do not protect arbitrary processes; Git indices, branch switching, and public build outputs within the same directory still require separate coordination and cannot execute shared repository state changes in parallel just because source files differ. Weekly plan based on dependencies: Week 1 I-113 and verify lock recovery; Week 2 I-114 and I-116 in order; Week 3 I-115; Week 4 end-to-end verification of this node and real machine acceptance of the three providers via I-059. These are estimates based on actual commencement; Weeks 3 and 4 are especially affected by host versions, sub-assistant identities, and hook coverage. Several sub-ideas will modify the same engine or coordination module, so implementation stages will be handed over in file order; when existing in-progress ideas like I-082 occupy ideas.ts, their work must be coordinated first, rather than assuming the file is free based on the planning dependency order.
Why it is implemented this way
Leverage existing graph engines, file conflict checks, guards, wiring, and packaging instead of building a new scheduling platform. The basis within the repository is companion/ideas.ts:131, :778, :3478, :3645, companion/guard.ts:208, :1657, and companion/build.mjs:30. SQLite transactions, proper-lockfile, and resident serve have all been compared as actual alternatives (see sub-ideas and the current round of ideas/log.md research table), but under the current constraints of a local single directory and Node 20 single-file distribution, unified short-locks and a single-record stream can satisfy the confirmed requirements. Preempt by file rather than by function to avoid diff line number drift and automatic merging issues when modifying interfaces simultaneously; messages are responsible for semantic coordination, while claims are only responsible for writing ownership. The linear overhead of each log replay, explicit crash recovery, and non-instantaneous message receiving are explicit costs of the first version, rather than using "non-interference" to mask these boundaries.

Use process barriers and fault injection rather than pretending to have concurrency through sequential calls or three different names; real host interception and sub-assistant identities are still subject to manual verification by I-059.

Parent idea
Collaboration within the same directory
What it is
Provides independent identity and a shared message board for each participating assistant session, enabling the posting of startup instructions, progress, issues, replies, and handover summaries, with new messages read according to each user's respective reading position.
Why this idea exists
Shared code does not equal shared context; assistants need to know what others are doing and what constraints they have proposed. Model names or short-lived command processes are insufficient to identify the same assistant session.
Expected result
Two sessions of the same model can still be distinguished; multiple sessions sending messages simultaneously will not lose records or result in half-merged messages; one session reading messages does not affect the unread position of another; explicitly ensures that new progress and replies are visible after executing a read, without promising that file updates trigger automatic wake-ups.
How to implement
Added companion/coordination.ts as a regular function module that does not depend on the graph engine; the engine passes paths(projectDir).runtime to it to avoid mutual imports. Added coord join / say / inbox / ack / status via existing CLI. Shared data is placed in ideas/.runtime/coord/events.jsonl; does not establish a separate graph or modified files for each assistant, nor does it mix daily messages into the ideas/log.md project decision records. Each record contains a format version, sequence number, request number, action, session identity, and corresponding content; session registration, messages, read receipts, and subsequent claim changes are all written into the same record stream. State is recovered from the complete sequence of records; retrying the same request number does not result in duplicate execution, and reusing a number with different content must be rejected. Input validation includes type, length, identity, and action; arbitrary messages are not treated as operation commands; the message body limit is 8 KiB, and the total record limit is 64 KiB; exceeding these limits results in explicit rejection. Appending and reading snapshots share withProjectLock: uses non-recursive mkdirSync to create a write.lock directory under runtime; if the directory already exists, it performs a bounded wait, defaulting to a maximum of 3 seconds, then returns the holder and a retry prompt; upon success, it records a random owner tag, PID, and timestamp, verifying the tag and releasing it in the finally block. No automatic expiration, no time-based lock deletion; locks left behind by a crash are only explicitly recovered according to the detected owner after all coordination writing processes have stopped; an incomplete owner also requires a shutdown check, with no guessing. Success is only reported after the record is fully written and fsync succeeds. Reading only accepts complete JSON records ending with a newline; incomplete tails left by a crash are discarded by the next lock-holding write, while corruption in the middle of a complete record results in rejection. The first version recovers state from the record stream every time, with the cost growing linearly with the number of records; a ponytail comment is left in the implementation so that if cumulative messages in a real project make reading latency unacceptable, it can be optimized or migrated to SQLite. inbox is read-only and paginated, returning lastSeq; ack explicitly confirms the delivered sequence number, and the cursor only moves forward and does not skip existing records. Duplicate delivery is allowed when output fails or is unconfirmed; messages are not silently dropped. Identity, model, and PID are separated; independent sessions use a stable host identifier, while sub-assistants are given additional verifiable sub-identities. When no host is automatically connected, join generates a session identifier which is explicitly passed later; this command path only provides cooperative identity and is not used for security authentication. I-115 then brings in the host hook identity and context delivery.
Why it is implemented this way
Reuses the existing append record logic (companion/ideas.ts:489-505), but does not copy the lockless short-line append because group messages are longer and include claim decisions; unified lock-holding appends are required to link checks with state changes. The Node file system interface is sufficient to implement local short-term mutual exclusion; official documentation warns that exclusive creation may not be effective on network file systems (https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v20.x/api/fs.html), so the first version explicitly only supports local working directories on the same machine. Carefully compared proper-lockfile (https://github.com/moxystudio/node-proper-lockfile): it provides mkdir, retries, and mtime heartbeat recovery, which could save lock lifecycle code; however, synchronous graph rendering might delay heartbeats, and its automatic stale recovery differs from the current requirement of not accidentally preempting an active holder, so only its mkdir logic is borrowed; the first version adopts short-locks that do not expire automatically and require explicit recovery. SQLite has built-in serial write transactions (https://www.sqlite.org/isolation.html), but node:sqlite was only added in Node 22.5 (https://nodejs.org/api/sqlite.html), while the project is still built and distributed using Node 20 (companion/build.mjs:30, companion/install.ts:48); native plugins or higher runtime requirements are not introduced for the first version. The existing serve can handle messages, but relying on a resident service for all collaboration dependencies would add new startup and discovery processes, which was not chosen this time.

npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_coord_messages.test.ts → exit 0; use truly parallel subprocesses in a temporary directory to write messages containing Chinese characters, newlines, and lengths near the limit; assert that successfully returned records are fully preserved, sequence numbers are unique, and retries for the same request are not duplicated. The ack of two sessions is independent; unacked messages can be re-read, and future sequence numbers are rejected; when a lock-holding subprocess is paused, another process cannot steal the lock, and timeouts result in explicit failure; after killing a lock-holding process, the lock is retained and must be explicitly recovered after stopping writes; only corrupted tails are discarded, while middle-segment corruption results in rejection. Do not use sleep to coincidentally hit a race condition as a substitute for a process barrier.

Parent idea
Collaboration within the same directory
What it is
Make the program record which assistant session a file currently belongs to and what task is being processed, and handle claiming, releasing, and explicit takeover after abnormal termination; successful claim changes are automatically published to the shared message board.
Why this idea exists
Claiming a lock after seeing a message would allow two sessions to succeed simultaneously; the program needs to guarantee mutual exclusion for file claiming, and also needs to let teammates know whom they should contact.
Expected result
When two processes attempt to claim the same file simultaneously, exactly one succeeds, and the failed party receives the holder and the task; different files can be claimed separately; different path representations of the same actual path cannot be claimed repeatedly; one cannot release another's claim; a timeout alone will not automatically kick out a session that may still be working; after an explicit takeover, the old holder loses modification permissions.
How to implement
Add coord claim / release / takeover to the coordination module and record stream of I-113. claim accepts an explicit set of files, session, task description, and request number; it reads the latest claims within a short lock, checks the entire batch, and uses a single event to claim all files at once; if any single conflict occurs, the entire batch is rejected, returning the files, current holder, task, and claim number. This prevents two assistants from each taking half the files and then waiting for each other. Long-term ownership of different files is not mutually exclusive; short locks are only used to change records. Each claim has an independent random claimId; release must match both the session and claimId, and retries use the original request number. An old holder cannot release or overwrite a claim subsequently acquired by someone else. The claim event itself is a shared message, avoiding the dual-write problem where a claim is written but another log entry fails. File ownership and idea status are managed separately: release occurs only upon task completion or explicit handover; ordinary conversation ends and Stop hooks do not trigger automatic release. Reuse the same-path comparison logic (companion/ideas.ts:774), and complete the handling for resolve/realpath, Windows case-sensitivity, real paths with existing parent directories, and uncreated filenames; once normalized, they must reside within the project root. Reject directory claims, out-of-bounds access, .git, coordination internal files, and hard links that could cause multiple identities for the same file; check required source and target paths during creation, deletion, and renaming. Graphs and their HTML are not handed over for long-term session occupation; they follow the I-116 update command uniformly. Claims do not expire automatically via heartbeat. Normal release is executed by the holder after all in-flight writes are completed; takeover must explicitly specify the observed old claimId, the new session, and the reason, and must first stop the original assistant and its writing commands. The old claimId is verified again within the short lock before the handover. A hook with an interval between checks cannot be claimed as an operating system lock; a takeover will not revoke tools that have already been released, and a takeover must not occur while the original write is still in flight.
Why it is implemented this way
Reuse the mutual exclusion and event stream of I-113, where a single claim event provides both the machine state and group messages, eliminating the need for cross-file transactions between lock file states and announcement logs. Reuse the fileClash (companion/ideas.ts:780) from I-089 to detect overlapping task plans, but since it operates at the idea level and lacks session ownership, it cannot replace actual claiming. Compared placing a lock next to each source file versus a global state table: the former requires handling rollbacks and lock ordering for multi-file claims and easily leads to cluttered generated directories; making batch decisions within a unified record stream is easier to verify. The stale/mtime of proper-lockfile is suitable for process locks that accept expiration; this long-term claim spans multiple short-lived CLI processes, where neither PID nor time can prove an assistant has abandoned a task, therefore explicit handover is adopted.

How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_coord_claims.test.ts → exit 0; two processes use a barrier to claim the same file simultaneously, and exactly one succeeds; claiming different files both succeed; a set of partially conflicting files results in none being written to disk. Windows path case-sensitivity, relative/absolute paths, symbolic links, or junction aliases cannot bypass conflicts; out-of-bounds access and hard links are explicitly rejected. An old claimId from A cannot release a claim taken over by B; time progression does not steal locks; takeover after explicit stopping leaves a reason and a new claimId. The claim and its announcement come from the same record.

Parent idea
Collaboration within the same directory
What it is
Allow all supported image update entries to read the latest content and submit local changes under program coordination, protecting node numbers, states, and fields; similarly, avoid old rendering results overwriting new results when generating web pages.
Why this idea exists
Current atomic replacement can only prevent writing half a file; multiple processes modifying from the same old image may still overwrite each other, and web pages may also be rolled back by an old rendering that ends later.
Expected result
Parallel creation of new nodes will not result in duplicate IDs or lost nodes; updates to different nodes are both preserved, and explicit rejection occurs if the old value of the same field has changed; command-line and web write-backs follow the same concurrency constraints as other graph writing paths, and static rendering does not roll back; assistants can directly submit local changes without each assistant needing to first create a change file; locks are only held during the brief submission process and do not cover the entire development task.
How to implement
Reuse the withProjectLock from I-113, provided by the graph engine to uniformly execute "acquire short lock—read current YAML—validate and modify—atomic write-back—render latest HTML—release lock". Do not just add a lock around atomicWrite, and do not pass the doc loaded at startup into it. Avoid nested lock acquisition: internal submissions and lock-holding rendering are explicitly used only within call chains that have already acquired the lock; public entry points must uniformly wrap the boundaries. The coordination module must not inversely import the graph engine. Sequentially integrate the manual verification write-back for main's init/new/set/apply, migrate, POST /changes of serve, and applyApproval, as well as independent render. The "existence of target" check for init and migrate is also moved into the lock. The snapshot reading of request-approval and the manual receipt processing verify the graph under the same short lock to avoid signing into a new graph after reviewing old content. The GET of serve still performs immediate rendering from the full disk snapshot; both web confirmation and application re-read, preserving the behavior of rejecting if the old envelope baseDigest does not match. Add edit <id> --field <field> --old-json <old_value> --value-json <new_value>; complex inputs support standard input JSON with the same structure, avoiding Windows command-line escaping and the need for every person to create a file. Fields are explicitly limited to planning and reference fields, validating types, unknown fields, parent/needs cycles, etc.; code/verify can be submitted as a whole but is prohibited from using this to write signed_off; status continues to use set, and field changes revoke expired approvals and return done to blocked according to existing rules. The old value is structurally compared with the latest field within the lock: updates to different nodes can be preserved simultaneously, but if the same field has changed, it is rejected and the current value is returned. new adds similar structure inputs for planning fields/parent; numbering is taken from next_id only within the lock. Existing apply continues the full graph fingerprint check and does not quietly replay old web drafts. All successful graph modification entry points and independent render use the same short lock to generate HTML, avoiding disk writes after an old rendering; if rendering fails after saving the YAML, explicitly return "Graph saved, web page needs reconstruction" instead of claiming total failure and letting assistants blindly replay. YAML, HTML, and review receipts remain multiple files and do not promise simultaneous submission during power failure; YAML is the re-renderable truth. Long tests, network operations, and user waiting do not hold locks. Once collaboration is enabled, paths for directly editing graph.yaml/graph.html are intercepted by I-115, and all skills switch to using update commands.
Why it is implemented this way
The existing independent temporary names of atomicWrite and Windows retries can be reused directly (companion/ideas.ts:131); load/save, addIdea, setStatus, applyChanges, and redraw have already covered parsing, validation, and rendering, so a second graph engine will not be rebuilt. The problem lies in the read-modify-write transaction boundary: applyChanges:1805 only compares the passed snapshot, and there is no mutual exclusion between main:3952 and disk writing. Locking only the HTML does not solve YAML modification loss; calculating a hash one extra time before writing to disk still leaves a gap between checking and replacing. One graph per assistant violates the rule that a project has only one intent; a resident single-writer service increases O&M overhead and the CLI still needs a unified interface. Since I-113 already has a local short lock, all graph entry points sharing its changes will be most concentrated. Local edit is more stable than quietly relaxing the existing full graph fingerprint of the web page: the new interface promises per-field old-value checking, while the old interface retains its original conflict semantics.

How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_graph_concurrency.test.ts → exit 0; truly parallel execution of new guarantees consistency in node count, numbering, and next_id; two edits changing different nodes are both preserved, while competing for the same field with the same old value accepts only one; invalid code/verify, unauthorized signed_off, and circular dependencies are not written to disk. Mixed CLI set/edit, HTTP apply, and manual sign-off entry points verify the same mutual exclusion; old baseDigest is rejected. Use a controlled barrier to let the old render and new modifications compete, ensuring the final HTML is consistent with the current YAML fingerprint; simulate rendering failure to confirm the YAML has been committed and return an accurate, repairable state. Cover init/migrate competition and do not miss these special entry points.

Parent idea
Collaboration within the same directory
What it is
Integrate file ownership checks and message reading into the assistant's actual workflow: read relevant messages at the start of work, before modification, and during wrap-up; confirm the current session has the right to operate the target file before modification; publish a summary and release the claim upon completion.
Why this idea exists
The existence of a command does not mean the assistant will use it; only by validating the owning session at the actual write entry point can cases of assistants forgetting to claim or mistakenly modifying a teammate's file be reduced, while also avoiding the need for humans to constantly move group messages.
Expected result
Sessions participating in collaboration can continue modifying files they have claimed, but attempting to modify files occupied by others or unclaimed files will result in an explicit rejection and next steps; a session cannot impersonate another's claim when the writing session identity is missing; work nodes can obtain new messages; verify the actual interception range of editing and command-line writing across platforms one by one; clearly state any write paths that are not integrated, and do not claim that ordinary file locks can restrict arbitrary processes.
How to implement
Retain host identity, subagent identifiers, and tool call numbers at the common exit of the three normalize functions; generate coordination sessions under the platform namespace. Claude uses session_id if agent_id exists; Cursor uses conversation_id and must not use the per-turn changing generation_id; Codex uses session_id for independent tasks, but official documentation states subagents inherit the parent session_id, which must provide verifiable sub-identities through real write payloads or isolated startup wrappers. The appearance of agent_id in SubagentStart does not mean it is included in every PreToolUse; unless proven on actual machines, specify that this subagent path can only use commands in a cooperative manner, and do not treat sharing parent identity as successful isolation. Extend decideOnePath/rulePreWrite and allow commands to verify current session file ownership in addition to existing approval, testing, and task scope checks; retain and reuse fileClash. Validate all targets of a multi-file tool call before allowing it, and renaming requires both source and target to have ownership. In coordination mode, naked writes of graph.yaml/graph.html and coordination records are prohibited; updates must go through I-116 or the coord command. Unknown targets and missing identities are explicitly rejected; any --session within a command cannot be used as a basis for host identity. CLI collaborative identity itself is merely a cooperative agreement and does not constitute a defense against malicious forgery of the same OS user. Review all allow branches of ruleShell; do not allow existing "approved test commands" or commands claiming to be read-only to skip ownership rules. Writes that can parse targets must check by target; commands that cannot determine the write scope shall only be used in execution entries that explicitly declare and claim output and where boundaries are actually verifiable, otherwise reject and explain the reason for restriction. Arbitrary background processes, editors, or shells that bypass hooks cannot be constrained by ordinary claim records; real access reports must list these boundaries. Confirm that in-flight tools have ended before releasing or taking over; write-pre-permission granted by a hook cannot be revoked retroactively. Shared messages are injected as ordinary data with sources and must not be treated as higher-priority instructions or tool execution requests. The inbox is paginated and does not automatically ack; for Claude/Codex, write-pre messages use the document-supported hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext, while Cursor uses additional_context or agent_message based on actual events. Complete the discard branches for currently encoded messages; if delivery cannot be confirmed, do not advance the cursor. Skill steps before startup, commencement, submission, and wrap-up must read messages and explicitly ack; a regular Stop only prompts that handover is incomplete and does not automatically release claims or allow infinite re-runs. Reuse existing manifests and single-file builds, placing capabilities into distribution sources; verify installation and identity payloads in temporary target repositories. Do not automatically reinstall retired hooks in this repository or other user repositories. Explicitly enable via coord enable and record in the event stream; internal short locks for existing graph/coord commands do not depend on the enabled status; the enabled status only controls assistant claims and write-pre constraints. The status report indicates whether there is only a command agreement or a verified host interception; a guard must not be displayed as protected when it is turned off, missed, or released due to host timeout. Synchronously update the D18/D24/D30 in FORMAT and the direct image modification instructions in skills to ensure that the prohibition of naked writes is consistent with the actually usable ccthink/ccbuild commands.
Why it is implemented this way
Reuse the unified events from guard.ts:40, decideOnePath:205, ruleShell:1243, normalizeClaude:1657 / normalizeCursor:1713 / normalizeCodex:1783, and the wiring in manifests.ts. Currently, only the prompt branch passes session_id, while the write branch loses identity; adding functionality to the coord CLI cannot bridge this gap. Official sources are https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, https://cursor.com/docs/hooks, and https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks. The difference between Cursor's stable conversation_id and Codex subagents inheriting the parent session_id must be handled; real host events are more reliable than a model self-reporting its name. Compared only writing skill agreements, sending only group messages, and OS-level strong isolation: the former two do not provide mandatory checks, while the latter is disproportionate to the scope of using shared directories and native tools. Choose to integrate existing hooks and accurately report their coverage boundaries, retaining the manual inbox as an explicit operation when context injection is unsupported.

Allow each session to publish progress, ask questions, and read new messages. CompletedI-113

Parent idea
I-112
What it is
Provides independent identity and a shared message board for each participating assistant session, enabling the posting of startup instructions, progress, issues, replies, and handover summaries, with new messages read according to each user's respective reading position.
Why this idea exists
Shared code does not equal shared context; assistants need to know what others are doing and what constraints they have proposed. Model names or short-lived command processes are insufficient to identify the same assistant session.
Expected result
Two sessions of the same model can still be distinguished; multiple sessions sending messages simultaneously will not lose records or result in half-merged messages; one session reading messages does not affect the unread position of another; explicitly ensures that new progress and replies are visible after executing a read, without promising that file updates trigger automatic wake-ups.
How to implement
Added companion/coordination.ts as a regular function module that does not depend on the graph engine; the engine passes paths(projectDir).runtime to it to avoid mutual imports. Added coord join / say / inbox / ack / status via existing CLI. Shared data is placed in ideas/.runtime/coord/events.jsonl; does not establish a separate graph or modified files for each assistant, nor does it mix daily messages into the ideas/log.md project decision records. Each record contains a format version, sequence number, request number, action, session identity, and corresponding content; session registration, messages, read receipts, and subsequent claim changes are all written into the same record stream. State is recovered from the complete sequence of records; retrying the same request number does not result in duplicate execution, and reusing a number with different content must be rejected. Input validation includes type, length, identity, and action; arbitrary messages are not treated as operation commands; the message body limit is 8 KiB, and the total record limit is 64 KiB; exceeding these limits results in explicit rejection. Appending and reading snapshots share withProjectLock: uses non-recursive mkdirSync to create a write.lock directory under runtime; if the directory already exists, it performs a bounded wait, defaulting to a maximum of 3 seconds, then returns the holder and a retry prompt; upon success, it records a random owner tag, PID, and timestamp, verifying the tag and releasing it in the finally block. No automatic expiration, no time-based lock deletion; locks left behind by a crash are only explicitly recovered according to the detected owner after all coordination writing processes have stopped; an incomplete owner also requires a shutdown check, with no guessing. Success is only reported after the record is fully written and fsync succeeds. Reading only accepts complete JSON records ending with a newline; incomplete tails left by a crash are discarded by the next lock-holding write, while corruption in the middle of a complete record results in rejection. The first version recovers state from the record stream every time, with the cost growing linearly with the number of records; a ponytail comment is left in the implementation so that if cumulative messages in a real project make reading latency unacceptable, it can be optimized or migrated to SQLite. inbox is read-only and paginated, returning lastSeq; ack explicitly confirms the delivered sequence number, and the cursor only moves forward and does not skip existing records. Duplicate delivery is allowed when output fails or is unconfirmed; messages are not silently dropped. Identity, model, and PID are separated; independent sessions use a stable host identifier, while sub-assistants are given additional verifiable sub-identities. When no host is automatically connected, join generates a session identifier which is explicitly passed later; this command path only provides cooperative identity and is not used for security authentication. I-115 then brings in the host hook identity and context delivery.
Why it is implemented this way
Reuses the existing append record logic (companion/ideas.ts:489-505), but does not copy the lockless short-line append because group messages are longer and include claim decisions; unified lock-holding appends are required to link checks with state changes. The Node file system interface is sufficient to implement local short-term mutual exclusion; official documentation warns that exclusive creation may not be effective on network file systems (https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v20.x/api/fs.html), so the first version explicitly only supports local working directories on the same machine. Carefully compared proper-lockfile (https://github.com/moxystudio/node-proper-lockfile): it provides mkdir, retries, and mtime heartbeat recovery, which could save lock lifecycle code; however, synchronous graph rendering might delay heartbeats, and its automatic stale recovery differs from the current requirement of not accidentally preempting an active holder, so only its mkdir logic is borrowed; the first version adopts short-locks that do not expire automatically and require explicit recovery. SQLite has built-in serial write transactions (https://www.sqlite.org/isolation.html), but node:sqlite was only added in Node 22.5 (https://nodejs.org/api/sqlite.html), while the project is still built and distributed using Node 20 (companion/build.mjs:30, companion/install.ts:48); native plugins or higher runtime requirements are not introduced for the first version. The existing serve can handle messages, but relying on a resident service for all collaboration dependencies would add new startup and discovery processes, which was not chosen this time.
Where is the code
companion/coordination.ts:1-259 · withProjectLock / readEvents / appendEvent / joinSession / readInbox / acknowledge / coordMain
companion/ideas.ts:3674-3749 · main / SUBCOMMANDS
.devcompanion/tests/test_coord_messages.test.ts:1-154 · Messaging, mutual exclusion, and fault recovery testing
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_coord_messages.test.ts → exit 0; use truly parallel subprocesses in a temporary directory to write messages containing Chinese characters, newlines, and lengths near the limit; assert that successfully returned records are fully preserved, sequence numbers are unique, and retries for the same request are not duplicated. The ack of two sessions is independent; unacked messages can be re-read, and future sequence numbers are rejected; when a lock-holding subprocess is paused, another process cannot steal the lock, and timeouts result in explicit failure; after killing a lock-holding process, the lock is retained and must be explicitly recovered after stopping writes; only corrupted tails are discarded, while middle-segment corruption results in rejection. Do not use sleep to coincidentally hit a race condition as a substitute for a process barrier.

How to use in the future
Subsequent file claiming will reuse the same record stream and short-lock; in the future, the same messages can be displayed on the existing web interface, or storage can be changed while keeping the command and event semantics unchanged.
