idea Arrange by dependency order

Allow sessions to claim, release, and hand over files that need modification. In progressI-114

Parent idea
I-112
What it is
Make the program record which assistant session a file currently belongs to and what task is being processed, and handle claiming, releasing, and explicit takeover after abnormal termination; successful claim changes are automatically published to the shared message board.
Why this idea exists
Claiming a lock after seeing a message would allow two sessions to succeed simultaneously; the program needs to guarantee mutual exclusion for file claiming, and also needs to let teammates know whom they should contact.
Expected result
When two processes attempt to claim the same file simultaneously, exactly one succeeds, and the failed party receives the holder and the task; different files can be claimed separately; different path representations of the same actual path cannot be claimed repeatedly; one cannot release another's claim; a timeout alone will not automatically kick out a session that may still be working; after an explicit takeover, the old holder loses modification permissions.
How to implement
Add coord claim / release / takeover to the coordination module and record stream of I-113. claim accepts an explicit set of files, session, task description, and request number; it reads the latest claims within a short lock, checks the entire batch, and uses a single event to claim all files at once; if any single conflict occurs, the entire batch is rejected, returning the files, current holder, task, and claim number. This prevents two assistants from each taking half the files and then waiting for each other. Long-term ownership of different files is not mutually exclusive; short locks are only used to change records. Each claim has an independent random claimId; release must match both the session and claimId, and retries use the original request number. An old holder cannot release or overwrite a claim subsequently acquired by someone else. The claim event itself is a shared message, avoiding the dual-write problem where a claim is written but another log entry fails. File ownership and idea status are managed separately: release occurs only upon task completion or explicit handover; ordinary conversation ends and Stop hooks do not trigger automatic release. Reuse the same-path comparison logic (companion/ideas.ts:774), and complete the handling for resolve/realpath, Windows case-sensitivity, real paths with existing parent directories, and uncreated filenames; once normalized, they must reside within the project root. Reject directory claims, out-of-bounds access, .git, coordination internal files, and hard links that could cause multiple identities for the same file; check required source and target paths during creation, deletion, and renaming. Graphs and their HTML are not handed over for long-term session occupation; they follow the I-116 update command uniformly. Claims do not expire automatically via heartbeat. Normal release is executed by the holder after all in-flight writes are completed; takeover must explicitly specify the observed old claimId, the new session, and the reason, and must first stop the original assistant and its writing commands. The old claimId is verified again within the short lock before the handover. A hook with an interval between checks cannot be claimed as an operating system lock; a takeover will not revoke tools that have already been released, and a takeover must not occur while the original write is still in flight.
Why it is implemented this way
Reuse the mutual exclusion and event stream of I-113, where a single claim event provides both the machine state and group messages, eliminating the need for cross-file transactions between lock file states and announcement logs. Reuse the fileClash (companion/ideas.ts:780) from I-089 to detect overlapping task plans, but since it operates at the idea level and lacks session ownership, it cannot replace actual claiming. Compared placing a lock next to each source file versus a global state table: the former requires handling rollbacks and lock ordering for multi-file claims and easily leads to cluttered generated directories; making batch decisions within a unified record stream is easier to verify. The stale/mtime of proper-lockfile is suitable for process locks that accept expiration; this long-term claim spans multiple short-lived CLI processes, where neither PID nor time can prove an assistant has abandoned a task, therefore explicit handover is adopted.
Where is the code
companion/coordination.ts · canonicalTarget / claimFiles / releaseClaim / takeoverClaim / coordMain
.devcompanion/tests/test_coord_claims.test.ts · Multi-process file claiming and handover testing
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_coord_claims.test.ts → exit 0; two processes use a barrier to claim the same file simultaneously, and exactly one succeeds; claiming different files both succeed; a set of partially conflicting files results in none being written to disk. Windows path case-sensitivity, relative/absolute paths, symbolic links, or junction aliases cannot bypass conflicts; out-of-bounds access and hard links are explicitly rejected. An old claimId from A cannot release a claim taken over by B; time progression does not steal locks; takeover after explicit stopping leaves a reason and a new claimId. The claim and its announcement come from the same record.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Have the assistant check ownership before modification, and read messages and perform handovers at work nodes. To doI-115

Parent idea
I-112
What it is
Integrate file ownership checks and message reading into the assistant's actual workflow: read relevant messages at the start of work, before modification, and during wrap-up; confirm the current session has the right to operate the target file before modification; publish a summary and release the claim upon completion.
Why this idea exists
The existence of a command does not mean the assistant will use it; only by validating the owning session at the actual write entry point can cases of assistants forgetting to claim or mistakenly modifying a teammate's file be reduced, while also avoiding the need for humans to constantly move group messages.
Expected result
Sessions participating in collaboration can continue modifying files they have claimed, but attempting to modify files occupied by others or unclaimed files will result in an explicit rejection and next steps; a session cannot impersonate another's claim when the writing session identity is missing; work nodes can obtain new messages; verify the actual interception range of editing and command-line writing across platforms one by one; clearly state any write paths that are not integrated, and do not claim that ordinary file locks can restrict arbitrary processes.
How to implement
Retain host identity, subagent identifiers, and tool call numbers at the common exit of the three normalize functions; generate coordination sessions under the platform namespace. Claude uses session_id if agent_id exists; Cursor uses conversation_id and must not use the per-turn changing generation_id; Codex uses session_id for independent tasks, but official documentation states subagents inherit the parent session_id, which must provide verifiable sub-identities through real write payloads or isolated startup wrappers. The appearance of agent_id in SubagentStart does not mean it is included in every PreToolUse; unless proven on actual machines, specify that this subagent path can only use commands in a cooperative manner, and do not treat sharing parent identity as successful isolation. Extend decideOnePath/rulePreWrite and allow commands to verify current session file ownership in addition to existing approval, testing, and task scope checks; retain and reuse fileClash. Validate all targets of a multi-file tool call before allowing it, and renaming requires both source and target to have ownership. In coordination mode, naked writes of graph.yaml/graph.html and coordination records are prohibited; updates must go through I-116 or the coord command. Unknown targets and missing identities are explicitly rejected; any --session within a command cannot be used as a basis for host identity. CLI collaborative identity itself is merely a cooperative agreement and does not constitute a defense against malicious forgery of the same OS user. Review all allow branches of ruleShell; do not allow existing "approved test commands" or commands claiming to be read-only to skip ownership rules. Writes that can parse targets must check by target; commands that cannot determine the write scope shall only be used in execution entries that explicitly declare and claim output and where boundaries are actually verifiable, otherwise reject and explain the reason for restriction. Arbitrary background processes, editors, or shells that bypass hooks cannot be constrained by ordinary claim records; real access reports must list these boundaries. Confirm that in-flight tools have ended before releasing or taking over; write-pre-permission granted by a hook cannot be revoked retroactively. Shared messages are injected as ordinary data with sources and must not be treated as higher-priority instructions or tool execution requests. The inbox is paginated and does not automatically ack; for Claude/Codex, write-pre messages use the document-supported hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext, while Cursor uses additional_context or agent_message based on actual events. Complete the discard branches for currently encoded messages; if delivery cannot be confirmed, do not advance the cursor. Skill steps before startup, commencement, submission, and wrap-up must read messages and explicitly ack; a regular Stop only prompts that handover is incomplete and does not automatically release claims or allow infinite re-runs. Reuse existing manifests and single-file builds, placing capabilities into distribution sources; verify installation and identity payloads in temporary target repositories. Do not automatically reinstall retired hooks in this repository or other user repositories. Explicitly enable via coord enable and record in the event stream; internal short locks for existing graph/coord commands do not depend on the enabled status; the enabled status only controls assistant claims and write-pre constraints. The status report indicates whether there is only a command agreement or a verified host interception; a guard must not be displayed as protected when it is turned off, missed, or released due to host timeout. Synchronously update the D18/D24/D30 in FORMAT and the direct image modification instructions in skills to ensure that the prohibition of naked writes is consistent with the actually usable ccthink/ccbuild commands.
Why it is implemented this way
Reuse the unified events from guard.ts:40, decideOnePath:205, ruleShell:1243, normalizeClaude:1657 / normalizeCursor:1713 / normalizeCodex:1783, and the wiring in manifests.ts. Currently, only the prompt branch passes session_id, while the write branch loses identity; adding functionality to the coord CLI cannot bridge this gap. Official sources are https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, https://cursor.com/docs/hooks, and https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks. The difference between Cursor's stable conversation_id and Codex subagents inheriting the parent session_id must be handled; real host events are more reliable than a model self-reporting its name. Compared only writing skill agreements, sending only group messages, and OS-level strong isolation: the former two do not provide mandatory checks, while the latter is disproportionate to the scope of using shared directories and native tools. Choose to integrate existing hooks and accurately report their coverage boundaries, retaining the manual inbox as an explicit operation when context injection is unsupported.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Retain each other's modifications when multiple sessions update the same image. To doI-116

Parent idea
I-112
What it is
Allow all supported image update entries to read the latest content and submit local changes under program coordination, protecting node numbers, states, and fields; similarly, avoid old rendering results overwriting new results when generating web pages.
Why this idea exists
Current atomic replacement can only prevent writing half a file; multiple processes modifying from the same old image may still overwrite each other, and web pages may also be rolled back by an old rendering that ends later.
Expected result
Parallel creation of new nodes will not result in duplicate IDs or lost nodes; updates to different nodes are both preserved, and explicit rejection occurs if the old value of the same field has changed; command-line and web write-backs follow the same concurrency constraints as other graph writing paths, and static rendering does not roll back; assistants can directly submit local changes without each assistant needing to first create a change file; locks are only held during the brief submission process and do not cover the entire development task.
How to implement
Reuse the withProjectLock from I-113, provided by the graph engine to uniformly execute "acquire short lock—read current YAML—validate and modify—atomic write-back—render latest HTML—release lock". Do not just add a lock around atomicWrite, and do not pass the doc loaded at startup into it. Avoid nested lock acquisition: internal submissions and lock-holding rendering are explicitly used only within call chains that have already acquired the lock; public entry points must uniformly wrap the boundaries. The coordination module must not inversely import the graph engine. Sequentially integrate the manual verification write-back for main's init/new/set/apply, migrate, POST /changes of serve, and applyApproval, as well as independent render. The "existence of target" check for init and migrate is also moved into the lock. The snapshot reading of request-approval and the manual receipt processing verify the graph under the same short lock to avoid signing into a new graph after reviewing old content. The GET of serve still performs immediate rendering from the full disk snapshot; both web confirmation and application re-read, preserving the behavior of rejecting if the old envelope baseDigest does not match. Add edit <id> --field <field> --old-json <old_value> --value-json <new_value>; complex inputs support standard input JSON with the same structure, avoiding Windows command-line escaping and the need for every person to create a file. Fields are explicitly limited to planning and reference fields, validating types, unknown fields, parent/needs cycles, etc.; code/verify can be submitted as a whole but is prohibited from using this to write signed_off; status continues to use set, and field changes revoke expired approvals and return done to blocked according to existing rules. The old value is structurally compared with the latest field within the lock: updates to different nodes can be preserved simultaneously, but if the same field has changed, it is rejected and the current value is returned. new adds similar structure inputs for planning fields/parent; numbering is taken from next_id only within the lock. Existing apply continues the full graph fingerprint check and does not quietly replay old web drafts. All successful graph modification entry points and independent render use the same short lock to generate HTML, avoiding disk writes after an old rendering; if rendering fails after saving the YAML, explicitly return "Graph saved, web page needs reconstruction" instead of claiming total failure and letting assistants blindly replay. YAML, HTML, and review receipts remain multiple files and do not promise simultaneous submission during power failure; YAML is the re-renderable truth. Long tests, network operations, and user waiting do not hold locks. Once collaboration is enabled, paths for directly editing graph.yaml/graph.html are intercepted by I-115, and all skills switch to using update commands.
Why it is implemented this way
The existing independent temporary names of atomicWrite and Windows retries can be reused directly (companion/ideas.ts:131); load/save, addIdea, setStatus, applyChanges, and redraw have already covered parsing, validation, and rendering, so a second graph engine will not be rebuilt. The problem lies in the read-modify-write transaction boundary: applyChanges:1805 only compares the passed snapshot, and there is no mutual exclusion between main:3952 and disk writing. Locking only the HTML does not solve YAML modification loss; calculating a hash one extra time before writing to disk still leaves a gap between checking and replacing. One graph per assistant violates the rule that a project has only one intent; a resident single-writer service increases O&M overhead and the CLI still needs a unified interface. Since I-113 already has a local short lock, all graph entry points sharing its changes will be most concentrated. Local edit is more stable than quietly relaxing the existing full graph fingerprint of the web page: the new interface promises per-field old-value checking, while the old interface retains its original conflict semantics.
Where is the code
companion/ideas.ts · mutateGraph / main / SUBCOMMANDS / migrate / applyApproval / requestApproval / serve / redraw / editIdeaField
.devcompanion/tests/test_graph_concurrency.test.ts · Graph transaction and static rendering competition testing
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_graph_concurrency.test.ts → exit 0; truly parallel execution of new guarantees consistency in node count, numbering, and next_id; two edits changing different nodes are both preserved, while competing for the same field with the same old value accepts only one; invalid code/verify, unauthorized signed_off, and circular dependencies are not written to disk. Mixed CLI set/edit, HTTP apply, and manual sign-off entry points verify the same mutual exclusion; old baseDigest is rejected. Use a controlled barrier to let the old render and new modifications compete, ensuring the final HTML is consistent with the current YAML fingerprint; simulate rendering failure to confirm the YAML has been committed and return an accurate, repairable state. Cover init/migrate competition and do not miss these special entry points.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Sub-ideas can be expanded in place on the parent page to view the eight questions; clicking a node on the graph locates its corresponding line on the current page; there is another button when entering the details page. CompletedI-117

Parent idea
I-124
What it is
On any page that has sub-ideas (including the home page), every row in the sub-idea list can be expanded in place: click the row itself, and the full text of the eight questions for this sub-idea, its prerequisites, its prerequisites' prerequisites, and its modification records will expand below the row; click again to collapse. The expanded content is read-only—no edit boxes, no sign-off buttons, and no markers for positioning by ID, so it is not that card itself, but merely a summary of the card. Each row has an independent "Enter →" button on the right; only clicking it will jump to the idea's own page, where the editable card is located. Clicking a node on the graph no longer jumps pages: the page does not change, the address bar does not change, the corresponding row on the current page expands, scrolls into view, and flashes. Breadcrumbs and cross-page links within cards still jump pages.
Why this idea exists
Currently, every row of sub-ideas on the parent page is a single link, so clicking anywhere causes a jump; to compare several sibling ideas, one must enter one and exit another, losing context every time. Clicking a node on the graph also jumps pages directly, making that graph merely a directory, whereas it should be the map for this page—clicking a node should show its position and content on this page, not take you elsewhere. In-place expansion allows a person to read one layer completely on a single page; "Enter" is reserved for when one truly needs to edit or view everything.
Expected result
When collapsed, each line remains the same as it is now: Name, Status, and the first sentence of "What it is". Clicking the line itself expands it, allowing you to see the full text of the eight questions for this sub-idea, prerequisites, the prerequisites of its parent, and the modification record; click again to collapse. Expanding one line does not affect other lines. In the expanded area, there are no input boxes, no sign-off buttons, and no positioning markers like id or data-idea; within the entire document, each idea's numbered editable card still appears only once, so the existing two "cards appear only once" tests pass as is. Each "Enter →" link is independently clickable and jumps to that idea's own page. Clicking a node on the graph: the address bar remains unchanged, the page does not change, the corresponding line expands and scrolls into view with a flash. There is a function in the page script that can be called directly to perform this, allowing testing to verify it without loading the graphing library. Breadcrumbs, prerequisite links within cards, and "is a prerequisite for these ideas" links behave unchanged, jumping to pages as before. Top-level ideas on the homepage can also be expanded. Pages without sub-ideas are unaffected.
How to implement
**Structure of the line.** Each line changes from a single link to a native browser disclosure element: the summary line contains the Name, Status, the first sentence of "What it is", and the "Enter →" link; the disclosure body contains the read-only eight questions. The labels for the eight questions are read from the engine's unique question list (QUESTIONS); for questions 6 and 7, the same text as the card's existing codeOf and verifyOf is used but without the sign-off button; prerequisites and successors are constructed using existing links, and modification records are listed following the card's format. All text uses the existing escape function. **Invisible to positioning mechanisms.** The disclosure body does not add an idea class name, id, data-idea, data-edit, data-remove, or data-sign markers — the three mechanisms for editing, draft recovery, and sign-off look for elements using these markers, and this area does not exist to them. **"Enter →"** is a link within the summary line (href points to that number) and carries a data-brief marker; clicking it triggers a page change; clicking elsewhere on the summary line only toggles the expansion. **Positioning on the graph.** A new function focusRow(number) is added to the page script: it finds the disclosure element on the current page where data-row equals that number, opens it, scrolls it into view, and adds a flashing style (reusing the card's existing flash animation). The nodeClick in the graphing module is changed to call this; if the line is not found (which should not happen), it falls back to the original page-change behavior. **Styles.** The disclosure element inherits the appearance of the current brief line; the expanded body is indented and the font color is slightly darker; add scroll-margin-top to the disclosure element so it is not obscured by the top when scrolling into position. **Update existing tests accordingly.** The three assertions in lines 64 to 71 of test_render_order.test.ts state "one line is one link, summary is inside the link"; these are updated to the new structure: the line is a disclosure element with data-row, and the link is the one with data-brief within the line. This change is recorded in I-082. **New tests.** test_render_expand.test.ts: use happy-dom to render a sample graph with three ideas, asserting that when collapsed there is only the summary; when expanded there is the eight questions text but no input boxes or positioning markers; there is still only one numbered card in the entire document; focusRow opens the corresponding line; the "Enter" link's href is correct; pages without sub-ideas have no disclosure elements.
Why it is implemented this way
**Why the expanded block is read-only.** The rule "editable cards appear only once" in I-082 is not a layout preference, but a mechanism: editing, draft recovery, and sign-off all look for elements by number; if the same number appears twice, it will silently target the wrong one. If expansion were to allow editing, the entire positioning mechanism would need to be rebuilt, which is a much larger task and is explicitly not being done this time. **Why use native browser disclosure elements instead of custom show/hide logic.** This page already uses them in three places (card modification records, two indices below the graph, and the project origin on the homepage); keyboard navigation, screen readers, and in-page search auto-expansion are all built-in with zero lines of script. "Not writing the open attribute" defaults to collapsed; writing open="false" actually expands it — we learned from this pitfall with previous ideas. **Why "Enter" is a separate link in the line instead of the whole line being clickable.** If the whole line were clickable, it would have to handle both toggling expansion and jumping pages; these two actions would compete for a single click, requiring double-clicks or modifier keys to distinguish — no one remembers those conventions. One action, one control. **Why clicking a node on the graph positions rather than jumps.** The graph depicts the sub-ideas of the current layer of this page; jumping away when clicking it would be like treating a map as a portal; positioning to the corresponding line on this page makes the graph and the list two views of the same thing. **Why extract positioning into a page script function.** The graphing module fetches its library from the web, so tests cannot load it; by placing the function in the module that can be executed by tests and having the graphing module call it, we achieve the same method used when I-086 handles the page header. **Why change existing tests.** Those three assertions were written for the old design where "one line is one link"; since the design has changed, updating them is a normal cleanup of an outdated idea, not changing tests just to make them pass. The change is recorded in I-082.

How to verify

How to use in the future
Once lines can expand in place, "comparing sibling ideas on the parent page" has a concrete implementation point: in the future, we can display the same question of two siblings side-by-side within the expanded bodies, or filter the entire layer by a specific question. Positioning graph nodes to lines is also the first step on the path of "the graph and the list are the same thing" — the next step is the reverse: highlighting the corresponding node on the graph when a line is expanded.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Make the text in the repository tell the truth: ensure every assertion in the documentation, specifications, source code comments, and test descriptions matches the code, and ensure the most critical ones are guarded by tests. CompletedI-118

Parent idea
I-128
What it is
Go through every sentence in the repository that "describes how the code works" and cross-reference it with the code, correcting any errors. A full-repository inspection was conducted on 2026-09-06 (searching from six angles, with each instance being verified once by two read-only reviewers against both the code and the original text), confirming 40 instances: two in README.md, three in CLAUDE.md, twenty in companion/FORMAT.md, six comments in companion/guard.ts, one comment in companion/ideas.ts, and nine instances of descriptions and fixture strings in five test files. Every instance has been changed to reflect the actual state of the code today; only the incorrect half of the sentence was modified, without reordering paragraphs or adding embellishments. At the same time, a new test file was created to pin down those sentences that can be verified by a program: whether a guard is installed, whether the archive directory is empty, whether the event types listed in the specification match the set in the engine, which fields are recognized during write-back, which line number formats are valid, whether the numbering references in the initial unimplemented list can be matched, and whether deleted directories and constant names are still being referenced as active. In the future, if these statements drift again, the tests will fail first. The specification and source files located under .companion/ must be byte-for-byte identical, so after modifying the source files, use the installer to refresh that copy instead of manual transcription. Explicitly excluding three items from this entry: two instances in the two skill files (ccbuild says "if something is missing when entering doing, supplement it," omitting the "plan approval" item; ccgraph says status can show which blocked idea is waiting, but it actually prints nothing) — those two files are claimed by I-049 and will be absorbed by it; two dated audit snapshots (companion/AUDIT-2026-09-01*.md) — those are history, and being overturned by subsequent work is their duty; and the fact that the D20 line lacks an "implementation status" section — the review opinions are split one-to-one on this, so this entry leaves it untouched.
Why this idea exists
This set of tools treats "what the specification says must be the current code" as a hard rule. The specification itself states: if a ruling says "it is already like this" but it is not in the code, the next assistant will treat it as fact and act according to a non-existent guarantee. This inspection proves it actually happened: both README and CLAUDE.md say this checkout has no guard installed, while a guard is currently blocking commands in this session; the first item in the "unimplemented list" at the beginning of the specification says not a single guard is effective; the specification says there are eight types of events in total and not to invent a ninth, but the engine already has a ninth type (fetching web pages) and is using it; the specification says the D21 gate has four stages, but the code has five, and the one missed is precisely the only one that blocks by target path rather than by verb; the specification says a single line number "12" is invalid, even though the engine clearly recognizes it. A specification with tests guarding it versus one without differs not today, but after the next change: without tests, every "implemented" statement will quietly become false after some modification, and it will look exactly like the truth. This repository already has a precedent guarding this (the group in test_base_skills stating "what the specification says must be the current engine"), and this idea expands it into a dedicated test file.
Expected result
After the changes, every one of those 40 sentences can be verified word-for-word against the code as true; the new test test_docs_truth passes, and if any of its sentences are changed back to the incorrect version, it fails. Specifically, what is pinned down includes: README.md and CLAUDE.md no longer say this checkout has no guard installed, and they specify where it is installed (.companion/companion.mjs and the three connections); both documents and the specification no longer describe what is contained in an empty archive directory, and clearly state that the old implementation only exists in the commit history; every "Item N" reference in the unimplemented list at the beginning of the specification points to an existing item; the event types listed in specification D22 are completely consistent with the members of the union type in companion/guard.ts, with no more or less in either direction; the set of fields that can be modified listed in specification D24 is consistent with the SET_FIELDS table in companion/ideas.ts; specification D32 acknowledges that single line numbers and comma-separated segments are valid; the deleted constant name MUTATING_SHELL no longer appears in the specification or the guard source code; the D21 description counts five gates and explains the one that blocks by target; specification D35 and the comments in guard.ts no longer say the claude-companion directory still exists or is still being pointed to by connections; in test_base_contract, the Codex read event cell changed from "cannot receive" to the actual payload, the deficiency list now only contains Cursor, and the sentence "Codex reads will never reach the guard" no longer appears; in test_base_skills, the engine path assertion is derived from constants rather than re-copying a literal. .companion/FORMAT.md and companion/FORMAT.md are byte-for-byte identical (the installer's --status reports "all up to date"). The full suite of tests passed.
How to implement
**Sequence.** First write `test_docs_truth.test.ts` and run it until it fails (it asserts the state after changes are made); then modify files one by one; finally refresh the installation copy, run it until it passes, and run the full suite. **README.md.** Line 3: Retain the history "2026-09-05 Uninstalled and archived as requested"; change "This checkout is not running guard" to "Reinstalled on that day, guard is running, installed in .companion/companion.mjs, connected to five events from .claude/settings.json and .cursor/hooks.json, .codex/hooks.json, skills are in .claude/skills/ and .agents/skills/". Line 10: `archive/` is an empty directory; the old implementation only exists in the commit history (the files deleted in commit 48e1f51). **CLAUDE.md.** Line 3 is the same as above; Line 7 `archive/` is the same as above; Line 9 change "Because nothing is installed here, modifying `guard.ts` does not affect this session" to "This session runs the installed product .companion/companion.mjs, modifying the source code itself does not affect it; `build.mjs` only writes companion/dist/companion.mjs, the installer is what installs the product into `.companion/`". **companion/FORMAT.md, twenty places.** Item 1 of the Unimplemented Checklist at the beginning: This checkout has the guard installed and is running, specify where it is installed, and state that this item was previously written incorrectly; Lines 28–31: claude-companion/FORMAT.md was deleted along with the entire directory on 2026-09-05, and no skills or commands point to it anymore; Lines 304–305: `set` recognizes the name, six prose segments plus `parent`, totaling eight fields, consistent with `SET_FIELDS`; Line 335: Guard can receive Bash (all three wiring setups subscribe to shell), change the sentence "Guard is attached to the editor and cannot see Bash" to the real reason; Lines 720–721: D21 consists of five gates, not four; add the fourth gate "intercept protected ledger files according to target path", and update the index references in lines 758 and 777 accordingly; Lines 768–772: The five verbs `truncate`, `dd`, `shred`, `patch`, and `Clear-Content` have already mentioned `MUTATING_HEAD`; ask about every command instead of only asking when adjacent to the engine; Lines 782, 788–790: Change the constant name `MUTATING_SHELL` to `MUTATING_HEAD`, and change it to "judge by command head segment by segment" instead of "judge by whole line"; Line 815: Change "Item 7" to "Item 6"; Lines 616–618: The five skills are Markdown, and the paths are written literally; change "all read the same constant" to "the engine, guard, installer, and wiring read the constant, while the skill body writes literals, which are pinned to the constant by `test_base_skills`"; Lines 835–836: Add `urls` to the field list of normalized events; Lines 841–842: There are nine types of events in total, the ninth type is `fetch`; change "don't invent a ninth" to "don't invent a tenth"; Lines 1027–1028, 1033–1034: Single line numbers and comma-separated segments are valid; only non-numeric values, start points less than 1, or end points less than the start point are invalid; Lines 1086–1087, 1092–1096, 1100–1102: In D35, the three statements "`claude-companion` directory still exists, four hooks still point to it, and unfreezing is unclaimed" are no longer true; change them to "already deleted" and "wiring has switched to `.companion/`". **companion/guard.ts, modify comments only.** Lines 1041–1042, 1058–1065, 1079–1080: In `ENGINE_PATHS` and `INSTALL_PATHS`, the comments for the `claude-companion` and `cursor-companion` entries saying "This repository still carries these two sets of engines, CLAUDE.md still teaches people to use them" — change to "Directories deleted, entries retained by identity, whether to remove them is a matter for another idea"; Change `MUTATING_SHELL` in the comments of lines 1160, 1188, and 1300 to `MUTATING_HEAD` / `mutatingShell`. **Do not delete the whitelist entries themselves** — deleting them would change behavior, and three test assertions allow those paths; that is a separate issue to be decided. **companion/ideas.ts, one comment.** Lines 1755–1756: Change the sentence above `SET_FIELDS` "name plus six prose segments" to "name, six prose segments, plus `parent`". **Text in five test files.** `test_base_guard_message_truth` lines 9–10, 63, 66; `test_base_guard_engine_identity` lines 17–18, 117; `test_base_guard_readonly` line 163: All say "CLAUDE.md still teaches this way, this checkout is still running the old engine"; change to "these paths are historical entries retained by identity"; `test_base_contract` lines 201–207: Replace the Codex read cell with the real payload (the sibling case in line 293 has already proven its normalization and judgment are consistent); the gap checklist in lines 283–286 now only has Cursor; `test_base_approval` lines 251–252: `show` has already printed `test_files` via `questionLines`, only the web card `verifyOf` is missing; correct the comment; `test_base_skills` line 61: Derive the engine path regex from `ENGINE_RELATIVE` in `manifests.ts`. **New test `test_docs_truth.test.ts`.** Read the source code of `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `companion/FORMAT.md`, `companion/guard.ts`, and `companion/ideas.ts`, and assert every item listed in the "Expected Results" above; for the event types item, extract the union type members from `guard.ts` using regex and perform a set equality check with the types named in the D22 section; for the `set` fields item, similarly extract `SET_FIELDS` from `ideas.ts` and compare it with the specification in D24; for the unimplemented checklist item, count the number of entries, find all "Item N" in the text, and assert that N does not exceed the number of entries; for the deleted directory item, perform a consistency check between the `existsSync` result and the text description (if the directory does not exist, the text cannot say it does). **Installation copy.** After modifying `companion/FORMAT.md`, run `npx tsx companion/install.ts --update` (this repository is in the installation list) or reinstall this repository once to refresh `.companion/FORMAT.md` along with the products; do not copy by hand.
Why it is implemented this way
**Why use tests to pin things down instead of just correcting the text.** Correcting text only manages today; this repository has already paid the price once for "specification says it is implemented, but code is not," and the moment those sentences are corrected looks identical to the moment they become false again. The set of "specification must match the current engine" assertions in test_base_skills has proven that this type of testing can catch drift, so we are expanding this into a dedicated file rather than relying on human reading again. **Why is this one idea, not forty.** A specification should have one idea per acceptance; if multiple acceptances are needed, it should be split. Here, there is exactly one acceptance — "text matches code" — and forty places are just forty locations of the same thing. Splitting it into forty items, where the verification of each is the same sentence, would only turn the frontier into a wall. **Why guard.ts only changes comments and does not delete invalid whitelist entries.** If a comment is wrong, it is a text issue, which this item handles; whether an entry should remain is a behavioral issue — three tests assert that those specific paths are allowed, and deleting them would be equivalent to changing the guard's judgment, which must be thought through and approved separately. One idea performs only one type of change, so the reader knows exactly what they are approving. **Why installation copies use the installer instead of manual copying.** The installer is the only thing that should write to .companion/; manual copying is exactly how the twin specification drifted apart back then (D14). **Why two skill corrections are not here.** Those two files are claimed by I-049, and the engine does not allow two ongoing ideas to claim the same file (D18); forcing them in would only prevent this item from entering "doing." Writing them into the I-049 record is cheaper than breaking the rules. **Why not touch the two audit snapshots.** They carry dates and record how things looked on that specific day; being overturned by later work is the very reason for their existence. Modifying them would be equivalent to tampering with history. **Why D20 remains untouched.** Two reviewers disagree: one says it is wrong, while the other says it is correct within its own declared scope; where opinions are split, this item should not act as a judge for others; leave it to the next round.

Format for recording idea nodes: every idea must answer the eight questionsCompletedFormat of an idea node: id / name / status / needs, plus the eight mandatory questions (what it is, why it exists, expected results, how to implement, why implement it this way, which lines the code is in, how to verify, how to use it in the future), plus an append-only log.Open →
Parent idea
An idea graph that a program can read and verify.
What it is
Format of an idea node: id / name / status / needs, plus the eight mandatory questions (what it is, why it exists, expected results, how to implement, why implement it this way, which lines the code is in, how to verify, how to use it in the future), plus an append-only log.
Why this idea exists
AI hallucinations, prompts not aligning with requirements, and being unable to understand the project framework after rework — the root cause of these three things is the same: ideas have never been written down, only code has been written down.
Expected result
For the same idea, humans and AI read the same record to reach the same understanding; a cold-start stranger agent can continue working just by reading this file, without needing extra context.
How to implement
YAML, a flat list of ideas, one type of node, and one type of edge. The specification is written in FORMAT.md: companion/FORMAT.md is the version shared by the three agents, and claude-companion/FORMAT.md is the version still running on the Claude side before the migration was completed; the node templates, the eight questions table, and the two ways of writing "how to verify" in both versions must match word for word. The previous statement "each of the three companions has a basically identical copy" is now obsolete: writing separately is the source of wording drift, and it is also inconsistent with the facts — Codex does not have this file at all, the Cursor version is an old version from before 2026-08-28 and lacks the entire "how to write this graph" section. Now, only the table in the common specification counts for the wording of the eight questions.
Why it is implemented this way
Choosing a flat structure instead of a four-layer requirement/feature/module/function structure — FORMAT.md specifies at the end: the goal is "all ideas become individual modules"; a module is not a classification method, and the four-layer structure itself is the kind of complexity that makes people unable to understand the project. YAML instead of JSON, because the eight answers are all prose paragraphs.

Parent idea
An idea graph that a program can read and verify.
What it is
Read graph.yaml, check that IDs are unique, needs point to existing ideas, the graph has no cycles, done nodes must have code and verify, the code paths of done nodes actually exist, and manual verification must have a human sign-off; fields not filled in the eight questions are reported as warnings.
Why this idea exists
Without validation, the graph will quietly rot: done nodes without code, code pointing to deleted files, or two ideas depending on each other. A rotten graph is worse than no graph, because it looks complete.
Expected result
A healthy graph passes the check and exits with code 0; every way of being rotten can be pointed out and the corresponding ID can be specified.
How to implement
DFS three-color marking to check for cycles; reverse traverse from endpoints through needs to find orphans that do not reach any endpoint; use existsSync to verify the code paths of done nodes (todo nodes are not checked — those are planned locations).
Why it is implemented this way
Turn "done must have code + verify" into a hard error instead of a warning —— the code comments state that this is the prerequisite for the entire system to hold: if "done" can exist without evidence, this graph is merely a wish list. The code path for todo is intentionally not checked, otherwise the plan itself would be treated as an error.

Write the ID counter and the change file format into the format specification.CompletedAdd two things to the format specification. First, the ID counter at the top level of the graph file: a number that only increases; new IDs are issued uniformly by the engine when writing back changes, and the web page only issues temporary IDs and does not touch it. Second, the format of the change file: what is in the envelope and what each of the six operations looks like.Open →
Parent idea
An idea graph that a program can read and verify.
What it is
Add two things to the format specification. First, the ID counter at the top level of the graph file: a number that only increases; new IDs are issued uniformly by the engine when writing back changes, and the web page only issues temporary IDs and does not touch it. Second, the format of the change file: what is in the envelope and what each of the six operations looks like.
Why this idea exists
"IDs are never reused" is a hard rule of the format, but the web page cannot see history. If the web page calculates "max ID + 1" based on the current graph, after deleting the idea with the largest ID, the next creation will obtain the ID that was just deleted; if two people open their own web pages, they will also simultaneously calculate the same new ID, and no one will notice after merging. The change file is the sole interface between the web page and the write-back command; a cross-component format that is not written into the specification would force the next person to read the implementation to understand it.
Expected result
Perform "create, delete, create" in succession; the obtained IDs increase strictly and never repeat; two change files from parties unaware of each other are written back sequentially, each obtaining a different ID. The specification allows looking up the counter field and the complete format of the change file without reading code.
How to implement
The counter is written as a field at the top level of the graph file, incremented only by the command that issues IDs; any other place is read-only. **The initial value is written as a rule, not as a number**: when the field does not yet exist in the graph, calculate it once as "the maximum ID that has appeared in this graph + 1" and write it in. The original text "the maximum ID is I-075, so the initial value is 76" is now obsolete — when that sentence was written, the graph had not yet grown to I-080; initializing according to 76 would cause I-076 to I-080 to be reissued, which is exactly what this field is meant to prevent. A hardcoded number will inevitably expire as long as the graph continues to grow. The specification clearly states two hard rules: the web page only issues temporary IDs; real IDs are issued all at once during write-back and all temporary IDs are replaced, and if replacement is incomplete, the entire write-back is rejected. The format of the change file is written out item by item according to the envelope and the six operations, with one example for each.
Why it is implemented this way
Put the counter in the graph file instead of letting the web page calculate it: ID non-reuse is a format rule, and the web page cannot see deleted IDs at all. Incidentally, correct an erroneous reason previously written in the graph — the original text said "old graph I-001~I-040 has been retired, and the page calculating max based on the current graph will collide with them," which is wrong: the living IDs are I-041~I-075, and max+1 yields I-076, which does not collide with any retired IDs. The real vulnerability occurs after deletion: if the idea with the largest ID is deleted, max retreats, and the next creation obtains the ID that was just deleted. Two web pages calculating the same ID simultaneously is a concurrent version of the same bug — this is also why Rails abandoned sequential ID migration years ago. The two matters are combined into one node because they are two halves of the same thing: both are "new things added to this pipeline that must be searchable in the specification," and both involve modifying the same managed file. Splitting them into two nodes would cause the same specification to be approved twice.
Where is the code
companion/FORMAT.md:156-170,245-342 · next_id · The change file
How to verify
Read both FORMAT.md files: the field name of the ID counter, its initial value, and "incremented only by write-back" are clearly stated; the envelope and the six operations of the change file each have an example; "web page only issues temporary IDs" is an explicit rule.

When modifying an idea's status, automatically leave a modification recordCompletedChange an idea's status and simultaneously append a record to its own log; preserve YAML comments when writing back; reject done without code/verify, and reject manual verification without human sign-off.Open →
Parent idea
An idea graph that a program can read and verify.
What it is
Change an idea's status and simultaneously append a record to its own log; preserve YAML comments when writing back; reject done without code/verify, and reject manual verification without human sign-off.
Why this idea exists
Detailed records must exist for what code, what documentation, and what idea was changed, while the reason must be placed next to the idea, not in another file —— if it is placed too far away, no one will read it.
Expected result
Re-read after set: the status has changed, a new log entry is added, and the original comments remain; setting done for an idea without code will fail and explain the reason.
How to implement
Use yaml's parseDocument to preserve comments and formatting, use setIn for targeted modification, write to a temporary file, and then rename.
Why it is implemented this way
Use Document instead of parse → modify → stringify: the latter will wipe out all comments and layout of the entire file, and comments are exactly what humans leave for themselves. rename is atomic, so a crash mid-write will not destroy the original graph (code comment: a crash mid-write leaves the old graph intact).

Parent idea
An idea graph that a program can read and verify.
What it is
At the start of /ccscan, list the files worth reading in the project as a list (ideas/.scan-todo); every time a file is Read, a hook strikes it off; check continues to warn while the list is not empty. ideas/.scanignore can exclude by path prefix (third-party packages, parallel versions from other agents).
Why this idea exists
"I have finished reading" is a sentence an agent can say casually. If a graph is built from only half a project, it looks exactly the same as a complete one — this is worse than having no graph at all.
Expected result
Scanning progress is a number like "Read 37/42" rather than a mere guarantee; Grep / Glob do not count, because they do not put file content into the context.
How to implement
git ls-files -z --cached --others --exclude-standard generates the list (degrades to directory traversal when git is unavailable), filtering by extension and .scanignore; strike() strikes off a line based on a case-insensitive relative path.
Why it is implemented this way
Use git ls-files instead of manual traversal because it already understands .gitignore, submodules, and case sensitivity; -z is added because without it, git escapes non-ASCII paths into octal, making those files impossible to strike off (this is explicitly stated in the code comments). node_modules is explicitly excluded because the repository might actually have committed it.

It is a prerequisite for these ideas Seven mandatory rules attached to hooks that agents cannot bypass. Fix the issue where scan list records are lost when multiple processes write to it simultaneously.

Fix the issue where scan list records are lost when multiple processes write to it simultaneously.CompletedEnsure that strike() does not lose writes or write corrupted files when multiple hook processes strike out files simultaneously.Open →
Parent idea
An idea graph that a program can read and verify.
What it is
Ensure that strike() does not lose writes or write corrupted files when multiple hook processes strike out files simultaneously.
Why this idea exists
This /ccscan personally encountered it: during the same round, five files were read in parallel, which meant the hook also ran five guard processes in parallel, each performing readWorklist → filter → writeFileSync. The later write overwrote the earlier write, leaving evidence in the log ("Read .gitignore (32 remaining)" immediately followed by "Read package.json (32 remaining)", the number did not decrease), and a line of incomplete content `n` was written into the list. The result was: the files were indeed read, but the ledger said they were not read — the number reported by R7 actually became inaccurate.
Expected result
After reading N files in parallel, the list should be exactly N lines short, and no lines other than file paths should appear.
How to implement
Make strike no longer rewrite the list, but change it to append only, so that race conditions no longer exist. .scan-todo becomes a list written only once (generated by scan, which is truly a single process); add a new append-only .scan-done, where strike finishes after appending one line using appendFileSync, without reading, modifying, or rewriting anything; "what remains" becomes the set difference of "list minus already read," so duplicate appending is harmless, and a torn half-line will simply not match anything. Appending must be a single write call (passing a pre-constructed full string, without using WriteStream or multiple calls), otherwise atomicity is not established. Change the return value of strike from true/false to the remaining count in its own snapshot, so that the guard does not need to read a second time when logging — otherwise, the symptom "two consecutive writes both say 7 remaining" will still appear after the fix. The contract of the return value must be able to distinguish two things, otherwise it will silently corrupt R7: if not in the list, or if no scan is running, return -1; if truly struck out, return the remaining count of this snapshot (which can be 0). Raw numbers cannot achieve this — "not in the list" and "struck out with 0 remaining" would both be 0, and guard.ts currently branches based on truthy/falsy values (`if (!struck) return OK`), and the two existing green tests happen to cover these two directions: one asserts that no log is recorded when there is no list, and one asserts that when striking out the last one, it must log "0 remaining in scan." Change the fixed temporary filename ${file}.tmp in save to a name with a process ID and a random suffix (copying the codex implementation), and add EPERM/EBUSY/EACCES retry to rename: renaming to overwrite an existing file is unreliable on Windows. .scan-done must be added to both the guard's write-protection list and ideas/.gitignore, otherwise an agent could write its own "I have read it," which is the entire reason R7 exists. Finally, perform a one-time migration for scan: list = the current project file list, already read = list minus the old remaining, and the already read items must be reconciled with the list, discarding anything that is not a known path in the list — the incomplete line `n` currently stuck in the list will therefore automatically disappear.
Why it is implemented this way
The original implementation of "align save temporary file + rename" was only a half-fix, and this repository provides immediate counter-evidence: rename makes "writing" atomic, but it does not serialize "reading". strike reads first, then writes; another process may have already read the old list in the interim, so when it writes back, it overwrites the results of others. The evidence is in lines 301 and 302 of ideas/log.claude.md — both lines write "7 remaining scanned", yet the file that was supposedly struck out remains the first line of the list to this day. The command_reviewed on the codex side is a more advanced version of the same error: it uses correct atomic writes, but it is still "read-modify-write", which still results in lost writes. Even the most complete of the three implementations failed here. Changing to append-only resolves both symptoms simultaneously: the operating system handles positioning for each append, N concurrent processes produce N complete records, and no locks, retries, waiting, or any new dependencies are required. This also holds true on Windows: the underlying library adds FILE_APPEND_DATA to append mode, which is the Windows equivalent of the POSIX semantics. I must clarify the boundaries of this evidence to avoid overstating: guard uses append for logging, and in log.claude.md, there are only three moments that truly prove "simultaneous writing" (the remaining count 32 appears three times, 19 twice, and 7 twice); the other hundreds of lines were written sequentially and do not prove concurrency. Therefore, the real guarantee is not "we tried many times and it didn't break," but rather "the growth of file length is atomic, and the upper limit for non-interleaved content is the disk sector size (512B to 4KB), while each of our records is a path of only a few dozen bytes." The first step of implementation is to measure this — first write the concurrency test, run it against the current code to confirm it actually fails (red), and then modify the implementation. Additionally, I am noting a more thorough approach that was considered but not adopted this round: Claude Code has a PostToolBatch event, which triggers only once after an entire batch of parallel tool calls has finished. Moving the strike action there would mean only one process is writing, eliminating concurrency at the source, which is simpler than any concurrency-safe implementation. The reason for not adopting it is that it would require modifying the installer to register a new event, depend on newer versions, and it would change the semantics of R7 itself (striking out by batch rather than by each Read), which is a matter for FORMAT.md to adjudicate, not something a bug fix should handle casually. The append-only approach does not conflict with it: regardless of which event triggers it, the writing method is safe, and it remains valid for the uncapped concurrency brought by sub-agents. No locks: approximately thirty lines of code would be exchanged for three new ways to fail, and stale locks are a long-term cost rather than an edge case — hook processes can be killed by the outer layer, and locks often outlive the processes. By design, guard must "allow through on error," so every lock path would need a "give up striking on timeout" branch, which would effectively reintroduce undercounting, and undercounting is exactly what R7 aims to eliminate. Node also lacks a built-in file lock to fall back on. No third-party packages: this engine has the design prerequisite that "installing in other repositories requires nothing," and since guard starts a new process for every Read, every dependency incurs a cost on every tool call. More directly, those atomic write packages only serialize writes within a single process, whereas the five writers here are in five separate processes; they do not solve the fundamental problem. Lock packages have not been maintained for years and have documented failure loops on Windows. The common foundation D30 has already ruled on this divergence: all generated state atomic writes must use process locks or single atomic appends for append logs. Known boundaries, written here to avoid being treated as a bug later: append atomicity does not hold on network drives; it is only safe on local disks when a single line is much smaller than a sector — here we store file paths, which is more than enough.

Change logbook: field changes and structural changes use the same format, and browser drafts and disk files also use the same format.CompletedThe logbook that records "what a person changed this time" on the page changes from a table of "idea ID + field name → new value" to a sequence of ordered operation records: changing a field, changing a status, creating a new idea, deleting an idea, connecting a prerequisite arrow, or breaking a prerequisite arrow. Parent idea
An idea graph that a program can read and verify.
What it is
The logbook that records "what a person changed this time" on the page changes from a table of "idea ID + field name → new value" to a sequence of ordered operation records: changing a field, changing a status, creating a new idea, deleting an idea, connecting a prerequisite arrow, or breaking a prerequisite arrow. This sequence of records is simultaneously the format for browser drafts and the format for the change file submitted to the disk later — one format, not three.
Why this idea exists
Currently, this logbook can only express "what a certain field of a certain idea became." When creating a new idea, there is no ID to use as a key; when deleting an idea, there is no field name; and prerequisite relationships are a list — the current logbook compares new and old values by treating the list as a single string, so "changing two prerequisites to one" is judged as "no change" and then discarded. Structural editing has no place to land in the current format.
Expected result
All six types of operations can be recorded, saved to drafts, and read back, without missing a single one; when changing an idea's prerequisites from two to one, the log shows "which one was broken" instead of "no change"; after the page is reopened, structural operations can be restored item by item, just like field changes.
How to implement
The ledger is changed from a single table to a sequence of ordered operations, consisting of six types: modify field (with old and new values), modify status (with original and new status), create (the page only provides a temporary ID and the content of the first three questions), delete (with ID), connect a prerequisite arrow, and disconnect a prerequisite arrow. Connecting and disconnecting edges are written as a pair of "from which to which," rather than a new value for the entire prerequisite list. An envelope wraps the entire sequence of operations: format version number, project path, and the embedded image fingerprint from the page — the fingerprint is brought back exactly as is; the page never calculates it itself. This envelope serves as both the format for browser drafts and the format for modified files on disk: one single format, not three. Incidentally, this fixes an existing adjacency defect: when a draft is written, the fingerprint is stored, but when it is read back, it is never compared, meaning a draft written against an old image would be silently restored. Once operations like "delete a certain idea" exist, this is no longer harmless.
Why it is implemented this way
The existing ledger cannot be expanded further; this is based on empirical testing, not speculation: its method of comparing old and new values involves converting both sides to strings before comparing, and a list with only one element converted to a string happens to equal the element itself — therefore, "deleting two prerequisites to leave one" will be judged as "no change" and subsequently deleted from the ledger. Raw strings also cannot express "non-existence" (an empty string means empty, not deleted), and the current implementation of splitting keys by delimiters when restoring drafts will produce garbage when encountering structural operations. Therefore, this is a reconstruction, not an expansion. This sentence must be written in the node, because it is precisely the difference between "two lines of changes" and "one new module," and it is also the reason why the original sentence "make deletion a mark for deletion" sounded trivial. We choose an ordered list instead of several parallel tables: "create a temporary ID" and "connect an edge to that temporary ID" only have a deterministic meaning when there is a sequence. Edges are written as a pair instead of the entire list: this prevents two edge changes on the same idea from overwriting each other. We do not borrow JSON Patch: it locates by array index, and once this chain can add nodes, all indices become incorrect — this is also why configuration tools generally abandon it. We do not borrow JSON Merge Patch: it can only replace arrays as a whole, and it uses null to represent deletion, which directly conflicts with the "human sign-off: not yet signed" that exists in this graph. The custom operation list, addressed by ID, aligns semantically with the Kubernetes precedent of key merging, and the implementation is only about thirty lines. For the version number, we adopt the approach of online flowchart editors: add a prefix so that the write-back end can explicitly reject an old format instead of reading it in ambiguously.

Layer the ideas: each idea must specify which idea it belongs under; the web page shows only one layer to a person at a timeCompletedAn idea can specify that it belongs under another idea —— add a field called "parent idea," fill in the ID of the first-level idea; if left blank, it is the top-most layer.
