Parent idea
A graph drawn layer by layer according to sequence.
What it is
An idea can specify that it belongs under another idea —— add a field called "parent idea," fill in the ID of the first-level idea; if left blank, it is the top-most layer. The entire graph is thus a tree: a person reads from the top few ideas, and upon clicking one, sees only the layer directly below it, with a maximum of seven items per layer. This rule must be implemented in four places; if missing one, it cannot be carried to other repositories. One, define it strictly in the format specification: what the field looks like, a maximum of seven per layer, what the validation manages, how the page is split, and how the name and sentence of the top-most layer should be written. Two, the validation program recognizes this field: if attached to a non-existent ID or forming a loop, it reports an error immediately; if a layer exceeds seven, it reports a warning. Three, the web page splits according to this tree: the home page only shows the top-most layer; upon clicking an idea, the top of the page shows its own complete card, and the line below shows its direct descendants one by one; an idea's complete card appears only once in the entire text, right on its own page. Four, the instructions for the assistant regarding graph building and adding new ideas are both changed to "build the tree first, then connect prerequisites." This matter has gone through two versions, and the second version tore down the first. The first version was a flat "step-by-step overview": a list of sequential steps at the top of the graph file, with each idea tagged with a step label —— it was only one layer, and it wasn't drawn on the page. On 2026-09-05, per human request, it was changed to a tree that can be opened layer by layer; those two old fields were deleted together, the original five steps each became an idea in the top-most layer, and the sixty-six ideas replaced step labels with parent idea IDs. One matter that does not belong to this idea is written here to avoid being mistaken as completed together: the title at the top of the web page and the paragraph below it change according to the current page; that is the work of another idea (I-086), which is already finished and is not included here.
Why this idea exists
Once a graph grows to seventy-one ideas, listing them flat makes them unreadable —— the first thing seen upon opening the web page is a wall, making it impossible to see what the project is doing or where to start reading. This is not a flaw unique to this repository, but a flaw that every repository equipped with this set of tools will eventually encounter: ideas will only increase, they will not decrease on their own. Writing a few lines of introductory text for this repository only solves the problem once; defining "ideas must be layered, and how to layer them" as a rule in the specification allows any repository to follow it and obtain its own version of layering. The flat overview produced first did indeed answer half the question —— sentences like "how many things this project is doing in total, and what capabilities the project gains after each thing is finished" were the first times these were forced to be clarified when writing that overview. But it failed on two points proven by testing: it only had one layer, so seventy-one ideas spread across five steps meant that clicking any step still resulted in a long string of ten or twenty ideas, meaning the "wall" was merely cut into five pieces; furthermore, it only existed in the graph file and was not drawn on the web page at all, so a person opening the web page saw nothing extra. To make people truly able to read it, "belonging" cannot just be a list printed in a file; it must become the structure of the graph itself, with the page serving it layer by layer according to that structure.
Expected result
Open the webpage; you will only see the top layer of ideas, one per line, each with its name, status, and the first line of its "what is"; click one to enter, and the top of the page shows its own eight questions, while the bottom shows its direct descendants; click again to enter another layer. The complete card of each idea appears only once in the entire file, right on its own page. Ideas in the same layer are sorted by dependency order: a prerequisite is placed before its successor. If an idea is attached to a non-existent ID, the validation reports an error and simultaneously reports both IDs; if it forms a loop (including attaching to itself), it reports one error and prints the loop in order, reporting the same loop only once; if any layer exceeds seven, a warning is reported instead of an error, specifying which layer it is. If an idea does not have its affiliation written, the validation says nothing about it — the top layer originally has no affiliation. The boundary of this statement must be clear: if the entire graph has no affiliation written and there are more than seven ideas, the "top layer exceeds seven" warning will still appear, because that is counting the top layer, not picking out ideas without affiliation. When creating a new idea on the webpage or changing an idea's affiliation, that field is saved as a single line of plain text when writing back to the graph file, not as a collapsed paragraph; validation is performed after writing back, resulting in zero errors. If an idea's affiliation is written as a non-existent ID, the page treats it as part of the top layer and displays it accordingly — an idea cannot be lost on the page due to a typo; errors that should be reported are left to the validation to report. One more thing: running a graph construction once in a strange repository produces a tree directly, not a flattened list. The verification command below this sentence will not be triggered — those two tests check validation rules, writing back, and the page; none of them will run graph construction in another repository; and the only time that sentence received a human sign-off (2026-09-04) was for the flattened overview of the first version, not this tree, and its referenced receipt file no longer exists on the disk today. This sentence remains here waiting for a real graph construction on a strange repository, without pretending it has already been covered.
How to implement
**Field.** Add a field to an idea where the value is the ID of the parent idea; if left blank, it is part of the top layer. Only add this one direction from child to parent; do not add a reverse "child idea list." **Validation is split into two levels, intentionally.** Attaching to an ID not in the graph or forming a loop will cause the page to lose ideas or fail to render — these report errors; exceeding seven in a layer is just hard to read — this reports a warning. The method for finding loops is to climb up from each idea following the affiliation; if you climb back to yourself, it is a loop; the members of the loop are recorded, and the same loop is reported only once, using the same convergence method as finding dependency cycles in a graph. **Webpage.** All pages are written into the same file and are all hidden initially; the script in the page displays one specific page based on the ID in the address bar; changing the ID changes the page, and the browser's forward and back functions work as usual. The home page is the top layer; an idea's page consists of "its own complete card + direct descendants, one per line." The dependency graph is shared across all pages, and when switching pages, it is redrawn using the descendants of the current page; if the current page has no descendants, the entire graph is hidden without leaving an empty frame. At the top of the page, there is a path counted down from the home page, constructed by following the affiliation all the way up. The order within the same layer follows the already established dependency sorting (that was a task completed by someone else; this is just another user of it). The "how many ideas in a group, how many completed" functionality uses the shared small function left over from the first version, so the count and legend on every page always share the same source and cannot conflict — that piece of code survived, and the comments still bear the version number of the first version. **Writing back.** Both creating a new idea and changing a field recognize this field; it is an ID, not prose, so it is saved as a single line of plain text. An idea created by a person on a specific page defaults to being attached to the idea on that page — wherever the person builds it, that is where it grows. **Specifications and two commands.** A new section is added to the specifications, clearly defining the field, the maximum of seven per layer, the four validation rules, and the appearance of page switching; it also separately defines the name of the top layer and how that specific sentence should be written — four rules plus one real counter-example (the graph in this repository itself once had three "buckets" used for categorizing authors like "known defects," "endpoint," and "reading order," which, if copied as top-level ideas, would cause readers to immediately ask "is reading order something this project needs to do"); a "provenance" section is left at the end, stating that the predecessor was that flattened overview and why/when it was changed. The exported specification and the source file are identical byte-for-byte. The graph construction command is changed to "after extracting ideas, before connecting prerequisites, first build the tree"; the new idea command is changed to "fill in the first three questions before writing the affiliation; to start a new top layer, you must explain why this project has a large new block." **Cost, stated clearly.** The two fields from the first version were deleted, and the step labels already attached to sixty-six ideas are also invalidated. This is tearing down and restarting a task that was already completed and tested; this cost is being paid because it was known to be necessary. **One unfinished task, written here to avoid being mistaken for completed.** The tree in this repository itself only has two layers: among the five top-level ideas, four each have eleven to twenty-three descendants, and the validation is currently reporting these four warnings. The rules are established, but the middle layer has not yet been built.
Why it is implemented this way
**Why is it "one parent per idea" instead of adding another type of arrow?** In this record, "prerequisite" is the only relationship. Adding a second type of arrow would mean every time a reader sees a line, they have to ask what kind it is. Ownership only answers one question: under whom does this idea belong. It does not participate in "who must finish first," so an idea can still be a prerequisite for an idea on another branch; the page renders that prerequisite as a cross-page link. If this point is ambiguous, layering will be mistaken for a new sequence of precedence, and someone will attempt to schedule project timelines based on it. **Why replace the entire flat step-by-step overview with a tree instead of adding a layer to it?** There are three concrete reasons. First, a flat layout is inherently single-layered: its shape is "a sequential table at the top of the file + one tag per idea." To add a second layer, you would need another table and another tag, and both tables would each require maintaining their own order; a tree uses only one field to support arbitrary layers. Second, "steps" are a second type of thing that appears out of thin air: they are not ideas, they cannot be depended upon by other ideas, they have no status, and they do not have their own page. After changing to a tree, a "step" becomes just an ordinary idea—answering the eight questions, following the status flow, and having its own page—meaning the specification, engine, and write-back each require one fewer field. Third, the word "step" itself implies precedence, whereas there is no precedence between several ideas belonging under the same idea—precedence only exists via prerequisites. Credit must be given to the first version: the five sentences it wrote have today become the five ideas in the top layer, word for word, without a single change; this is empirical proof that it got half the answer right. **Why not use the existing section comments in the graph file for grouping?** This was the approach chosen by humans at the start of the first version, but it was rejected after research, and the reasons remain valid today. Comments can be used today—tests show they can be split into ten sections, and the numbers and legends match perfectly. However, they will **silently tell lies**: new ideas created on the web are appended to the end of the file, so every idea created via the web will automatically fall into the last section. This cannot be seen in the change logs or on the page; only the sentence "this section has X ideas" quietly becomes a lie. Two other reasons: comments are a verbal convention, they have never been written in the specification, they do not exist in newly created empty graphs, and if moved to another repository, they become a blank void; furthermore, the library that reads and writes this file format states in its own documentation that its comment handling is not entirely stable. **Rules must be portable; they cannot be built upon something that cannot be carried away.** **Why set the limit at seven?** A layer exceeding seven lines is not an overview, it is a table of contents—a human cannot scan it in one glance, so they won't scan it. This number can be checked by a machine, so it is a rule, not a suggestion. Fewer than seven is not a complete set, because the few that do make a set tend to become "buckets": this repository itself has produced three ("Known Defects", "Endpoint", "Reading Order"), and they fail to explain "what capability this project gained after completion." Therefore, even that counter-example is written into the specification—if you only write rules and not counter-examples, the next person will make the same mistake. **Why is a wrong attachment an error, while exceeding seven per layer is only a warning?** Attaching to a non-existent ID, or attaching in a loop, will cause the page to actually lose an idea or fail to render, while the page looks perfectly normal—that is bad, not just unattractive. "This layer has eight" simply means a human cannot scan it in one glance, but the graph itself is still correct; reporting it as an error immediately would cause every repository that has installed this tool to turn red instantly, which would be making others' repositories pay for our new rules. The cost must be stated: warnings are often overlooked, so "maximum seven per layer" currently relies on self-discipline rather than enforcement; once this field has stabilized across various repositories, we will consider tightening it. **Why does an idea say nothing if it doesn't write its own ownership?** In the first version, this had to be split into two tiers: if steps were declared but an idea had no ownership, a warning would be issued. The cost was that the numbers on the page would be undercounted, and warnings are often overlooked—that was a conscious trade-off. A tree does not have this cost: an idea without written ownership is simply an idea in the top layer, which is a valid state; the page will still display it and include it in the count. Thus, that tier of warning, along with its cost, has disappeared—it wasn't overlooked. **Why does each idea only write "who I belong to," and not "who belongs to me"?** Storing both directions would result in two sets of potentially contradictory facts, and when contradictions occur, no one knows which one counts. To clarify the weight of this statement: this repository has never actually stored a reverse subordinate list, so this rule is avoiding a problem based on experience elsewhere, rather than fixing a problem that occurred here. The half that can be verified is: by only storing the child-to-parent direction, the parent's subordinate list is recalculated every time. The cost is that retrieving an idea's subordinates requires scanning the entire graph, but with only dozens or hundreds of ideas, this overhead is negligible. **Why does a complete card for an idea only appear on its own page, with only one line placed on the parent page?** This is not a layout preference, but a mechanism: editing, draft recovery, and human sign-off on the web all find elements in the document by ID. If the same ID appears twice, these processes will silently misidentify one. A single line containing the name, status, and the first line of "what it is" is sufficient to decide whether to click into it. **"The entire graph is one file" was not a choice this time, but an inheritance.** It is written here because it explains why the page looks the way it does, not because other methods were compared this time: from day one, this web page has been a file that can be double-clicked to open and sent in its entirety to others; write-back, human sign-off, and drafts all find elements by ID within the same document. Therefore, page splitting can only be "all pages are in this one document, hidden first, and then one page is displayed according to its address." The cost must still be noted: rendering seventy-one ideas results in 1.44 million bytes, and it still opens very quickly; if it becomes ten times longer, the math should be recalculated. **Why is ownership stored as a line of plain text, rather than as a collapsed paragraph like other answers?** It is used for precise comparison with the IDs of other ideas. When a collapsed paragraph is read back, it has an extra newline at the end, making the comparison result always "no one," and this is completely invisible on the page—this is the most expensive kind of error. **Why are the descriptions of two commands being modified, rather than injecting logic into the program?** A machine cannot determine how to divide a project into major blocks or how to describe each block in plain language; this can only be done by the party that has read the project. What the program can do is validation; what it can write are only descriptions. The reason the description only references that section of the specification and does not copy the rules into it is because this tool has already paid the price for "writing the same thing in three different places" once before—the copied version will inevitably differ from the original, and no one will know which one counts. **Why is this one idea, rather than three?** The rules, the validation, and the two commands were originally three separate ideas. What actually happened was: the rules were written without validation to support them, the validation was done without the commands following, and all three were describing the same thing. The only effect of splitting them was to make people think that two-thirds of the layering work had already been completed. After merging, according to the rules of the specification, the smallest ID is kept; the other two retain their IDs, are set to blocked, and the record specifies which one they were merged into—IDs are never recycled, and the human sign-off on one of them remains exactly where it was.

How to use in the future
From now on, whenever adding any new structure to an idea graph, follow this procedure: the specification defines the rules, the validation catches violations, the page displays accordingly, and the two creation commands are written accordingly — if any of these four elements is missing, this rule will fail to propagate to other repositories. The first version was missing the latter two. This round also leaves behind one piece of experience specifically for "replacing an already implemented structure": retain the old idea's ID, set it to blocked, and clearly record in the notes which idea it was merged into; at the end of the specification section, leave a "provenance" paragraph stating what the predecessor was and why/when it was changed — this way, if someone asks six months later "did this field used to look different", they can find it through the specification without having to dig through commit records. The most important next step is to build the middle layer: currently, the four ideas that carry eleven to twenty-three sub-items each should be split into one more layer, so that those four warnings drop to zero. The rules are already there; this will be the first time they are executed through the entire process. Moving further down, the most natural step is to draw cross-layer prerequisites more clearly on the page — currently, the same page only draws dependencies between siblings, while cross-page prerequisites only appear as links within cards. Once installed into a foreign repository, its first time building a graph will directly yield a tree belonging to itself, without needing anyone to teach it.

Parent idea
A graph drawn layer by layer according to sequence.
What it is
The engine recognizes the top-level step list and the affiliation field for each idea; the validation command checks these things: assigning to a non-existent step is an error; if steps are declared but some ideas have no affiliation, or the step count is outside the three-to-seven range, or if a step has no ideas, it is a warning; a graph with no steps written at all reports nothing. Newly created ideas on the webpage are allowed to include an affiliation field. Simultaneously, all existing ideas in this repository are assigned to steps in one go.
Why this idea exists
A rule without validation is just a suggestion. Misassigned steps, missing affiliations, and uncontrolled step counts — if these are not reported on the spot via validation, they will become lies on the page that no one notices — and since the numbers on the page will always look correct, that is exactly where the danger lies.
Expected result
Assigning an idea to a non-existent step triggers a validation error; missing affiliation, out-of-range step counts, or empty steps trigger validation warnings; a graph with no steps written at all (such as a newly created empty graph) reports nothing. After all ideas in this repository are assigned to steps, validation shows zero errors.
How to implement
Two additions to the engine's graph structure: the top-level step list and the affiliation field for each idea. **Validation is split into two levels, intentionally**: assigning to a non-existent step — reports an **error** (that is a definite typo, and it would cause the numbers on the page to decrease for no reason); if steps are declared but some ideas have no affiliation, the step count is outside three to seven, or a step has no ideas — reports a **warning**; if the entire graph has no steps written — **reports nothing**. The fields allowed for new ideas include affiliation; otherwise, ideas created from the webpage could never be assigned to steps. Then, extract a small two-line function to count "how many in a group of ideas, how many completed," so that the page legend and the step-by-step overview share the same calculation method. Finally, assign all existing ideas in this repository to steps at once — this is the first example following the newly defined rules, and it also tests whether the rule is written clearly enough: if it cannot be written, the rule is not clear. The write command also recognizes this field (both the "new idea" and "modify field" paths recognize it; values are stored as a single line, not as a collapsible paragraph). For this repository, the step assignment was intended to be written via a single change file using apply, but the guard does not allow the agent to create change files on any unclaimed paths (D16), and adding paths to this idea's code would invalidate the recently obtained plan approval (D7), so the 61 steps were written into the graph one by one using the edit tool, with comments preserved as is.
Why it is implemented this way
**Why misassigned steps are an error, while missing affiliation is only a warning**: Assigning to a non-existent step is a definite typo with no second interpretation; whereas "not yet assigned" is a normal state in a world where this field has just been added — reporting an error immediately would cause every repository that has installed this tool to turn red instantly, which would be making other people's repositories pay for our new field. We must be honest about the cost: **reporting missing affiliation only as a warning means the number on the page will be undercounted, and warnings are easily overlooked by people**. This is a conscious trade-off, not an oversight; once this field has stabilized across all repositories, we will tighten it into an error. **Why nothing is reported when no steps are written at all**: A newly created empty graph, or a project that hasn't decided how many steps it has, should not be nagged by the tool. Rules are for those who want to use them, not to punish those who do not. **Why "count how many, completed how many" was extracted into a small function**: The page legend currently flattens the entire graph count into a single string, which cannot be parsed. The step-by-step overview counts by step; if they use different methods, the legend and the overview will eventually disagree — and having two conflicting numbers is more damaging to the page's credibility than having no numbers at all. **Why step assignment is included in this idea rather than being a separate one**: It is the first user of the rule. If done separately, the rule would be written but never used, and no one would know if it was written clearly enough.

Render the idea graph into a clickable, zoomable webpageCompletedRender into a self-contained webpage: at the top is a complete project graph showing only idea names, which can be panned and zoomed; click any node to jump to the detail card below, which contains all answers to the eight questions, as well as its prerequisite ideas and "which ideas it is a prerequisite for", allowing for continuous clicking in both directions.Open →
Parent idea
A graph drawn layer by layer according to sequence.
What it is
Render into a self-contained webpage: at the top is a complete project graph showing only idea names, which can be panned and zoomed; click any node to jump to the detail card below, which contains all answers to the eight questions, as well as its prerequisite ideas and "which ideas it is a prerequisite for", allowing for continuous clicking in both directions.
Why this idea exists
Projects without a visible shape will inevitably be rewritten. Graphs are for humans to look at, not for machines; the three things humans need to judge (too many nodes, missing edges, or failing to reach the endpoint) can only be judged if they are drawn.
Expected result
Double-click to open graph.html to see the project shape at a glance; lines remain sharp after zooming; dragging will not be misidentified as clicking a node.
How to implement
Mermaid flowchart TD (CDN) handles the layout, node labels only contain the name, and click callbacks jump to details. Zooming relies on modifying the SVG's own width/height to trigger a vector redraw, while panning relies on the wrapper's translate.
Why it is implemented this way
Use Mermaid instead of d3 / cytoscape: static HTML, no build steps, and no need to start a server. Zooming deliberately avoids CSS scale() — code comments specify that scale() rasterizes the layer once before stretching, which is exactly why it previously looked blurry; fit only scales up and never down, because putting a small image at 235% is not what anyone means when they say "fit to window."

Arrange ideas according to dependency order: prerequisites always come first.CompletedGiven a graph, return a list of ideas sorted by topological order: each idea is placed after all its prerequisites; within the same layer, sort by id (topological order is not unique, so a fixed rule is needed to ensure the same output order every time); if the graph has cycles or edges pointing to non-existent ids, do not enter an infinite loop and do not lose any nodes.Open →
Parent idea
A graph drawn layer by layer according to sequence.
What it is
Given a graph, return a list of ideas sorted by topological order: each idea is placed after all its prerequisites; within the same layer, sort by id (topological order is not unique, so a fixed rule is needed to ensure the same output order every time); if the graph has cycles or edges pointing to non-existent ids, do not enter an infinite loop and do not lose any nodes.
Why this idea exists
Now 'reading from top to bottom is the dependency order' is just a coincidence — this graph is built bottom-up all at once. /ccthink will make this coincidence fail by appending each new idea to the end of the file.
Expected result
Given a graph where prerequisites are written later, each idea in the returned list is still placed after all its prerequisites; the same input always gives the same output; graphs with cycles will not cause it to hang or swallow nodes.
How to implement
Add an independent function `topoOrder` in the graph query section using Kahn's algorithm: First, calculate the in-degree of each idea based on the number of `needs`; skip edges pointing to non-existent IDs directly (following the existing convention in this file—dangling edges are silently ignored, and `check` will report errors); then proceed layer by layer: extract the entire batch of nodes with an in-degree of zero, sort them by ID, and output them together, then use the nodes they unlock as the next layer, repeating this process. This is the literal meaning of "sorting by ID within the same layer"—depth comes first, ID comes second; it is neither a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue nor a greedy approach that takes the minimum at each step (both of those would move an idea from the second layer ahead of an idea from the first layer that has not yet been output). After finishing, take the nodes whose in-degree is still greater than zero (i.e., those in a cycle), sort them by ID, and append them to the end, losing none. The three orders look very similar, and a three-node linear fixture cannot distinguish them, so the tests must use the following two small graphs (I have run all three implementations, and the numbers are actual outputs, not conjectures): I. I-002 needs I-001, I-004 needs I-003 — both layer-by-layer and FIFO give I-001, I-003, I-002, I-004, while taking the minimum at each step gives I-001, I-002, I-003, I-004. This fixture catches "taking the minimum at each step." II. I-003 needs I-002, I-004 needs I-001 — layer-by-layer gives I-001, I-002, I-003, I-004, while FIFO gives I-001, I-002, I-004, I-003. This fixture catches "copying codex." Both are required; having only one would allow the other incorrect implementation to pass. The return value is the idea objects themselves, accessed by array index without going through the ID lookup table: the lookup table only keeps the last entry for duplicate IDs, and the command-line `render` never runs `check` first, so duplicate IDs would cause a card to vanish into thin air. Do not modify the existing `findCycle`.
Why it is implemented this way
This algorithm does not need to be invented from scratch—there is already a version in the Python implementation of this repository, which even defines two contracts: skip dangling edges instead of erroring, and return nodes in a cycle as data instead of throwing an exception. Borrow its shape, but the queue must be replaced: it uses FIFO (sorting only at the initial seed and each expansion), which is neither "sorting by ID within the same layer" nor "taking the minimum at each step"—the three orders are distinct, and copying it will result in the third type. To distinguish between layer-by-layer and FIFO, use the second fixture in `how`: I-003 needs I-002, I-004 needs I-001 — layer-by-layer gives I-001, I-002, I-003, I-004, while FIFO gives I-001, I-002, I-004, I-003. (The counter-example written here previously was wrong and is now void: "Four ideas A B C D, the only edge is C needs A, FIFO gives A B D C" — layer-by-layer also gives A B D C; this fixture can only catch "taking the minimum at each step" and cannot distinguish FIFO. I have manually derived the three orders one by one and am writing them here to prevent the next person from being misled by it.) This point is explicitly required by `expected`, so it must be decided and clearly documented. I choose layer-by-layer because its sole consumer, I-061, requires exactly this: "Cards are arranged from the foundation with no prerequisites all the way to the end"—read all ideas without prerequisites first, then read those built upon them. Taking the minimum at each step cannot achieve this: it would output an idea from the second layer with a smaller ID before an idea from the first layer has been output. The divergence between these three orders must be recorded in the divergence adjudication table in `FORMAT.md`, because `codex` is already running another one. Why not merge with `findCycle`: it breaks the entire traversal when it encounters the first cycle, and merging would return a truncated order, losing nodes—whereas "not losing nodes" is exactly what `expected` forbids violating. Furthermore, the required return values differ: `check` prints the path of the cycle (which only depth-first can provide), while `topoOrder` requires the complete sequence. `findCycle` is code already completed by someone else (I-042). Why not use an existing sorting library: this engine has zero-dependency as a design prerequisite; moreover, existing libraries do not provide the two things truly needed here—deciding same-layer order by ID and returning nodes in a cycle as data; re-implementing them would require an extra wrapper. To answer an obvious counter-question: I-043 once wrote "do not perform topological sort." That adjudication has not been overturned—`frontier` answers a state question (which ones can start working now), while `topoOrder` answers a structural question (in what order should this graph be read). The two are mutually exclusive, and `topoOrder` must never become aware of state, nor should `frontier` be changed to be built upon it. Known boundary: "sorting by ID" means sorting by characters. Current IDs are three-digit numbers with zero-padding, so character order happens to equal numerical order; a project using a mix of one-digit and two-digit IDs would sort in reverse. Use standard sorting (consistent with the other two places in this file) without locale-dependent comparisons—that would cause the same input to produce different outputs on different machines.

Parent idea
A graph drawn layer by layer according to sequence.
What it is
`render()` uses topological order when outputting the detail cards below, rather than the writing order in the YAML. IDs remain unchanged, and the YAML source files remain unchanged—only the rendered web page changes.
Why this idea exists
Humans read the web page. If the order is incorrect, readers must manually trace every `needs` in their heads to know what to look at first.
Expected result
Open `graph.html`: the foundation with no prerequisites is at the front, and every card is placed after all its prerequisites; reshuffle the writing order of ideas in the YAML and re-render, the card order remains unchanged.
How to implement
Only one change: in the line that outputs the detail cards when generating the webpage, replace "traverse by writing order" with "sort by topoOrder before traversing". topoOrder is a function already built by I-060, and to date, it has no production callers — only its own tests in the entire repository use it. This idea is its first consumer, so no additional sorting logic needs to be written, and the order does not need to be redefined (I-060 has already selected "by layer, and by id within the layer" for this consumer). There are three things that must remain untouched, each with a specific reason. 1. The flowchart above: its node declaration order comes from the shared drawing function, and existing tests assert that "the graph drawn on the page is word-for-word equal to what that function calculates"; touching it means touching the already established visual, and since the layout engine's result depends on the node declaration order, the graph would change its appearance for no reason. 2. The JSON data model embedded in the page: I-062 defines that "JSON is the sole data model for the page, and the DOM is merely its view"; card order is a matter of the view and should not move the model in reverse; a more practical reason is that every time the page structure changes, it recalculates the flowchart source code according to the order of this JSON. Once the JSON is reordered while the initial graph is not, if a person breaks a prerequisite for the first time, the entire graph will re-layout and jump instantly because the declaration order changed. 3. Anchors and jumps: card ids, links, and click jumps all find elements by id and are independent of order; after reordering, clicking a node will still jump to it — this point must be pinned down in the tests, not just relied upon through reasoning. Additionally, add a line of explanation for humans under the "Idea Details" title: "Cards are arranged by dependency order, not by the writing order in the file," otherwise readers will think the rendering is wrong if they see an order different from the YAML.
Why it is implemented this way
Compared four approaches. Sorting by id: ids are assigned sequentially as they are written, so sorting by id is basically equivalent to sorting by writing order, which is exactly the problem this idea aims to fix; furthermore, it directly violates the sentence "how it will be used in the future" — the id of a new idea is always the largest and will only appear last. Sorting by status (completed first, todo later): that answers "which ones can start working now," but frontier is already answering that question; I-043 ruled on this once, and I-060 reaffirmed it: status issues and structural issues are two different things, and the order of reading the graph is a structural issue. Moreover, sorting by status would split a dependency chain into four segments, giving the reader even more prerequisites to track. Directly reordering the ideas in the YAML to make the file order equal to the dependency order: the "What is it" section explicitly states the source file remains untouched, and this path hits two hard constraints — approval is bound to the hash of the graph content, so reordering the file is changing the content, making a graph just approved invalid instantly; the expiration check used during webpage submission also uses the same fingerprint. Changing a file that has just been human sign-off for the sake of layout involves costs and risks that are disproportionate. Reordering using a script in the browser: this is equivalent to rewriting the topological sort in the page, whereas I-076 just spent an entire idea refactoring the "graph drawing algorithm" into a single piece of source code shared by the engine and the page, precisely because a second hand-copied version would inevitably drift; since the engine side already has topoOrder, sorting once during rendering adds zero extra bytes to the page and avoids the jump caused by reordering after loading. Choosing "sort during rendering, only sort cards" is because it is the only approach that only moves the view, without moving the model or the files: the YAML remains unchanged, the ids remain unchanged, the JSON data model remains unchanged, and the flowchart remains unchanged; only the order seen by a person opening the webpage changes. Also need to correct one sentence in the original "Expected Result": it says "cards are arranged from the foundation with no prerequisites all the way to the end," but a layered topological order cannot provide this — in actual testing in this repository, five endpoints fall at positions 29, 30, 33, 34, and 40, with only the last one being exactly at the end. Topological order guarantees that "every card is placed after all its prerequisites," but does not guarantee "the endpoint is last": a shallow endpoint will naturally be placed before a deep non-endpoint. Rewritten according to what can actually be achieved.

Parent idea
A graph drawn layer by layer according to sequence.
What it is
Currently, the algorithm for "one idea graph → flowchart source text" only lives inside the function that generates the web page, and it references several variables outside that function. Extract it into an independent function that references no external variables, so that the engine side and the browser side run the exact same source code — text purification, long name line wrapping, coloring by status, and click binding are all moved into this function.
Why this idea exists
Once the structure can be modified (adding an idea, breaking an arrow), the browser must be able to recalculate the flowchart source text and redraw it itself. There are only two ways to do this: hand-copy this algorithm again in the web page, or have both sides share the same one. A hand-copied second version will inevitably drift — if the line-wrapping rule is changed on only one side, the same idea graph will look different in two places, and no test will detect it.
Expected result
For the same idea graph, when the engine calls this function and the web page calls this function, they obtain identical flowchart source text, character for character; the existing web page's appearance, connections, and click behavior remain unchanged by a single pixel.
How to implement
Move the entire loop that generates the flowchart source text into a new function. It only accepts one idea graph and references nothing outside the function — the six items currently used by it: index lookup table, endpoint set, index-to-node-name conversion, classification by status, long name line wrapping, and text purification, are all moved inside the function body. Then, embed the function body into the web page script as a **string constant**, rather than using Function.prototype.toString to retrieve its source code at runtime. The engine side calls this function directly, and the web page side executes the same text. The way to lock in "the same source code" is a single test: for the same idea graph, calculate once on both sides and assert that the outputs are identical character for character.
Why it is implemented this way
The original plan was to "inject the page using Function.prototype.toString during rendering." This path is broken in this repository; I have tested it: tsx hard-codes esbuild's keepNames to enabled (searchable in installed packages, and there is no environment variable to turn it off), so any named const in the function body will be compiled into a call to __name(...), and __name is a free variable injected by the compiler — in other words, the prerequisite of "zero closure" is precisely destroyed by the compiler itself. I ran a function of the same shape with real tsx, evaluated the injection result, and it reported __name is undefined. What is even more fatal is that it cannot be caught: the transformation suite used for running tests does not depend on esbuild, so tests will all be green, while the page opened by double-clicking will error out directly. A failure mode that a test can never discover should not be chosen. Remediation is not impossible — write a __name shim before injection and add a test that actually spawns a child process to watch it — but that would be to preserve a mechanism that provides no benefit here, adding two new things out of thin air. Since the page generation script is already hand-written using template strings (as is already done in this file), writing the function body as a string constant involves zero extra mechanisms. The cost must be stated clearly: the string constant version loses type checking. Therefore, that test of "identical character-for-character output on both sides" is not just a bonus; it is the safety net for this decision, and without it, this choice is invalid.

Parent idea
Three gates: Start, Write Implementation, and Complete
What it is
Add capabilities to the common engine that were first implemented in the Cursor version: new (creates a new idea, takes a number from the next_id counter at the top of the graph, and increments it after use), allow (asks "Can I write now?" before writing a specific file, and the answer must be exactly consistent with the guard), status (provides an overview of where each idea is blocked); before changing the status to doing, the program checks if the plan fields are complete, if all prerequisites are finished, and if the file to be written overlaps with another ongoing idea; status can only follow a small state transition table; skipping steps will be rejected.
Why this idea exists
These checks are a unique advantage of the Cursor version; the D17/D18/D19/D28 adjudication table has ruled that they are required. Rules written only in prompts are forgotten as soon as the agent gets busy; by turning them into program checks, the precedence in the graph truly holds authority.
Expected result
If one plan field is missing, one prerequisite is lacking, or one file overlaps, the transition from todo→doing is rejected, and the rejection must specify what is missing; numbers issued by new must only come from next_id, so creating a new idea after deleting the idea with the maximum number will not cause number collisions; allow's permission/rejection for any file must be consistent with the actual result of running the guard once.
How to implement
Port three pure functions (isBuildReady / needsUnmet / fileClash) and three subcommands (new / allow / status) from cursor-companion/ideas.ts; modify new to take numbers from the top-level next_id of the graph (when the field does not yet exist in the graph, initialize and write it all at once as "maximum existing number plus one", thereafter it only increments); add a four-state small transition table in set, which runs the three checks in sequence during todo→doing, and prints exactly what is missing for the user to see.
Why it is implemented this way
Option 1: Rely only on the guard to block during code writing (I-093) — by then the human has already started working, and errors are exposed too late; rejecting on the spot during set doing has the lowest cost of correction. Option 2: Follow the current Cursor status of issuing numbers via "maximum number plus one" — explicitly rejected by format specifications (re-issuing the same number after deleting the maximum number), must use next_id. The three functions are moved directly without rewriting because they already have behavioral test endorsement from test_companion_gate.

Parent idea
Three gates: Start, Write Implementation, and Complete
What it is
A guard.ts is attached to PreToolUse / PostToolUse / Stop / UserPromptSubmit, dispatching seven rules based on events: R1 automatically logs every edit; R2 the status of an existing idea can only be changed via set; R3 implementation writing is forbidden if the test file does not exist; R4 code cannot be touched if how / why_this_way are not filled; R5 the turn cannot end if the graph has errors; R6 implementation cannot start if the graph has no human sign-off; R7 a file is only considered scanned if it has truly been Read.
Why this idea exists
The five commands are merely prompts — an agent can skip research, fabricate why_this_way, directly Edit to change the status to done to bypass all checks, or self-answer "it looks reasonable" and continue. Discipline written in prompts becomes meaningless by the thirtieth round of dialogue.
Expected result
Skipping tests to write implementation will be rejected, and it will be told which file to write first; manually changing status will be rejected, and the required set command will be provided; if the graph is broken, the turn cannot end; every edit leaves a line in ideas/log.md, requiring no cooperation from the agent.
How to implement
Exit code 2 + stderr = "intercept and tell Claude the reason"; this is the only universal mechanism across the four hook events, so a script dispatching by hook_event_name is sufficient. install.ts is responsible for writing into the target repository's .claude/settings.json without overwriting others' hooks.
Why it is implemented this way
Only enforce things a machine can judge: whether a file exists, whether fields are filled, whether status has changed, and whether it passed check. The quality of eight questions or the honesty of web searches cannot be forced; the only line of defense is to make omissions visible in check and rendering — hard-blocking something that cannot be judged accurately is worse than not blocking at all. All exception paths fail open (code comment: a guard that crashes must never block work); if the guard itself crashes, it must not lock humans out; AIDEV_GUARD=off is the escape hatch.

Parent idea
Three gates: Start, Write Implementation, and Complete
What it is
The run-check command runs verification commands on behalf of the agent, recording the exit code, the end of the output, and the content fingerprint of the test files into ideas/.runtime/: Before implementation, there must be one record of "test actually failed" (called RED); every time an implementation file is written, the old passing record (called GREEN) expires; marking done must have a currently valid GREEN or a manual verification signed by a human. If a test passes unexpectedly before being implemented, a human must approve an exemption to continue.
Why this idea exists
Only checking "test file exists" cannot distinguish between a truly failed test and an empty file (current Claude version status); the Cursor version has no defense against test-first at all. Codex has proven that "test before implementation" can be implemented with evidence; the adjudication table D8/D20 rules that the common base is not allowed to be weaker than it.
Expected result
When there is no RED record, writing implementation files is rejected; if implementation is changed after GREEN and marked done without re-running, it is rejected; if the test file is changed, old evidence is immediately invalidated; if it unexpectedly turns Green first without a human-approved exemption, progress cannot proceed.
How to implement
The run-check subcommand carries --phase red|green: run verify.command at the project root (reusing Cursor version's 120-second timeout and retries when Windows cannot find the command), saving the exit code, the last two thousand characters of the output, and the sha256 of each file in verify.test_files into each idea record in ideas/.runtime/; the guard's write-after record increments a monotonic counter for product file writes, and the GREEN record stores the counter value at the time of its execution; when setting done, re-verify that GREEN exists, the counter has not fallen behind, and the test hash has not changed. If the exit code in the red phase is 0, it is recorded as "unexpected early pass"; thereafter, implementation writing can only be released after a I-090 exemption receipt.
Why it is implemented this way
An alternative is to retain the Claude version's "test file exists is enough" — which cannot distinguish between a truly failed test and an empty file; the D8 adjudication explicitly refuses to regress the Codex evidence chain. Use a monotonic counter instead of a timestamp to judge "expiration," because timestamp resolution is low and they may roll back, whereas the counter is driven only by hooks; test file hashes are bound to prevent "post-hoc test modification." The mechanism is ported from the verified behavior of codex-companion; its corresponding Python tests are rewritten as vitest to serve as the porting checklist.

Clean up expired hook configurations pointing to deleted code.CompletedThere are still two hooks in .claude/settings.json pointing to packages/hook/dist/*.js, but packages/ has already been deleted in ca7e956.Open →
Parent idea
Three gates: Start, Write Implementation, and Complete
What it is
There are still two hooks in .claude/settings.json pointing to packages/hook/dist/*.js, but packages/ has already been deleted in ca7e956.
Why this idea exists
These two hooks run once during every edit and fail every time. This repository itself is the first user of this workflow; its own configuration points to non-existent files, indicating that the promise that "installation is reversible and re-entrant" has not yet covered uninstallation.
Expected result
Only the claude-companion/guard.ts set of hooks remains in settings.json; there are no longer failing hook processes when editing files.
How to implement
Manually delete those two hook group objects in .claude/settings.json that are holding packages/hook/dist; the uninstallation feature will not be implemented in this round. The arrays for the two events will not become empty because of this, so no logic for cleaning up empty objects is required. After deleting, maintain the same shape generated by the installer (two-space indentation, one newline at the end), otherwise, the next time the installer runs, it will create a change to the entire file out of thin air. At the same time, add a regression test: extract the word that looks like a script from each hook command in settings.json (ends with .js/.ts/.mjs/.cjs/.py, remove quotes, parse relative path against the project root), and assert that the file it points to actually exists. This test is currently red and will turn green after deletion. Add one more assertion: each of the four events (PreToolUse / PostToolUse / Stop / UserPromptSubmit) must still retain at least one hook containing guard.ts in its commands. Without this, deleting the entire guard section would also make the first assertion turn green — a "pass by deleting everything" test, which perfectly rewards the exact kind of failure this idea should not cause.
Why it is implemented this way
First, why "delete" instead of "disable": Claude Code does not have a switch to disable individual hooks; the only switch would disable all hooks together, including the guard itself; and the hooks in settings.local.json are additive and merged, with no syntax to "negate a specific item from a previous layer." Therefore, deletion is the only way to avoid accidentally harming the guard. Second, why not just implement an uninstallation feature: the D14 of the common base has already adjudicated the scope of responsibility for install.ts — local development, old installation migration, and viewing/refreshing installed repositories; formal distribution and uninstallation are handled by each agent's own plugin layer. Creating an uninstallation subcommand now would be equivalent to building something that the common base has explicitly decided not to own. In the history of this repository, there actually was an uninstallation script (in the parent commit of ca7e956); its approach was to filter out its own entries based on characteristic substrings in the commands, and then remove the resulting empty groups — which is also the standard solution across the entire ecosystem. However, it relies on a different registry format and several files that no longer exist; bringing the whole thing back would be the kind of scope expansion that was rejected. When actually implemented, it would be a dozen lines of inversion of the four lines of filtering logic in installHooks, not something new. Finally, why a manual deletion read by a human instead of creating a new mechanism: the commit message for ca7e956 explicitly states "also deleted references interrupted by the archiving action: pointing to the hook in packages/hook/dist," and the change to settings.json in that commit only rearranged those two items from single lines into indented JSON, without deleting a single one. The reason is that the installHooks filter only recognizes its own command names, so it cannot structurally delete others'. This file has already been fooled once by an automatic fix that "looked successful"; we shouldn't let it happen a second time. There is also one risk that must be stated: this is the agent modifying the file that "decides whether the agent is managed." Cursor's specification directly prohibits this (it lists hook configuration as a locked file, with the reason being that agents are not allowed to uninstall their own constraints), whereas the common base's D24 did not put hook configuration on the protection list. The mitigation is for a human to read the changes before committing.
Where is the code
.claude/settings.json:21-64 · hooks
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_settings_hooks.test.ts → exit 0
How to use in the future
With an uninstallation path, this set of tools becomes truly reversible when installed into someone else's repository.

Parent idea
Three gates: Start, Write Implementation, and Complete
What it is
Write only one version of the guard's judgment logic: the input is a normalized event (which event, which tool, which files to modify, what the human said), and the output is allow or deny plus a reason. Rules include: files without an idea claim are denied write access by default; writing is not allowed if the idea is not ready; writing is not allowed without approval; implementation is not allowed without failure test records; no one is allowed to directly write to evidence files managed by the program; file writing tricks in shell commands (redirection, in-place replacement, one-liner file writing via interpreter) are also blocked; write operations where the target cannot be identified are directly denied; the idea graph must pass verification before the session ends. If a crash occurs during the pre-write or approval stage, block it; if a crash occurs during post-write recording, only warn and do not block (Decision Table D9); AIDEV_GUARD=off is the only escape hatch; using it will trigger a loud warning and be recorded.
Why this idea exists
The three sets of guards each have unique strengths and fatal weaknesses: the Claude version is comprehensive but "allows through on crash"; the Cursor version lacks approval and testing prerequisites; the Codex version cannot see writes from MCP tools. Rules must be written only once, so that fixing one place affects all three simultaneously, to truly qualify as a common foundation.
Expected result
Every rule has a corresponding test: out-of-bounds writes, unapproved, no failure records, shell bypass, unknown targets—all are denied with human-readable reasons; failure in post-write recording does not block a completed write; the guarantees expressed by the existing tests of the three providers are all restored under the common rules.
How to implement
A pure function decide(normalized_event, idea_graph, evidence) in companion/guard.ts executes the rule table in order: evidence files managed by the program and generated files can only be modified via CLI; idea graphs and logs are editable, but if a direct modification to the status or signed_off fields is detected compared to the old idea graph, it is denied (plugging the hole where the Cursor version "agent modifies the ledger itself to unlock"); the product path must hit a code or test_files of a ready doing idea, otherwise deny by default; then check the approval receipt (I-090) and failure test evidence (I-091); shell commands must pass three layers of regex (ported from codex-companion: redirection, in-place replacement, interpreter one-liners, package managers); write operations where the target cannot be identified are directly denied; run check at Stop. In the catch blocks for pre-write, approval, and Stop, return deny; in the catch block for post-write recording, only warn and do not block (D9); AIDEV_GUARD=off allows everything but issues a prominent warning every time and attempts to record it.
Why it is implemented this way
Rather than patching three separate guards, it is better to write the rules as a pure function and feed normalized events directly into the fixture—the closest online precedent, Probity (a TypeScript program serving the three Claude/Codex/Copilot providers), uses this architecture, proving it is feasible. The rejection order checks protected files before claims, because the most common agent transgression is touching evidence first; the crash direction is categorized by event (block before write, allow after write), where Codex's hybrid model wins among the current status of the three: Claude's full allowance would miss irreversible out-of-bounds writes, while Cursor's full blocking would halt the entire repository due to logger bugs.
Where is the code
companion/guard.ts:1-316 · decide / record and rule table
How to verify

How to use in the future
Modify only this single function for the new rules; the thin layer between the three I-094 providers and this function is the only interface.

Parent idea
Three gates: Start, Write Implementation, and Complete
What it is
The guard can recognize if an agent is driving the browser. Today, any MCP call that does not include a file path or a content field is categorized as "other" and allowed through (companion/guard.ts:1510, original comment: "a read-shaped MCP call is not ours to block"). Change it to: first check if this call points to the local service — any address falling within the loopback address plus the serve port must be blocked with a clear explanation of why; calls to execute scripts on the page should also be blocked. The reason for blocking must be a human-readable sentence, and it must honestly state that this is a guardrail, not a sandbox.
Why this idea exists
Any button on the page with authority is effectively zero if an agent can click it. Today, this path is open: the browser tool's navigate opens pages, computer clicks buttons, and javascript_tool runs scripts directly on the page; none of these three include a file path or a content field, so they all hit that "allow" branch. Meanwhile, the entire downloader family on the shell side has long been blocked as a "write file" verb (companion/guard.ts:705), and the interpreter wall also blocks node --eval — in other words, the front door is locked tight, but a back door is left open that no one sees. This hole exists today, regardless of whether web approval is implemented later.
Expected result
If an agent attempts to open the browser to the local service address, it is rejected on the spot, with a clear explanation of which rule was triggered and why. A human opening the same address in a browser is unaffected. If the guard crashes or fails to recognize a call, allow it through as before, so as not to lock humans out.
How to implement
Three steps. First, add the rule to the dispatch table in decideInner (companion/guard.ts:164 area), **do not write it into mcpEvent**. normalize() runs outside of decide's try/catch (:1821), and there is no .catch after readStdin().then() — throwing an exception in mcpEvent is equivalent to an unhandled promise rejection, exit code 1, and the host allowing it through; furthermore, in that specific hook, both the shell wall and the pre-write wall failed to run. To effectively block it, it must be placed where try/catch can manage it. Second, the criterion must be **identified by target, not by tool name**: extract the URL from the calling parameters, and block anything falling on a loopback address — the entire loopback family, regardless of port. serve has --port (:3681), so if the port is hardcoded, the rule will be missed as soon as a parameter is added. Third, block calls that execute scripts on a page as a separate reason. The rejection message should follow the structure of the existing three: which rule, why, and where the way out is, and explicitly state that this is a guard, not a sandbox. The new event type must also modify encodeClaude (:1588-1603), otherwise the rejection will fall through to a bare exit code 2 — the host recognizes this code, but cannot obtain the structured reason, so a human only sees a single failure without explanation.
Why it is implemented this way
Why identify by URL instead of tool name: enumerating browsers by name (e.g., matching tool names containing 'browser') would both miss various differently-named integrations and immediately trigger a red failure in test_base_guard_shell_targets.test.ts:231 for "navigating to example.com must be allowed" — that test is correct; letting an agent access the internet is normal work, and only the specific instance of targeting a local service should be blocked. Why block the entire loopback family instead of just the serve port: the guard and the service are two separate processes, and the guard has no reliable way to know which port the service is currently running on. Why not assume browser tools will all be allowed today: MCP_WRITEISH (:1410) includes create and write; calls like opening a new tab or writing to the clipboard have already been rejected by the sentence in :193 "this call might write a file, but it is unclear where it writes" — new rules must avoid this, otherwise a single call will stack two sets of contradictory reasons. **The honest boundary must be written into the rejection message**: Local testing on 2026-09-05 — clicking a button with a browser tool resulted in isTrusted being true, navigator.userActivation.isActive being true, and navigator.webdriver being false, exactly the same as a manual click. Therefore, the value of this rule is to turn "something that can be done easily" into "something that requires an explicit bypass," not to make it impossible. Claiming the latter will cause the next person reading the code to overestimate this wall.

Parent idea
Three gates: Start, Write Implementation, and Complete
What it is
The hook wiring lists for the three parties (.claude/settings.json, .cursor/hooks.json, .codex/hooks.json) currently only send edit-type, shell-type, and calls starting with mcp__ into the guard. Web-fetching tools (called WebFetch on the Claude side) belong to neither category, so the guard cannot even see these calls. Supplement each of the three lists with it, and also supplement the one planted by the installer into the new repository. Add one more test: if a tool that should be seen by the guard is missing from the list, it must turn red.
Why this idea exists
The rule established by I-104 in the guard adjudicates "this call is targeting the local service." But no matter how correct the rule is, if the event cannot reach the guard, it is as if it does not exist — web-fetching tools are exactly such a path: they can directly request the local service on 127.0.0.1, but neither of the two PreToolUse matchers (edit and shell types for .claude/settings.json:54, and the mcp__ prefix for :68) matches it. Currently, there is nothing guarding this type of misconfiguration: test_base_manifests.test.ts has a GUARDED whitelist, but it only asserts those things already written in the list and will not turn red if one is missing — meaning the same error will be repeated in the future, and no one will notice it.
Expected result
Send the web-fetching tools into the guard for all three lists, and do the same for the new repository planted by the installer. When an agent is blocked while using a web-fetching tool to request a local service, the reason should be consistent with the I-104 rule. If a tool that should be seen by the guard is deleted from any list, the test must turn red immediately. A human accessing the same address in a browser should remain unaffected.
How to implement
Three steps. First, for the PreToolUse of the three manifests (.claude/settings.json, .cursor/hooks.json, .codex/hooks.json), supplement the tool names used for fetching web pages on this platform. Claude's current two matchers are .claude/settings.json:54 (editor and shell types) and :68 (mcp__ prefix), neither of which covers the web-fetching tools. Second, supplement the manifest used for installing new repositories into the installer (companion/install.ts) — if not supplemented, every time a new repository is installed, the same hole will be created. Third, change the GUARDED whitelist in test_base_manifests.test.ts from "asserting these are written in the manifest" to "the manifest must cover this table; if one is missing, it turns red." Since the tool names differ across the three providers, the whitelist is divided by platform.
Why it is implemented this way
Why split I-104 into two ideas: I-104 modifies the guard's judgment, while this item modifies whether the event can actually reach the guard. Their failure modes are completely different — a wrong rule will block the wrong things, which is immediately visible to humans; a misconfigured connection results in nothing happening, with no signs at all. If merged into one idea, verification could only cover one half. Why change the whitelist to a reverse assertion: currently, this table only asserts what has already been written, so missing an entry won't turn red — meaning the same error will recur in the future without anyone noticing. This time, the hole was not caught by tests, but by a human reading the connections; the fact itself is evidence. Why not just list all tools capable of sending requests: it's impossible to list them all, and the list would expire. The true safety net is the rule in I-104 based on the target URL; what is being supplemented here is "allowing the event to reach the guard" — both are required to work together; neither is sufficient alone. This must be clearly stated to prevent anyone from thinking that supplementing the list solves everything.
Where is the code
.claude/settings.json
.cursor/hooks.json
.codex/hooks.json

How to use in the future
From now on, the three connection manifests are managed by a single table. Adding a tool that should be seen by the guard simply means adding a row to the table. All three providers follow suit, and if one misses it, the test will report it immediately.

Parent idea
Approval can only come from a single sentence manually replied by a human
What it is
Set up an approval gate for both splitting and planning: when the agent requests approval, the program creates a summary of "the content the human needs to see" and generates a one-time approval code; approval only takes effect when the human manually replies with this approval code in the conversation, and the receipt (who, when, which summary approved) is stored in ideas/.runtime/ and kept by the program. If even one character of the content changes, or if the approval code is used once, the approval becomes invalid. Human sign-off follows the same path.
Why this idea exists
Claude's current approval is the word "approve" for the entire message, bound to the full graph hash — this prevents agent impersonation, but approving the full graph in batches does not prove the human has seen a specific split; Cursor has no approval at all. Codex's one-time approval code plus content summary is the strongest among the three, and the D7/D26/D27 adjudication table has ruled to transform it into two regular gates.
Expected result
Replying with the same approval code twice results in failure on the second attempt; if the approved content is modified and used again after approval, it fails; if the receipt file is written directly by the agent, it will be rejected by the guard; the splitting gate and the planning gate can request and approve independently.
How to implement
Reconstruct in TypeScript based on the verified behavior of codex-companion: request-approval generates a one-time approval code (cryptographically random, CC-XXXXXXXX), and writes it into ideas/.runtime/pending/ along with the gate name, involved nodes, and content summary; the summary follows the "sha256 after newline normalization" method; the splitting gate creates a summary of the full graph's numbering/name/edge/eight questions projection, while the planning gate creates a summary of the single node's eight questions plus path plus verification projection; in the UserPromptSubmit event, the entire message must strictly match "approve [approval code]" or "APPROVE [approval code]" to be consumed, and the receipt (who, when, which summary approved, original text hash) is written into .runtime/approvals/; if the approved content changes, the pending files are deleted and the reason is explained. Human sign-off and unexpected green exemptions follow the same challenge/receipt path.
Why it is implemented this way
Option 1: Follow Claude's current "the entire message is the approval, bound to the full graph hash" — the same "approve" can be replayed if the graph is unchanged, and it cannot prove the human has seen any specific split; D7 has ruled this obsolete. Option 2: Codex's five gates — too heavy; D7 has reduced them to two regular gates and two on-demand gates. The behavior of single-use approval codes and content binding is copied from codex-companion (its Python tests directly assert these properties); online Baseline projects use the same "human generates markers, agent cannot forge" approach, supporting this direction.
Where is the code
companion/ideas.ts:564-709 · requestApproval / applyApproval / validApproval / approvalSnapshot
How to verify

How to use in the future

Parent idea
Approval can only come from a single sentence manually replied by a human
What it is
Approval is bound to the first 12 characters of the graph's sha256; it is only written into ideas/.approved when the entire message in the UserPromptSubmit event is exactly "批准 / approve / 同意"; if a single character in the graph is changed, the approval becomes invalid. The files .approved and .scan-todo, which record approval and scanning progress respectively, are blocked by PreToolUse; the agent cannot use Write to write to them directly.
Why this idea exists
Any marker that an agent can write, an agent can forge. If a "I have confirmed" marker is written by the constrained party themselves, it cannot constrain anything.
Expected result
Modifying an unapproved graph will be rejected and will require showing it to a human first; "I do not approve" will not be counted as an approval; no tool event can produce an approval.
How to implement
APPROVALS is a set that compares the entire prompt after trim + lowercase + removing trailing punctuation; newline characters are normalized before hashing to prevent CRLF detection from being read as a different graph.
Why it is implemented this way
Bind "I did it" to an event that cannot be produced without actually doing it: UserPromptSubmit is only triggered when a human manually types the message. Judge "the entire message is an approval" rather than "the message contains an approval", otherwise "I do not approve" will be counted as an approval. Known ceiling (as truthfully stated in README): an agent can still use Bash to feed a fake UserPromptSubmit directly to guard.ts. R6 blocks accidental skipping, not an agent determined to bypass it.
