Parent idea
Synthesize the three implementations into one
What it is
The migrate command reads three old formats — suffix-bearing graph.claude.yaml, graph.cursor.yaml, and Codex's one-node-one-file JSON — and converts them into one ideas/graph.yaml; transferable approval and verification evidence are also moved into .runtime/; if multiple old graphs exist in the same repository, stop and let a human choose or merge, never automatically pick a winner; fields that cannot be converted are listed in a report for a human to see. Old files are kept as-is, read-only.
Why this idea exists
Adjudication table D10 rules that graphs belong to the project, not the agent; only implementation is unified, state is not migrated; changing an agent still won't allow it to take over. Migration is a one-time, lossy, and risky operation, so it must be explicit, must be auditable, and must let humans make choices.
Expected result
Each of the three old formats has one migration sample, and verification passes after migration; when two old graphs coexist, the command stops and presents the differences to a human; the migration report lists every field that could not be converted losslessly; old files remain unchanged after migration.
How to implement
The migrate subcommand scans graph.claude.yaml, graph.cursor.yaml under ideas/, and JSONs under .codex-companion*/nodes/: when there is only one source, convert directly (Codex fields are mapped according to D2 — expected_result becomes expected, implementation.how becomes how, code_refs becomes code, eight states are compressed back to four states, and extra fields are listed one by one in the report); when there are multiple sources, print a difference table and exit, waiting for a human to explicitly choose using --pick or --merge; transferable approval receipts and test evidence are moved into .runtime/; run a check before writing, and do not commit to disk if it fails; old files are all left untouched.
Why it is implemented this way
Alternative one: The installer automatically picks the "most recently modified graph" as the winner — explicitly forbidden by D10. Alternative two: Do not migrate and let humans hand-copy — hand-copying a graph with over fifty nodes will surely result in errors, and evidence files are even harder to hand-copy. Explicit commands, human choices, and issuing a report before committing to disk is the direction already adjudicated in the I-070 original text; this is simply making it into an independent, verifiable step.

Parent idea
Synthesize the three implementations into one
What it is
Currently, `migrate` rejects as long as ideas/graph.yaml exists, replying "project graph is in place, no migratable location." Even before rejecting, it has clearly already calculated the source of the old graph (findLegacySources), yet it doesn't mention it in a single word. The three repositories ErrorRecoveryBenchmark, LifeCopilot, and LiveCaption are exactly stuck here: the `graph.yaml` planted by the installer is only 68 to 111 bytes with zero ideas, while lying next to it is a `graph.claude.yaml` of 57 to 148 KB with 31 to 68 ideas—yet the message says "no migratable location." The fix is split in two: if there are no ideas in ideas/graph.yaml (empty seed), treat it as non-existent and migrate directly, recording "overwrote empty seed" in the migration report; only reject if `graph.yaml` already contains ideas—but tell the truth: how many ideas the current graph has, the path and idea count of each adjacent old graph, and the word "move" (to indicate which one to move). Also, modify step 0 of the `ccscan` skill: a rejection from `migrate` does not equal "confirmed no old graph"; it only counts if it explicitly says "no old format graph found."
Why this idea exists
This lie is creating opportunities for data loss, and it is happening through a process we wrote ourselves: step 0 of `ccscan` tells the agent to run `migrate --dry-run`, and if rejected, it is treated as "confirmed no old graph," after which a new graph is built next to the real data. In these three repositories, 136 ideas are being blocked by a single sentence, invisible to both humans and agents. The installer side (seedWouldLockOut) already wrote this logic correctly; it is just that `migrate` itself did not.
Expected result
An empty seed is next to an old graph: `migrate` succeeds directly, `graph.yaml` is replaced with the old graph content, and `migrate-report.md` records that the empty seed was overwritten; multiple old graphs are next to an empty seed: require `--pick` as before, do not select automatically. An old graph is next to a `graph.yaml` that has ideas: reject, with the reason including the current graph's idea count, the path and idea count of each old graph, and the word "move"; `graph.yaml` remains untouched. No old graphs exist: reply "no old format graph found" as before, regardless of whether `graph.yaml` exists. `npx vitest run --dir .devcompanion/tests test_base_migrate` is all green.
How to implement
companion/ideas.ts's migrate: First, check if sources.length === 0 (if there are no old idea graphs, there is nothing to say, so do not check if graph.yaml exists first); then, if plain exists, read its number of ideas — if zero, let it pass through the original migration path and add a line to converted.report: "Overwrote a ideas/graph.yaml that contains only a seed and no ideas"; if non-zero, reject it, using sources to list the kind, path, and number of ideas for each item in the reason (reuse the counting logic from the multiple old idea graphs section), and append at the end: The engine does not merge (D10); to migrate old graphs, move ideas/graph.yaml out of the way first; to keep the current graph, move the old graph away. If graph.yaml cannot be read (YAML is corrupted), treat it as "having something," reject it, and state that it cannot be read. In step 0 of companion/skills/ccscan/SKILL.md, add a sentence: Only "no old format graphs discovered" counts as having no old graphs; all other rejections must stop for human review. test_base_migrate.test.ts: Change the line "an existing plain graph.yaml means there is nothing to migrate onto" to allow direct migration with an empty seed, add a new case for rejecting non-empty graphs with a truthful reason, and a case for rejecting bad YAML.
Why it is implemented this way
The reason for not just speaking correctly but still rejecting empty seeds is that the agent cannot perform the step of "moving graph.yaml away" (mv is a write-disk verb, blocked by D21), so it can only wait for a human — and since an empty seed contains no information to begin with, rejecting it protects nothing; it just locks three repositories for an extra day. The decision to reject non-empty graphs instead of merging them is the ruling of D10: a human decides which of the two graphs is the truth, and the engine does not automatically pick a winner; this is the same rule as requiring --pick when multiple old graphs are present. Do not change the installer's sentence "once planted, it can never be migrated into again" (seedWouldLockOut): it was the truth at the time, and after the change, its situation (not planting when an old graph is next to an empty seat) remains correct; only the reason changes from "permanently locked" to "let a human decide first." Leave this sentence to be changed together the next time it is touched; do not expand the scope this time.

Another pitfall encountered during development: receipts generated by request-approval --gate decomposition --node X can never pass set doing (it validates against the whole graph, not the node), yet the command neither blocks nor provides a prompt, causing humans to perform an extra unnecessary approval. Parent idea
Synthesize the three implementations into one
What it is
companion/guard.ts normalizes events from the three providers and executes the same set of policies: unassigned files are rejected by default, doing readiness/prerequisite/path range, two approvals, RED→GREEN, state and runtime protection, shell mutation and Stop completion checks. Reject during pre-write/approval/Stop crash; allow with a warning when recording a crash after writing; each platform only encodes input/output protocols.
Why this idea exists
Directly moving Claude guard will miss Codex apply_patch, MCP, and Bash, and will also change Cursor's default rejection to default allowance. A common guard must share the "decision"; it cannot pretend the original JSONs are exactly the same.
Expected result
Three sets of real event fixtures produce the same allow/deny for the same behavior; unknown write paths, unapproved, no RED, out-of-bounds files, and shell bypasses are all rejected; PostToolUse recording a failure will not block an already completed write; AIDEV_GUARD=off will show and record warnings.
How to implement
Keep three small normalize functions and three output encoders within the same file, without building an adapter class hierarchy; policy functions only receive normalized events. Port Cursor gate and Codex hook tests, covering apply_patch multi-file parsing, MCP, local editing, and Stop continuation.
Why it is implemented this way
The three providers' hooks are close enough to share a policy, but not close enough to safely delete normalization. A few pure functions are the smallest thin layer, which is shorter than copying three sets of rules or introducing a general adapter framework.

Parent idea
One command to install into any repository.
What it is
If ideas/graph.yaml is empty, use it and write agent: claude in the file; if it is taken by someone else, use ideas/graph.claude.yaml. Add the corresponding .approved / .scan-todo / log.md suffixes together. Once chosen, keep it fixed, because the fact that "the file with the suffix already exists" is itself the answer.
Why this idea exists
Three companions—Claude, Codex, and Cursor—reside in the same repository and all want ideas/graph.yaml. Whoever writes later will destroy the previous one.
Expected result
Three sides coexist without overwriting each other; a graph.yaml without an agent: key is treated as belonging to someone else (assuming the reverse would destroy others' work).
How to implement
For nameIsTaken, first check if the file with the suffix exists (exists = already selected), then check the agent: line in the file without the suffix; for agentName, determine whether the suffix is inserted or appended based on whether an extension exists (dotfiles have no extension to split).
Why it is implemented this way
The first to arrive keeps the clean name. Use "file existence" as the state instead of saving a separate configuration—this reduces the number of places where reality might become inconsistent. The agent: key is not decoration; code comments state that without it, the next call will misidentify our own suffix-less graph as someone else's, thereby quietly switching to the file with the suffix and discarding the graph we just wrote.

What it is
Copy the five commands into the target repository's .claude/commands/ (rewrite the path to an absolute path), create an empty ideas/graph.yaml, attach the guard to the four events in .claude/settings.json, and write a ideas/.gitignore to distinguish "records that should enter git" from "local machine state."
Why this idea exists
This process must be used on all projects, not just in this single repository.
Expected result
In other repositories, all five slash commands can be invoked; do not overwrite existing command files that do not belong to this tool (unless using --force); repeated installations result in no change, and hooks will not pile up indefinitely.
How to implement
Copy commands/*.md one by one and replace `claude-companion/` with the absolute path of the current directory; when installing hooks, filter out your own old one before adding it back, while keeping others exactly as they are.
Why it is implemented this way
The engine (ideas.ts / guard.ts) is intentionally not copied—all repositories share one copy, so fixing it once fixes it everywhere, preventing five repositories from running five different versions. The cost is that if this directory is moved, it needs to be reinstalled. graph and log.md go into git (as they are records), while .scan-todo and .approved do not (a partial scan and a human sign-off are local machine states).

Record which repositories are installed, and be able to check if they are expired and perform batch updates.CompletedEvery installation records the target absolute path into claude-companion/.installs.json; --status reports current / stale / missing / foreign file by file; --update refreshes everything, but does not touch foreign files.Open →
Parent idea
One command to install into any repository.
What it is
Every installation records the target absolute path into claude-companion/.installs.json; --status reports current / stale / missing / foreign file by file; --update refreshes everything, but does not touch foreign files.
Why this idea exists
The engine is shared so it never expires, but the five command files are copies, and copies can expire—and in the past, there was no way to know where they were installed or if they were the latest versions.
Expected result
After modifying the command file, running --status will show stale, and after running --update, everything changes to current; if someone else occupies a file with the same name, it reports foreign and will not be overwritten.
How to implement
Perform a word-for-word comparison with "what the current source file will generate now"; unify line endings before comparison.
Why it is implemented this way
No version numbers: the commit specifies "a number you must remember to bump, which will eventually be wrong, but the content knows itself whether it is correct". Normalizing line endings is mandatory — the source files provided by git on Windows are CRLF, while the installed ones are LF; if not normalized, every installation will be forever reported as outdated, rendering this check useless.

Bundle the engine, guard, and dependencies into a single-file program; as long as node is available, it can run anywhere it is installed CompletedA build script bundles the companion's engine, guard, and yaml parsing dependencies into a single dist/companion.mjs file; running it only requires node in the system, no npx required, no tsx required, and the target repository does not require npm install. Parent idea
One command to install into any repository.
What it is
A build script bundles the companion's engine, guard, and yaml parsing dependencies into a single dist/companion.mjs file; running it only requires node in the system, no npx required, no tsx required, and the target repository does not require npm install. The source code remains a single TypeScript version.
Why this idea exists
Today there are three different running methods across three providers: Claude uses absolute paths with npx tsx to run source code (which breaks when switching machines), Cursor copies source code into the target repository and then runs npm install (which will expire), and Codex is a complete replica in another language (the source of drift). Adjudication Table D34 adjudicates single-file artifacts.
Expected result
Copy dist/companion.mjs separately into an empty directory without node_modules; verification, rendering, and guard judgments can all run; artifacts can be repeatedly regenerated by build scripts.
How to implement
companion/build.mjs is about a dozen lines: call esbuild --bundle --format=esm --platform=node --target=node20 to output companion/dist/companion.mjs, with the banner injecting two things — the first-line shebang and a createRequire shim. The shim is indispensable: the CJS build of the yaml package contains require('process'), and without the shim, the build will show all green but will crash immediately upon the first parse — this investigation has reproduced this failure on a local machine and verified the fix. The entry point companion/cli.ts simultaneously mounts the engine command and the guard subcommand.
Why it is implemented this way
Use esbuild directly; do not use tsup (it is no longer maintained, and its repository points to a successor), do not use rollup (it requires three or four plugins to be equivalent, and the artifact is only a few dozen KB), do not use bun (it has a known defect of writing the build machine's absolute path into the artifact, which hits the core requirement of a "portable single file"), and do not use node single executables (hundred-megabyte binaries that still require running esbuild first). This is the only path that has been tested and passed with this set of dependencies on a local machine.
Where is the code
companion/build.mjs:1-25
companion/cli.ts:1-14
How to verify
npx vitest run .devcompanion/tests/test_base_bundle.test.ts → exit 0
Test file:.devcompanion/tests/test_base_bundle.test.ts
How to use in the future
The hook wiring and the installer for all three providers issue this same file; the risk of npx tsx cold starts swallowing approvals under a thirty-second UserPromptSubmit timeout is eliminated.

Parent idea
One command to install into any repository.
What it is
Three platform lists: four hook events in Claude's settings, Cursor's .cursor/hooks.json, and the hooks.json of the Codex plugin — each list only writes "which event, which command"; the commands are all node dist/companion.mjs plus a parameter describing itself; all skills point to the same companion/skills/. The Cursor version's "injecting a briefing of the current work status into the conversation at the start of a session" is also included in the wiring, shared by all three.
Why this idea exists
Hook event names and invocation methods truly differ across providers, which is the natural location for platform differences (Adjudication Table D14/D15); besides this, nothing else should exist in three separate versions.
Expected result
Format validation for the three lists passed; the Claude version truly triggers the guard in this repository; the two Cursor/Codex versions align with the event samples (acceptance in the real product belongs to I-073/I-074).
How to implement
companion/manifests.ts exports three wiring generation functions: Claude — in addition to the four existing events in settings, it includes ConfigChange (to intercept when the agent modifies its own wiring) and SessionStart (to inject the current graph's status briefing into the session, absorbing the unique advantage of the Cursor version); commands use the officially recommended exec form with the ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} placeholder instead of hardcoding machine absolute paths, and the UserPromptSubmit entry explicitly increases the timeout; Cursor — .cursor/hooks.json, events preToolUse/afterFileEdit/beforeSubmitPrompt/stop/sessionStart/ beforeShellExecution/beforeMCPExecution, with the critical interception item failClosed set to true; Codex — .codex/hooks.json uses an event table of the same form as Claude, the matcher covers the Bash/apply_patch/Edit/Write/mcp__ prefix (same as Probity), and the command remains a stable single-line string — Codex's trust binding uses the hook definition hash, so artifact updates should not trigger re-trusting.
Why it is implemented this way
Retaining three versions of the wiring is the D14 adjudication: event names and invocation forms are truly different, which is the natural location for platform differences; only the event tables are in the three versions, with no rules included. The exec form and placeholders are explicit suggestions from official Claude documentation for Windows (regarding shell quoting issues); absolute path wiring for the current status fails when switching machines, which is a gap recorded in this audit.

Parent idea
One command to install into any repository.
What it is
companion/install.ts: install the target repository path, install the three platform manifests, skill pointers, and single-file programs into the target repository, and register them in the local installation list; --status performs a byte-by-byte comparison to check if each installation is consistent with the source (normalizing newlines first so Windows CRLF does not cause false positives); --update refreshes expired installations. All tests inject a temporary installation list and never read the real list —— the bug where existing tests write temporary directories into the real list is also fixed.
Why this idea exists
The user explicitly requested that "the experience of installing into other repositories should be the same as today's claude-companion"; today's installer only installs Claude. To achieve "one installation, three beneficiaries," the hooks for all three must be connected in a single installation.
Expected result
After executing install on a temporary repository, the three manifests and runnable single-file programs are in place, and the guard takes effect on Claude events; --status reports the latest first, reports expired after source code changes, and restores the latest after --update; after running all tests, the real installation list remains unchanged by a single character.
How to implement
companion/install.ts follows the skeleton of claude-companion/install.ts (CRLF normalization, byte-by-byte comparison, unknown target files are judged as "external" and skipped, idempotent hook merging): install copies dist/companion.mjs to the target repository (one set of artifacts shared by three parties), merges the three connection sets of I-097 into .claude/settings.json, .cursor/hooks.json, and .codex/hooks.json respectively (without overwriting others' entries), copies skills to .agents/skills/ and bridges .claude/skills/ (uses symbolic links if possible, otherwise defaults to copying on Windows), seeds ideas/graph.yaml and .gitignore; perform smoke testing immediately after installation: send one synthesized out-of-bounds write event to the Claude connection command, expecting exit code 2 —— official documentation explicitly states that incorrect hook paths will fail silently, so it must be verified on the spot. Registry functions must all accept registry path parameters, with tests injecting temporary paths.
Why it is implemented this way
Aligning the experience with today's claude-companion is a user-specified requirement; however, it has changed from "absolute path sharing engine" to "copying single-file artifacts," because the artifacts have been decoupled from the source repository dependency (D34), and absolute paths are precisely the biggest portability issue in the current state (the connections in this repository itself would fail if moved to another machine). Smoke testing is written into the installer rather than the documentation, because "silent hook failure" is a trap explicitly mentioned in the platform documentation that humans cannot rely on memory to avoid.
Where is the code
companion/install.ts:1-231

Three assistantsAccess the same idea graph.
What it is
The same set of idea graphs for Cursor: five skills (idea-onboard / discuss / build / debug / record), one preToolUse gate that intercepts before writing files, one afterFileEdit recording hook, and one sessionStart prompt hook.
Why this idea exists
The workflow should not serve only one agent; Cursor's hook model is different from Claude Code, so the same guard.ts cannot be attached.
Expected result
When no idea is in the doing state, product code cannot be written; only the code / verify files of ideas that are both doing and build-ready are unlocked; two doing ideas cannot share the same code file.
How to implement
gate-lib.mjs is a pure Node ESM shared decision layer (hooks cannot wait for tsx to start), both ideas.ts and hooks/gate.mjs call decideWrite; the harness file itself is locked, so agents cannot remove this set of gates.
Why it is implemented this way
Contrary to the Claude side, the Cursor side is fail closed — the top comment of gate.mjs states "a crash or missing yaml denies the edit". The trade-offs between the two sides are different: the guard on the Claude side consists of seven independent rules, where a crash allows passage; the Cursor side has only one rule (interception before writing files), where a crash blocks passage. No record was found in the repository explaining why opposite failure directions were chosen within the same project.

Parent idea
Three assistantsAccess the same idea graph.
What it is
Place three input conversion functions and three output encoding functions in the same file: Claude's events include file_path; Cursor's native hooks.json has different event field names and requires permission JSON for judgments; Codex's apply_patch carries multiple files in one patch and requires parsing for exec and MCP tools, requiring another JSON type for judgments. Each provider is assigned a set of real event samples, which are converted before entering the same rule core. The gap where the current Codex version cannot see MCP writes is filled here.
Why this idea exists
Official compatibility only guarantees that events can be triggered, not that the JSON formats of the three providers are identical (Decision Table D15/D22). Without normalization, rules would have to be copied three times, and copying three times leads to drift—which is exactly what has already happened in this repository.
Expected result
Real event samples from the three providers result in the same allow/deny for the same behavior; every file in a single apply_patch is checked; MCP writes no longer bypass the guard; output formats can be correctly parsed by all providers (Claude exit code 2, Cursor permission JSON, Codex decision JSON).
How to implement
In guard.ts, there are three input conversions and three output encodings. The entry point selects via --platform=claude|cursor|codex: Claude reads hook_event_name/tool_name/tool_input.file_path events (backslash normalization) and rejects using exit code 2 plus a permissionDecision JSON; Cursor uses native preToolUse/beforeShellExecution/beforeMCPExecution/afterFileEdit/ beforeSubmitPrompt/stop events and returns a flat permission / continue / followup_message; Codex official hooks share the same event names as Claude, and apply_patch parses all paths one by one from the Add/Update/Delete File lines within tool_input.command (if one line cannot be parsed entirely, the whole order is rejected). MCP tools match via mcp__service_name__tool_name, and response packets only use allow/deny — official documentation explicitly states that 'ask' is not supported in Codex before writing, so returning 'ask' is equivalent to granting permission. A set of real event samples for each provider is stored in the test directory.
Why it is implemented this way
Research confirmed that Codex hooks have been officially released and deliberately use event names compatible with Claude, and Cursor also includes a Claude compatibility layer — however, the response formats and field names of the three providers remain different (Cursor uses flat permission, Codex does not support ask); pretending they are the same will cause the most critical "rejection" to fail silently. Using three small functions instead of an adapter class hierarchy is the ruling from the I-071 original text; the apply_patch parser is ported from codex-companion's regex (with test endorsement).
Where is the code
companion/guard.ts:317-612 · normalizeClaude / normalizeCursor / normalizeCodex with three encoders, entry

Integrating a fourth agent is equivalent to adding a pair of conversion functions and a set of event samples.

Parent idea
Three assistantsAccess the same idea graph.
What it is
Claude, Cursor, and Codex are simultaneously available within the same repository, jointly reading and writing project-level ideas/graph.yaml, logs, and evidence; when switching agents, there is no reconstruction, no copying, and no selection of another graph. This round of expansion enables multiple assistant sessions to collaborate within the same working directory simultaneously, communicating through shared messages and coordinating the writing of files and graphs.
Why this idea exists
The same project will be taken over by different agents. If switching to a different agent requires rebuilding the idea graph, then that graph is not a record of the project, but merely the memory of a specific agent.
Expected result
Once all three sides are installed, there is only one canonical graph.yaml; if any side modifies the graph, records, or completes a node, the other two sides can see the same state by re-reading. Old suffix graphs are only retained as read-only inputs before an explicit migration. During multi-session parallelism, different files can be developed simultaneously, conflicts in claiming the same file are visible and constrained, messages can be read by each other, graph updates are not lost; after an abnormal termination, an explicit handoff can be performed.
How to implement
Retain the common base migration and the relay acceptance by the original three parties, and add parallel acceptance within the same directory for I-112. First, explicitly install the products of this round in a disposable real test repository; use the actual hosts of Claude, Cursor, and Codex to open one session each to work in parallel, respectively claiming files, publishing messages, reading messages from others, and performing local updates to the same graph. Subsequently, create contention for the same file and conflicts with old values, then stop the old sessions and all in-flight writes to perform an explicit handoff. At the same time, verify that opening two sessions of the same model type does not merge identities; check the identity payload of the actual write hook for sub-assistants, rather than just checking the startup notification. Retain platform versions, input events, visible prompts, and actual file results, distinguishing between cooperative commands and verified host interceptions. Do not mark as complete until all three parties have verifiable write identities and blocking results; report unintegrated hosts or write paths item by item.
Why it is implemented this way
Continue to reuse the original common graph and the three-party connection, expanding the endpoint acceptance instead of creating another endpoint representing the same goal. Multi-process testing of I-112 can verify the file protocol but cannot prove that the real host called the hook, so manual verification is retained here. Official documentation https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks clearly states that the Codex sub-assistant follows the parent session_id; https://cursor.com/docs/hooks distinguishes between conversation_id and generation_id; identity must be verified in the actual host, and different model names cannot be used as evidence of isolation.
Where is the code
companion/FORMAT.md · Acceptance steps for three real experiments collaborating in the same directory
.devcompanion/tests/test_coord_end_to_end.test.ts · Reusable temporary project and protocol acceptance scenarios
How to verify
Explicitly install products in a disposable real repository, using Claude, Cursor, and Codex to collaborate simultaneously: each message is visible, different files can be parallelized, contention for the same file is rejected and notifies the holder, concurrent local modifications to the same YAML are preserved, conflicts with old values are explicitly rejected, and handoff occurs after stopping in-flight writes with old claims becoming invalid. Add dual-session checks for the same model type and identity checks for sub-assistants, recording host versions and actual hook input/output. Host paths that have not proven write identity or interception cannot be marked as complete. Throughout the process, only one project intent graph is retained; do not automatically modify this repository or other user repositories.

Common code does not equal a common workflow; only when state can be relayed, rules can be updated once, and original guarantees do not regress, is the common base truly established.

After acceptance, use dry-run to view the seven old local installations and perform explicit migration one by one; stop any repository that has multiple legacy graphs for human sign-off.
Why it is implemented this way
The endpoint is observable behavior rather than directory reorganization; use a temporary repository before real installation to avoid testing and migration accidentally modifying user projects again.

What it is

Why this idea exists
A specification that claims to be 'implemented' when the code is not is more harmful than having no specification at all.

Parent idea
The base delivers on its promises.
What it is
After moving the three old implementations into archive/ and switching this repository to the common base on 2026-09-02, two items remain for wrap-up. One is three test assertions: they require claude-companion/FORMAT.md to reside in the repository root, reasoning that "the five command files installed in the seven repositories point to it by name" — but those command files were also archived, and the six external repositories now install skills, so this prerequisite itself is no longer valid, and the assertions must be moved under archive/. The other is that the guard's shell gate misidentified 2>&1 as a file write: it only sees the greater-than sign and fails to recognize this as a file descriptor operation merging standard error into standard output, which does not result in a file.
Why this idea exists
The second issue is something encountered every day: a very ordinary `npx vitest run ... 2>&1 | grep` will be rejected, and the rejection message even advises people to "remove the redirection"—that is an impossible suggestion to follow, because what needs to be seen is precisely the standard error. Once the guard blocks legitimate work too many times, people will start disabling AIDEV_GUARD entirely, which is the real loss: a bypassed gate is worse than no gate at all, because it still gives the illusion of protection. Failing to fix the first issue leaves three red tests, and this repository has just established a rule that "documentation and code must not contradict each other"; those red assertions are the most glaring counterexamples.
Expected result
npx vitest run --dir .devcompanion/tests is all green; `node .companion/companion.mjs allow` answers with permission for a read-only command containing `2>&1`; meanwhile, redirections that actually result in files, such as `printf ... > src/x.ts`, are still rejected.
How to implement
On the guard side: the REDIRECT in companion/guard.ts is now `/(?:^|[^<])(<>|>{1,2})/`. We need to extract "file descriptor copying" from "writing files"—syntax like `数字>&数字` and `>&数字` results in a descriptor rather than a file; first exclude them from the match, then judge the remaining redirections. The same applies to `2>/dev/null` and `2>NUL`: the target is a null device, not a product file; judge by the target rather than by the symbol. On the testing side: in the "the frozen twin spec" section of `test_base_skills.test.ts`, `twin()` points to archive/claude-companion/FORMAT.md, and invert the assertion "must exist in the root directory"—there must not be a second copy in the root directory; there must be one in `archive/`.
Why it is implemented this way
The reason for not directly adding the entire `2>&1` string to the whitelist is that the whitelist only recognizes this specific spelling, whereas `2>&1`, `1>&2`, `>&2`, and `3>&1` are four ways of writing the same thing; adding them one by one will inevitably lead to omissions. Judging by "whether the redirection target is a file" is what this rule originally intended to ask—this follows the same logic as this round's change of protected evidence to "defend by target rather than defend by verb," where we previously had to patch it after missing `dd`, `install`, and `tar` in the enumeration.
Where is the code
companion/guard.ts:731-742,832-838 · NON_FILE_REDIRECT, mutatingShell
.devcompanion/tests/test_base_skills.test.ts:109-143 · the frozen twin spec (H25)

Parent idea
The base delivers on its promises.
What it is
Go through every sentence in the repository that "describes how the code works" and cross-reference it with the code, correcting any errors. A full-repository inspection was conducted on 2026-09-06 (searching from six angles, with each instance being verified once by two read-only reviewers against both the code and the original text), confirming 40 instances: two in README.md, three in CLAUDE.md, twenty in companion/FORMAT.md, six comments in companion/guard.ts, one comment in companion/ideas.ts, and nine instances of descriptions and fixture strings in five test files. Every instance has been changed to reflect the actual state of the code today; only the incorrect half of the sentence was modified, without reordering paragraphs or adding embellishments. At the same time, a new test file was created to pin down those sentences that can be verified by a program: whether a guard is installed, whether the archive directory is empty, whether the event types listed in the specification match the set in the engine, which fields are recognized during write-back, which line number formats are valid, whether the numbering references in the initial unimplemented list can be matched, and whether deleted directories and constant names are still being referenced as active. In the future, if these statements drift again, the tests will fail first. The specification and source files located under .companion/ must be byte-for-byte identical, so after modifying the source files, use the installer to refresh that copy instead of manual transcription. Explicitly excluding three items from this entry: two instances in the two skill files (ccbuild says "if something is missing when entering doing, supplement it," omitting the "plan approval" item; ccgraph says status can show which blocked idea is waiting, but it actually prints nothing) — those two files are claimed by I-049 and will be absorbed by it; two dated audit snapshots (companion/AUDIT-2026-09-01*.md) — those are history, and being overturned by subsequent work is their duty; and the fact that the D20 line lacks an "implementation status" section — the review opinions are split one-to-one on this, so this entry leaves it untouched.
Why this idea exists
This set of tools treats "what the specification says must be the current code" as a hard rule. The specification itself states: if a ruling says "it is already like this" but it is not in the code, the next assistant will treat it as fact and act according to a non-existent guarantee. This inspection proves it actually happened: both README and CLAUDE.md say this checkout has no guard installed, while a guard is currently blocking commands in this session; the first item in the "unimplemented list" at the beginning of the specification says not a single guard is effective; the specification says there are eight types of events in total and not to invent a ninth, but the engine already has a ninth type (fetching web pages) and is using it; the specification says the D21 gate has four stages, but the code has five, and the one missed is precisely the only one that blocks by target path rather than by verb; the specification says a single line number "12" is invalid, even though the engine clearly recognizes it. A specification with tests guarding it versus one without differs not today, but after the next change: without tests, every "implemented" statement will quietly become false after some modification, and it will look exactly like the truth. This repository already has a precedent guarding this (the group in test_base_skills stating "what the specification says must be the current engine"), and this idea expands it into a dedicated test file.
Expected result
After the changes, every one of those 40 sentences can be verified word-for-word against the code as true; the new test test_docs_truth passes, and if any of its sentences are changed back to the incorrect version, it fails. Specifically, what is pinned down includes: README.md and CLAUDE.md no longer say this checkout has no guard installed, and they specify where it is installed (.companion/companion.mjs and the three connections); both documents and the specification no longer describe what is contained in an empty archive directory, and clearly state that the old implementation only exists in the commit history; every "Item N" reference in the unimplemented list at the beginning of the specification points to an existing item; the event types listed in specification D22 are completely consistent with the members of the union type in companion/guard.ts, with no more or less in either direction; the set of fields that can be modified listed in specification D24 is consistent with the SET_FIELDS table in companion/ideas.ts; specification D32 acknowledges that single line numbers and comma-separated segments are valid; the deleted constant name MUTATING_SHELL no longer appears in the specification or the guard source code; the D21 description counts five gates and explains the one that blocks by target; specification D35 and the comments in guard.ts no longer say the claude-companion directory still exists or is still being pointed to by connections; in test_base_contract, the Codex read event cell changed from "cannot receive" to the actual payload, the deficiency list now only contains Cursor, and the sentence "Codex reads will never reach the guard" no longer appears; in test_base_skills, the engine path assertion is derived from constants rather than re-copying a literal. .companion/FORMAT.md and companion/FORMAT.md are byte-for-byte identical (the installer's --status reports "all up to date"). The full suite of tests passed.

`test_base_contract` lines 201–207: Replace the Codex read cell with the real payload (the sibling case in line 293 has already proven its normalization and judgment are consistent); the gap checklist in lines 283–286 now only has Cursor; `test_base_approval` lines 251–252: `show` has already printed `test_files` via `questionLines`, only the web card `verifyOf` is missing; correct the comment; `test_base_skills` line 61: Derive the engine path regex from `ENGINE_RELATIVE` in `manifests.ts`. **New test `test_docs_truth.test.ts`.** Read the source code of `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `companion/FORMAT.md`, `companion/guard.ts`, and `companion/ideas.ts`, and assert every item listed in the "Expected Results" above; for the event types item, extract the union type members from `guard.ts` using regex and perform a set equality check with the types named in the D22 section; for the `set` fields item, similarly extract `SET_FIELDS` from `ideas.ts` and compare it with the specification in D24; for the unimplemented checklist item, count the number of entries, find all "Item N" in the text, and assert that N does not exceed the number of entries; for the deleted directory item, perform a consistency check between the `existsSync` result and the text description (if the directory does not exist, the text cannot say it does). **Installation copy.** After modifying `companion/FORMAT.md`, run `npx tsx companion/install.ts --update` (this repository is in the installation list) or reinstall this repository once to refresh `.companion/FORMAT.md` along with the products; do not copy by hand.
Why it is implemented this way
**Why use tests to pin things down instead of just correcting the text.** Correcting text only manages today; this repository has already paid the price once for "specification says it is implemented, but code is not," and the moment those sentences are corrected looks identical to the moment they become false again. The set of "specification must match the current engine" assertions in test_base_skills has proven that this type of testing can catch drift, so we are expanding this into a dedicated file rather than relying on human reading again. **Why is this one idea, not forty.** A specification should have one idea per acceptance; if multiple acceptances are needed, it should be split. Here, there is exactly one acceptance — "text matches code" — and forty places are just forty locations of the same thing. Splitting it into forty items, where the verification of each is the same sentence, would only turn the frontier into a wall. **Why guard.ts only changes comments and does not delete invalid whitelist entries.** If a comment is wrong, it is a text issue, which this item handles; whether an entry should remain is a behavioral issue — three tests assert that those specific paths are allowed, and deleting them would be equivalent to changing the guard's judgment, which must be thought through and approved separately. One idea performs only one type of change, so the reader knows exactly what they are approving. **Why installation copies use the installer instead of manual copying.** The installer is the only thing that should write to .companion/; manual copying is exactly how the twin specification drifted apart back then (D14). **Why two skill corrections are not here.** Those two files are claimed by I-049, and the engine does not allow two ongoing ideas to claim the same file (D18); forcing them in would only prevent this item from entering "doing." Writing them into the I-049 record is cheaper than breaking the rules. **Why not touch the two audit snapshots.** They carry dates and record how things looked on that specific day; being overturned by later work is the very reason for their existence. Modifying them would be equivalent to tampering with history. **Why D20 remains untouched.** Two reviewers disagree: one says it is wrong, while the other says it is correct within its own declared scope; where opinions are split, this item should not act as a judge for others; leave it to the next round.

Close the three gaps where decisions were made but not implemented: old graphs are read-only, files that were read but have since changed automatically revert to unread, and allow provides the complete decision from the guard CompletedThree small tasks, each corresponding to a signed decision: (1) The guard treats migration inputs (old graphs in ideas/ with the agent suffix) as read-only and directly rejects writes (D10); (2) The scan manifest recognizes content fingerprints —— when striking out, record the file's fingerprint at that time, so that if the content changes later, it automatically reverts to unread (D12); (3) The allow command is upgraded to the guard's complete decision: it must answer all three layers—claim, approve, and failed test record—ensuring the real decision for the same file by the guard comes from the same function (fulfilling the I-089 expectation of "consistency with the guard").Open →
Parent idea
The base delivers on its promises.
What it is
Three small tasks, each corresponding to a signed decision: (1) The guard treats migration inputs (old graphs in ideas/ with the agent suffix) as read-only and directly rejects writes (D10); (2) The scan manifest recognizes content fingerprints —— when striking out, record the file's fingerprint at that time, so that if the content changes later, it automatically reverts to unread (D12); (3) The allow command is upgraded to the guard's complete decision: it must answer all three layers—claim, approve, and failed test record—ensuring the real decision for the same file by the guard comes from the same function (fulfilling the I-089 expectation of "consistency with the guard").
Why this idea exists
An audit after the implementation of I-093/I-094 found these three instances of "decision written, code not done": old graphs could still be written, so it cannot be said that "only graph.yaml is the real truth"; it only recognized read events rather than content, so files modified after being read were still considered read; allow missed two layers, causing agent self-checks to receive answers opposite to the guard.
Expected result
Edits to old-suffix graphs are rejected by the guard with the reason pointing to migrate; changing a single character in a read file causes scan to show it has returned to unread (legacy un-fingerprinted records continue to be treated as read to avoid punishing existing stock); allow answers "deny" for files that are "claimed but not approved" or "approved but not red," matching the source and answer of the guard's decision.
How to implement
(1) guard's decideOnePath rejects the pattern graph.<agent>.yaml in the ideas/ branch; (2) when striking out, append the sha256 to the read record (append only, without breaking I-055's concurrent fixes), and readWorklist compares the current fingerprint, so if it changes, it is no longer considered read; (3) extract the guard's decision on product files into decideProductWrite and export it from guard, and change the allow command to call it —— add approval and red records to the fixtures for the two CLI tests in I-089, while the assertion semantics (answer allow if writable) remain unchanged.
Why it is implemented this way
All three tasks involve connecting existing functions rather than creating new mechanisms: the read-only rule goes into decideOnePath because it already holds relative paths; fingerprints go into the read record because .scan-done is already append-only, and adding a hash column does not affect concurrency behavior; decideProductWrite is extracted instead of having the engine call guard in reverse, because guard depends on ideas.ts, and reverse calling would create a circular dependency. The alternative "allow writing its own judgment" is exactly the kind of duplication this foundation aims to eliminate. Codex's "render fingerprint handshake" is explicitly not moved: set/apply's automatic re-rendering and checking before Stop already serves the same purpose, which is recorded as a design choice rather than an omission.

When writing back the real issued number, also replace the temporary number in the parent field value. CompletedI-129

Parent idea
I-123
What it is
When changing the `parent` of an idea `set` in a change file to `tmp:N` (a newly created intermediate layer), the write-back step during the real number issuance must also replace this value with the real number; if a temporary number remains after replacement, the entire operation is rejected as usual.
Why this idea exists
The specification states that temporary numbers only appear in four positions (the id of set/status and both ends of link/unlink); this was written before the parent field existed. After adding parent, a single write-back for 'creating a new idea on the web and moving other ideas under it' is impossible—this collided during the layering on 2026-09-06: 62 set parent operations pointed from tmp:1 to tmp:10, the validation reported 'parent is not an idea in the graph', the entire file was rejected, and it could only be done in two steps by copying the fingerprint in between.
Expected result
A change file contains both 'add tmp:1' and 'set I-041 parent → tmp:1'; a single apply succeeds, and the parent of I-041 in the graph is the newly issued real number; the specification 'temporary numbers will appear in four positions' is changed to five.
How to implement
In the section of applyChanges where numbers are replaced, apply the same temporary number mapping table to set operations where the field is parent; add a test: add plus set parent pointing to a temporary number, and after write-back, the parent equals the new number; change the 'The change file' entry in FORMAT.md from four positions to five.
Why it is implemented this way
Continue using the existing mapping table and the fallback 'reject if temporary numbers remain' without adding another reference format; no changes are needed on the web side, as it already sends set operations with parent as a regular field.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Open any page and you know what it is talking about, where it is stuck, and what has moved recently, even without clicking into it. To doI-130

Parent idea
I-110
What it is
Let every idea on the webpage speak for itself: three bullet points under the title explain what it is doing; expanding one line reveals which ideas are hanging under it; blocked ideas print why they are blocked; at the bottom of every page is a timeline of changes for this idea and its descendants.
Why this idea exists
To understand an idea today, you must click into it and read all eight questions; blocked ideas only show the two words "Blocked", so no one knows what is stopping them; change records are hidden inside each card, making it impossible to see which part of the project has been moving in the last few days. If you send this graph to someone who hasn't opened this repository, they won't be able to read it.
Expected result
Open any layer, and there are three bullet points under the title explaining what this page is about; expanding one line allows you to see what its own sub-ideas are and their respective statuses; blocked ideas come with a sentence stating "why they are blocked"; at the bottom of the page, a list of every change for this idea and its descendants is shown in reverse chronological order.
How to implement
Three bullet point introductions (I-131), the list of its own sub-ideas in the expanded line (I-132), the reason for being blocked (I-133), and the change timeline at the bottom of every page (I-134). All four items only modify the render section in companion/ideas.ts and its adjacent engine functions; no new files or dependencies are added.
Why it is implemented this way
These four things could have been attached separately, but they are placed under the same idea because they share the same set of read-only derivatives—sub-idea list (kidsOf), status count (tally plus countsOf), first sentence extraction (the expression that is identical word-for-word between the line summary and the page header today), and collapsible blocks (worklist)—and every single item in the repository already exists in only one copy. By grouping them together, all four changes will pull from that single copy; if dispersed into I-123 and I-124, a second copy will inevitably grow. Another path was to stuff everything into I-124, but that was rejected by the "maximum seven per layer" rule, and furthermore, I-124 is about "who is waiting for you to process," which is not the same thing as "has this page explained itself clearly."

companion/ideas.ts · render

idea Arrange by dependency order

At the top of every page, three bullet points explain the idea of that page, automatically summarized by the program from the eight questions and the relationships.To doBetween the title and the flowchart, use three bullet points to answer "what exactly is this idea on this page talking about": the program automatically extracts these three sentences from its eight questions, plus its prerequisites, successors, parent idea, and sub-idea completion status, without adding any fields that require manual writing.Open →
Parent idea
Open any page and you know what it is talking about, where it is stuck, and what has moved recently, even without clicking into it.
What it is
Between the title and the flowchart, use three bullet points to answer "what exactly is this idea on this page talking about": the program automatically extracts these three sentences from its eight questions, plus its prerequisites, successors, parent idea, and sub-idea completion status, without adding any fields that require manual writing.
Why this idea exists
Today, that position only has the first line of "what it is"—a sentence with the beginning and end clipped. The reader still has to click open the eight questions to know what this idea is doing, why it is being done, and what the result looks like once finished.
Expected result
Click into any idea, and three bullet points consistently appear under the title; not a single word needs to be backfilled for the eighty-nine existing ideas; when switching to a different idea, the three bullet points change accordingly.
How to implement
Expand companion/ideas.ts's showHeader—it is the only page header redraw point on the page, and all page changes and address bar updates go through it—to insert a read-only block between the breadcrumbs and the flowchart, writing in the three bullet points: the first is the first sentence of "what it is," the second is the first sentence of "expected result," and the third is the facts calculated on the graph (which idea it belongs to, how many direct sub-ideas are finished written as "2/4" with the count specified, which prerequisites are still waiting to be completed, and whom it is blocking). The first sentence extraction follows the existing expression in the page (the line summary and page header are identical word-for-word today), first by paragraph boundary and then by period, with abbreviation guards; if it cannot be retrieved, fall back to the previous question, and if still not found, write "this idea has not been clearly written," do not make things up. Relationship data is derived from snapshot and pageGraph, without creating new indices; the wording of the eight questions is taken from QUESTIONS. The entire block has no numbering or positioning markers, and like the read-only summary in the expanded line, it is invisible to the three mechanisms for finding elements by number: editing, drafts, and human sign-off. If it exceeds fifty words, a warning is reported during rendering; no silent truncation is performed.
Why it is implemented this way
Research investigated four types of existing approaches. Jira, Linear, Notion, and Backstage do not automatically summarize prose; that line must be written by a human—copying it would be equivalent to backfilling a paragraph for each of the eighty-nine ideas, so this was rejected. Documentation generators (Sphinx, rustdoc, Doxygen) do indeed perform first-sentence extraction, but all three treat it as a "fallback for when humans haven't written a summary," and Doxygen has it turned off by default; therefore, we only copy its algorithm (Sphinx's extract_summary is about fifteen lines, including abbreviation guards) and not its status. The third bullet point is handed to calculated facts rather than a summary, a reason derived from the ACL 2023 classification of unfaithfulness in extractive summarization: sentences extracted from prose can distort the original meaning, but facts on a graph will not, because it does not touch the original text at all. The writing style of "2/4," and whether "the count must be specified for direct sub-ideas or the entire subtree," comes from Org mode; "saying it is waiting for 2 unfinished ideas instead of saying there are 3 links" comes from Linear—relationship facts must be filtered by the current status of the other end, otherwise that number is static. Reporting a warning for ultra-long text instead of silent truncation comes from the Clippy approach.

Expand a line on a parent idea page to see what its own sub-ideas are and their respective statuses.To doOn a parent idea page, each sub-idea is a line; clicking it allows you to see its eight questions, prerequisites, and change records; additionally, add a section called "its own sub-ideas" to this expanded area, listing the names and statuses of the next layer, allowing you to look one layer deeper without changing pages.Open →
Parent idea
Open any page and you know what it is talking about, where it is stuck, and what has moved recently, even without clicking into it.
What it is
On a parent idea page, each sub-idea is a line; clicking it allows you to see its eight questions, prerequisites, and change records; additionally, add a section called "its own sub-ideas" to this expanded area, listing the names and statuses of the next layer, allowing you to look one layer deeper without changing pages.
Why this idea exists
Clicking a node on the graph will locate and expand that line on the current page; this path is already working; however, after expanding, you cannot see what else is hanging under this idea—to know if it has sub-ideas or how many are finished, you can only click "Enter" to change pages, and then return after viewing.
Expected result
Expand any row that has sub-ideas; an extra section will appear listing its next layer; every item can be clicked to return to that idea; rows without sub-ideas will not have this extra section.
How to implement
Add a section "Its own sub-ideas" at the end of the briefDetail of companion/ideas.ts: use the existing kidsOf from the same closure to fetch the next layer, use links to produce jump links, and use STATUS_ZH and cls for status text and color schemes; if there are no sub-ideas, do not output the entire section. Do not place data-row in this new section — the node positioning on the graph to locate the corresponding row on the page uses the .children data-row selector; nesting one would break both the positioning and the four sets of assertions; sub-idea names also do not use the .bname class; renaming the selector is a document-wide change and would be taken away. The entire block continues to remain without numbering, without edit markers, and without human sign-off markers.
Why it is implemented this way
Two other paths were tested on paper. First, making sub-ideas into expandable rows (recursively expanding row summaries) was rejected due to the positioning method — the page finds rows via data-row, and after nesting, the same ID would appear twice on the page. Second, embedding an entire page directly into the expansion area would create a duplicate of the editable card, but since the three mechanisms of editing, draft recovery, and human sign-off all find elements by ID, the appearance of a duplicate would result in two elements with the same ID. Therefore, we only list the name and status and only provide links, without providing a second interactive object — this is exactly the rule originally set for this expansion area, which has already been locked down by four zero-count assertions in testing.

Blocked ideas must state why they are blocked; this sentence is printed under the eight questions.To doAdd an explicit field to ideas to hold "why blocked"; if the status is blocked but this sentence is not written, the validation will report it immediately; the web cards and expansion rows both print this under the eight questions.Open →
Parent idea
Open any page and you know what it is talking about, where it is stuck, and what has moved recently, even without clicking into it.
What it is
Add an explicit field to ideas to hold "why blocked"; if the status is blocked but this sentence is not written, the validation will report it immediately; the web cards and expansion rows both print this under the eight questions.
Why this idea exists
Currently, a blocked idea on the command line and the web only shows the two words "Blocked". Why it stopped and what must be waited for to restart are only scattered in the modification records, and the last entry in the modification record is not guaranteed to be about this matter. This repository currently has four blocked ideas, and not one of them states a reason.
Expected result
Setting an idea to blocked must simultaneously provide a reason; validation will report blocked ideas that lack a reason; on the web, blocked ideas will have an extra line "Blocked Reason" under the eight questions; supplement a sentence for each of the existing four blocked ideas.
How to implement
Add an optional field blocked_because to the idea type, placed next to the status, not in the line of the eight questions. Only one function must be forced to change: setStatus is the only place in the entire repository where the status of an existing idea is written (covering the three paths of command line, web envelope, and local service); there, judge that "transitioning to blocked must include a reason", passed via --because in the command line; for the path where the behavior field is changed and automatically reverts to blocked, use the existing text and write it directly into the new field. Add one error to check following the "Completed" templates: report if the status is blocked but this sentence is missing, and name which idea it is. On the web, cards use a field (including edit state, escaping, and draft wiring), and expansion rows manually write a pair of labels and values, both placed after the eighth question. Do not expand the plan field list, do not enter the eight questions' wording table, and do not enter questionLines — it shares the approved prompts, and adding a column would hit two assertions; on the command line, it must be printed under the eight questions, specifically as a single line after the show loop. The reasons for the four existing blocked ideas and the validation rules will be implemented at once: the guard will turn every error from check into "session not allowed to end"; adding rules before backfilling would freeze the session.
Why it is implemented this way
No online tracking tool natively enforces this — Jira's Flagged is a locked boolean, and reasons can only be written in optional comments; the request to turn it into a required field has been pending since November 2021 with 59 votes and has not been implemented; Trello's custom fields do not even have conditional requirements. Therefore, there is no product to copy, only two practices from actual usage: enforce it at the moment of status transition rather than enforcing it on static files (Azure DevOps attaches required rules to status changes, and this repository's setStatus is exactly at this position); and conditional validation must include a sentence naming the item, otherwise no one can understand the error. Two suggestions were not adopted: selecting the reason from a fixed category — its benefit is statistics on the recurrence of the same reason, and the four blocked ideas in this repository are not even at that volume; saving a separate blocked start date — that would be a redundant field, as setStatus already automatically tracks a dated modification record, and how long it has been blocked can be calculated from there. Both are explicit postponements, not omissions.

The home page aggregates the entire project.Open →
Parent idea
Open any page and you know what it is talking about, where it is stuck, and what has moved recently, even without clicking into it.
What it is
Add a collapsible modification timeline at the bottom of each page: aggregate the modification records of the idea on this page itself and all its descendant ideas, sort them by date from newest to oldest, and every item can be clicked to return to which idea was modified. The home page aggregates the entire project.
Why this idea exists
The modification records for each idea are currently hidden inside its own card. To know which part of the project has been moving in recent days, one can only flip through card by card.
Expected result
A modification list in reverse chronological order appears at the bottom of each page, containing only the ideas of this page and its descendants; clicking an item goes to that idea; when there are many items, it does not bloat the page.
How to implement
Add a collapsible block at the end of the page in companion/ideas.ts, after the sub-ideas section: take the idea of this page itself plus all descendants provided by descendants, merge their modification records into a single timeline, sort them by date from newest to oldest, group them by day, print the date, who modified it, and what was modified for each entry, along with a link to jump back to that idea. The home page follows the same path, aggregating the entire graph. The container uses the native folding element similar to the worklist (with the count in the title), the row styles follow the two existing families of styles, and not a single line of CSS is added. The entire block is read-only and carries no edit markers — modification records are lifecycle fields and are not in the whitelist for web write-backs. No pagination: render everything, tuck the old ones into a default collapsed folding element, write the exact number of hidden items in the title; do not place title elements inside the folding title.
Why it is implemented this way
The item "What to do if there are too many entries" is where the research directly overturned the original plan. GitHub's "N more items / Load more" approach is to save server round-trips, but here we have a static file and no server at all; community discussion records how that approach breaks in-page search and deep links. Since Chrome M96, collapsed elements automatically expand due to in-page search, text fragment jumping, and anchor navigation — therefore, "rendering everything + putting old items into collapsed elements" neither loses search nor links, and requires zero lines of script. Reverse order with grouping by day, and every aggregated record must be able to link back to its specific sub-idea, comes from the activity streams of GitHub and Google Drive; "Whether to aggregate descendants must be two explicit parameters and cannot be ambiguous" comes from the Drive activity API's practice of splitting "this one" and "this branch" into two parameters — the choice here is that every page aggregates its own descendants and specifies this in the title. The cost is explicitly stated: the same record will be statically copied into every level of its ancestors' pages; the two existing indexes are already paying this cost.
Where is the code
companion/ideas.ts · page

How to use in the future
With this timeline, "who has been working on which part lately" no longer needs to be asked of people; in the future, filtering by person or jumping by date will simply be adding a filter within the same block, as the data is already on the page.

Add a collapsible modification timeline at the bottom of each page: aggregate the modification records of the idea on this page itself and all its descendant ideas, sort them by date from newest to oldest, and every item can be clicked to return to which idea was modified. The home page aggregates the entire project.
Why this idea exists
The modification records for each idea are currently hidden inside its own card. To know which part of the project has been moving in recent days, one can only flip through card by card.
Expected result
A modification list in reverse chronological order appears at the bottom of each page, containing only the ideas of this page and its descendants; clicking an item goes to that idea; when there are many items, it does not bloat the page.
How to implement
Add a collapsible block at the end of the page in companion/ideas.ts, after the sub-ideas section: take the idea of this page itself plus all descendants provided by descendants, merge their modification records into a single timeline, sort them by date from newest to oldest, group them by day, print the date, who modified it, and what was modified for each entry, along with a link to jump back to that idea. The home page follows the same path, aggregating the entire graph. The container uses the native folding element similar to the worklist (with the count in the title), the row styles follow the two existing families of styles, and not a single line of CSS is added. The entire block is read-only and carries no edit markers — modification records are lifecycle fields and are not in the whitelist for web write-backs. No pagination: render everything, tuck the old ones into a default collapsed folding element, write the exact number of hidden items in the title; do not place title elements inside the folding title.
Why it is implemented this way
The item "What to do if there are too many entries" is where the research directly overturned the original plan. GitHub's "N more items / Load more" approach is to save server round-trips, but here we have a static file and no server at all; community discussion records how that approach breaks in-page search and deep links. Since Chrome M96, collapsed elements automatically expand due to in-page search, text fragment jumping, and anchor navigation — therefore, "rendering everything + putting old items into collapsed elements" neither loses search nor links, and requires zero lines of script. Reverse order with grouping by day, and every aggregated record must be able to link back to its specific sub-idea, comes from the activity streams of GitHub and Google Drive; "Whether to aggregate descendants must be two explicit parameters and cannot be ambiguous" comes from the Drive activity API's practice of splitting "this one" and "this branch" into two parameters — the choice here is that every page aggregates its own descendants and specifies this in the title. The cost is explicitly stated: the same record will be statically copied into every level of its ancestors' pages; the two existing indexes are already paying this cost.

idea Arrange by dependency order

If sub-ideas are not all completed, the parent idea is not allowed to be marked as completed, nor is it allowed to undergo human sign-off. CompletedI-135

Parent idea
I-108
What it is
Add a predicate to the "Completion" gate: as long as a sub-idea of an idea is not completed, the idea itself cannot be set to completed, cannot request human sign-off, and even if a human returns an approval code, it cannot be signed; the sign-off button on the webpage will be grayed out; every instance must clearly state which sub-ideas are still missing.
Why this idea exists
Today, a parent idea can be marked as completed or signed off even when none of its sub-ideas are finished; that signature is equivalent to being meaningless. This rule is currently only written in the manual verification sentences of a few parent ideas themselves — I-121 says "all seven sub-ideas completed", I-124 says "six sub-ideas completed" — those are handwritten prose, no program manages them, and adding a sub-idea turns those sentences into lies.
Expected result
When sub-ideas are unfinished, the command line will reject a completion request and state which ones are missing; sign-off requests will be rejected; the manual sign-off button on the webpage turns gray, with the specific sub-ideas blocking it written next to it; all three locations unlock simultaneously once all sub-ideas are completed; the handwritten "N sub-ideas completed" no longer requires manual counting. The "Complete" on the webpage is not within the scope of this idea — no idea can be changed to completed via the webpage; to achieve completion, one must have valid current GREEN evidence, which can only be done via the command line (D20).
How to implement
In the setStatus of companion/ideas.ts, after the existing four interceptions in the "Completed" branch, add a fifth: if this idea still has any direct sub-idea that is not completed, reject it and name which ones are missing. The predicate shape mimics needsUnmet verbatim (returning either empty or a sentence naming the items) and relies only on the graph itself (both parent and status are in the graph), because pure unit calls without the project directory also use this function; move the private kidsOf and parentKey from the rendering closure to the module scope for shared use, so "who is whose sub-idea" does not need to be written twice. Block two points on the sign-off side: the manual check prerequisite block in requestApproval blocks sending the approval code, and applyApproval performs one more check before writing the signature — if a sub-idea reverts to unfinished after the approval code is sent, only blocking the first point would allow the signature to be applied via that code. On the webpage, gray out the manual sign-off button instead of hiding it, and write in text who is blocking it; first change this button to call the existing awaitingSignature, otherwise the same thing must be modified in two places; grayed-out buttons do not carry data-sign, so the sign-off panel cannot be opened. Do not touch the "Complete" on the webpage — that gate belongs to D20; no idea can be changed to completed via the webpage. Blocked sub-ideas are counted as "not completed" per the ruling, blocking it in the same way. In FORMAT.md, add one sentence to each of the three places stating "parent is inclusion, not sequence": the completion of a parent idea implies the completion of all its sub-ideas, which is a direct consequence of the inclusion relationship, not a second type of sequential relationship; synchronize the copy stored next to the engine.
Why it is implemented this way
Every tool seen in research converges to the same skeleton: the status carries a terminal state marker, and the invariant is written on that marker, not on a state name called "Completed". What cannot be copied is their failure — Jira and Redmine have completely different architectures but identical user complaints, because both companies implement interception as "control disappearance," making it impossible for users to distinguish between a rule and a defect; therefore, here we gray out instead of hiding, and name the items when rejecting. What is explicitly not copied is "automatically marking sub-ideas as completed when the parent idea is completed": Linear makes this an option that is off by default, and GitHub rejected it directly, reasoning that a parent idea's completion does not imply all sub-ideas are completed, as some sub-ideas might be optional. We only look at direct sub-ideas rather than the entire subtree because once each layer holds its own, the entire tree is automatically established, and rejection can name an idea visible on the current page; the prerequisite for these two being equivalent is that setStatus is the only place in the entire repository where status can be changed, which holds true today. Blocked sub-ideas are not counted as completed because in this format, the destination for "Deprecated" is to retain the number, set it to blocked, and write the reason — that is a record of "this thing was not done," not "this thing was finished"; the cost is explicitly stated: a deprecated sub-idea will continue to block its parent idea; if truly stuck, one must either delete it from the graph or add an "Annulled" status (the more sophisticated approach online is that a sub-idea being annulled satisfies the parent idea, but a parent idea whose sub-ideas are all annulled should be considered annulled rather than completed), but we will not do that now.
