Parent idea
—
What it is
Allow users to open a URL on any device to see the idea graphs of all their repositories that have this tool installed; modify ideas and approve plans there; after each repository pulls the code, the idea graph files will already contain the new content, requiring no manual YAML editing. Division of labor: the engine in this repository is responsible for each repository's own graph pages, write-backs, approvals, and git commits; the URL, login, and multi-repository index are handled by the portal repository LifeCopilotBeta (specifically the I-009 branch in its idea graph). First, connect both sides on the local machine, then move to a machine that is always on.
Why this idea exists
As the number of repositories increases, there is no single place to overview all projects or manage them directly on any device. Each repository's idea graph can only be viewed and modified within that specific machine and directory. What is needed is a common management terminal.
Expected result
Click into a graph of a certain repository within the portal and change an idea to blocked while writing the reason; after performing a git pull on another checkout of the same repository, that idea in graph.yaml will already be blocked and the reason will be present. Reply with an approval code on the portal's graph page, which has the same effect as replying in the terminal. Run it through on the local machine first, then repeat it from a mobile phone.
How to implement
Three things on the engine side in this repository: I-137 connect the local small service to git, I-138 move approval codes and receipts into git, I-139 open an approval entry that only recognizes host credentials (including an additional segment for I-105). On the portal side, there is one branch for LifeCopilotBeta's idea graph I-009: starting child processes and proxying (I-010), making the project page the highest level (I-011), login (I-012), forwarding approvals (I-013), and deploying to an always-on machine (I-014). Order of implementation: I-137 → Portal I-010, I-011 → I-138 → I-139 → Portal I-013 → Local endpoint I-142 → Portal I-014, I-015. companion/FORMAT.md add a section "Portal", clearly defining the division of labor and three boundaries: host credentials shall not appear in pages or logs; the identity used for synchronization and approval shall never be a human login; receipts are written only by the engine and shall not be generated or rewritten by the portal.
Why it is implemented this way
Why place the portal in LifeCopilotBeta instead of letting the engine grow its own multi-repository index: users want to eventually merge into LifeCopilot, which already has graph_repos scanning (lifecopilot/graphs.py:82), the /projects interface (lifecopilot/api.py:274), FastAPI, and a background task running once per minute; if the engine grows another one, it would be redundant. Why not use Plane (research conducted on 2026-09-09): the free tier workspace webhook cannot add request headers, so it cannot wake up GitHub Actions; the prerequisite relationship interface paths differ between the cloud and self-hosted versions, and it did not exist at the end of 2024; squeezing eight questions into the work item description box makes the dependency graph invisible; the mapping table, push, and pull components would all require new code. The always-on machine solution moves the editing, human sign-off, and submission capabilities already completed by serve and graph.html as they are; only the three git commands, one directory move, and one entry point are newly written. Why not use rclone to sync to a cloud drive: it only moves files, has no editing interface, does not produce git commits, and would result in two different truths compared to the version in git.

Parent idea
Multiple repositories sharing one management website
What it is
Add a switch to serve: when enabled, perform a git pull before every page render, and after every successful write-back, commit and push graph.yaml, log.md, and the receipt directory; if pulling or pushing fails, print the error on the page instead of swallowing it. Simultaneously ensure that serve can be started as a background process by other programs: specify a port, do not open a browser, print its own address and token on the first line of standard output, and exit cleanly.
Why this idea exists
The prerequisite "after pulling the repository, it is already updated" assumes someone has performed commits and pushes on behalf of others. Since serve is already the sole place receiving web changes, letting it handle the commit conveniently avoids the need to build another synchronization pipeline. The portal needs to start a serve instance for each repository, so it must act like a background program rather than a window opened by double-clicking.
Expected result
Two checkouts of the same repository: modify an idea and commit it on the serve page of one checkout, and after a git pull on the other, graph.yaml will already contain the new content, and git log will show one additional commit written by serve; when the switch is off, serve behaves exactly as it does today, running not a single git command.
How to implement
Add an option gitSync to serve(), with the command-line flag --git-sync, disabled by default. When enabled: before rendering GET /, run git pull --ff-only; if it fails, return a plain text 503 page where the body is the git error output; after a POST /changes with confirm and a successful atomicWrite, execute git add ideas/graph.yaml ideas/log.md ideas/approvals (the latter only if it exists), git commit -m "Web write-back N times (serve)", and git push in sequence; if any step fails, do not roll back files, but put the error into the git field of the response and append it to log.md. All three commands run through a small function gitRun(projectDir, args) using execFileSync with a 30-second timeout. The background contract adds nothing new: --port and --no-open already exist, and the first line of standard output is already "Idea graph opened at http://127.0.0.1:Port」"; pin this line during testing so the portal can read the address from it.
Why it is implemented this way
Why put it in serve instead of apply: apply is the path for humans to manually move modified files, so it is reasonable for humans to perform commits themselves; serve is the unattended path, so only it needs to commit on behalf of humans. Why --ff-only instead of merging: serve does not resolve conflicts for humans; if a conflict occurs, it stops and reports it, following the same principle as the envelope fingerprint lock (FORMAT.md "The change file" baseDigest). Why execFileSync instead of libraries like simple-git: there are only three commands, and the single-file artifact (D28) should not carry an extra dependency for it. Why disabled by default: the version opened by double-clicking on a local machine should not silently push to the remote. Why not print the token to standard output: the page carries the token back itself, and the portal is a transparent proxy, so it does not need it.

Parent idea
Multiple repositories sharing one management website
What it is
Today, the approval codes and receipts waiting for answers are only written to each machine's respective ideas/.runtime/, and do not enter git. Move these two items into a git-tracked directory ideas/approvals/ (pending/ for approval codes waiting for answers, receipts/ for receipts); the guard's protection for it is the same as .runtime/: it can only be written by CLI and hooks. Receipts in the old directory .runtime/approvals/ remain valid and are read-only compatible. Test pass/fail evidence is not moved and remains in .runtime/. Update format specification D24 and the "Generated files" list with this entry.
Why this idea exists
Approval codes are generated on a human's computer by request-approval, approvals must be returned on an always-on machine, and the receipt must return to the human's computer for set doing to see. Only git connects these three places. Approval codes do not enter git, so the always-on machine does not know what is waiting for approval; receipts do not enter git, so the human's computer will never see that approval, making a web approval equivalent to no approval.
Expected result
Request approval and commit at one checkout, then after pulling at another location, it can answer that approval code, and the receipt lands in ideas/approvals/receipts/; commit it back, and after the first location pulls, set doing allows the same idea; if the content of that idea is modified and run again, it is rejected as before (the rule that receipts are bound to content remains unchanged); an agent attempting to write any file under ideas/approvals/ is blocked by the guard.
How to implement
paths() adds one more field, approvals, pointing to ideas/approvals; pendingDir and approvalsDir are changed to point to pending/ and receipts/ under it. When applyApproval looks for an approval code file, it first checks the new directory, then the old .runtime/pending/; validApproval first scans receipts/, then scans the old .runtime/approvals/. decideProductWrite adds ideas/approvals to the "only produced by CLI and hooks" group, with the reasoning text citing D24. The path string for the sentence written into the receipt (signed_off) is changed to the new directory. Do not change GITIGNORE_SEED in install.ts: the new directory is intended to enter git. FORMAT.md: D24 adds a section on implementation status, and the Generated files list adds a line for ideas/approvals/.
Why it is implemented this way
Why approval codes also enter git instead of only moving receipts: the always-on machine needs to know which approval codes are waiting for a response, and approval code files only contain the stage and content fingerprint; request-approval already prints them in full to the terminal (I-102), so there is no secret. Why not change to deterministic approval codes calculated from content (to avoid moving files): it would change the "one-time, random" semantics of D7/D26, and the scope of impact would be much larger than moving a directory. Why pass/fail evidence remains in .runtime/: it is evidence that this specific machine has run the tests; moving it to another machine would mean it is no longer evidence. Why the old directory is read-only compatible instead of migrated: there are not many existing receipts, and scanning two locations is cheaper than writing a migration.

Parent idea
Multiple repositories sharing one management website
What it is
serve adds a POST /approve entry point, receiving the human's response "approve CC-XXXXXXXX" and a host credential; the credential is a random string passed to it via environment variables when the portal starts serve, which does not appear on the page and is not printed in logs. The validation is identical to the terminal (approval code exists, content fingerprint unchanged, used only once); if successful, it writes the receipt to the git-tracked directory. If there is no credential or the credential is incorrect, it is rejected, just like today.
Why this idea exists
Users require that approval can also be done on the web. I-105 rules that local pages cannot distinguish between humans and automation, but it itself wrote that the only structurally valid method is an out-of-band second location; the portal login is that second location: only after a person passes the portal login does the portal pass that sentence along with the credential to serve, whereas an agent has neither a login nor a credential. Therefore, this does not overturn I-105, it only adds a clause: forwarding after out-of-band login counts, provided the credential does not appear in the page or logs.
Expected result
Sending an approval with the correct credential results in the receipt landing in the git-tracked directory and set doing allowing it; sending the same approval code a second time is rejected; sending without a credential, with an incorrect credential, or after content has been modified is rejected and no receipt is left; the credential cannot be found in the serve page source code or standard output.
How to implement
When serve() starts, it reads the environment variable AIDEV_APPROVE_SECRET. If not set: POST /approve returns 404, same as having no such entry point today. If set: request body {secret, words}, uses timingSafeEqual to compare the secret; if incorrect, returns 403; if correct, calls applyApproval(projectDir, words, {date, session_id: "serve", turn_id: request sequence}), and returns its result as-is; if it returns ok and gitSync is enabled, it commits ideas/approvals/ according to I-137. The credential does not enter the render output, the console, or log.md; standard output only adds one line: "approval entry enabled". Add a fourth paragraph to the "how" section of I-105: forwarding after out-of-band login counts, subject to three conditions (the credential does not appear in the page or logs; the portal login is not something an agent can obtain; receipts are only written by the engine). FORMAT.md D26 adds a section on implementation status, citing these three points.
Why it is implemented this way
Why use environment variables for credentials instead of command-line arguments: arguments are visible to everyone in Task Manager and ps. Why is it received by serve instead of the portal running the CLI directly: applyApproval must run on the machine where the repository is located, and serve is located there; furthermore, the guard rule blocking agents from accessing local services (I-104) still applies to this entry point. Why not change a single word in the ANSWER regex: the portal forwards the exact original words spoken by the human, and the validation must be identical to the terminal to claim "equivalent effectiveness." Why does it 404 instead of opening by default if environment variables are not set: the version opened by double-clicking on the local machine should not have an extra entry point.

Parent idea
Multiple repositories sharing one management website
What it is
A real drill, all on the local machine: check out two copies of the same repository; the portal (LifeCopilotBeta) starts the serve for the first copy; modify the text of an idea and reply with an approval code in the portal; do not manually run any engine commands; go to the second checkout and git pull, the part in graph.yaml is already modified, and that idea is released via set doing. Moving this to an always-on machine and re-enacting it from a mobile phone constitutes the endpoint on the portal side.
Why this idea exists
This is the acceptance criterion for the entire top-level idea; if it cannot be achieved, it is equivalent to not having been done.
Expected result
Pass the drill in one go; keep the git log and set doing output from both checkouts in the records.
How to implement
Perform manually step-by-step without writing code: 1. Clone this repository into two copies in temporary directories A and B, sharing one bare remote; 2. Point LifeCopilotBeta's graph_repos to A, and start the portal (portal I-010 to I-013 completed); 3. Open the portal in a browser, enter the idea graph of this repository, modify an idea's 'what', and commit; 4. In the terminal of A, request-approval for that idea and submit the approval code file; 5. Reply "Approve CC-XXXXXXXX" on the portal page; 6. Go to B, git pull, see that the part in graph.yaml is modified, and run set doing to release that idea; 7. Paste the git log and set output from both sides into the I-142 section of ideas/log.md.
Why it is implemented this way

It is a prerequisite for these ideas —

Connect the local small service to git: pull before starting the service, and after a successful write-back, commit and push; other programs should be able to start it as a background process. CompletedI-137

Parent idea
I-136
What it is
Add a switch to serve: when enabled, perform a git pull before every page render, and after every successful write-back, commit and push graph.yaml, log.md, and the receipt directory; if pulling or pushing fails, print the error on the page instead of swallowing it. Simultaneously ensure that serve can be started as a background process by other programs: specify a port, do not open a browser, print its own address and token on the first line of standard output, and exit cleanly.
Why this idea exists
The prerequisite "after pulling the repository, it is already updated" assumes someone has performed commits and pushes on behalf of others. Since serve is already the sole place receiving web changes, letting it handle the commit conveniently avoids the need to build another synchronization pipeline. The portal needs to start a serve instance for each repository, so it must act like a background program rather than a window opened by double-clicking.
Expected result
Two checkouts of the same repository: modify an idea and commit it on the serve page of one checkout, and after a git pull on the other, graph.yaml will already contain the new content, and git log will show one additional commit written by serve; when the switch is off, serve behaves exactly as it does today, running not a single git command.
How to implement
Add an option gitSync to serve(), with the command-line flag --git-sync, disabled by default. When enabled: before rendering GET /, run git pull --ff-only; if it fails, return a plain text 503 page where the body is the git error output; after a POST /changes with confirm and a successful atomicWrite, execute git add ideas/graph.yaml ideas/log.md ideas/approvals (the latter only if it exists), git commit -m "Web write-back N times (serve)", and git push in sequence; if any step fails, do not roll back files, but put the error into the git field of the response and append it to log.md. All three commands run through a small function gitRun(projectDir, args) using execFileSync with a 30-second timeout. The background contract adds nothing new: --port and --no-open already exist, and the first line of standard output is already "Idea graph opened at http://127.0.0.1:Port」"; pin this line during testing so the portal can read the address from it.
Why it is implemented this way
Why put it in serve instead of apply: apply is the path for humans to manually move modified files, so it is reasonable for humans to perform commits themselves; serve is the unattended path, so only it needs to commit on behalf of humans. Why --ff-only instead of merging: serve does not resolve conflicts for humans; if a conflict occurs, it stops and reports it, following the same principle as the envelope fingerprint lock (FORMAT.md "The change file" baseDigest). Why execFileSync instead of libraries like simple-git: there are only three commands, and the single-file artifact (D28) should not carry an extra dependency for it. Why disabled by default: the version opened by double-clicking on a local machine should not silently push to the remote. Why not print the token to standard output: the page carries the token back itself, and the portal is a transparent proxy, so it does not need it.

idea Arrange by dependency order

One approval receipt enters git: a receipt generated on an always-on machine, which is also recognized by a human's computer after a pull. CompletedI-138

Parent idea
I-136
What it is
Today, the approval codes and receipts waiting for answers are only written to each machine's respective ideas/.runtime/, and do not enter git. Move these two items into a git-tracked directory ideas/approvals/ (pending/ for approval codes waiting for answers, receipts/ for receipts); the guard's protection for it is the same as .runtime/: it can only be written by CLI and hooks. Receipts in the old directory .runtime/approvals/ remain valid and are read-only compatible. Test pass/fail evidence is not moved and remains in .runtime/. Update format specification D24 and the "Generated files" list with this entry.
Why this idea exists
Approval codes are generated on a human's computer by request-approval, approvals must be returned on an always-on machine, and the receipt must return to the human's computer for set doing to see. Only git connects these three places. Approval codes do not enter git, so the always-on machine does not know what is waiting for approval; receipts do not enter git, so the human's computer will never see that approval, making a web approval equivalent to no approval.
Expected result
Request approval and commit at one checkout, then after pulling at another location, it can answer that approval code, and the receipt lands in ideas/approvals/receipts/; commit it back, and after the first location pulls, set doing allows the same idea; if the content of that idea is modified and run again, it is rejected as before (the rule that receipts are bound to content remains unchanged); an agent attempting to write any file under ideas/approvals/ is blocked by the guard.
How to implement
paths() adds one more field, approvals, pointing to ideas/approvals; pendingDir and approvalsDir are changed to point to pending/ and receipts/ under it. When applyApproval looks for an approval code file, it first checks the new directory, then the old .runtime/pending/; validApproval first scans receipts/, then scans the old .runtime/approvals/. decideProductWrite adds ideas/approvals to the "only produced by CLI and hooks" group, with the reasoning text citing D24. The path string for the sentence written into the receipt (signed_off) is changed to the new directory. Do not change GITIGNORE_SEED in install.ts: the new directory is intended to enter git. FORMAT.md: D24 adds a section on implementation status, and the Generated files list adds a line for ideas/approvals/.
Why it is implemented this way
Why approval codes also enter git instead of only moving receipts: the always-on machine needs to know which approval codes are waiting for a response, and approval code files only contain the stage and content fingerprint; request-approval already prints them in full to the terminal (I-102), so there is no secret. Why not change to deterministic approval codes calculated from content (to avoid moving files): it would change the "one-time, random" semantics of D7/D26, and the scope of impact would be much larger than moving a directory. Why pass/fail evidence remains in .runtime/: it is evidence that this specific machine has run the tests; moving it to another machine would mean it is no longer evidence. Why the old directory is read-only compatible instead of migrated: there are not many existing receipts, and scanning two locations is cheaper than writing a migration.

idea Arrange by dependency order

Web approval implementation: the small service adds an approval entry point that only recognizes host credentials, following the same validation logic as the terminal. In progressI-139

Parent idea
I-136
What it is
serve adds a POST /approve entry point, receiving the human's response "approve CC-XXXXXXXX" and a host credential; the credential is a random string passed to it via environment variables when the portal starts serve, which does not appear on the page and is not printed in logs. The validation is identical to the terminal (approval code exists, content fingerprint unchanged, used only once); if successful, it writes the receipt to the git-tracked directory. If there is no credential or the credential is incorrect, it is rejected, just like today.
Why this idea exists
Users require that approval can also be done on the web. I-105 rules that local pages cannot distinguish between humans and automation, but it itself wrote that the only structurally valid method is an out-of-band second location; the portal login is that second location: only after a person passes the portal login does the portal pass that sentence along with the credential to serve, whereas an agent has neither a login nor a credential. Therefore, this does not overturn I-105, it only adds a clause: forwarding after out-of-band login counts, provided the credential does not appear in the page or logs.
Expected result
Sending an approval with the correct credential results in the receipt landing in the git-tracked directory and set doing allowing it; sending the same approval code a second time is rejected; sending without a credential, with an incorrect credential, or after content has been modified is rejected and no receipt is left; the credential cannot be found in the serve page source code or standard output.
How to implement
When serve() starts, it reads the environment variable AIDEV_APPROVE_SECRET. If not set: POST /approve returns 404, same as having no such entry point today. If set: request body {secret, words}, uses timingSafeEqual to compare the secret; if incorrect, returns 403; if correct, calls applyApproval(projectDir, words, {date, session_id: "serve", turn_id: request sequence}), and returns its result as-is; if it returns ok and gitSync is enabled, it commits ideas/approvals/ according to I-137. The credential does not enter the render output, the console, or log.md; standard output only adds one line: "approval entry enabled". Add a fourth paragraph to the "how" section of I-105: forwarding after out-of-band login counts, subject to three conditions (the credential does not appear in the page or logs; the portal login is not something an agent can obtain; receipts are only written by the engine). FORMAT.md D26 adds a section on implementation status, citing these three points.
Why it is implemented this way
Why use environment variables for credentials instead of command-line arguments: arguments are visible to everyone in Task Manager and ps. Why is it received by serve instead of the portal running the CLI directly: applyApproval must run on the machine where the repository is located, and serve is located there; furthermore, the guard rule blocking agents from accessing local services (I-104) still applies to this entry point. Why not change a single word in the ANSWER regex: the portal forwards the exact original words spoken by the human, and the validation must be identical to the terminal to claim "equivalent effectiveness." Why does it 404 instead of opening by default if environment variables are not set: the version opened by double-clicking on the local machine should not have an extra entry point.
